Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: Which factor about the aerosol itself most influences whether inhaling it could cause Legionnaires' disease?
o: Whether the droplets are fine enough to be breathed deep into the lungs
Whether the spray simply looks coloured or clear
Whether droplets are large enough to be seen falling
Whether the water tastes unpleasant when swallowed

n.2: Large droplets that quickly fall are less likely to be inhaled deeply into the lungs.
n.3: Taste relates to swallowing, which is not the route of infection.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: A member of the public asks whether they can catch Legionnaires' disease from a family member who has it. What is the correct explanation?
o: No, it is not passed between people; it comes from inhaling contaminated aerosols

No, but only because the family member is no longer contagious after about a week
Yes, close contact within the family is the most common way that it spreads
Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.w: Legionnaires' disease is not transmitted between people; it is contracted only by inhaling contaminated aerosols, so a family member cannot catch it from the patient.

n.1: Sharing drinking water does not transmit it; drinking is not a route.
n.2: There is no person-to-person spread, so contagiousness over time is not the reason.
n.3: There is no person-to-person spread, so close contact is not a route.

Legionella & Legionnaires' Disease.q: Considering both aerosol sources and susceptible people, why is a care home with communal showers a setting that deserves particular attention?
o: Because Legionnaires' disease spreads very easily between residents living close together

Because the residents there are generally young and at very low risk
Because showers cannot generate any aerosols in communal settings

n.2: Care home residents are frequently older and at higher risk, not young and low-risk.
n.3: Showers do generate inhalable aerosols, including in communal settings.

How Legionella Grows.q: Within which water temperature range does Legionella bacteria actively multiply?
o: Between 61°C and 80°C
Between 20°C and 45°C

How Legionella Grows.w: Legionella multiplies in water between roughly 20°C and 45°C.

How Legionella Grows.q: At roughly what water temperature does Legionella grow fastest?
o: Around 5°C, where the cold water keeps the bacteria dormant

Around 37°C, which is close to human body temperature
Around 70°C, which is hot enough to kill the bacteria quickly

n.3: 70°C is hot enough to kill the bacteria quickly.

How Legionella Grows.q: Why is around 37°C an especially dangerous water temperature?
o: It is the legal minimum temperature for storing hot water safely
It is far too cold for any bacteria to survive in the water
It is the temperature at which legionella is instantly killed off
It is close to body heat, where legionella multiplies fastest
How Legionella Grows.w: Around 37°C is close to body temperature and is the ideal condition for the fastest Legionella growth.

n.1: 37°C is warm, well within the range bacteria multiply in.
n.2: Legionella is not killed at 37°C, it thrives there.

How Legionella Grows.q: A stored water sample is measured at 40°C. In terms of Legionella, this temperature is:
o: Hot enough to kill the bacteria within a few minutes
Cold enough to hold the bacteria completely dormant for now
Inside the range where the bacteria actively multiply
Of no real relevance to how quickly legionella grows
How Legionella Grows.w: 40°C sits within the 20– 45°C band where Legionella actively multiplies.

How Legionella Grows.q: Which of the following best describes the temperature band that most favours Legionella?
o: Any cold water sitting at a temperature below 10°C
Boiling water held at 100°C straight from the kettle
Near-freezing water held very close to 0°C in unheated cold pipes
Warm water roughly between 20°C and 45°C, around body heat

n.1: Boiling water destroys the bacteria.
n.0: Below 10°C the bacteria are cold and dormant.

How Legionella Grows.q: Cold water in a building should ideally be kept below which temperature to discourage Legionella growth?
How Legionella Grows.w: Keeping cold water below 20°C keeps the bacteria dormant and out of the growth range.

How Legionella Grows.q: Below which temperature does Legionella become dormant and stop multiplying?
o: Below 25°C, a temperature still comfortably within the active growth range
Below 20°C, where the bacteria stop multiplying and turn dormant
Below 37°C, which is the point of most rapid multiplication
Below 45°C, sitting right at the top of the active growth range
How Legionella Grows.w: Below 20°C the bacteria are dormant and do not multiply, though they can survive.

n.0: At 25°C the bacteria are still within the active growth range.
n.2: 37°C is the temperature of fastest growth, not dormancy.
n.3: 45°C is the upper end of active growth, not where it stops.

How Legionella Grows.q: At approximately what temperature is Legionella killed quickly?
o: About 40°C, a warm temperature that suits the bacteria well
About 45°C, sitting near the top of the growth band
About 60°C, hot enough to destroy the bacteria rapidly
About 30°C, only mildly warm to the touch

How Legionella Grows.q: Does keeping water below 20°C destroy Legionella?
o: No, cold only makes them dormant; they revive when warmed

No, cold water actually makes them grow faster
Yes, cold water below 20°C kills them for good

n.2: Cold slows the bacteria down, it does not speed them up.

How Legionella Grows.q: Hot water leaving a correctly set system should reach at least what temperature to keep Legionella controlled?
How Legionella Grows.w: Hot water stored at 60°C is hot enough to kill Legionella and keep the system controlled.

n.2: 40°C is squarely inside the growth range.
n.1: 45°C is at the top of the growth band and still allows the bacteria to survive.
n.0: 50°C slows growth but is not reliably lethal to the bacteria.

How Legionella Grows.q: Why is water held at a steady 15°C generally lower risk for Legionella?
o: It is above 60°C, so the bacteria are all killed
It is at body temperature, so the growth is slowed
Cold water simply contains no nutrients at all
It is below 20°C, so the bacteria stay dormant

How Legionella Grows.q: Which pair of temperatures correctly describes the safe zones either side of Legionella growth?

How Legionella Grows.q: Why are little-used or infrequently used taps and outlets a Legionella concern?

How Legionella Grows.q: What is the main purpose of regularly flushing rarely-used outlets?

To deliberately add extra nutrients into the water held in the system
To move fresh water through and prevent stagnation
To warm the standing water up to around body temperature

How Legionella Grows.q: What is a 'dead leg' in a water system, and why does it matter?

A length of little-used pipe where water stagnates and bacteria grow
A section of pipe that self-cleans with fresh flowing water

How Legionella Grows.q: A section of pipework was capped off but left connected to the live system. Why is this a risk?

The cap keeps the trapped water permanently above 60°C
A blanked branch will always stay safely below 20°C

A slimy layer on wetted surfaces that shelters and feeds bacteria
A protective surface coating that instantly kills bacteria on contact

How Legionella Grows.q: Why does scale build-up inside a system raise Legionella risk?

How Legionella Grows.q: Rust and corrosion inside a tank are a concern for Legionella because they:

They sterilise the water and prevent any bacteria growing

How Legionella Grows.q: Sludge and sediment settling at the bottom of a storage tank are a problem because they:

Keep the stored water constantly disinfected and clean
Make the water flow through the tank faster
Raise the whole tank above 60°C on their own

How Legionella Grows.q: Organic matter such as leaves or dead insects getting into a water tank is a risk because it:

Cools the stored water to well below 20°C
Cannot affect the water quality in any way
Instantly kills all bacteria already present
How Legionella Grows.w: Organic debris adds nutrients that help feed Legionella growth.

n.2: Contamination of stored water is a genuine, well-known risk.
n.3: Debris feeds bacteria, it does not kill them.

How Legionella Grows.q: How does contaminated water usually become dangerous to people?

Only when it is frozen solid into ice cubes
When it is broken into a breathable spray and inhaled
When it is swallowed as ordinary drinking water

How Legionella Grows.q: By what route does Legionella infect a person?
o: Breathing contaminated water droplets deep into the lungs
Passing directly from person to person like a common cold
Swallowing food that has been contaminated with the bacteria

How Legionella Grows.q: Which everyday piece of equipment is a classic Legionella aerosol risk?

How Legionella Grows.q: Why are cooling towers regarded as a significant Legionella hazard?
o: They throw off a fine spray of droplets that can drift a distance
They keep all of their water above 60°C at all times
They store the building's drinking water in a large warm open tank
They hold no water at all while the fans are running

How Legionella Grows.q: Which situation is LEAST likely to create a breathable Legionella aerosol?

How Legionella Grows.q: Why is a cold-water supply that has warmed up above 20°C a concern?
o: It has entered the temperature range where legionella multiplies
Warmed cold water no longer contains any nutrients at all
It is now easily hot enough to kill the bacteria present
Warming cold water always sterilises it completely and makes it safe to drink

How Legionella Grows.q: Why is a hot-water system that has cooled to around 40°C a Legionella risk?
o: Cooled hot water like this is far too cool to hold any bacteria at all
At 40°C the bacteria are kept completely dormant
The water has dropped into the active growth range
40°C is now hot enough to kill the bacteria outright

How Legionella Grows.q: Which set of conditions in a building water system raises Legionella risk?

Warm cold-water, cool hot-water, and underused oversized pipework
Clean, well-used outlets that are flushed thoroughly every day

n.3: Cold below 20°C and hot above 60°C are the correct control temperatures.

How Legionella Grows.q: Why does an underused, oversized system tend to raise Legionella risk?

Large systems are always kept running above 60°C from end to end
Bigger systems are automatically self-cleaning and need no attention
Low demand lets water sit still and drift into the warm growth range

How Legionella Grows.q: A little-used outlet sits at the far end of a long warm pipe run. Why is it higher risk?

The length of pipe strips out all the nutrients in the water
Outlets this far away never actually hold any water
Stagnant water there warms up and lets Legionella multiply
How Legionella Grows.w: The stagnant, warmed water in a rarely-used far outlet lets Legionella numbers build up.

How Legionella Grows.q: Which change would most reduce Legionella risk in a warm, stagnant section of pipework?

Restoring regular flow so water does not stand and warm
Insulating the pipe so that it stays even warmer
Leaving it capped, still and completely undisturbed

How Legionella Grows.q: Where can Legionella shelter to survive and resist water treatment?

Inside biofilm and within amoebae (protozoa)
Only in water kept above 70°C for long periods
Only on completely dry and clean surfaces

How Legionella Grows.q: Why does biofilm make Legionella harder to control?
o: It shields the bacteria from disinfectant and heat
It raises the water temperature above 60°C
It makes the bacteria die within a few minutes
It strips every last nutrient out of the water

n.2: Biofilm protects the bacteria, helping them survive.

How Legionella Grows.q: How do amoebae in a water system affect Legionella?
o: They graze on and permanently destroy all the legionella present
They raise the surrounding water above the lethal temperature
They have no meaningful relationship with legionella at all

How Legionella Grows.q: Why is simply raising the temperature briefly sometimes not enough to control Legionella hidden in biofilm?

Biofilm makes the sheltered bacteria multiply faster when heated
Heat cannot affect any bacteria in a water system at all
Biofilm always sits above 60°C so added heat does nothing

How Legionella Grows.q: You open an inspection hatch and find a tank of tepid, still water. What is the main concern?

Still water in a tank is always perfectly safe to leave
It is warm and stagnant, ideal conditions for legionella to grow

How Legionella Grows.q: During a survey you find a shower that has not been used for several weeks. Before anyone uses it, the safest action is to:

How Legionella Grows.q: You spot heavy rust and brown sludge in the bottom of a storage tank. Why is this a Legionella risk?

The layer of rust keeps the stored water above 60°C at all times

How Legionella Grows.q: A plant room is warm and a cold-water storage tank there feels warm to the touch. What is the concern?

How Legionella Grows.q: An outlet produces a fine warm spray and the surrounding water sits at about 35°C. Why is this combination especially concerning?
o: At 35°C the water is far too cold for bacteria
A breathable spray of growth-range water reaches the lungs
A fine spray always means the water must be completely sterile
Fine sprays are unable to carry any bacteria at all
How Legionella Grows.w: Water at 35°C can be heavily colonised and a fine spray turns it into a breathable aerosol, the key infection route.

n.2: Spraying does not sterilise the water.
n.0: 35°C is near the ideal growth temperature, not too cold.
n.3: Fine sprays are the main way Legionella is carried into the lungs.

How Legionella Grows.q: During a check you find slimy film coating the inside of a tank wall. What is the significance?
o: It proves the stored water is safely above 60°C
It is biofilm, which shelters, feeds and protects Legionella
It shows the inside of the tank is perfectly sterile
It is a harmless coating that actively kills bacteria
How Legionella Grows.w: The slimy film is biofilm, which both shelters and feeds Legionella and makes it harder to treat.

n.0: Biofilm has nothing to do with the water being hot.
n.2: Biofilm is a sign of bacterial growth, the opposite of sterile.
n.3: Biofilm protects bacteria, it does not kill them.

How Legionella Grows.q: A rarely-used spray tap in a back room is fed by warm water. A colleague says 'no one uses it, so it's fine.' What is the correct view?
o: The colleague is right, because taps that no one uses are always perfectly safe
It is completely safe, because warm water reliably kills off any Legionella
It is higher risk, as warm stagnant water breeds Legionella and it sprays
It is safe, because spray taps are unable to carry bacteria of any kind
How Legionella Grows.w: A little-used warm spray tap combines stagnation, warmth and aerosol, so it is a raised risk, not a safe one.

n.0: Unused outlets stagnate and are a recognised higher risk.
n.1: Warm water encourages Legionella; it does not kill it.
n.3: Spray taps are exactly the outlets that produce a breathable aerosol.

How Legionella Grows.q: You notice sediment has settled in the base of a large, slowly-used cold tank. Why does this raise the risk?
o: The sediment feeds bacteria while the slow turnover lets water stagnate and warm
A large tank turns its stored water over much faster than a small one
The settled sediment keeps the whole tank below 20°C and dormant
The settled sediment gradually disinfects the stored water
How Legionella Grows.w: Settled sediment supplies nutrients while the slow, stagnant turnover lets numbers build up.

n.1: A large tank with low demand turns its water over more slowly, not faster.
n.2: Sediment does not keep water cold; it insulates and enriches it.
n.3: Debris harbours bacteria rather than disinfecting.

How Legionella Grows.q: A calorifier (hot-water cylinder) is found storing water at 45°C. In Legionella terms this is a problem because:
o: At 45°C the stored water is held safely in a dormant state
It is warm enough to grow Legionella but not to kill it
45°C is above the kill temperature, so the store is safe
Storage temperature has no real bearing on Legionella risk
How Legionella Grows.w: At 45°C the stored hot water is in the growth range and below the ~60°C needed to kill Legionella.

n.0: Dormancy is below 20°C; 45°C is warm and favourable.
n.2: The kill temperature is about 60°C, so 45°C does not kill it.
n.3: Storage temperature is one of the most important Legionella controls.

How Legionella Grows.q: In what water temperature range does legionella multiply most readily?
o: Between 20°C and 45°C, the growth band
Below minus 10°C, hard frozen solid
Between 0°C and 5°C, near freezing point
Between 60°C and 80°C, hot enough to kill
How Legionella Grows.w: Legionella multiplies in water between 20°C and 45°C, with around 37°C being ideal.

n.1: Freezing temperatures do not allow the bacteria to multiply.
n.2: At these cold temperatures the bacteria stay dormant and do not multiply.
n.3: At 60°C and above the bacteria are killed rather than multiplying.

How Legionella Grows.q: What happens to legionella bacteria in water held below 20°C?
o: They multiply faster than at any other temperature
They stay dormant and do not multiply
They immediately die within seconds
They turn the water into a spray on their own
How Legionella Grows.w: Below 20°C legionella becomes dormant and does not multiply, though it is not killed.

n.0: Cold water slows growth; it does not speed it up.
n.2: Cold water does not kill the bacteria; it only makes them dormant.
n.3: Bacteria cannot create a spray; aerosols come from equipment like showers and taps.

How Legionella Grows.q: At roughly what temperature is legionella killed quickly?
o: Around 60°C and above, which is hot enough to kill it quickly
Around 37°C, which is close to the ideal temperature for growth
Around 20°C, where the bacteria are just beginning to multiply
Around 10°C, where the bacteria stay dormant but are not killed
How Legionella Grows.w: Water at 60°C and above kills legionella quickly, which is why hot water should be stored hot.

n.1: 37°C is close to the ideal growth temperature, not for killing.
n.2: At 20°C the bacteria begin to multiply rather than die.
n.3: At 10°C the bacteria are dormant but not killed.

How Legionella Grows.q: Which condition helps legionella to multiply in a water system?
o: Water that is kept constantly moving and very hot throughout the system
Water that is stored below 5°C at all times of the day
Stagnant water with sludge, scale, rust or biofilm to feed on
Water that is regularly flushed and turned over often
How Legionella Grows.w: Stagnation together with nutrients such as biofilm, scale, rust and sludge provides ideal conditions for legionella to grow.

n.0: Keeping water moving and hot discourages growth.
n.1: Very cold water keeps the bacteria dormant, preventing multiplication.
n.3: Regular flushing removes stagnation and helps prevent growth.

How Legionella Grows.q: Which of these acts as a nutrient source that helps legionella grow?
o: Biofilm, scale, rust and organic sediment inside pipes and tanks
Fresh air circulating around the inside of the system
Clean, well-treated and chlorinated flowing water
Bright natural sunlight falling directly on the tanks
How Legionella Grows.w: Deposits such as biofilm, scale, rust, sludge and organic matter feed the bacteria and shelter them from disinfectant.

n.1: Air is not a nutrient source for the bacteria.
n.2: Clean, treated flowing water lacks the nutrients and stagnation needed.
n.3: Sunlight is not a food source and does not promote growth in systems.

How Legionella Grows.q: Which situation is most likely to create the aerosol that spreads legionella?
o: A sealed, full cold water storage tank with a tight lid
Still water sitting quietly in a tightly covered bucket
A running shower or spray tap that breaks the water into a fine breathable mist
A closed dead-end pipe that has no outlets at all
How Legionella Grows.w: Showers, spray taps and cooling towers break water into fine droplets that can be inhaled, which is how the bacteria reach the lungs.

n.0: A properly sealed storage tank does not create a breathable spray.
n.3: A closed pipe with no outlet produces no aerosol.
n.1: Still water in a covered container does not form an inhalable mist.

How Legionella Grows.q: You find a shower in a spare room that has not been used for several weeks. What is the safest way to bring it back into use?
o: Turn it on at full mist and stand close to it to check the temperature
Flush it through at a high temperature, keeping clear of the spray to avoid a mist
Give the shower head just a quick wipe over with a dry cloth only
Leave it exactly as it is, because unused showers are always safe
How Legionella Grows.w: Little-used outlets should be flushed regularly, avoiding breathing in the spray, because stagnant water is where legionella multiplies.

n.0: Standing in the mist of a long-unused shower risks inhaling any bacteria.
n.2: A dry wipe does not remove bacteria or clear the stagnant water inside.
n.3: Unused, stagnant outlets are a higher risk, not a safe one.

How Legionella Grows.q: Why are little-used ('dead leg') sections of pipework a particular legionella risk?
o: Water stagnates in them, letting bacteria multiply undisturbed
They are nearly always exposed to freezing outdoor conditions
The water held in them is always kept above 60°C at all times
They contain extra chlorine that actually feeds the bacteria
How Legionella Grows.w: Water sits still in rarely used pipe sections, and stagnation lets legionella grow and form biofilm.

n.1: Dead legs are a risk because water stagnates, not because they freeze.
n.2: Dead legs often sit at warm room temperature, not above 60°C.
n.3: Chlorine is a disinfectant that kills bacteria; it is not a food source.

How Legionella Grows.q: A stored hot water calorifier is found running at 48°C rather than the intended 60°C. Why does this specific reading matter for Legionella growth?
o: 48°C is cold enough to keep the bacteria fully dormant
48°C instantly kills any legionella that is present
48°C is too cool to kill it yet warm enough for growth
Temperature has no effect because nutrients control growth
How Legionella Grows.w: Stored hot water should be at 60°C. At 48°C the water is near or within the range where Legionella multiplies and is not hot enough to kill it, so numbers can rise. HSG274 Part 2 requires 60°C storage and 50°C at outlets within one minute.

n.0: Dormancy occurs below 20°C, not at 48°C; at 48°C the bacteria are active and can multiply.
n.1: Legionella is killed reliably around 60°C, not at 48°C, which is too cool to disinfect.
n.3: Temperature is the primary control; keeping water hot or cold prevents multiplication even where nutrients exist.

How Legionella Grows.q: Legionella bacteria multiply most rapidly at a temperature closest to which of the following?
o: Around 55°C, typical of correctly distributed hot water
Around 8°C, typical of chilled mains water
Around 70°C, typical of a boiler flow
Around 37°C, close to human body temperature
How Legionella Grows.w: Legionella multiplies across roughly 20–45°C, with the fastest growth near 37°C, close to human body temperature. This is why lukewarm water is the highest-risk condition.

n.1: Around 8°C the bacteria are dormant and do not multiply; cold water should be kept below 20°C.
n.0: Around 55°C the bacteria begin to die rather than multiply.
n.2: Around 70°C Legionella is killed almost immediately, so no growth occurs.

How Legionella Grows.q: Cold water drawn from an infrequently used outlet is measured at 24°C after running for two minutes. What does this tell you about Legionella risk?
o: The reading is irrelevant, because cold water can never support legionella at all
The cold water is above 20°C, now in the range where legionella multiplies
The outlet is fine, because only hot water systems grow legionella
The water is safely cold and needs no further attention here
How Legionella Grows.w: Cold water should stay below 20°C. At 24°C after two minutes' run-off, the cold system has warmed into the 20–45°C growth band, so Legionella can multiply. HSG274 Part 2 targets below 20°C for cold water.

n.3: Water at 24°C is above the 20°C threshold and is not safely cold.
n.0: Warm cold-water systems are a well-recognised source of Legionella growth.
n.2: Cold water systems that run warm are just as capable of supporting growth as hot systems that run cool.

How Legionella Grows.q: At which approximate temperature is Legionella reliably killed within a short time?
How Legionella Grows.w: Legionella is killed rapidly at around 60°C, which is why hot water is stored at that temperature. At 60°C the great majority of bacteria die within a couple of minutes.

n.0: 20°C is the lower edge of the growth band, where the bacteria become active rather than being killed.
n.2: 37°C is near ideal for multiplication, not for killing the bacteria.
n.1: 45°C is still within the growth range; the bacteria are not reliably killed until much hotter.

How Legionella Grows.q: Why is a layer of biofilm on the inside of a pipe or tank important to how Legionella grows?
o: Biofilm removes every nutrient from the water and starves the bacteria
Biofilm raises the water temperature above 60°C and destroys bacteria
Biofilm only forms in water hotter than 50°C where growth is impossible
Biofilm shelters Legionella and supplies nutrients that aid growth
How Legionella Grows.w: Biofilm is a slime layer of micro-organisms that both shelters Legionella from disinfectants and temperature and supplies nutrients, promoting growth. Controlling biofilm is central to HSG274 Part 2.

n.0: Biofilm supplies nutrients rather than removing them.
n.1: Biofilm does not heat water; it protects the bacteria.
n.2: Biofilm forms readily in warm, stagnant water, not only hot water.

How Legionella Grows.q: A capped-off length of redundant pipework still connected to a live main is left in place. Why does this 'dead leg' increase Legionella risk?
o: It cools the whole system below 20°C and forces the bacteria into dormancy
It sterilises the connected pipework by trapping heat inside it
Water stagnates in it, warms to room temperature and gathers nutrients
It continuously flushes fresh chlorinated water through the system
How Legionella Grows.w: A dead leg holds water that does not move, allowing it to reach ambient temperature and collect sediment and nutrients, creating ideal conditions for Legionella. HSG274 Part 2 recommends removing dead legs.

n.0: A dead leg sits at room temperature within the growth range, not below 20°C.
n.1: Trapped stagnant water is not sterile; it favours growth rather than preventing it.
n.3: By definition there is no flow through a dead leg, so no flushing occurs.

How Legionella Grows.q: Besides suitable temperature, which combination of conditions most favours Legionella multiplication?
o: High pressure running through completely sterile, deposit-free pipework
Frequent draw-off and a total absence of any deposits at all
Fast continuous flow with freshly chlorinated incoming water
Stagnation together with nutrients such as scale, rust, sludge and organic matter
How Legionella Grows.w: Legionella needs warmth plus stagnant water and nutrients. Scale, rust, sludge, sediment and organic matter feed the bacteria and support biofilm, so still, dirty water in the growth range is highest risk.

n.0: High pressure and sterile pipework do not provide the stagnation and nutrients needed.
n.1: Frequent draw-off and clean pipework work against growth.
n.2: Continuous flow and disinfectant residual suppress growth rather than promoting it.

How Legionella Grows.q: How do free-living amoebae and other protozoa in a water system affect Legionella?
o: They raise the surrounding pH so high that the legionella bacteria simply cannot survive at all
They have no meaningful interaction with the legionella bacteria whatsoever
They host the bacteria, letting legionella multiply inside and shelter from disinfection
They consume all of the legionella that is present and eliminate it from the system entirely
How Legionella Grows.w: Legionella can invade and multiply inside protozoa such as amoebae, which shelter the bacteria from heat and biocides and provide nutrients. This is why controlling biofilm, where protozoa live, is important.

n.0: The relationship is hosting and shelter, not a pH change.
n.1: There is a strong interaction: protozoa are a recognised reservoir.
n.3: Rather than being destroyed, legionella exploits protozoa as hosts.

How Legionella Grows.q: Growth of Legionella in a system only becomes a health risk to people when which of the following occurs?
o: A person touches a tap handle contaminated with the bacteria
The contaminated water is swallowed while drinking a glass of it
The water is heated above 60°C before it reaches the outlet
The contaminated water is dispersed as a fine, breathable aerosol
How Legionella Grows.w: The risk is realised when water containing Legionella is broken into a fine aerosol of droplets small enough to reach the lungs, for example from showers, sprays or cooling towers. Inhalation is the route of infection.

n.0: Touching a contaminated surface is not the recognised route of infection.
n.1: Legionnaires' disease is contracted by inhaling aerosol, not from drinking.
n.2: Heating above 60°C kills the bacteria, reducing rather than creating risk.

How Legionella Grows.q: Why is an oversized cold water storage tank that serves only a small daily demand a Legionella concern?
o: The extra capacity guarantees a strong disinfectant residual throughout
The water turns over slowly, so it stagnates and warms into the growth range
The large surface area cools the water enough to kill the bacteria
The large volume keeps the water permanently below 20°C and dormant
How Legionella Grows.w: An oversized, underused tank has a low turnover, so water sits for long periods. Slow-moving water stagnates and can drift up towards ambient temperature, favouring growth. HSG274 Part 2 advises matching capacity to demand.

n.0: Slow turnover lets any disinfectant residual decay, not stay strong.
n.2: A large tank does not chill water to a killing temperature.
n.3: Slow turnover in a warm room lets water rise, not stay cold and dormant.

How Legionella Grows.q: A cold water tank sits in an unventilated roof space next to hot flow pipework in summer, and its temperature climbs to 26°C. What is the significance?
o: It is unimportant, since roof tanks are always exempt from temperature control
The heat gain has pushed the cold water into the 20–45°C growth range
The warmth actually kills the bacteria before they can multiply at all
The water is now hot enough to be treated as safely pasteurised
How Legionella Grows.w: Heat gain from the surroundings has warmed the cold water above 20°C into the growth range. Cold water should be kept below 20°C, so tanks should be insulated and kept away from heat sources.

n.3: Cold water storage temperature control applies to roof tanks; they are not exempt.
n.2: 26°C is well within the growth range and does not kill the bacteria.
n.0: Pasteurisation needs far higher temperatures; 26°C is simply warm, high-risk water.

How Legionella Grows.q: What happens to Legionella bacteria in water held steadily below 20°C?
o: They multiply faster there than at any other water temperature
They are immediately and completely destroyed by the cold water
They convert the surrounding water into a solid layer of biofilm
They can survive in a dormant state but do not multiply
How Legionella Grows.w: Below 20°C Legionella survives but remains largely dormant and does not multiply. This is why keeping cold water below 20°C is a key control, even though it does not kill the bacteria.

n.0: Fastest multiplication is near 37°C, not below 20°C where they are dormant.
n.1: Cold does not kill Legionella; the bacteria persist and can grow if it warms.
n.2: Bacteria do not turn water into biofilm; biofilm is a separate slime layer.

How Legionella Grows.q: Why does scale build-up from hard water inside a pipe or fitting contribute to Legionella growth?
o: Scale provides surface area and nutrients that harbour biofilm and shelter bacteria
Scale raises the water temperature above 60°C and completely sterilises it
Scale dissolves the surrounding biofilm and starves the bacteria of nutrients
Scale prevents any water from ever contacting the inside of the pipe wall
How Legionella Grows.w: Scale creates a rough surface and, with rust and sediment, forms deposits where biofilm establishes and Legionella shelters and feeds. Removing scale and sediment is part of controlling growth under HSG274 Part 2.

n.1: Scale does not heat water; it insulates surfaces and can even protect bacteria from heat.
n.2: Scale supports biofilm rather than dissolving it, so it encourages growth.
n.3: Scale is a deposit water flows over and around; it does not seal the bacteria away from water.

How Legionella Grows.q: A building has been closed for six weeks with no water use. Regarding Legionella growth, what is the main concern on reopening?
o: The lack of use will have sterilised the system completely
The pipework will have cooled to a temperature that kills bacteria
There is no concern because bacteria die without people present
Prolonged stagnation let bacteria multiply and biofilm form
How Legionella Grows.w: Six weeks with no flow means water has stagnated, temperatures have drifted towards ambient, disinfectant residual has decayed and biofilm has grown, all favouring Legionella. Systems should be flushed and checked before reuse.

n.0: Stagnation promotes growth; it does not sterilise a system.
n.1: Lack of use does not create killing temperatures; water tends towards room temperature.
n.2: The absence of occupants does not remove the water conditions that let Legionella multiply.

How Legionella Grows.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between temperature and Legionella across a water system?
o: Keep water below 20°C or hot enough to kill them; 20–45°C is where it thrives
Keeping water in the 20–45°C band is the safest way to control growth
Legionella grows just as well at every temperature from freezing to boiling point
Only nutrients matter; the temperature makes no difference to growth at all
How Legionella Grows.w: Temperature control works by avoiding the 20–45°C danger band: cold water below 20°C keeps bacteria dormant and hot water around 60°C kills them. The band between is where multiplication occurs.

n.1: The 20–45°C band is precisely the danger range, not a safe target.
n.3: Temperature is the primary control alongside stagnation and nutrients; it matters greatly.
n.2: Growth is confined to a specific range; the bacteria are dormant when cold and killed when hot.

How Legionella Grows.q: Rubber, natural fibre washers and some jointing compounds are discouraged in water systems mainly because they can influence Legionella growth. How?
o: They release nutrients that feed bacteria and biofilm
They chill the surrounding water below the growth range
They release a continuous disinfectant that suppresses growth
They have no real effect on microbial growth at all
How Legionella Grows.w: Certain materials such as some rubbers and natural fibres can degrade and provide nutrients that encourage bacterial and biofilm growth. Water fittings should meet approved standards to limit this, supporting HSG274 Part 2 control.

n.1: These materials do not cool water; they can be a nutrient source.
n.2: They tend to feed growth rather than release disinfectant.
n.3: The choice of materials does affect microbial growth.

How Legionella Grows.q: Hot water reaching a distant outlet on a large system is measured at only 43°C. Why is this a growth concern even though the water leaves the calorifier at 60°C?
o: 43°C means the water was never actually heated at the calorifier at all
Heat loss has cooled the water into the 20–45°C growth range here
43°C at that outlet is easily hot enough to kill Legionella straight away
Outlet temperature is irrelevant as long as storage still sits at 60°C
How Legionella Grows.w: Hot water should reach outlets at 50°C within one minute. At 43°C the water has cooled into the growth band during distribution, allowing multiplication near the outlet despite correct storage. This points to heat loss or poor circulation.

n.0: The water was heated to 60°C but lost heat on the way, which is the problem.
n.2: 43°C is within the growth range and does not kill the bacteria.
n.3: Distribution matters too; outlets must reach 50°C.

How Legionella Grows.q: Why is sediment or sludge collecting at the base of a calorifier or cold water tank a particular concern for Legionella growth?
o: It settles out all the bacteria and safely removes them from the water
It provides both nutrients and shelter where legionella and biofilm can thrive
It has no bearing on growth, as bacteria live only in flowing water
It keeps the stored water held at a lethal temperature
How Legionella Grows.w: Accumulated sludge, rust and sediment supply nutrients and a protected surface for biofilm, where Legionella multiplies and is shielded from temperature and disinfectant. Removing deposits by cleaning is a recognised control.

n.0: Settled sediment concentrates nutrients and bacteria rather than safely removing them.
n.2: Legionella thrives in stagnant, sediment-rich zones, not only in flowing water.
n.3: Sediment does not heat water; the base of a tank is often cooler and higher-risk.

How Legionella Grows.q: A little-used shower in a plant room delivers warm, cloudy first-draw water and is rarely run. Which factors combine to make this a Legionella growth hotspot?
o: High flow, cold water and clean, deposit-free pipework throughout
Stagnation, growth-range warmth and nutrients, plus shower aerosol
Frozen water combined with a total lack of any available nutrients
Continuous circulation together with effective ongoing disinfection
How Legionella Grows.w: Infrequent use means stagnation, the plant room warms the water into the growth band, and cloudiness suggests sediment and nutrients. A shower also generates fine aerosol, combining growth conditions with a route of exposure.

n.0: This outlet has low flow and warm water, the opposite of these protective conditions.
n.2: The water is warm and cloudy with nutrients, not frozen and clean.
n.3: Rare use means no circulation and decayed disinfectant, not continuous protection.

How Legionella Grows.q: Which of the following best explains why simply keeping a system clean of deposits helps control Legionella growth?
o: Cleaning permanently lowers the water temperature to below 20°C right through the entire system
Cleaning does away entirely with the need for any form of temperature control at all
Cleaning makes the water so pure that aerosols can no longer form at the outlets
Removing scale, rust, sludge and biofilm takes away the nutrients and shelter bacteria need
How Legionella Grows.w: Legionella depends on nutrients and shelter from deposits and biofilm. Removing them by cleaning and descaling reduces the food source and protective habitat, an important part of HSG274 Part 2 control alongside temperature.

n.0: Cleaning removes deposits but does not set the water temperature.
n.1: Cleaning complements temperature control; it does not replace it.
n.2: Water purity does not stop aerosols; aerosol is a physical process.

How Legionella Grows.q: In terms of Legionella, why is a mixer tap or thermostatic mixing valve (TMV) area sometimes described as a higher-risk point for growth?
o: Because the water at that point is always stored well above 60°C
Because the mixing process removes all nutrients from the water
Because hot and cold blend to a warm temperature within the growth range
Because it only ever delivers cold water held well below 20°C
How Legionella Grows.w: A TMV blends hot and cold to a comfortable warm temperature, which sits in the 20–45°C growth band right at the outlet and downstream fittings. This is why TMVs are fitted close to the outlet and maintained carefully.

n.0: The blended water is deliberately warm, not stored above 60°C.
n.1: Mixing does not remove nutrients; it produces a warm temperature ideal for growth.
n.3: The output is warm mixed water, not cold water below 20°C.

How Legionella Grows.q: Which description of Legionella's nutrient needs is correct?
o: It manufactures all of its own food from sunlight and needs none from the water
It grows only in chemically pure, completely nutrient-free water
It obtains nutrients from biofilm, scale, rust, sludge and organic matter
It requires added sugar to be dosed into the water in order to survive
How Legionella Grows.w: Legionella draws nutrients from the organic and inorganic matter found in water systems, including biofilm, corrosion products, scale and sediment. Limiting these deposits limits the food available for growth.

n.0: Legionella does not photosynthesise; it feeds on organic matter.
n.1: Pure, nutrient-free water is unfavourable; the bacteria need food.
n.3: No dosing is needed; ordinary system deposits supply nutrients.

How Legionella Grows.q: A section of hot water pipework is poorly lagged and runs through a cool basement, so the water in it drifts to around 40°C between draw-offs. What is the growth implication?
o: The section is fully protected, since hot water can never grow Legionella at all
The cooled hot water sits in the growth range, so Legionella can multiply there
The water freezes in the pipe and the bacteria are all destroyed
The cooling makes the water safe because it is now below 45°C
How Legionella Grows.w: Hot water that cools to about 40°C between uses sits squarely in the 20–45°C growth band, so Legionella can multiply there. Adequate lagging and circulation keep hot water hot and prevent this cool-hot-water risk.

n.3: Being below 45°C does not make water safe; it is inside the growth range.
n.0: Hot water systems that run cool are a recognised growth risk, not protected.
n.2: 40°C is warm, not freezing; the bacteria are not destroyed and can multiply.

How Legionella Grows.q: Why is regular use, or planned flushing, of every outlet important in controlling how Legionella grows?
o: It permanently sterilises the pipework, with no further action ever needed
It heats all of the cold water in the system to above 60°C
It stops water stagnating, drawing fresh water through and refreshing any residual
It replaces the need to keep hot water hot and cold water cold
How Legionella Grows.w: Movement of water stops stagnation, brings through fresh water at the correct temperature and helps maintain any disinfectant residual, denying Legionella the still conditions it needs. Weekly flushing of little-used outlets is standard practice.

n.0: Flushing manages stagnation but does not permanently sterilise; it must be repeated.
n.1: Flushing moves water through; it does not heat cold water to 60°C.
n.3: Flushing supports temperature control but does not replace it.

How Legionella Grows.q: Which everyday piece of equipment is a classic aerosol generator that can turn Legionella growth in a system into a health risk?
o: A sealed, mains-fed drinking water bottle filler with no spray
A shower head producing a fine spray of warm water
A closed radiator circuit that never opens to air
A kettle used only to boil water for drinks
How Legionella Grows.w: A shower head breaks warm water into fine, breathable droplets, the aerosol that can carry Legionella into the lungs. Aerosol-producing outlets are a priority for control because they link growth to exposure.

n.0: A non-spraying bottle filler produces little or no breathable aerosol.
n.2: A sealed radiator circuit does not disperse water as an aerosol into the room air.
n.3: A kettle boils water, killing bacteria, and does not generate a fine warm spray.

How Legionella Grows.q: Why can Legionella survive a short-term rise in temperature or a dose of disinfectant that would be expected to kill free-floating bacteria?
o: Because biofilm and host protozoa shelter it from heat and chemicals
Because it forms heat-proof spores like some other bacteria
Because it multiplies faster than any treatment can act
Because it changes the water chemistry to neutralise the disinfectant
How Legionella Grows.w: Legionella hidden within biofilm or inside protozoa is protected from heat and biocides that would kill bacteria suspended in the water. This is why control must tackle biofilm and sediment, not just treat the bulk water.

n.1: Legionella does not form the resistant spores that some other bacteria produce; its protection comes from biofilm and hosts.
n.2: Its resistance comes from shelter, not from outpacing treatment by rapid multiplication.
n.3: The bacteria do not chemically neutralise disinfectant; they are shielded from it.

How Legionella Grows.q: A maintenance report notes 'low system turnover and warm ambient conditions'. Why does this phrasing point to a Legionella growth risk?
o: Neither factor has any genuine link to Legionella growth at all
Low turnover keeps the water permanently below 20°C at all times
Together they mean stagnant water warming into the legionella growth range
Warm ambient conditions somehow kill off the bacteria on contact straight away
How Legionella Grows.w: Low turnover means water stands still (stagnation) while warm surroundings raise it into the 20–45°C band. Combined, these give Legionella the still, warm conditions it needs to multiply, so both should be addressed.

n.0: Both stagnation and warmth are core drivers of Legionella growth.
n.1: Low turnover lets standing water warm towards ambient, not stay cold below 20°C.
n.3: Warm ambient conditions promote growth; they do not kill the bacteria.

How Legionella Grows.q: Which statement about where Legionella typically grows within a system is correct?
o: Only inside completely sealed pressure gauges
Only suspended free in fast-flowing water, never on surfaces
Mainly on inner surfaces, in biofilm, scale and sediment
Only in the open air above the water surface
How Legionella Grows.w: Much Legionella growth occurs on wetted surfaces within biofilm and among scale and sediment, which shelter and feed it. Water sampling can under-represent this, so surfaces and deposits must be controlled.

n.0: It is not confined to sealed gauges; it colonises pipework, tanks and fittings.
n.1: Surfaces and biofilm are a primary habitat; the bacteria are not limited to flowing water.
n.3: Legionella is a waterborne organism that grows in the water and on wetted surfaces, not in open air above it.

How Legionella Grows.q: Why is it misleading to assume a system is safe just because a water sample taken from a tap shows low bacterial numbers?
o: Legionella can persist in biofilm and sediment a single sample may miss
Because tap samples heat the water and kill everything inside the pipe
Because water samples always overstate the true amount of legionella that is present
Because low numbers prove the system can never grow legionella at all
How Legionella Grows.w: Legionella sheltered in biofilm, sediment and protozoa may not appear in a one-off water sample, yet it can seed the system later. This is why temperature, cleanliness and flow controls matter, not just sample results.

n.3: A low result does not prove the system cannot grow Legionella; conditions can change and biofilm persists.
n.2: Samples can under-represent, not overstate, bacteria held in biofilm and deposits.
n.1: Taking a sample does not heat or sterilise the pipework; the hidden reservoir remains.

How Legionella Grows.q: Two adjoining outlets are compared: one used many times daily, one used once a month. Why is the monthly outlet the greater Legionella growth risk?
o: Rarely used outlets are physically incapable of forming biofilm
Its frequent flushing keeps it constantly fresh and clean
Its water stagnates and warms between uses, gathering debris
It is always supplied with much hotter water than usual
How Legionella Grows.w: The monthly outlet leaves water standing for weeks, allowing stagnation, temperature drift into the growth band and nutrient build-up. Frequently used outlets refresh their water and are less prone to these conditions.

n.0: Rarely used outlets are especially prone to biofilm as water sits still.
n.1: A monthly outlet is not frequently flushed; that describes the busy one.
n.3: There is no reason a rarely used outlet gets hotter water.

How Legionella Grows.q: Which set of conditions together represents the greatest risk of Legionella multiplying to harmful levels?
o: Water at 65°C, circulating, freshly cleaned, with no spray
Water frozen solid, with no nutrients present at all
Water at 6°C, high turnover, clean pipework and no aerosol
Water at 40°C, stagnant, sediment-laden, feeding a spray outlet
How Legionella Grows.w: Warm water in the growth range, standing still, rich in nutrients and feeding an aerosol-producing outlet brings together every factor: temperature, stagnation, nutrients and a route of exposure. This is the highest-risk combination.

n.0: At 65°C and circulating, Legionella is killed and there is no aerosol.
n.1: Frozen, nutrient-free water offers none of the conditions needed.
n.2: At 6°C with turnover and no aerosol, exposure is unlikely.

How Legionella Grows.q: How does poor circulation in a hot water return loop encourage Legionella growth?
o: It removes almost all of the available nutrients from the returning water
It keeps the water moving far too fast for any bacteria to settle
It forces the whole loop above 60°C and kills off all the bacteria
Parts of the loop cool into the growth range and water stagnates
How Legionella Grows.w: Inadequate circulation lets sections of the loop and its branches fall below the target hot temperature into the 20-45°C band and stagnate, giving Legionella warm, still conditions. Balanced circulation keeps the whole loop hot.

n.0: Poor circulation does not strip nutrients; deposits build up in the sluggish areas.
n.1: The problem is water moving too slowly, allowing stagnation, not too fast.
n.2: Poor circulation causes cool spots below 60°C, not uniform killing temperatures.

How Legionella Grows.q: Why is corrosion (rust) inside steel pipework relevant to Legionella growth?
o: Corrosion continuously releases a natural biocide that suppresses growth
Corrosion seals the pipe so that no water can touch the bacteria at all
Corrosion raises the local water temperature above the killing point
Corrosion gives nutrients and a rough, sheltered surface for biofilm
How Legionella Grows.w: Rust and corrosion debris supply nutrients and create rough, sheltered surfaces where biofilm forms and Legionella lodges. Controlling corrosion and removing debris helps limit the conditions for growth.

n.0: Corrosion products feed growth rather than releasing any biocide.
n.1: Corrosion roughens and pits surfaces; it does not seal water away from bacteria.
n.2: Corrosion does not heat water to a killing temperature; it provides food and shelter.

How Legionella Grows.q: An expansion vessel and a rarely opened emergency safety shower are both on a site risk assessment. Why are components like these flagged for Legionella growth?
o: They keep large volumes of the water constantly hot, above 60°C at every hour of the day
They are completely self-cleaning inside and never accumulate any deposits at all
They hold water that seldom moves, allowing stagnation, warming and nutrient build-up
They contain no water whatsoever and so cannot support any bacteria
How Legionella Grows.w: Expansion vessels and emergency showers hold water that is rarely exchanged, so it stagnates, drifts into the growth range and gathers nutrients. Such infrequently used components need regular flushing and inspection.

n.0: These are not maintained hot at 60°C; the water sits at ambient.
n.1: Little-used components accumulate sediment and biofilm.
n.3: They do hold water, which is why they can support growth.

How Legionella Grows.q: Which single summary best captures the conditions Legionella needs to grow to harmful numbers?
o: Sterile, nutrient-free water held at any temperature at all
Warm, stagnant 20–45°C water with nutrients, then dispersed as aerosol
Water kept constantly below 20°C or above 60°C and always moving
Fast-flowing water with a strong disinfectant residual and no deposits
How Legionella Grows.w: Legionella multiplies when water is warm (20–45°C), still and nutrient-rich, and becomes a health risk when that water is dispersed as a breathable aerosol. Controls target each of these factors under HSG274 Part 2.

n.0: Sterile, nutrient-free water lacks the food the bacteria need.
n.2: Water kept cold or hot and moving is a control condition, not what favours growth.
n.3: Fast flow, disinfectant residual and no deposits all suppress growth.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Under the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974, what is the main duty an employer owes to their employees?
o: To provide free protective clothing to every worker whatever the cost involved
To hold employers' liability insurance and take no further steps
To pay compensation to a worker whenever any accident happens on site
To ensure their health, safety and welfare at work so far as is reasonably practicable
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Section 2 of the Act places a general duty on employers to ensure the health, safety and welfare of employees so far as is reasonably practicable.

n.0: PPE is provided where the risk assessment requires it; the duty is qualified by reasonable practicability.
n.1: Employers' liability insurance is separate and does not discharge the safety duty.
n.2: The Act prevents harm; paying out after an accident is not the primary duty.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: The Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 also places a duty on employees. What must every employee do?
o: Personally write all of the company's risk assessments on their own
Ignore any hazards that fall outside their own particular trade
Only follow the site's safety rules while a manager is actually watching them
Take reasonable care of themselves and others and co-operate with the employer
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Section 7 requires employees to take reasonable care for their own safety and that of others and to co-operate with the employer on health and safety.

n.0: Producing risk assessments is the employer's duty, not the operative's.
n.1: The duty to take reasonable care extends to others affected by your work.
n.2: The duty of care applies at all times, not only when supervised.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Which set of regulations treats legionella bacteria as a biological hazard that must be assessed and controlled at work?
o: The Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations 2002
The Road Traffic Act governing the use of vehicles on the highway
The Data Protection Act covering the handling of personal data
The Working Time Regulations covering workers' hours and rest breaks
The Law & Responsibilities.w: COSHH 2002 covers biological agents such as legionella and requires the risk to be assessed and adequately controlled.

n.1: The Road Traffic Act governs driving, not workplace health hazards.
n.2: The Data Protection Act governs personal data, not hazardous substances.
n.3: The Working Time Regulations deal with hours of work, not biological hazards.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: What does the abbreviation ACOP stand for in relation to L8?
o: Approved Code of Practice
Annual Certificate of Practice
Approved Contractor Order Policy
Advisory Committee on Plumbing
The Law & Responsibilities.w: L8 is the Approved Code of Practice, giving practical advice on complying with the law on legionella.

n.3: There is no such committee behind L8; ACOP is a defined legal term.
n.1: L8 is not a certificate; it is guidance with special legal status.
n.2: ACOP does not refer to a contractor order policy.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: What is the special legal status of an Approved Code of Practice such as L8?
o: It is purely optional advice that has no bearing on the law and may be freely ignored
Follow it and you comply; if not, you must show an equally effective method
It applies only inside hospitals and to nowhere else at all
It completely replaces the Health and Safety at Work Act
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Following an ACOP is normally enough to comply; departing from it means you must demonstrate compliance by some equally good means.

n.0: An ACOP has a defined legal standing and can be cited in court, so it is not merely optional.
n.3: An ACOP supports the law; it does not replace primary legislation.
n.2: L8 applies wherever there is a legionella risk, not only hospitals.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: HSG274 is best described as which of the following?
o: Practical technical guidance on controlling legionella in water systems
A criminal statute passed by Parliament that can carry a prison sentence
A product warranty document supplied with new plumbing equipment
A first aid manual for treating people who fall ill on site
The Law & Responsibilities.w: HSG274 is HSE technical guidance giving practical detail on controlling legionella in different types of water system.

n.1: HSG274 is guidance, not an Act of Parliament.
n.2: It is not a warranty; it is health and safety guidance.
n.3: It concerns water system control, not first aid.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Which part of HSG274 covers hot and cold water systems?
o: Part 1, which covers evaporative cooling towers and condensers
Part 3, which covers other risk systems such as spa pools
Part 6, said to cover large cold water storage reservoirs
Part 2, the guidance covering hot and cold water systems
The Law & Responsibilities.w: HSG274 Part 2 gives the practical guidance for controlling legionella in hot and cold water systems.

n.0: Part 1 covers evaporative cooling systems, not hot and cold water.
n.1: Part 3 covers other risk systems such as spa pools, not hot and cold water.
n.2: There is no Part 6; hot and cold water is Part 2.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Who is the 'duty holder' with the legal responsibility to assess and manage the legionella risk on a site?
o: The water company that supplies the incoming mains
Whichever operative last carried out work on the tank
Anyone who happens to report a fault on the system
The employer or the person in control of those premises
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The duty holder is the employer or person in control of the premises, and they carry the legal responsibility to assess and manage the risk.

n.0: The mains supplier is not responsible for the building owner's internal systems.
n.1: An individual operative is not the duty holder simply because they did the last task.
n.2: Reporting a fault is a good act but does not make someone the duty holder.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: The duty holder appoints a competent person to take day-to-day charge of controlling the legionella risk. What is this person usually called?
o: The insurance assessor who settles claims
A general site visitor passing through
The appointed responsible person
The water mains inspector for the area
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The appointed competent person who manages the control measures is known as the responsible person.

n.1: A 'site visitor' has no defined role in the control scheme.
n.3: A mains inspector is not the appointed manager of the internal water system risk.
n.0: An insurance assessor deals with claims, not day-to-day legionella control.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Which regulations place a clear duty on employers to carry out a suitable and sufficient risk assessment?
o: The Highway Code covering the use of public roads
The Consumer Rights Act covering goods and services
The Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999
The Building Societies Act covering financial firms
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations require employers to make a suitable and sufficient assessment of the risks.

n.0: The Highway Code concerns road use, not workplace risk assessment.
n.1: The Consumer Rights Act deals with goods and services to consumers.
n.3: The Building Societies Act is financial legislation.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Legionnaires' disease diagnosed as caught at work must be reported to the authorities under which reporting requirement?
o: PAT, the portable appliance testing scheme for electrical items
MOT, the annual roadworthiness test for motor vehicles
GDPR, the regulations governing the protection of personal data
RIDDOR, the work-related injury and disease reporting rules
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Legionnaires' disease contracted at work is reportable to the HSE under RIDDOR.

n.0: PAT is portable appliance testing, not disease reporting.
n.1: MOT covers vehicle roadworthiness, not disease reporting.
n.2: GDPR governs personal data protection, not disease reporting.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Which body is the main enforcing authority for the legionella duties under health and safety law?
o: The Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency
The Advertising Standards Authority
The Environment Agency
The Health and Safety Executive (HSE)
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The HSE is the principal enforcing authority for health and safety law covering legionella.

n.2: The Environment Agency deals mainly with environmental discharges, not this enforcement.
n.1: The Advertising Standards Authority regulates advertising.
n.0: The DVSA regulates drivers and vehicles.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: A written scheme for controlling the risk has been prepared for a site. What is your duty as an operative in relation to it?
o: Rewrite the control scheme yourself to suit your own preferred way of working
Carry out your tasks as the scheme sets out and record what you do
Ignore it, since the scheme is only advisory guidance
Keep it locked away and unread to keep it in good condition
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Operatives must follow the written scheme, complete their tasks correctly and keep records as required.

n.0: Altering the control scheme is the responsible person's role, not an operative's.
n.2: The scheme is a legal control measure that must be followed, not ignored.
n.3: The scheme must be used and understood, not hidden away.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Under COSHH, what must be done before employees are exposed to a substance or agent hazardous to health such as legionella?
o: Every employee must be issued a respirator whatever the task
The water system must be permanently shut down and drained
A sample must be sent to the local police for testing first
The risk must be assessed and adequate controls put in place
The Law & Responsibilities.w: COSHH requires the risk to be assessed and controlled adequately before exposure occurs.

n.0: Respirators are only required where the assessment identifies the need.
n.1: Permanent shutdown is not required; the risk is managed, not eliminated.
n.2: There is no requirement to involve the police with samples.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: You are flushing a rarely used outlet as instructed. Part-way through you notice a nearby tap has no cold water at all. It is outside your task. What should you do?
o: Report the fault to the responsible person so it can be investigated
Turn off the whole building's water supply yourself without asking anyone
Wait a few weeks to see whether the fault fixes itself
Say nothing at all because it is not on your job sheet today
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Everyone has a duty to report problems so the responsible person can act, even where it falls outside their own task.

n.1: Isolating the whole building without authority is not your decision and could cause harm.
n.2: Delaying a report lets a potential risk persist.
n.3: Ignoring a fault because it is off your sheet breaches the duty to report.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Why must a person appointed to manage legionella control be 'competent'?
o: Competence simply means the person holds a driving licence
They need the training, knowledge and experience to do the work safely
It is only a courtesy title and carries no real practical meaning
Competence is decided purely by a person's length of service
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Competence means having the necessary training, knowledge, skills and experience to carry out the duties properly.

n.0: A driving licence is unrelated to competence in legionella control.
n.2: Competence is a genuine legal requirement, not a courtesy.
n.3: Time served does not by itself prove the required knowledge and skills.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: The responsible person is away on leave for two weeks. How should continuity of legionella control be maintained?
o: All monitoring simply stops until the responsible person returns
Control measures are suspended and then restarted on their return
The tasks pass to whoever happens to be on site that day
A trained and competent deputy is appointed to cover the duties
The Law & Responsibilities.w: A competent deputy should be appointed so the control duties continue without a gap during absences.

n.0: Stopping monitoring during absence would break the control regime.
n.1: Suspending controls allows conditions for legionella to develop.
n.2: Duties should go to a competent deputy, not any untrained bystander.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: An operative argues that because L8 is 'only a code of practice' it can be ignored. Why is this wrong?
o: Codes of practice are fully binding statutes in their own right
Only the Environment Agency, not the HSE, is allowed to quote L8 in court
L8 has been formally withdrawn and no longer exists at all
An ACOP has special legal status and can be cited in court as evidence
The Law & Responsibilities.w: An ACOP carries special legal standing, and failing to follow it can be used in court unless equal compliance is shown.

n.0: An ACOP is not itself a statute, but it still carries legal weight; the claim it can be ignored is the error.
n.2: L8 is current guidance, not withdrawn.
n.1: The HSE, not the Environment Agency, is the enforcing authority that relies on L8.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Under the Health and Safety at Work Act, what must an employee NOT do to safety equipment provided for their protection?
o: Report it to a supervisor whenever it is found to be damaged
Store it correctly and securely in the proper place after use
Clean it carefully after every use to keep it serviceable
Interfere with it or deliberately misuse it
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Section 8 makes it an offence to intentionally interfere with or misuse anything provided for health and safety.

n.0: Reporting damage is exactly what an employee should do.
n.1: Storing equipment correctly is expected, not prohibited.
n.2: Cleaning equipment properly is good practice, not prohibited.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Who has the ultimate legal responsibility for ensuring the legionella risk assessment is carried out?
o: The visiting auditor
The duty holder
The chemical supplier
The most junior operative
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The duty holder holds the legal responsibility for ensuring a suitable risk assessment is carried out.

n.3: A junior operative carries out tasks but does not hold the legal duty to ensure assessment.
n.2: A chemical supplier provides products, not the site's legal duty of assessment.
n.0: An auditor checks compliance but does not carry the duty holder's responsibility.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: During a routine temperature check you find a hot outlet running well below the expected temperature. What is the correct action?
o: Cross out the low figure and write in a passing temperature instead
Record the reading and report it to the responsible person
Assume the thermometer must be faulty and move on to the next outlet
Adjust the boiler yourself without telling anyone about the reading
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Out-of-range readings must be recorded accurately and reported so control can be reviewed and corrective action taken.

n.0: Falsifying records is dishonest and hides a real risk.
n.2: Dismissing the reading without checking could conceal a genuine control failure.
n.3: Altering plant settings without authority is not the operative's role.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between L8 and HSG274?
o: L8 is the approved code of practice; HSG274 gives the detail
They are simply two different names for one single document
HSG274 legally overrides L8 in every situation without exception
Neither of them has any connection to legionella control
The Law & Responsibilities.w: L8 sets the code of practice while HSG274 provides the supporting practical and technical detail.

n.1: They are separate publications, not one document.
n.2: HSG274 supports L8 rather than overriding it.
n.3: Both are specifically about controlling legionella.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: You are a contractor asked to do work not covered by the site's written scheme or your training. What should you do?
o: Stop and check with the responsible person first
Guess at a method and carry on anyway to save time
Refuse to talk to anyone and quietly leave site
Sign the work off as complete regardless
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Work must be within your competence and the written scheme; if it is not, you should stop and consult the responsible person.

n.1: Guessing a method on a safety-critical system risks creating a hazard.
n.2: Leaving without informing anyone abandons the duty to communicate.
n.3: Signing off work not properly done is falsifying records.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Under COSHH, how often should the assessment for a legionella risk be reviewed?
o: Only once, at the time the building is first constructed
Only after an outbreak of illness has already happened
Never again, once it has been signed off
Regularly, and whenever it may no longer be valid
The Law & Responsibilities.w: COSHH requires the assessment to be reviewed regularly and whenever it may no longer be valid, such as after changes to the system.

n.0: A single assessment at construction cannot reflect later changes.
n.1: Waiting for an outbreak defeats the purpose of assessment.
n.2: Assessments must be kept up to date.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: An operative says the risk assessment is 'the water company's job'. Why is this incorrect?
o: Nobody at all is legally required to assess this water risk
The duty holder in control of the premises assesses their own systems
The water company is legally bound to assess the pipework in every building
Only the HSE is permitted to carry out any risk assessment
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Responsibility for assessing the risk in the building's own water systems rests with the duty holder, not the mains supplier.

n.0: The law clearly requires the risk to be assessed by the duty holder.
n.2: The water company is not responsible for risks inside private premises.
n.3: The HSE enforces the law but does not do duty holders' assessments for them.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: What is the purpose of keeping records of the checks and tasks carried out under the control scheme?
o: To show the control measures are working and to help identify any problems
To replace the need to actually carry out the physical tasks on site
To satisfy the marketing department's promotional needs
To generate paperwork that no one will ever need to read
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Records demonstrate that control measures are being applied and provide a history that helps spot trends and problems.

n.1: Recording a task does not remove the need to actually perform it.
n.2: Record keeping is a legal and technical requirement, not a marketing exercise.
n.3: Records are a working tool that must be available for review, not pointless paperwork.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: You arrive to service a cold water storage tank and find the lid missing and debris inside. It is not the job you were sent for. What is the responsible action?
o: Scoop the debris out with your bare hands and mention nothing
Report the open tank and debris to the responsible person now
Fit any spare lid from another site without checking it suits
Leave the tank open and simply finish your original task
The Law & Responsibilities.w: An uncovered, contaminated tank is a clear risk that must be reported promptly so it can be dealt with correctly.

n.0: Using bare hands is unhygienic, and saying nothing hides the problem.
n.2: An unsuitable random lid could add further contamination and is not authorised.
n.3: Leaving the tank open ignores an obvious, reportable hazard.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: The Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations require the significant findings of a risk assessment to be recorded when the employer has how many or more employees?
o: Two hundred or more
Fifty or more
Five or more
One or more
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Employers with five or more employees must record the significant findings of their risk assessment.

n.3: The recording threshold is five, not one, although good practice is to record in any case.
n.1: The threshold is far lower than fifty.
n.0: The threshold is not set at two hundred employees.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Which of the following best describes 'so far as is reasonably practicable' in the Health and Safety at Work Act?
o: Ignoring a risk whenever controlling it would be inconvenient to arrange
Balancing the level of risk against the time, trouble and cost of controlling it
Always choosing whatever option happens to be the cheapest available
Spending an unlimited amount of money no matter how small the risk
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Reasonably practicable means weighing the level of risk against the effort and cost needed to control it.

n.0: Inconvenience does not excuse leaving a significant risk uncontrolled.
n.2: Cost cannot be put ahead of a serious risk; it is a balance, not the cheapest option.
n.3: The test is proportionate, not a requirement to spend without limit.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: An operative on your team says they were never trained but has been told to carry out chlorination. What should happen?
o: They should not do the task until they are trained and competent
They should ask a passing member of the public to help them do it
They should just sign the record to say the work was done anyway
They should attempt it anyway and simply learn the job as they go
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Tasks must only be done by people with the training and competence to do them safely and correctly.

n.1: Members of the public are not trained operatives and must not do control tasks.
n.2: Signing a record for work not properly done is falsification.
n.3: Attempting a chemical task untrained risks harm to themselves and others.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Why is legionella specifically covered by COSHH?
o: Because it is a biological agent that is hazardous to health
Because it is a highly flammable liquid stored on the premises
Because it is a controlled explosive requiring a licence
Because it is classed as a road transport hazard in transit
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Legionella bacteria are a biological agent hazardous to health, which brings them within COSHH.

n.1: Legionella is a living organism, not a flammable liquid.
n.2: It is not an explosive substance.
n.3: COSHH covers it as a health hazard, unrelated to transport rules.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: You are working on a customer's site and are unsure who the responsible person is. What is the best course of action?
o: Assume there is simply no responsible person on this site
Ask before starting so you know who to report to and take instruction from
Just start the work and hope that somebody eventually tells you who it is later
Report only to another contractor you happen to know on site
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Knowing who the responsible person is ensures you can take instruction and report problems to the right person before work begins.

n.2: Starting blind means faults may not reach the right person.
n.0: A duty holder should have appointed a responsible person; assuming none exists is unsafe.
n.3: Reporting to an unrelated contractor does not put the information where it needs to go.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Which statement about the duty holder's responsibilities is correct?
o: They are only responsible for water they can see
They only need to act after someone becomes ill
They can pass all legal responsibility to a cleaning contractor by verbal agreement
They must identify and assess the risk and put in place a means of controlling it
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The duty holder must identify and assess the risk and ensure control measures are in place and maintained.

n.2: Legal responsibility for the duty cannot simply be handed off by a casual arrangement.
n.1: The duty is preventive and does not wait for illness to occur.
n.0: The duty covers the whole system, including parts not readily visible.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: A supervisor tells you to skip a scheduled temperature monitoring round because 'it's always fine'. What should you do?
o: Do just half of the outlets this time so the round is quicker
Skip it as instructed and record on the sheet that it was done
Carry out the monitoring the scheme requires and record the results
Delete that outlet from the record permanently to avoid the issue each time
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The written scheme's monitoring must be carried out and recorded honestly, as it is a legal control measure.

n.0: Partial monitoring does not meet the requirements of the scheme.
n.1: Recording monitoring as done when it was skipped is falsification.
n.3: An operative has no authority to remove monitoring points from the scheme.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: What does the term 'suitable and sufficient' mean when applied to a risk assessment?
o: It is kept as brief as possible, deliberately leaving out almost all detail
It properly identifies the risks and the measures needed to control them
It is copied word for word from a completely different building
It simply lists all of the equipment installed across the site
The Law & Responsibilities.w: A suitable and sufficient assessment properly identifies the significant risks and the control measures required.

n.0: An assessment must contain enough detail to be useful, not be deliberately brief.
n.2: A copied generic assessment may not reflect the actual system and its risks.
n.3: Listing equipment alone does not assess how the risk arises or is controlled.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Legionnaires' disease is reportable under RIDDOR when it is believed to have been caught in what circumstance?
o: Only when the affected person is over 65 years of age
Where the person's work exposed them to legionella
Only if the person happens to work outdoors regularly
Never, because it is not considered work-related at all
The Law & Responsibilities.w: A case is RIDDOR-reportable where there is reasonable evidence the illness was linked to work exposure to legionella.

n.0: Age does not determine whether a case is reportable.
n.2: The setting need not be outdoors; indoor water systems are a common source.
n.3: Work-related cases are reportable, so it is not correct that it is never reportable.
