The Law & Responsibilities.q: You find that a colleague has been signing monitoring sheets without actually taking the readings. What is the correct response?
o: Copy their approach so you can keep up with the workload
Say nothing at all so as not to cause any trouble
Report it, since the records are false and the risk is unmanaged
Backdate your own sheets to match the ones they signed
The Law & Responsibilities.w: False records mean the risk is not truly being monitored, so this must be reported so control can be restored.

n.0: Copying false record-keeping compounds the danger and the dishonesty.
n.1: Staying silent allows an unmanaged risk to continue.
n.3: Backdating records is itself falsification and hides the problem further.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Which of these is a duty placed on employees rather than the employer under health and safety law?
o: Funding and buying all of the control equipment on site
Preparing the site's legionella risk assessment
Appointing the site's own responsible person
Co-operating with the employer so they can meet their duties
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Employees have a legal duty to co-operate with their employer on health and safety matters.

n.0: Providing and funding equipment is an employer duty.
n.1: Preparing the risk assessment is the duty holder's duty.
n.2: Appointing the responsible person is a duty holder responsibility.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: If a duty holder chooses not to follow the exact advice in ACOP L8, what must they be able to demonstrate?
o: That the decision saved them a good amount of money overall
That some other company can now be blamed for it instead
That they controlled the risk to the same standard another way
That the risk no longer needs to be controlled at all now
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Departing from an ACOP is permitted only if you can show you achieved compliance to an equally effective standard.

n.0: Saving money does not justify a lower standard of control.
n.1: Shifting blame does not discharge the duty to control the risk.
n.3: The legal duty to control the risk always remains.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: A cold water storage tank temperature is found to be rising toward the range where legionella can multiply. Whose job is it to make sure this is acted upon?
o: The water meter reader who calls to read the supply meter
The member of the public who reported feeling unwell that day
The HSE inspector whenever they next happen to visit
The responsible person, acting on the operative's report
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The operative reports the finding and the responsible person ensures corrective action is taken.

n.0: A meter reader has no responsibility for the control scheme.
n.1: A member of the public has no role in managing the control scheme.
n.2: Action cannot wait for a possible future HSE visit.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Under the Health and Safety at Work Act, an employer's duty to non-employees such as visitors and the public is:
o: Non-existent, because the Act is written only to protect an employer's own staff
Owed only to paying customers who happen to be inside the premises
Conduct the work so they are not exposed to risks, so far as is reasonably practicable
Met simply by displaying a warning sign somewhere near the hazard
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Section 3 extends the duty to persons not in the employer's employment who may be affected by the work.

n.0: The Act clearly protects people beyond the direct employees.
n.1: The duty is owed to anyone affected, not only paying customers.
n.3: A sign alone does not discharge the wider duty to control the risk.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Why should an operative understand the site's written scheme of control before starting work?
o: So they can justify charging the customer a higher price for the job
So they can decide for themselves that the whole scheme is unnecessary here
So they are able to change the system's control temperatures as they see fit
So they carry out the correct tasks in the correct way and know what to report
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Understanding the scheme ensures tasks are done correctly and that faults are recognised and reported properly.

n.0: The scheme controls risk; it is not about adjusting charges.
n.1: The scheme is a legal control measure, not something an operative can dismiss.
n.2: Changing control temperatures is a decision for the responsible person.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: A landlord manages a block of flats with shared water systems. Under the law, they are best described as:
o: Exempt from any duties because they do not live in the building
An ordinary member of the public with no legal duties at all
A duty holder who must assess and control the legionella risk
Responsible only for keeping the boiler's warranty valid
The Law & Responsibilities.w: A landlord in control of premises with a water system is a duty holder and must assess and control the risk.

n.0: Not living in the building does not remove the duty for premises they control.
n.1: As the person in control, the landlord has clear legal duties.
n.3: The duty covers the whole system risk, not just a warranty.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: You notice the site risk assessment on the wall is dated over five years ago and the building has since been extended. What does this suggest?
o: The assessment likely needs reviewing because the system has changed
Only the HSE is allowed to point this problem out to the site
Nothing at all, because risk assessments never expire once written
The extension automatically makes the old assessment correct and current
The Law & Responsibilities.w: A material change such as an extension is a trigger to review whether the assessment is still valid.

n.1: Anyone noticing this should raise it; it is not solely for the HSE.
n.2: Assessments must be reviewed after changes, so they are not timeless.
n.3: An extension adds new pipework and risk, so the old one cannot be assumed valid.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Which of the following is the correct order of legal weight, from primary law to practical guidance?
o: ACOP L8 first, then the Act, then HSG274 guidance
They all carry exactly equal legal force in every case
The Health and Safety at Work Act, then ACOP L8, then HSG274 guidance
HSG274 guidance first, then ACOP L8, then the Act
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The Act is the primary legislation, L8 is the approved code of practice supporting it, and HSG274 is practical guidance.

n.3: Guidance does not sit above the primary Act; the order is reversed.
n.0: An ACOP supports the Act rather than outranking it.
n.1: They have different standings; primary law, ACOP and guidance are not equal.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: A member of the public tells you a shower in a leisure centre changing room has not worked for months. You are on site to service the pool plant. What should you do?
o: Ignore it because servicing showers is not part of your job today on a busy site
Tell the responsible person so the little-used outlet can be assessed
Tell the member of the public to go and fix the shower themselves
Turn the shower on and simply leave it running there unattended
The Law & Responsibilities.w: A little-used outlet can allow stagnation, so the information should reach the responsible person to be assessed and acted upon.

n.0: The duty to report a potential risk applies even outside your task.
n.2: Members of the public should not be carrying out control work.
n.3: Leaving a shower running unattended is not a safe response.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: What is the main reason an operative must report faults promptly rather than at the end of the month?
o: There is no real reason at all, since the timing genuinely does not matter
Monthly reporting simply looks tidier and neater on the paperwork records
A delay can let conditions for legionella develop and put people at risk
Prompt reports mainly serve to annoy the responsible person on site
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Prompt reporting allows quick corrective action before conditions favour legionella growth.

n.0: Timing matters greatly because delay increases risk.
n.1: Appearance of paperwork is irrelevant next to controlling a health risk.
n.3: Reporting promptly supports the responsible person's duties rather than hindering them.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Which document would an operative primarily follow for the day-to-day tasks and frequencies on a site?
o: The company's staff holiday and annual leave policy
A generic advertising brochure for the company
The building's fire safety certificate document
The site-specific written scheme of control
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The written scheme of control sets out the specific tasks, methods and frequencies for that site.

n.0: A holiday policy is unrelated to water hygiene tasks.
n.1: A brochure is marketing material, not a control document.
n.2: A fire certificate concerns fire safety, not legionella control tasks.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: If the HSE inspects a site and finds the legionella risk is not being managed, which of these can they do?
o: Only give friendly advice, since they hold no enforcement powers whatsoever
Repair the entire water system for the site free of charge
Issue an on-the-spot parking ticket for a car parked outside
Serve an improvement or prohibition notice and prosecute serious cases
The Law & Responsibilities.w: As the enforcing authority the HSE can serve enforcement notices and bring prosecutions where the law is breached.

n.0: The HSE has real enforcement powers, not just advice.
n.1: The HSE enforces the law; it does not carry out the duty holder's repairs.
n.2: Parking tickets are nothing to do with the HSE's health and safety role.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: An operative completes a task but realises they did it slightly wrong. What is the responsible thing to do?
o: Do nothing and simply hope that it was fine
Record it as fully correct to avoid any questions
Tell the responsible person so it can be corrected
Blame the previous contractor in the written record
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Being honest about a mistake lets it be corrected and keeps the records accurate and reliable.

n.0: Ignoring a known error leaves a potential problem unaddressed.
n.1: Recording a wrong task as correct is falsification and hides risk.
n.3: Shifting blame does not fix the error or keep the record truthful.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Which document is the Approved Code of Practice (ACOP) for controlling legionella?
o: The Highway Code covering the safe use of public roads
The building's daily cleaning and housekeeping rota
L8, the HSE approved code of practice for legionella
A shower manufacturer's product installation leaflet
The Law & Responsibilities.w: L8 is the HSE Approved Code of Practice that sets the standard for controlling legionella, supported by the HSG274 guidance.

n.0: The Highway Code deals with road use, not water hygiene.
n.1: A cleaning rota is a local task list, not the ACOP.
n.3: A product leaflet is not an official code of practice.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Under health and safety law, who is the 'duty holder' with overall responsibility for controlling the legionella risk?
o: Whichever is the most junior member of staff on the site that day
The employer or person in control of the premises
Any visitor who happens to use the building that day
The water company that supplies the mains to it
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The duty holder is the employer or person in control of the premises, who must assess and control the risk.

n.2: Visitors have no legal duty to control the risk.
n.3: The water supplier is responsible only up to the boundary, not for the building's internal systems.
n.0: Responsibility rests with the duty holder, not automatically with junior staff.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: What must the duty holder do about managing the day-to-day legionella controls?
o: Appoint a competent responsible person to manage them
Simply wait until someone actually becomes ill before acting
Rely only on tenants happening to notice any problems
Leave the whole system alone once it is installed
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The duty holder must appoint a competent responsible person to take day-to-day charge of managing and monitoring the controls.

n.1: The law requires prevention in advance, not waiting for illness.
n.2: The legal duty cannot be passed to tenants noticing faults.
n.3: Water systems need ongoing management, not fit-and-forget.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Which two pieces of legislation place general legal duties to control the legionella risk?
o: The Working Time Regulations and the Equality Act 2010
The Road Traffic Act and the Licensing Act 2003 together
The Data Protection Act and the Consumer Rights Act 2015
The Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 and COSHH 2002
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 and the COSHH Regulations 2002 create the legal duties to assess and control the risk.

n.0: These cover working hours and discrimination, not legionella.
n.1: These cover driving and alcohol licensing, not legionella.
n.2: These cover data and consumer purchases, not water hygiene.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: What is the role of HSG274 in relation to legionella control?
o: A promotional marketing brochure for water-treatment cleaning products
A manufacturer's warranty document covering hot water boilers
A criminal court sentencing guideline for such offences
HSE technical guidance on controlling legionella in water systems
The Law & Responsibilities.w: HSG274 is the HSE's practical technical guidance that supports the L8 ACOP, including Part 2 on hot and cold water systems.

n.0: It is official guidance, not sales material.
n.1: It is not a product warranty.
n.2: It is health and safety guidance, not a court sentencing document.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: You are carrying out water hygiene checks and notice a stored hot water temperature is far too low. What should you do?
o: Say nothing about it at all so as to avoid causing extra work
Ignore it entirely, because it is simply not on your written task list
Wait several months and just mention it at the next annual review
Record the reading and report it promptly to the responsible person
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The written scheme requires readings to be recorded and problems reported promptly so control can be restored quickly.

n.0: Staying silent leaves a known risk uncontrolled.
n.1: Everyone has a duty to report problems they find, even outside usual tasks.
n.2: A control failure needs prompt action, not delay until the next review.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: A colleague asks you why you bother writing down every temperature and inspection. What is the correct reason?
o: To show that the controls are working and give evidence that the risk is managed
Only to decorate the wall of the plant room with paperwork
Purely so that the staff on site can get some practice at their handwriting
They are not really needed at all and can be thrown away straight away
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Records demonstrate that the written scheme is being followed and that the risk is being properly controlled over time.

n.1: Their purpose is evidence and control, not decoration.
n.2: Their value is as proof of monitoring, not handwriting practice.
n.3: Records must be kept, not discarded; they are a legal expectation.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: What does 'competent' mean when appointing a responsible person for legionella control?
o: They simply happen to own the most tools of anyone
They have the right training, knowledge and experience
They just happen to be the ones available on the day
They are the longest-serving employee, regardless of knowledge
The Law & Responsibilities.w: A competent person has the necessary training, knowledge, skills and experience to carry out the control duties properly.

n.0: Owning tools is not a measure of competence for managing the risk.
n.2: Being available is not the same as being competent.
n.3: Length of service alone does not make someone competent.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: You are a new operative and have not read the site's written control scheme yet. Before you start work on the water system, what should you do?
o: Guess what to do for yourself so you do not have to ask anyone at all
Copy whatever the last operative did without any checking
Read and follow the written scheme, and ask if you are unsure
Skip the paperwork entirely because it only slows you down
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Everyone must follow the site's written scheme and raise any uncertainty with the responsible person before working on the system.

n.0: Guessing on safety-critical work risks leaving the system uncontrolled.
n.1: Copying past actions may repeat mistakes and ignores the scheme.
n.3: The written scheme sets out required controls and must not be skipped.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: An operative argues that because ACOP L8 is only an Approved Code of Practice and not an Act of Parliament, its guidance can be ignored so long as the job gets done. Under the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974, what is the true legal standing of L8?
o: It has no legal weight at all and is purely advisory background reading only
It applies only to the water supplier and places no duties on any contractor on the system
It is fully mandatory law, so any deviation is automatically a criminal offence whatever controls are in place
Following it is one way to comply; otherwise you must prove your controls are at least equally effective
The Law & Responsibilities.w: An ACOP has a special legal status: you may follow it, or adopt controls that are at least equally effective. If prosecuted for a breach of the law and it is shown you did not follow the ACOP, a court can find you at fault unless you prove you complied in some other equally effective way.

n.0: An ACOP is not merely advisory; it carries special evidential status.
n.1: L8 duties fall on anyone in control of the premises, including contractors.
n.2: An ACOP permits equally effective alternatives, so deviation is not automatic.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: A duty holder claims they have discharged all their legal duties simply by appointing a competent responsible person for Legionella control. Under the HSWA 1974 and MHSWR, is this correct?
o: No, but only because a deputy responsible person must also be appointed first
Yes, provided the responsible person holds a recognised certificate
Yes, appointing a competent person transfers the whole legal duty away completely
No, the duty holder keeps overall responsibility for controlling the risk
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Appointing a competent responsible person is required, but overall legal responsibility for assessing and controlling the risk stays with the duty holder (employer/person in control). They must resource, monitor and ensure the arrangements actually work.

n.2: Legal duty cannot be transferred away by appointing someone; the duty holder remains accountable.
n.1: A certificate does not remove the duty holder's ongoing responsibility to oversee the arrangements.
n.0: A deputy is good practice for continuity, but the real reason is that overall duty always remains with the duty holder.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: On a domestic hot and cold water system, which HSE guidance document sets out the technical guidance most directly relevant to National Water Hygiene work?
o: HSG274 Part 3, which covers other risk systems such as spa pools
INDG458, which is a short introductory leaflet only
HSG274 Part 1, which covers evaporative cooling systems
HSG274 Part 2, which covers hot and cold water systems
The Law & Responsibilities.w: HSG274 is HSE's technical guidance supporting ACOP L8, and Part 2 specifically addresses hot and cold water systems, which is the domain most relevant to water hygiene operatives.

n.2: Part 1 covers evaporative cooling systems such as cooling towers, not hot and cold water.
n.0: Part 3 covers other risk systems such as spa pools, not general hot and cold water systems.
n.1: INDG458 is a brief overview leaflet and is not the detailed technical guidance for hot and cold water systems.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Scenario: While flushing a rarely used outlet, an operative notices the thermostatic mixing valve is delivering blended water at only 35 degrees C and the local temperature monitoring records are two months out of date. What is the correct action under the written scheme and their legal duties?
o: Shut down the entire building water supply immediately without informing anyone
Record the finding and report the fault to the responsible person so it can be assessed and acted upon
Adjust the valve settings themselves and backdate the monitoring records to close the gap
Ignore it because temperature control of individual outlets is not part of a water hygiene operative's role
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Operatives must follow the written scheme and report faults or abnormal readings to the responsible person, who assesses and directs corrective action. Reporting creates the record and triggers the proper management response.

n.2: Adjusting valves outside your remit and falsifying records is unsafe and unlawful.
n.3: Monitoring and reporting temperature abnormalities is a core part of the operative's role.
n.0: Unilaterally shutting the whole supply without informing anyone is not the correct managed response; the fault must be reported and assessed.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Which single piece of legislation places the broad, overarching duty on employers to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health and safety of employees and others affected by the work, and underpins all Legionella control law?
o: The Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999
The Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations 2002
The Reporting of Injuries, Diseases and Dangerous Occurrences Regulations 2013
The Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974
The Law & Responsibilities.w: HSWA 1974 is the primary, overarching legislation placing general duties on employers and the self-employed to protect employees and others so far as is reasonably practicable. The other regulations sit beneath it.

n.1: COSHH deals specifically with hazardous substances, including biological agents, but is a regulation made under the wider Act.
n.0: MHSWR sets out risk-assessment duties but is subordinate to the primary Act.
n.2: RIDDOR is about reporting specified incidents, not the overarching general duty.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: A Legionella bacterium is a biological agent. Which regulations most directly require employers to assess and control the risk from exposure to it as a hazardous substance?
o: The Construction (Design and Management) Regulations 2015
The Personal Protective Equipment at Work Regulations 1992
The Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998
The Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations 2002 (COSHH)
The Law & Responsibilities.w: COSHH covers hazardous substances including biological agents such as Legionella bacteria, requiring assessment and control of exposure. L8 and HSG274 give the practical guidance for meeting these duties.

n.0: CDM concerns management of construction projects, not control of Legionella.
n.1: The PPE Regulations cover protective equipment, not the substance risk assessment.
n.2: PUWER concerns the safety of work equipment, not a biological agent.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Scenario: A site's responsible person leaves the company suddenly and no deputy was ever appointed. For several weeks nobody is directing the Legionella control scheme. From a legal standpoint, what does this situation primarily represent?
o: A matter only for the water supplier to resolve, not the duty holder at all
A problem that only becomes legally relevant if someone actually falls ill
A failing by the duty holder, who must ensure competent management of the risk continues
An acceptable temporary gap, since the control duties simply pause when nobody is in post
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The duty holder must ensure the risk continues to be managed by a competent person at all times, which is why appointing deputies and providing continuity is expected. A management gap is a failing of the duty holder's ongoing duty.

n.0: Responsibility for on-site control rests with the duty holder, not the water supplier.
n.1: The legal failing exists as soon as control lapses, regardless of whether illness has occurred.
n.3: Legal duties to control the risk do not pause when a post is vacant.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: An HSE inspector visits a site and finds a water system being operated in a way that involves a risk of serious personal injury. Which enforcement action allows the inspector to require that activity to stop, immediately or after a set time?
o: A prohibition notice
A fixed penalty ticket issued on the spot
An improvement notice
A simple caution letter with no legal force
The Law & Responsibilities.w: A prohibition notice is used where there is a risk of serious personal injury and can require an activity to stop immediately or by a specified time. It is the enforcement tool aimed at stopping dangerous activity.

n.2: An improvement notice requires a contravention to be remedied within a period but does not stop the activity.
n.3: A caution letter is not the formal power used to halt dangerous activity.
n.1: HSE does not use on-the-spot fixed penalty tickets for this; formal notices or prosecution are used.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: An HSE inspector identifies a breach of health and safety law that must be put right, but there is no immediate risk of serious injury. Which notice is most appropriate?
o: An improvement notice giving a time period to remedy it
A prohibition notice requiring the work to cease at once
A verbal warning that carries no obligation to act on
An automatic criminal conviction without any notice at all
The Law & Responsibilities.w: An improvement notice is served where there is a contravention that must be remedied; it specifies the breach and sets a time period for compliance. It is the appropriate tool when there is no immediate serious risk.

n.1: A prohibition notice is reserved for situations involving a risk of serious personal injury.
n.2: A verbal warning is not the formal legal instrument; an improvement notice imposes an enforceable obligation.
n.3: A conviction follows a prosecution and court process, not the serving of an improvement notice.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Scenario: A care home has a confirmed case of Legionnaires' disease traced to its hot and cold water system. Beyond controlling the immediate risk, what reporting duty does the responsible party have?
o: It only needs to be recorded in the site logbook and no external report is required
It is reportable to the enforcing authority under RIDDOR as a reportable disease
None, because Legionnaires' disease is a private medical matter for the individual only
It must be reported only if more than one person is affected
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Legionnaires' disease is a reportable disease under RIDDOR where it is linked to work exposure. The responsible party must report it to the enforcing authority as well as controlling the risk.

n.2: It is not solely a private medical matter; a work-linked case triggers a legal reporting duty.
n.3: The reporting duty does not depend on the number of people affected.
n.0: A logbook entry alone is insufficient; an external RIDDOR report is required.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Under the Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999, what is the fundamental first step an employer must take in managing the risk from Legionella?
o: Delegate all decisions to the water supplier and take no further action
Carry out a suitable and sufficient assessment of the risk of exposure
Wait for the HSE to inspect and tell them what to do
Immediately install chemical dosing on every water system before any assessment
The Law & Responsibilities.w: MHSWR requires a suitable and sufficient risk assessment as the foundation of managing any workplace risk, including Legionella. Controls then flow from what that assessment identifies.

n.3: Installing controls before assessing the risk is not the required first step and may be disproportionate or ineffective.
n.2: Employers must act proactively, not wait to be told by the regulator.
n.0: The duty cannot be delegated away to the water supplier; the employer must assess and act.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: A responsible person delegates temperature monitoring to an operative who has never been trained or shown competent to do the task. Under L8 and MHSWR, what is the primary legal problem with this?
o: The task must legally be carried out only by the HSE, not staff
The only problem is that the operative is not paid enough
There is no problem, since any employee can monitor water
Those doing control tasks must be competent, informed, instructed and trained
The Law & Responsibilities.w: L8 and MHSWR require that those carrying out Legionella control tasks are competent, with the necessary information, instruction and training. Assigning safety-critical monitoring to an untrained person breaches this.

n.2: Not any employee may do it; competence and training are legal requirements.
n.0: Monitoring is carried out by the duty holder's arrangements, not by the HSE.
n.1: Pay is not the health and safety issue; the issue is competence and training.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Scenario: A contractor is asked to sign a written scheme of control they have not read, being told 'it's just a formality'. What is the correct understanding of the written scheme's legal role?
o: It replaces the need for any risk assessment to be done
A formality with no bearing on how the work is done
The documented control plan operatives must follow
It only matters to office staff and never to the workers
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The written scheme of control sets out how the risk is to be prevented or controlled and must be implemented and followed. Operatives are expected to understand and work to it, not sign it blind.

n.0: The written scheme follows from, not replaces, the risk assessment.
n.1: It directly governs how the work must be done.
n.3: It is precisely the people doing the work who must follow it.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Which of the following best describes 'so far as is reasonably practicable', the standard applied to many duties under HSWA 1974?
o: Only doing something once the HSE has specifically ordered it
An absolute duty that must always be met regardless of any other factor
Balancing the risk against the time, cost and effort to control it
Whatever the duty holder can still afford after all other spending
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Reasonably practicable involves weighing the risk against the sacrifice (time, cost, effort) needed to reduce it; where the risk is significant relative to the effort, the control must be taken.

n.0: The duty exists independently of any HSE order.
n.1: It is not absolute; it explicitly allows a proportionate balance.
n.3: Affordability alone does not define the standard; risk is weighed.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: In the context of EUSR National Water Hygiene work on public water supplies, what additional overriding responsibility do operatives carry when working on systems connected to drinking water?
o: To disconnect the backflow protection to make their tasks easier
To sample the water only for taste and appearance, ignoring risk
To increase the water pressure at every opportunity to improve flow
To protect the public drinking-water supply from contamination
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Water hygiene work on drinking-water systems carries a duty to protect the public supply from contamination, which is central to why the water industry requires the National Water Hygiene scheme and Blue Card.

n.0: Backflow protection prevents contamination and must never be defeated for convenience.
n.1: Contamination risk cannot be ignored; taste and appearance are not adequate measures.
n.2: Raising pressure indiscriminately is not a responsibility and can cause harm.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: An employer wants to know who, in law, can be a 'duty holder' with responsibility for Legionella risk. Which description is correct?
o: Only a fully qualified plumber can ever be the duty holder here
Only the HSE inspectorate can ever act as the legal duty holder
Only the building's original architect stays the duty holder for its whole life
The employer, or anyone in control of the premises or system for their work
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The duty holder is the employer or any person in control of the premises or the water system in connection with a trade, business or undertaking. Control, not job title, determines the duty.

n.0: Being a plumber is not what makes someone a duty holder; control does.
n.1: The HSE is the enforcing authority, not the duty holder.
n.2: Duty follows current control, not the person who originally designed the building.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Scenario: An operative is told by a site manager to skip a scheduled flushing task because 'the risk assessment is overdue for review anyway'. What is the correct response consistent with legal duties?
o: Rewrite the risk assessment on the spot to remove the flushing task yourself
Continue to follow the current written scheme and report the overdue review
Do nothing, and assume the manager has authority to waive all the controls
Skip the task, since an overdue review cancels the whole control scheme
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The existing written scheme remains in force until properly reviewed and revised. The operative should keep following it and report the overdue review to the responsible person so it can be actioned.

n.0: Operatives do not unilaterally rewrite risk assessments.
n.2: A manager cannot lawfully waive required controls.
n.3: An overdue review does not cancel existing controls.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Under Section 7 of the HSWA 1974, what duties are placed directly on employees such as water hygiene operatives?
o: No duties at all, as every duty rests with the employer
To personally fund and buy any safety equipment they need
To take reasonable care of their own and others' safety and cooperate
To design the entire legionella control scheme themselves
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Section 7 places duties on employees to take reasonable care for the health and safety of themselves and others affected by their acts, and to cooperate with the employer on health and safety matters.

n.0: Employees do have personal legal duties under the Act.
n.1: Employers, not employees, provide necessary safety equipment.
n.3: Designing the whole control scheme is a management function.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: A responsible person keeps no records of monitoring, inspections or remedial actions for the water system. Why is this a legal and practical failing?
o: Because L8 and HSG274 expect monitoring and controls to be recorded to show the scheme is managed
Because records are only needed once the system is more than ten years old
Because only the water supplier is ever legally required to keep any records
Because records are entirely optional, and their complete absence has no practical consequence whatsoever
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Keeping records of the assessment, control scheme, monitoring and remedial actions is expected under L8/HSG274 so the duty holder can demonstrate the risk is being effectively managed and reviewed.

n.1: Record-keeping is not tied to the system being over a certain age.
n.2: The duty holder must keep records, not only the water supplier.
n.3: Records are not optional; their absence undermines showing control.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Scenario: During a prosecution following an outbreak, the duty holder states they had a risk assessment but never acted on its recommendations. How is this likely to be viewed under health and safety law?
o: As completely irrelevant, since risk assessments are said to carry no legal weight at all
As a serious failing, because the law requires identified controls to be put into effect, not just written down
As perfectly acceptable in law, provided that a manager had signed the assessment
Favourably, because merely having an assessment on file is said to satisfy the law
The Law & Responsibilities.w: An assessment must lead to the implementation of appropriate controls. Identifying risks but failing to act on them is a serious failing of the duty to prevent or adequately control exposure.

n.3: Having an assessment is not enough; the required controls must be put into effect.
n.0: Risk assessments are a legal requirement and carry significant weight.
n.2: A signature does not excuse failing to implement the identified controls.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Which statement best captures the relationship between ACOP L8 and HSG274?
o: L8 is the technical how-to guide and HSG274 is the actual legal ACOP document in the end
L8 is the ACOP and legal framework; HSG274 gives the detailed technical guidance
HSG274 replaced L8 entirely, so the L8 document simply no longer exists today
They are really just two different names for exactly the same one document
The Law & Responsibilities.w: L8 contains the ACOP and outlines the legal framework and duties, and HSG274 supplements it with detailed practical/technical guidance across its parts for achieving effective control.

n.0: The roles are reversed: L8 is the ACOP and HSG274 is the technical guidance.
n.2: HSG274 supplements L8; it did not abolish it.
n.3: They are distinct documents with different roles.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: An operative discovers a dead leg (a section of redundant pipework holding stagnant water) during routine work. Under their reporting duty, what should they do?
o: Leave it well alone, since dead legs are not really relevant to Legionella risk
Cap off the live supply so that nothing at all can be flushed anywhere on site
Record and report it to the responsible person so it can be assessed and removed
Cut it out themselves without telling anyone about it, just to save a little time
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Dead legs promote stagnation and Legionella growth. The operative's duty is to record and report the finding to the responsible person, who assesses and arranges appropriate remedial action such as removal.

n.0: Dead legs are a well-recognised Legionella risk factor and are relevant.
n.1: Capping the live supply is a disproportionate and unsafe response and does not address the dead leg.
n.3: Unauthorised modifications outside the managed scheme are not correct and may create new risks.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: What does the appointment of a 'competent' responsible person for Legionella control principally require?
o: That the person holds any first-aid certificate
That the person volunteers without understanding
That the person has the training, knowledge and skills needed
That the person is the most senior manager on site
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Competence means having sufficient training, knowledge, experience and skills to carry out the role of managing and controlling the Legionella risk effectively.

n.0: A first-aid certificate is unrelated to competence for Legionella management.
n.1: Willingness to volunteer does not substitute for the required competence.
n.3: Seniority alone does not equal competence for this specialised role.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Scenario: A landlord of let residential properties asks whether Legionella duties apply to them. Which answer is correct?
o: Only if the let residential property happens to have a cooling tower installed
No, these duties never apply to residential landlords in any way
Yes, landlords must assess and manage the risk of exposure to their tenants
Only if a tenant asks for a risk assessment in writing first
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Landlords who provide residential accommodation as part of their business have a duty to assess and control the Legionella risk to tenants, applying the same principles of assessment and proportionate control.

n.1: The duty does apply to landlords in connection with their letting business.
n.0: The duty is not limited to premises with cooling towers; hot and cold water systems are covered.
n.3: The duty exists regardless of whether a tenant requests an assessment.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Following a failure to control Legionella risk that leads to prosecution, which outcome is possible under the HSWA 1974 for the most serious cases?
o: Only a written apology to the HSE is ever required
Penalties are capped at a small fixed administrative fee
Unlimited fines and, in the worst cases, imprisonment
The HSE simply reissues its guidance with no action
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Breaches of the HSWA can lead to prosecution with unlimited fines and, in the most serious cases, imprisonment, reflecting the potentially fatal consequences of failing to control Legionella.

n.0: An apology is not the legal remedy; formal penalties can follow.
n.1: Fines can be unlimited, not capped at a small fee.
n.3: Prosecution and penalties, not merely reissuing guidance, follow.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Why does ACOP L8 place emphasis on the management arrangements (roles, responsibilities, lines of communication) rather than only on technical controls?
o: Because only paperwork, and not any physical control, ever reduces risk
Because good management arrangements remove any need to monitor the system
Because clear responsibility and communication make controls reliable
Because the technical controls themselves are entirely legally irrelevant
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Even good technical controls fail without clear roles, responsibilities and communication so that tasks are done, results reviewed and faults acted upon. L8 stresses management to make control effective in practice.

n.0: Physical control measures directly reduce risk; paperwork alone does not.
n.1: Management arrangements support monitoring; they do not remove it.
n.3: Technical controls are essential; management makes them work.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Scenario: An operative is offered a shortcut by a colleague to falsify a chlorination certificate for a new water main so the job can be signed off faster. Considering both health and safety law and the duty to protect the public supply, what is the correct course?
o: Sign it but keep a private note that it may well be inaccurate
Ask the colleague to sign it instead so the operative avoids being implicated
Refuse, and see that the disinfection is genuinely done and recorded
Accept it, since the paperwork rarely affects the actual water quality
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Falsifying records endangers the public water supply and breaches legal duties. The correct course is to ensure the disinfection is genuinely carried out and verified, and recorded truthfully.

n.0: Signing a document known to be false is dishonest and unlawful regardless of private notes.
n.1: Passing the falsification to a colleague does not make it lawful or safe.
n.3: Records underpin confidence that the water is safe; falsification directly risks public health.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Who is the enforcing authority responsible for the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 as it relates to Legionella control in most industrial and commercial premises?
o: The Environment Agency alone, in each and every case without exception
The Health and Safety Executive, or local authority for some premises
The building's insurance provider that underwrites the whole premises
The regional water company that supplies the mains, entirely on its own
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The HSE is the primary enforcing authority for the Act, with local authorities enforcing in certain premises such as some retail and office environments. They can issue notices and prosecute.

n.0: The Environment Agency has other roles but is not the enforcer of these duties.
n.2: Insurers are not statutory enforcing authorities.
n.3: The water company is not the enforcing authority for the Act.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Scenario: A duty holder installs a control measure that differs from the specific method described in ACOP L8 but can demonstrate, with evidence, that it controls the risk at least as effectively. Is this permissible?
o: Only if the HSE first grants a signed exemption certificate beforehand
Yes, because an ACOP allows alternative measures that are at least equally effective
No, any deviation at all from the exact wording of L8 is automatically unlawful
Only if the alternative measure works out cheaper than the L8 method does
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The special status of an ACOP allows compliance either by following it or by adopting measures that are at least equally effective. Evidenced equivalent control is legally acceptable.

n.0: No pre-issued exemption certificate is required.
n.2: Equally effective alternatives are permitted; deviation is not automatically unlawful.
n.3: Cost is not the test; equal effectiveness is.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: An operative's core legal contribution to Legionella control on site is best summarised as which of the following?
o: Setting the whole organisation's health and safety policy
Prosecuting other duty holders who fail to comply with the law
Deciding the overall control strategy and appointing the responsible person
Carrying out assigned tasks to the scheme and reporting faults
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The operative implements the written scheme, works safely and reports faults or abnormal readings so that management can act. Strategy, policy and enforcement sit with others.

n.0: Setting the health and safety policy is a management responsibility.
n.1: Prosecution is the role of the enforcing authority, not the operative.
n.2: Deciding strategy and appointing the responsible person are duty-holder functions.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Why does the law require a review of the Legionella risk assessment when there is reason to suspect it is no longer valid, for example after significant changes to the water system?
o: Because reviews exist only to satisfy the insurers and serve no genuine safety purpose whatsoever
Because the assessment expires automatically every seven days under the regulations
Because system changes can introduce new risks current controls may miss, so it must stay current
Because only the water supplier is ever allowed to change or review the assessment
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Changes such as new pipework, altered use or occupancy can create new risks. The assessment and written scheme must be reviewed so controls remain suitable, sufficient and effective.

n.0: Reviews serve a genuine safety purpose, not merely an insurance one.
n.1: There is no automatic seven-day expiry; change triggers review.
n.3: The duty holder, not only the supplier, keeps the assessment current.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Scenario: An operative repeatedly reports the same uncorrected temperature fault, but the responsible person takes no action over several months. What does the operative's continued reporting, properly recorded, principally achieve in law?
o: It shows the operative has discharged their duty to report and records that the failure to act lies with management
It removes any need for the responsible person to take further action
It transfers the entire legal liability squarely onto the operative instead
It automatically closes the fault once the third report has been filed
The Law & Responsibilities.w: By reporting and recording the fault, the operative fulfils their own duty and creates evidence. The failure to act then rests with the responsible person and duty holder, not the operative.

n.2: Proper reporting does not transfer liability onto the operative; it evidences they did their part.
n.1: The responsible person's duty to act is not removed by the operative's reports.
n.3: Reporting does not automatically resolve or close a fault; corrective action is still required.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Under COSHH and supported by L8/HSG274, what is the correct order of priority when deciding how to control the Legionella risk?
o: Rely first on personal protective equipment and only then consider anything else
Prevent the risk where reasonably practicable; otherwise control it by suitable measures
Always simply choose the very cheapest option regardless of how effective it is
Do nothing at all until an actual outbreak provides evidence a control is needed
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The principle is to prevent the risk of exposure where reasonably practicable, and where that is not possible, to control it using suitable measures such as temperature or treatment regimes.

n.0: PPE is a lower-order measure and is not the first line of control.
n.2: Cost alone must not override the effectiveness of control.
n.3: Controls must be proactive; waiting for an outbreak is unlawful and dangerous.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: A new operative asks why holding the EUSR National Water Hygiene card matters legally when working on public water supplies. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: It evidences the hygiene awareness and competence the water industry requires
It exempts the holder from all other health and safety duties on site
It is a personal souvenir with no bearing on competence or site access
It replaces the need for the duty holder to have any water control scheme at all
The Law & Responsibilities.w: The National Water Hygiene scheme and Blue Card evidence the hygiene awareness and competence the water industry expects, helping protect the public supply, and is widely required for access to water-industry sites.

n.1: It does not exempt the holder from other legal duties; those still apply.
n.2: The card is evidence of competence and is often required for site access, not a souvenir.
n.3: It does not remove the duty holder's obligation to have a control scheme.

The Law & Responsibilities.q: Scenario: An operative is unsure whether a task they have been given falls within the site's written scheme or their own competence. What is the legally and professionally correct action before proceeding?
o: Proceed anyway and interpret the scheme however seems fine
Stop and clarify the task with the responsible person first
Carry out a different task instead without recording it
Refuse to communicate and simply leave the site without notice
The Law & Responsibilities.w: Where scope or competence is unclear, the correct action is to stop and clarify with the responsible person, consistent with the duty to work within the scheme and to take reasonable care.

n.0: Proceeding on personal interpretation risks working outside competence and the scheme.
n.2: Substituting an unrecorded task neither resolves the uncertainty nor meets record and reporting duties.
n.3: Leaving without notice abandons the task and fails the duty to communicate and cooperate.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: What is the main purpose of a legionella risk assessment for a water system?
o: To identify the sources of risk in the system and who could be exposed
To set the price of any remedial plumbing work the building needs
To prove the water is safe to drink from every single outlet fitted
To record the water temperature just once a year for the site's building file
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A legionella risk assessment identifies and assesses the sources of risk in the water system and the people who could be exposed.

n.1: Costing remedial work is not the purpose of assessing the risk.
n.2: Legionella controls concern inhaled aerosols, not drinking quality.
n.3: A single annual temperature reading is not an assessment of the risk.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Under the ACOP L8 approach, which should you try to do FIRST when managing legionella risk?
o: Wait until a confirmed case of illness has actually been reported on site
Add extra biocide to every single part of the system straight away
Prevent the risk where reasonably practicable, then control the rest
Fit more monitoring meters before taking any other step
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: You should prevent the risk of exposure so far as is reasonably practicable first, and control any risk that cannot be prevented.

n.0: Waiting for illness means the risk was never managed.
n.1: Dosing biocide everywhere is a control, not the first-choice prevention step.
n.3: Monitoring measures a risk but does not prevent or control it on its own.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A legionella risk assessment should specifically consider people who are especially vulnerable. Which group is an example?
o: Delivery drivers who drop off at the gate and never go inside
Contractors who only ever work outside on the site grounds
People who merely park in the site car park and then leave
Elderly, sick or immunocompromised people who may be exposed
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: The assessment must consider those more susceptible to infection, such as the elderly, the sick and people with weakened immune systems.

n.0: People who do not enter the building are not exposed to its water aerosols.
n.1: Working outside on the grounds is not exposure to building water aerosols.
n.2: Using only the car park gives no exposure to the water system.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Which of these is a potential source of risk that a legionella risk assessment should look for?
o: Anywhere that water is stored, can stagnate or sits between 20 and 45°C
A mains power socket mounted on the plant room wall
The colour chosen for the pipework insulation in the plant room
The manufacturer's brand name printed on the side of the cold tank
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Stored, stagnant or warm water in the 20-45 degrees C range provides the conditions in which legionella can multiply.

n.1: An electrical socket is not part of the water system risk.
n.2: Insulation colour does not affect legionella growth.
n.3: The brand name has no bearing on the risk.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Why does a legionella risk assessment pay attention to outlets and equipment that create a spray or mist?
o: Because the fine spray makes the surrounding floor slippery underfoot
Because misting outlets are much harder to keep properly clean
Because aerosols can carry legionella deep into the lungs when breathed in
Because spraying outlets use far more water and push up the water bill
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Legionella causes illness when contaminated water aerosols are inhaled, so sources of spray or mist are key to assess.

n.0: Slip hazards are a separate safety issue, not the legionella reason.
n.1: Cleaning difficulty is not why aerosols matter for legionella.
n.3: Water cost is not the health reason for assessing aerosols.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A large office block closes one entire wing and takes its taps and showers out of use for several months. What is the correct action for the water system?
o: Review the risk assessment and flush the now little-used outlets
Do nothing at all, since the closed wing is no longer used by people
Turn off the whole building's cold water supply at the mains
Remove the wing from the asset register and forget about it
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A change of use creates stagnation risk, so the assessment must be reviewed and the disused outlets kept under control, such as by regular flushing.

n.1: Closed but still-connected outlets stagnate and become a growing risk.
n.2: Shutting the whole supply is disproportionate and affects occupied areas.
n.3: Ignoring the wing hides a real and increasing legionella risk.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: What is the written scheme of control (the written scheme) for?
o: To keep a running list of the names of everyone who has ever visited the site
To record only the total cost of the chemicals that were used
To advertise the building's facilities to prospective new tenants
To set out how the risk is prevented or controlled and managed safely
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: The written scheme describes the water system and sets out the measures to be taken to prevent or control the risk.

n.0: A visitor log has nothing to do with controlling legionella.
n.1: Chemical costs are not the purpose of the written scheme.
n.2: Marketing the building is unrelated to controlling the risk.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Which item should a written scheme of control include?
o: A recent photograph of the building's front door and entrance
Only the postcode of the building where the system is installed every time
The control measures, how they are monitored, and who is responsible
The favourite colour and hobbies of the current site manager
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: The written scheme should describe the control measures, the checks and monitoring, and the roles and responsibilities for carrying them out.

n.0: A photo of the door tells you nothing about the water system controls.
n.1: A postcode alone does not describe how the risk is controlled.
n.3: Personal preferences are irrelevant to the scheme.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A written scheme of control should also say what to do in one important situation. Which one?
o: What action to take if the control measures are found to be failing
How staff should go about booking a shared meeting room
Which nearby supermarket is closest to the site entrance
What background music should be played in the reception area
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: The written scheme must set out the remedial action to take if monitoring shows the control measures are not working.

n.1: Room booking has nothing to do with water safety.
n.2: The nearest shop is not a legionella control matter.
n.3: Reception music is irrelevant to the scheme.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: An up-to-date schematic diagram of the water system is useful in the risk assessment mainly because it:
o: It shows the layout, including tanks, pipe runs and outlets
It records the building's monthly electricity meter readings
It shows where the staff car park spaces are located
It proves the building fully meets fire safety regulations
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A schematic diagram maps the system so that storage, dead-legs and outlets that could pose a risk can be identified and managed.

n.1: Electricity readings are not part of the water schematic.
n.2: Car parking layout is unrelated to the water system.
n.3: Fire regulation compliance is a separate matter.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Why should an asset register or list of the water system's parts be kept with the assessment?
o: To help decide the paint colour and décor scheme of the plant room
To help work out the building's annual council tax banding
So all plant, tanks and outlets are known and none overlooked
So spare parts can be sold off second-hand later
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: An asset register records the system's components so that every relevant item is accounted for and included in the control scheme.

n.3: Selling parts is not the reason for the register.
n.0: Decor choices are irrelevant to managing risk.
n.1: Council tax has nothing to do with the water assets.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: When should a legionella risk assessment be reviewed?
o: Never again, once it has been signed off
Once every twenty years or so at the most
Only when the building is eventually put up for sale
Regularly, and whenever it may no longer be valid
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: The assessment should be reviewed regularly and specifically whenever there is reason to believe it is no longer valid.

n.0: An assessment that is never reviewed becomes unreliable.
n.1: A twenty-year gap leaves the assessment badly out of date.
n.2: Waiting until a sale ignores changes that happen in between.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Which of these changes would be a reason to review the risk assessment?
o: The office repaints one of its corridors in a new colour scheme
The car park's line markings are freshly repainted over a weekend
New plant or pipework is added, or the building's use changes
A new manager starts work on the building's reception desk
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Changes to the system, such as new plant or altered use, can create new risks and require the assessment to be reviewed.

n.0: Repainting a corridor does not alter the water system.
n.1: Repainting parking lines has no effect on water risk.
n.3: A new reception manager does not change the plumbing.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: An outbreak or suspected case of legionnaires' disease linked to a site should trigger which action for the assessment?
o: Removing the written scheme from the site file and archiving it
An immediate review of the risk assessment and controls
Painting over the affected pipework to seal the bacteria in
Ignoring it until the next scheduled annual check comes round
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A case or outbreak is a clear reason the assessment may no longer be valid and must be reviewed straight away.

n.0: Discarding the scheme removes the very controls needed.
n.2: Painting pipework does nothing to address the risk.
n.3: Delaying the review allows exposure to continue.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: The risk assessment and written scheme should be kept how?
o: Written once when first produced and then never changed again
Recorded and kept up to date to match the current system
Held only in the memory of one experienced member of staff
Shredded at the end of the first year to save on storage
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Records must be kept and updated so the assessment and scheme always reflect the current system and controls.

n.0: An unchanged document soon fails to match a changing system.
n.2: Relying on memory leaves nothing others can follow or audit.
n.3: Destroying the records loses the basis for managing the risk.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Who should carry out or oversee a legionella risk assessment?
o: Anyone at all who happens to be free on the site that day
The newest apprentice on their very first morning, working unsupervised
A competent person with the right knowledge, skills and experience
A passing visitor who has no knowledge of the water system
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: The assessment must be done by someone competent, with sufficient knowledge, skills and experience to identify and assess the risk.

n.0: Availability does not make a person competent to assess the risk.
n.1: An unsupervised first-day apprentice lacks the needed competence.
n.3: A visitor without knowledge cannot judge the system's risks.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A café installs a new decorative water feature that produces a fine spray in the seating area. What should happen to the legionella risk assessment?
o: It should be deleted, as the feature is only decorative
Nothing changes, as it only holds a small amount of water
It should be reviewed because a new aerosol-producing source is present
It should be swapped for the building's fire risk assessment
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Adding new plant that creates aerosols is a relevant change, so the assessment must be reviewed to cover the new source.

n.0: Being decorative does not remove the aerosol risk.
n.1: Even a small volume of sprayed water can carry legionella.
n.3: A fire assessment does not address legionella at all.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Storing hot and cold water at the wrong temperatures matters because legionella multiplies best:
o: In water roughly between 20 and 45 degrees C
Only in water that is actually boiling on the stove
Only in water chilled to below its freezing point
At any temperature equally, hot, cold or tepid alike
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Legionella grows most readily in water in the approximate range of 20 to 45 degrees C, which the assessment aims to avoid.

n.1: Boiling temperatures kill the bacteria rather than grow them.
n.2: Freezing water does not let the bacteria multiply.
n.3: Growth is strongly temperature-dependent, not equal at all temperatures.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A hotel converts several guest bathrooms into a rarely used storeroom, leaving the showers connected but unused. What is the key risk this creates?
o: A noticeable rise in the building's monthly electricity bill and nothing more
Stagnation in the unused showers, which should be flushed or removed
A shortage of clean towels for the remaining guest bathrooms
Gradual damage to the bathroom wall and floor tiles over time
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Little-used or dead outlets allow water to stagnate and legionella to grow, so they must be managed and the assessment reviewed.

n.0: Electricity cost is not the water safety concern here.
n.3: Tile condition is unrelated to legionella risk.
n.2: Towel supply has nothing to do with the water system.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Monitoring in the written scheme is mainly there to:
o: Increase the number of forms that staff are required to sign off
Remove the need for any control measures to be applied at all
Prove to inspectors that the building is completely fully occupied
Confirm the control measures are working as they are intended to
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Monitoring confirms whether the chosen controls are keeping the risk under control and flags when they are not.

n.0: Paperwork volume is not the purpose of monitoring.
n.1: Monitoring supports controls; it does not remove the need for them.
n.2: Occupancy levels are not what monitoring is checking.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Which statement about preventing legionella risk is correct?
o: Longer runs of unused pipework are generally the safer option
Prevention is basically impossible, so only ongoing monitoring matters
Removing needless storage and dead-legs cuts risk before controls are needed
Adding more storage tanks will nearly always reduce the overall risk
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Designing out storage, stagnation and dead-legs prevents conditions for growth, which is preferable to controlling them later.

n.0: Unused dead-legs stagnate and increase risk, not reduce it.
n.1: Prevention is a recognised and preferred step, not impossible.
n.3: Extra unnecessary storage adds stagnation risk rather than removing it.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A school is closed over a long summer holiday. What should the written scheme cover for this period?
o: Removing the site risk assessment for the holiday period
Leaving every tap running continuously day and night
Keeping water moving by flushing outlets so it cannot stagnate
Switching off all record keeping until the new term starts
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: During long closures the scheme should keep water fresh, such as by regular flushing, to prevent stagnation.

n.0: Removing the assessment leaves the closure unmanaged.
n.1: Leaving all taps running wastes water and is not the specified control.
n.3: Records should continue, as the risk does not stop over the holiday.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: The risk assessment should identify who could be exposed. What does 'exposed' mean here?
o: People who have merely read through the safety policy document
People who merely live nearest to the building
People who happen to pay the water bill each month
People who could breathe in droplets or mist from the system
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Exposure to legionella happens when people inhale contaminated aerosols, so the assessment identifies who could breathe them in.

n.0: Reading a policy is not the same as being exposed to aerosols.
n.2: Paying the bill has no bearing on inhalation exposure.
n.1: Simply living nearby is not exposure unless aerosols reach them.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A factory takes over the empty unit next door and connects it to the same mains water supply. What should be done?
o: Extend the assessment and scheme to cover the new pipework
Ignore the new pipework because the run is short
Only assess the new unit later if someone eventually falls ill
Assume the existing assessment already covers the new unit
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Adding pipework and outlets is a relevant change, so the assessment and scheme must be updated to cover the extended system.

n.1: Even short new pipework can contain dead-legs and outlets to manage.
n.2: Waiting for illness means managing the risk too late.
n.3: The old assessment cannot cover parts it never examined.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Which of these best describes a 'dead-leg' that a risk assessment should look for?
o: A pipe carrying hot water at high speed straight to an outlet
A length of pipe with little or no flow where water stagnates
The main incoming water supply that serves the whole of the building
A tap that is opened and used many times every single day
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A dead-leg is pipework with little or no throughput, allowing water to stagnate and legionella to grow.

n.0: Fast-flowing hot water is not a stagnation point.
n.2: The busy main supply is not a low-flow dead-leg.
n.3: A frequently used tap keeps water moving, not stagnant.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: If monitoring shows a control measure has failed, the written scheme should ensure staff know to:
o: Take the pre-agreed remedial action promptly and record what was done
Erase the failed reading from the monitoring log and carry on
Wait for a member of the public to complain about it first
Do nothing at all until the next scheduled annual review
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: The scheme sets out remedial actions so that a control failure is corrected promptly and the action recorded.

n.1: Deleting the reading hides the problem and breaks the record.
n.2: Relying on public complaints is not a control response.
n.3: Delaying to the annual review leaves the risk uncontrolled.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Why should roles and responsibilities be written down in the scheme of control?
o: To make the control document look longer and more thorough
So blame can be handed out to someone after any incident
To keep the duties secret from the staff who do the work
So each task has a clear owner and nothing gets missed
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Naming who does what ensures every control task has an owner and is actually carried out.

n.0: Length is not a goal in itself.
n.1: The aim is prevention and clarity, not apportioning blame.
n.2: Staff need to know their duties, not be kept in the dark.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A care home admits more residents who are frail and elderly than before. How does this affect the legionella risk assessment?
o: It has no effect whatsoever, since the pipework itself is unchanged
It means the control scheme can now safely be relaxed a little
It only matters if the incoming water pressure also changes
It should be reviewed, as more vulnerable people are now exposed
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A rise in the number of especially vulnerable people is a relevant change in who is exposed, so the assessment must be reviewed.

n.0: Risk depends on who is exposed, not only on the pipework.
n.1: More vulnerable people call for equal or tighter control, not relaxation.
n.2: Vulnerability of occupants matters regardless of water pressure.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: What kind of information about temperature is useful to record when assessing and controlling risk?
o: Hot and cold water temperatures at sentinel and other outlets
The surface temperature of the staff car park through the day
Only the outside air temperature, measured outdoors each morning
The temperature inside the ovens in the kitchen
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Recording water temperatures at outlets shows whether the system is kept out of the range that lets legionella grow.

n.1: Car park temperature is irrelevant to the water system.
n.2: Outside air temperature does not tell you the water's temperature.
n.3: Oven temperature is unrelated to water safety.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A previously vacant building is brought back into full use after standing empty for a year. What should be done before people use the water?
o: Only test the water if one of the occupants later reports a bad smell
Assume the standing water is fine and simply open up as normal
Review the assessment and clean, flush and prove the system is safe
Remove the assessment altogether because the building stood empty
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Long stagnation is a serious risk, so the assessment must be reviewed and the system brought back into safe condition before use.

n.0: Waiting for a complaint means exposing people first.
n.1: Water standing for a year can harbour heavy growth and is not fine.
n.3: An idle period is a reason to keep the assessment, not remove it.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Which of these is a reasonable prevention measure the assessment might recommend?
o: Removing redundant pipework and unused outlets that only hold stagnant water
Leaving all the disused showers permanently connected to the live water system
Adding several extra unused tanks in case they are needed one day
Fitting more dead-legs in order to balance out the whole system
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Taking out redundant pipework and outlets removes stagnation points and prevents conditions for legionella growth.

n.2: Extra unused tanks create more storage and stagnation, not less.
n.3: Adding dead-legs increases stagnation risk.
n.1: Leaving disused showers connected keeps a stagnation source.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: The written scheme describes the water system. Why is an accurate description important?
o: So the controls fit the system as it actually is, not an outdated layout
So the finished document looks professional and neatly presented
So the water used in the building can be billed to tenants correctly day to day
So the building itself can be insured against future flood damage
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: An accurate description ensures the control measures match the real system, so nothing risky is missed.

n.1: Appearance is not the reason an accurate description matters.
n.2: Water billing is separate from controlling legionella.
n.3: Insurance is not the purpose of the system description.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A gym adds a new communal shower block used by many members each day. What should the water safety arrangements do?
o: Only assess the showers if member attendance starts to fall
Exclude the showers from the scheme because they are used so often
Cover the new showers in the assessment and scheme, since they create aerosols
Treat the new showers exactly the same as the outdoor car park
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: New showers generate aerosols and are heavily used, so they must be brought into the assessment and control scheme.

n.0: Falling attendance would raise stagnation risk, not remove the need to assess.
n.1: Frequent use reduces stagnation but does not remove the aerosol risk.
n.3: A car park has no water aerosol risk to compare with.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Keeping the risk assessment 'live' means:
o: Storing it on the newest and fastest office computer
Updating it whenever the system or its use changes
Printing out a completely fresh paper copy each morning
Reading it aloud in full at every single staff meeting
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A live assessment is kept current by updating it whenever a relevant change occurs, so it always reflects the real risk.

n.0: Where it is stored does not make its content up to date.
n.2: Reprinting an unchanged document does not keep it current.
n.3: Reading it aloud does not update its content.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A hospital ward is temporarily closed for refurbishment, isolating part of the pipework. What is the correct approach?
o: Delete that whole ward from all of the site's records
Manage the isolated section so it cannot stagnate before reconnection
Leave the isolated pipe full of water and forget it
Increase the whole system's water pressure to compensate
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Isolated pipework can stagnate, so the assessment must be reviewed and the section managed before it is put back into use.

n.2: Leaving it full and forgotten lets legionella grow unchecked.
n.0: Deleting records loses control of a real part of the system.
n.3: Raising pressure does not address stagnation in the isolated section.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Which best describes 'sentinel outlets' referred to when monitoring a system?
o: The outlets that are never actually used anywhere in the building
Only the outlets located within the plant room itself
The nearest and furthest outlets, used as representative checks
The most expensive taps fitted anywhere in the building
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Sentinel outlets are the nearest and furthest points on hot and cold systems, chosen as representative places to monitor temperature.

n.0: Unused outlets are not representative of the working system.
n.1: Plant-room outlets alone do not represent the whole distribution.
n.3: Cost has nothing to do with choosing sentinel points.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: An office doubles its staff and adds a second kitchen with new taps and a boiling-water unit. What is the right response?
o: Only take any action if the tap water later starts to taste different
Remove the original kitchen from the water system records
Take no action, because ordinary tap water is always safe
Review the assessment and update the scheme for the new outlets
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Adding outlets and a water heater is a relevant change, so the assessment and scheme must be updated to cover them.

n.0: Taste is not a reliable indicator of legionella risk.
n.1: The original kitchen stays part of the system and the records.
n.2: Tap water is not automatically free of legionella risk here.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: The assessment should record the findings so that:
o: The stack of paperwork reaches a certain required weight
Only the assessor who originally wrote them ever needs to see them
They can be filed away neatly and then never opened again
The significant risks and chosen controls are clear to act on
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Recording the findings makes the significant risks and the chosen controls clear so responsible people can act on them.

n.0: The physical bulk of paperwork is not the point of recording.
n.1: Others must be able to follow the findings, not just the assessor.
n.2: Findings that are never opened cannot guide any control.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Why might a risk assessment recommend keeping cold water genuinely cold?
o: To keep it below the range where legionella multiplies
To reduce the building's overall water and energy bill
To make the exposed pipework easier to clean and repaint
To make the drinking water taste noticeably sweeter
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Keeping cold water below about 20 degrees C helps stop legionella multiplying, which is a core control.

n.1: It is not primarily a cost-saving measure.
n.2: Painting pipes is unrelated to the temperature control.
n.3: Temperature control is about safety, not taste.
