Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A landlord takes over a block of flats and finds no legionella risk assessment exists. What should be done first?
o: Arrange a competent legionella risk assessment of the water systems
Wait until one of the tenants complains before assessing anything
Only assess the flats that currently have tenants actually living in them
Assume the previous owner already dealt with it and simply move on
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Where no valid assessment exists, a competent assessment of the water systems must be carried out to identify and assess the risk.

n.1: Waiting for a complaint leaves the risk unassessed and unmanaged.
n.2: Empty flats can hold stagnant water and must also be assessed.
n.3: Assuming without evidence provides no basis for control.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: What should happen to the written scheme when a control method in it is changed, for example a new disinfection regime?
o: Only bother to update it at the next sale of the whole building
Update the written scheme to reflect the new control method
Leave the old method written down for the records
Throw the scheme away and simply rely on memory
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: The scheme must be kept up to date so it always describes the controls actually in use.

n.0: Delaying to a sale leaves the scheme wrong in the meantime.
n.2: Leaving the outdated method written down misleads whoever follows it.
n.3: Relying on memory removes the documented basis for control.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A risk assessment considers 'the water systems'. Which of these is part of that?
o: The surface-water drainage gullies serving the site's main car park
Cold water tanks, hot water cylinders, pipework, taps and showers
The internal and external telephone and data lines
The powered cradle used by the window cleaning contractors
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: The water systems assessed include storage, heaters, distribution pipework and the outlets people use.

n.0: Car park drainage is separate from the building's water system.
n.2: Phone and data lines are not part of the water system.
n.3: A window-cleaning cradle is not part of the assessed water system.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: An assessment finds a little-used tap at the end of a long pipe. Which control fits the 'prevent then control' principle best?
o: Paint the tap a bright colour to mark it as unused
Remove the redundant tap and pipe if it is not needed, otherwise flush it regularly
Leave it in place and simply hope it never becomes a problem
Cap the pipe but keep all the stagnant water sitting inside
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Removing redundant pipework prevents the stagnation risk; if it must stay, regular flushing controls the remaining risk.

n.2: Hoping is not a control and leaves the risk in place.
n.3: Capping while trapping stagnant water leaves a growth reservoir.
n.0: Painting the tap does nothing about the stagnant water.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Why should the person managing the scheme be told promptly about a temperature reading that is out of range?
o: So the faulty thermometer can be blamed for the poor reading
So the monitoring log can simply be closed off for the whole year
So the out-of-range reading can be quietly ignored and forgotten
So corrective action can be taken quickly before the risk grows
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Prompt reporting lets the responsible person act quickly to bring the control back on target before risk increases.

n.0: Blaming the instrument does not correct the water risk.
n.1: Closing the log does not address the failed control.
n.2: Ignoring an out-of-range reading leaves the risk uncontrolled.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A building changes from offices to a residential use with showers and baths in every unit. What must be reconsidered?
o: Just the colour and finish chosen for the new bathroom fittings throughout the units
Nothing at all, since it remains the very same building as before
The whole risk assessment, since use, outlets and exposed people have all changed
Only the wording shown on the reception signage at the main entrance
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A major change of use with new aerosol-producing outlets and different occupants requires the assessment to be reconsidered in full.

n.0: Fitting colour is irrelevant to the assessment.
n.1: The same walls do not mean the same water risk after a change of use.
n.3: Signage does not reflect the changed water risk.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Which of these is the best reason to keep records of monitoring and inspections?
o: To use up spare storage space in the filing cabinet
To hide the monitoring results from the site managers
To show controls were carried out and to spot trends
To avoid ever having to carry out the checks again
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Records demonstrate that controls were done and help identify trends so problems can be acted on early.

n.0: Using up space is not a reason to keep records.
n.1: Records are meant to inform managers, not be hidden from them.
n.3: Records do not replace the ongoing need to carry out checks.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A cooling tower is added to a site that previously had none. How significant is this for the risk assessment?
o: Very significant, as towers spread aerosols widely
Not significant at all, given that it is sited outdoors
Relevant only if it is painted a bright colour
Of concern only to the electricity supplier
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Cooling towers create and disperse aerosols that can carry legionella, so adding one is a major change the assessment must address.

n.1: Being outdoors can spread aerosols further, not remove the risk.
n.2: Colour has no bearing on the aerosol risk.
n.3: The electricity supplier is not who manages the legionella risk.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: What is the correct overall order of the approach in the written scheme of control?
o: Monitor first, then decide whether to write anything down
Describe, prevent, control, monitor, then act if control fails
Do nothing at all until the first case of illness appears
Dose the whole system with chemicals and skip describing it
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A sound scheme describes the system, prevents risk, controls what remains, monitors the controls and sets out remedial action for failures.

n.0: You cannot monitor sensibly before the system and controls are defined.
n.2: Waiting for illness abandons the preventive approach.
n.3: Skipping the description means controls may miss parts of the system.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A tenant reports that the hot water at their tap now runs only lukewarm, which was not the case before. What does this suggest about the assessment and controls?
o: A control may have slipped, so review the assessment and fix it
The tenant should simply be told to run the tap for longer each time
The written scheme of control should now be thrown away completely
Lukewarm water is always perfectly safe, so nothing needs doing
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Hot water failing to reach its intended temperature suggests a control has slipped, so the assessment should be reviewed and the cause put right.

n.1: Running the tap does not fix the underlying temperature fault.
n.2: Discarding the scheme removes the controls rather than correcting the fault.
n.3: Lukewarm water sits near the growth range and is not automatically safe.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Which statement about who is responsible for managing legionella risk is correct?
o: No one needs to be responsible as long as a contractor visits occasionally
Only the external water supplier is responsible for the building's systems
A named responsible person should be appointed to manage the scheme
Responsibility ends the moment the assessment is first written up
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A competent responsible person should be appointed to take day-to-day charge of the assessment, scheme and controls.

n.0: Occasional contractor visits do not remove the need for an appointed responsible person.
n.1: The water supplier is not responsible for the internal systems within the building.
n.3: Responsibility continues through ongoing review and control, not just the first write-up.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Under the ACOP L8, who is responsible for making sure a legionella risk assessment is carried out for a building's water system?
o: The water hygiene operative who takes the temperatures
The duty holder, such as the employer or person in control
The tenants who use the building's various outlets
The local water supply company that provides the mains water
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: The duty holder, such as the employer or person in control of the premises, has the legal duty to ensure a legionella risk assessment is done.

n.0: The operative carries out monitoring tasks but does not hold the legal duty for the assessment.
n.2: Tenants use the outlets but are not the ones legally responsible for the assessment.
n.3: The water company supplies the mains but is not responsible for the building's internal system.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: What is the main purpose of a legionella risk assessment?
o: To record the daily hot water bill for the whole of the building
To list every single member of staff who works in the building
To identify and assess the sources of legionella risk in the water system
To decide the colour coding used for the site's cleaning equipment in the end
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A risk assessment exists to identify and assess the sources of legionella risk so that suitable controls can be put in place.

n.0: Energy costs are not the purpose of a legionella risk assessment.
n.1: A staff list is not what the assessment is for.
n.3: Cleaning colour codes are a separate matter and not the aim.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: If the risk assessment finds a foreseeable legionella risk, what must the duty holder put in place?
o: A notice telling users they may run the taps whenever they wish
Nothing further, because the assessment on its own is quite enough
A single verbal instruction given to staff on just one occasion
A written scheme of control setting out how the risk is managed
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Where a risk is identified, a written scheme of control must be prepared describing how the risk is managed.

n.0: An informal notice does not meet the requirement for a written scheme of control.
n.1: The assessment alone is not enough; a written scheme is required when a risk is found.
n.2: A one-off verbal instruction is not a documented, controlled scheme.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Which of the following should a written scheme of control normally include?
o: A complete copy of the building's fire evacuation and assembly plan
Only the phone number of the local water supply company
The schematic, responsibilities, controls and monitoring regime
The names of everyone who has ever visited the site
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A written scheme should describe the system, responsibilities, control measures, monitoring and the action to take if control is lost.

n.0: The fire plan is a separate document and not part of the water control scheme.
n.1: A supplier phone number alone is nowhere near a complete written scheme.
n.3: A visitor list has nothing to do with controlling legionella.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Which change would most clearly make a legionella risk assessment need reviewing?
o: A new poster goes up in the staff canteen
The building is repainted the very same colour
A member of staff changes which car parking space they use
New plant is installed or the building's use changes
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Installing new plant or changing how the building is used can alter the risk, so the assessment must be reviewed.

n.0: A canteen poster does not affect the water system risk.
n.1: Repainting in the same colour does not change the water system.
n.2: A change of parking space has no bearing on legionella risk.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A legionella risk assessment should be reviewed following which of the following events?
o: A change of the office's usual stationery supplier
A staff member returning to work from their annual leave
A suspected case or outbreak linked to the system
The arrival of the end of the company financial year
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: An outbreak or suspected case is a clear trigger to review the assessment, as controls may need strengthening.

n.0: The stationery supplier has no link to water safety.
n.1: Routine staff leave does not change the water system risk.
n.3: The financial year end is an accounting date, not a risk trigger.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: What does keeping an up-to-date schematic drawing of the water system in the written scheme help operatives to do?
o: Decide the paint colour scheme chosen for the whole plant room
Understand the layout so every part, dead legs included, is found
Set the temperature on the building's central heating radiators upstairs
Work out the building's total monthly electricity charges
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: An accurate schematic lets operatives locate all parts of the system, including little-used sections, so nothing is missed.

n.0: Paint choices are unrelated to a water system schematic.
n.2: Radiator settings are part of heating, not water safety.
n.3: A schematic is not used for calculating electricity charges.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: What is the first thing a Legionella risk assessment must establish before any control measures are considered?
o: The precise temperature setpoint of the calorifier thermostat
The particular brand of biocide to be dosed into the system
Whether a risk of exposure exists and, if so, where its sources are
The name of the external contractor who will carry out the monitoring
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: L8 requires the assessment first to identify and assess the risk — whether a foreseeable risk of exposure to Legionella exists and where the sources of that risk are — as the basis for everything that follows.

n.1: Selecting a biocide is a control decision that can only be made after the risk and sources are understood.
n.3: Arranging who monitors is a management step that follows identification of the risk.
n.0: A specific setpoint is a control measure, not the initial finding the assessment must reach.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Besides identifying sources of risk, what else must the risk assessment identify about the people around the system?
o: Who could be exposed, especially the most at risk
Which members of staff currently hold a first-aid certificate
The job titles of everyone who enters the plant room
The home addresses of employees for emergency contact
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: The assessment must identify who may be exposed to the aerosol, paying particular attention to those who may be especially susceptible, such as the elderly, the very young or those with weakened immunity.

n.1: First-aid cover is unrelated to identifying who is exposed.
n.2: A list of who entered does not identify who is exposed to infection.
n.3: Home addresses have no bearing on exposure to the system.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A care home installs a new spa pool in a communal lounge but does not revisit its existing water risk assessment. Why is this a breach of L8?
o: Only the local authority, never the duty holder, can amend an assessment
Risk assessments only ever need reviewing once every five calendar years
A spa pool never has to appear in any written water risk assessment
The assessment must be reviewed after a significant change like new plant
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: L8 requires the assessment to be reviewed regularly and specifically whenever there is reason to suspect it is no longer valid, including significant changes such as new plant, a new aerosol source or a change of use.

n.0: The duty holder must keep the assessment current, not the local authority.
n.1: There is no fixed five-year rule; change triggers review.
n.2: A spa pool is a high-risk aerosol source and must be assessed.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Which record is central to a Legionella risk assessment because it shows every part of the water system?
o: The site fire evacuation plan for the whole building
A list of the approved cleaning-chemical suppliers used
A schematic diagram of the whole water system, kept fully up to date
The annual electrical installation inspection certificate
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: An up-to-date schematic (asset register/diagram) of the water system is fundamental; it lets the assessor see all plant, pipework, storage and outlets so no source of risk is missed.

n.0: A fire plan addresses a different hazard and does not map the water system.
n.1: A supplier list does not describe the physical water system.
n.3: An electrical certificate is unrelated to identifying water risk sources.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: The written scheme for controlling Legionella risk must set out several things. Which of the following is one of them?
o: The clear allocation of responsibilities for the control measures
The recent postcode lottery results for the surrounding local area
The marketing plan drawn up for the building's current owner
The purchase price of every single fitting in the building
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: The written scheme must set out the control measures, how and when they are checked and monitored, and who is responsible for carrying them out — clear allocation of duties is a required element.

n.1: This is irrelevant filler with no bearing on the scheme.
n.2: A marketing plan has nothing to do with managing water risk.
n.3: The cost of fittings is not a control-scheme requirement.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: In the hierarchy of managing Legionella, which approach should the duty holder consider first?
o: Preventing the risk, for example by avoiding storage and stagnation where practicable
Raising every single outlet temperature right up above boiling point around the whole site
Waiting for a positive water sample before taking any control action at all
Dosing the whole system continuously with the strongest available chemical biocide
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: The duty holder should first consider whether the risk can be prevented — for instance by removing dead legs, avoiding unnecessary storage and designing out stagnation — and only then control any residual risk.

n.1: Water cannot practically be held above boiling at outlets.
n.2: Waiting for a result is reactive and does not prevent the risk arising.
n.3: Continuous biocide dosing is a control, applied when prevention is not practicable.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Which temperature band is regarded as the range in which Legionella bacteria most readily multiply, and which prevention aims to keep water out of?
o: Between about 70 and 90°C
Between about 5 and 15°C
Between about 20 and 45°C
Below 0°C, around freezing point
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Legionella multiplies most readily between about 20°C and 45°C; prevention keeps cold water below 20°C and hot water hot so water spends as little time as possible in this band.

n.0: These temperatures kill the bacteria rather than allow multiplication.
n.1: This band is below the growth range; cold water sits here safely.
n.3: Below freezing the bacteria do not multiply, so this is not the band to avoid.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A newly appointed manager finds the site risk assessment was written by an office administrator with no water-hygiene training. What is the concern under L8?
o: The assessment simply needs rewriting in a clearer and more professional font
The assessment is fine, because anyone employed on the site may write it
Only assessments written by the local water supplier are ever valid
It may not be suitable and sufficient, as no competent person did it
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: L8 requires the risk assessment to be carried out by a competent person with the necessary knowledge, skills and experience; an untrained author casts doubt on whether it is suitable and sufficient.

n.0: Formatting is irrelevant to the validity of the assessment.
n.1: Employment on site does not confer the competence required.
n.2: A competent person acting for the duty holder may write it, not only the supplier.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: What must the written scheme state should happen if a control measure is found not to be working?
o: That the outlet is simply painted a warning colour
Nothing — the scheme only covers normal operation
That the failure is logged and reviewed at the next annual audit only
The remedial action to be taken when control limits are not met
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: The written scheme must describe the action to be taken, including remedial steps, if monitoring shows the control measures are not effective, so failures are corrected promptly.

n.2: Deferring action to an annual audit allows the risk to persist; response must be prompt.
n.1: A scheme that ignored failure would leave the risk uncontrolled; it must cover what to do when control fails.
n.0: Marking an outlet does not restore control of the risk.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Why does a Legionella risk assessment pay particular attention to sources that generate a spray or mist?
o: Because infection follows from breathing in an aerosol of contaminated droplets
Because misting fittings tend to use noticeably more electricity
Because spray taps are almost always the very cheapest fittings to replace on site
Because sprays and mists tend to look untidy around a plant room
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Legionnaires' disease is contracted by inhaling small airborne droplets containing the bacteria, so identifying aerosol-generating sources — showers, spray taps, cooling towers, spa pools — is a key part of the assessment.

n.3: Appearance is not a health consideration in the assessment.
n.1: Energy use is not the reason aerosol sources are prioritised.
n.2: Replacement cost is irrelevant to why aerosols are a risk.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A landlord's risk assessment lists 'monthly temperature checks' but names nobody to do them and gives no record sheet. Which required feature of a written scheme is missing?
o: The manufacturer's warranty document for the building's hot water boiler as well
The chosen colour scheme for the plant room walls and its pipework
A copy of the current tenant's signed rent agreement for the property
A statement of who is responsible and a means of recording the monitoring
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A written scheme must allocate responsibility for each task and provide for recording the results of monitoring; naming a frequency alone, with no responsible person or record, leaves the scheme incomplete.

n.0: A boiler warranty does not fulfil the monitoring or responsibility requirement.
n.1: Decor is not part of the control scheme.
n.2: A rent agreement is unrelated to water-hygiene monitoring.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: How long should records of the risk assessment and monitoring of control measures generally be retained?
o: For a suitable period, so trends can be reviewed and control demonstrated over time
Records are never really needed at all, as long as the water looks clear
Only until the end of the current working day, and then they are discarded
They may be destroyed the moment they have been written down on the sheet, if wished
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: L8 expects records to be kept for a suitable period so that the effectiveness of the scheme can be reviewed over time and compliance demonstrated; monitoring results in particular should be retained long enough to show trends.

n.1: Clear-looking water proves nothing; records are still required.
n.2: A single day is far too short to show whether control is being maintained.
n.3: Immediate destruction would defeat the purpose of recording and prevent trend review.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A building has stood empty during a long refurbishment and water has sat unused in the pipework. What does this change mean for the existing risk assessment?
o: The assessment only needs review once the building is gone
The assessment is automatically cancelled and not replaced
Nothing changes at all because the building is exactly the same shape
The assessment should be reviewed as stagnation changes risk
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A change of use or a period during which the system is left stagnant is exactly the kind of change that can invalidate an assessment, so it must be reviewed and controls applied before normal use resumes.

n.0: Waiting until demolition ignores the risk to people using the reoccupied building.
n.1: An assessment is never simply cancelled; it must be reviewed and kept current.
n.2: The physical shape is irrelevant; the water conditions have changed materially.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Which of these best describes the relationship between the risk assessment and the written scheme of control?
o: The written scheme entirely removes the need to assess the risk at all going forward
The scheme is prepared to manage the risks the assessment identifies
They are really the same single document under two names
The written scheme must be produced before any assessment
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: The assessment identifies the risks; where a risk is identified that cannot be prevented, a written scheme is then prepared to manage it, setting out the control measures. The scheme flows from the assessment.

n.2: They are distinct documents with different purposes, though they are linked.
n.3: The scheme cannot sensibly precede the assessment that defines what it must control.
n.0: A scheme does not remove the ongoing duty to assess and review risk.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: During a review, an assessor discovers a capped-off branch of pipe that no longer feeds any outlet. Why is this noted as a risk?
o: Capped pipework is always completely illegal to leave in place
It forms a dead leg where water stagnates and bacteria grow
It immediately voids the whole building's insurance policy
It noticeably reduces the water pressure at other taps
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A dead leg holds a volume of water that is not drawn through, allowing it to stagnate and warm into the growth range, so the assessment should flag it for removal or management.

n.0: Redundant pipework is not inherently unlawful, but should be removed.
n.2: Insurance status is not the water-hygiene reason.
n.3: The concern is stagnation and growth, not a pressure effect.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: The written scheme specifies checking that cold water reaches outlets below a set temperature. What is the purpose of setting such a control limit?
o: To justify buying rather more expensive thermometers for the job
To give a measurable standard for judging whether control holds
To limit how often the building's staff are allowed to use the taps
To make the completed paperwork look a good deal more detailed still
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Control limits give monitoring an objective benchmark; if a reading falls outside the limit, the scheme's remedial action is triggered, so the limit is what makes monitoring meaningful.

n.0: Equipment cost is not the reason for setting a limit.
n.2: Control limits govern water conditions, not tap usage.
n.3: The purpose is functional control, not the look of paperwork.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Who holds the legal duty to ensure a suitable and sufficient Legionella risk assessment is carried out for premises?
o: The duty holder — usually the employer or person in control
The most junior member of the site's maintenance team
Any visitor who happens to notice a problem while on site
The water regulator, acting on the duty holder's behalf entirely
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: The duty holder — the employer or person in control of the premises — is legally responsible for ensuring the assessment is done and kept up to date, even if the work itself is delegated to a competent person.

n.1: A junior worker may carry out tasks but does not hold the overarching legal duty.
n.2: Visitors have no legal duty for the premises' water safety.
n.3: The regulator enforces the law; it does not carry the duty holder's responsibility.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A risk assessment concludes that the risk from a small, simple system is 'insignificant'. What does L8 still expect the duty holder to do?
o: Stop using the building's water supply entirely from this point on
Record the conclusion and review it periodically and if circumstances change
Discard all of the paperwork at once, since no risk must mean no records
Install a cooling tower on the roof just to be on the safe side
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Even where the risk is assessed as insignificant, the duty holder should record the assessment and its conclusion and review it periodically, and again if anything changes, to confirm it remains valid.

n.0: Ceasing to use the supply is neither required nor practical for a low-risk system.
n.2: A conclusion of insignificant risk still has to be recorded and revisited.
n.3: Adding a cooling tower would introduce a major new risk, the opposite of what is needed.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: An outbreak of respiratory illness is linked to a site. Regarding the water risk assessment, what should the duty holder do?
o: Assume the assessment is still perfectly valid and change nothing at all
Delete the previous monitoring records so you can start again afresh
Review the assessment, since an outbreak is a clear trigger to check it is valid
Wait a full year before looking at the assessment again after this
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: An outbreak, or any reason to suspect the assessment is no longer valid, is a specific trigger to review it promptly and check whether the controls have failed or the risk has changed.

n.0: An outbreak is precisely when the assessment must not be assumed valid.
n.1: Records must be preserved, especially during an investigation.
n.3: Delaying review for a year during a suspected outbreak is indefensible.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Why does keeping the water-system schematic accurate matter so much when the risk assessment is reviewed?
o: An out-of-date schematic can hide dead legs or added plant
Schematics are required purely for planning-permission purposes only
A tidy diagram just makes the plant room easier to photograph
The diagram is only ever needed to satisfy the site architect
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: If the schematic does not reflect alterations — new branches, removed outlets, added storage — the reviewer cannot see all sources of risk, so keeping it current is essential to a suitable and sufficient review.

n.1: Its role is water-safety management, not planning permission.
n.2: Photographic tidiness is not the purpose of the schematic.
n.3: The diagram serves the risk assessment, not the architect's records.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A written scheme sets a monitoring frequency for flushing infrequently used outlets. What risk is this control primarily addressing?
o: The risk of limescale gradually forming on the tap spout
The risk of stagnation in rarely used outlets allowing bacterial growth
The risk of the site's overall water bill steadily increasing over the year
The risk of the outlet being stolen from the wall
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Little-used outlets let water sit and warm, favouring Legionella growth; scheduled flushing draws fresh water through and is a recognised control the written scheme should specify and record.

n.0: Limescale is a nuisance but is not why flushing is scheduled.
n.2: Flushing uses little water; controlling growth, not the bill, is the point.
n.3: Theft is not a water-hygiene risk addressed by flushing.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Which statement best reflects how often a Legionella risk assessment should be reviewed?
o: Regularly, and also whenever there is reason to suspect it is no longer valid
Just the once when it is first written down, and then never looked at again at all
Strictly every ten years to the exact day, and at no other time
Only if a member of the public makes a formal written complaint
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: L8 expects periodic review and, on top of that, review whenever there is reason to think the assessment is no longer valid — such as changes to the system, its use, or a suspected case of disease.

n.1: A one-off assessment cannot stay valid as systems and uses change over time.
n.3: A public complaint is not the only, or main, trigger for review.
n.2: There is no fixed ten-year rule; review is driven by suitability and change.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A duty holder argues that because they employ a specialist contractor to manage the water systems, they no longer need to understand the risk assessment. Why is this view mistaken?
o: Because contractors are simply not allowed to touch or work on water systems
Because employing a contractor doubles the number of assessments required
Because the assessment must instead be understood only by the site cleaner
The duty holder keeps legal responsibility and must ensure the assessment is acted on
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Delegating the work does not transfer the legal duty; the duty holder must still ensure a competent assessment is made, understand its findings and see that the controls are implemented and reviewed.

n.0: Contractors routinely and lawfully manage water systems; that is not the issue.
n.1: Using a contractor does not multiply the number of assessments required.
n.2: Responsibility does not pass to the cleaner; it remains with the duty holder.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Within the written scheme, what is the purpose of clearly recording who does each monitoring task?
o: So that the busiest person on site can be blamed if anything ever goes wrong later
So that the recorded names can then be shared with marketing partners
So the finished document reaches its required minimum page count
So responsibility is unambiguous and tasks are not left undone through confusion
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Allocating each task to a named, competent person ensures accountability and that nothing falls between roles; the scheme's controls only work if someone is clearly responsible for carrying them out.

n.0: The aim is reliable completion of tasks, not apportioning blame.
n.1: Sharing names with marketing is irrelevant and inappropriate.
n.2: Page count is not a consideration in the scheme.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: An assessor identifies a large cold-water storage tank that far exceeds the building's daily demand. Why is oversized storage recorded as a risk factor?
o: Bigger tanks always cost noticeably more to insure
Excess water turns over slowly and can stagnate and warm
The extra stored water makes the building harder to heat
Larger tanks are heavier and put stress on the roof beams
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Storage far above demand means water dwells longer before being drawn off, giving it time to warm into the growth range and stagnate; the assessment should flag it, favouring right-sized storage as prevention.

n.0: Insurance cost is irrelevant to the Legionella risk.
n.2: Heating the building is not why oversized storage is a hygiene risk.
n.3: Structural loading is a building concern, not the water-hygiene reason for the flag.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: What does 'suitable and sufficient' mean when applied to a Legionella risk assessment?
o: It uses the very same template as every other building
It has been signed off by the most senior director
It evaluates the actual risks in enough detail to decide the controls
It is long enough to fill a whole lever-arch file
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A suitable and sufficient assessment properly identifies the sources and who is exposed, and evaluates the risk in enough depth to determine what control measures are needed for that particular system.

n.3: Length alone says nothing about whether the real risks were identified.
n.0: A generic template ignoring the system's specifics is not sufficient.
n.1: A senior signature does not make an inadequate assessment suitable.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A hotel converts a disused wing back into guest bedrooms after two years. Which action best reflects L8 before the wing reopens?
o: Review the assessment and update the wing's controls first
Remove the wing from the schematic to simplify the records
Open the rooms and only monitor water if a guest complains
Leave the assessment unchanged since the rooms existed before
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Bringing dormant plant back into use is a change that can invalidate the assessment; it should be reviewed, the schematic updated and controls applied so the reoccupied wing is safe from the first day of use.

n.1: Deleting the wing from records hides a real part of the system.
n.2: Waiting for a complaint exposes guests before control is confirmed.
n.3: Existing rooms do not account for two years of stagnation.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Why is an accurate asset register or list of system components valuable to the risk assessment?
o: It is only ever needed by the finance department for depreciation
It sets the resale value of the water system's plant and equipment
It ensures every component that could harbour Legionella is managed
It records the guarantee dates needed for future warranty claims
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Knowing every component — tanks, calorifiers, showers, spray taps, cooling plant — lets the assessor account for each potential source and assign controls, so nothing capable of harbouring or spreading the bacteria is overlooked.

n.0: Depreciation accounting is not the register's purpose here.
n.1: Resale value is a financial matter, not a water-hygiene one.
n.3: Warranty tracking is incidental, not why the register matters.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A written scheme lists control measures but says nothing about how their effectiveness will be checked. What key element is missing?
o: The car-parking arrangements laid on for any visiting site contractors
Provision for monitoring the controls to confirm they stay effective
A full list of the building's previous owners over the years
A glossary of common plumbing terms provided for site visitors
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A written scheme must not only state the controls but set out how and when they are monitored, so the duty holder can confirm they are working; without monitoring, control failures would go undetected.

n.0: Parking arrangements are unrelated to water-safety controls.
n.2: Past ownership has no place in the control scheme.
n.3: A glossary is not a required element and does not verify the controls.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: When identifying who is at risk, why does the assessment give particular attention to groups such as the elderly, the very young and the immunocompromised?
o: They are more likely to tamper with the building's plumbing
They tend to be more susceptible to infection if exposed
They use the hot water more cheaply than most other people
They are legally exempt from paying any of the water charges
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: L8 highlights that some people are more susceptible — the elderly, the very young, those with weakened immunity or respiratory illness — so premises serving them warrant particular care in identifying and controlling the risk.

n.0: Tampering is not why these groups are singled out.
n.2: Cost of water use has no bearing on susceptibility.
n.3: Water charges are unrelated to the health-risk reasoning.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: A duty holder wants to reduce risk by design. Which of the following is a prevention measure rather than a control-and-monitor measure?
o: Taking routine water samples and sending them away for full laboratory analysis
Removing an unused length of pipework so water can no longer stagnate in it
Dosing the hot water with a chemical biocide to keep the numbers down
Recording the weekly shower-head temperatures onto a monitoring log sheet
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Prevention designs the risk out — here, removing a dead leg so stagnant water cannot accumulate. The others manage a risk that remains, by controlling or monitoring it, which the hierarchy places after prevention.

n.0: Sampling checks the system state; it does not prevent the risk.
n.2: Biocide dosing controls an existing risk rather than removing its cause.
n.3: Logging temperatures is monitoring of a retained risk, not prevention.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: An assessor reviewing a factory notes that its process uses a humidifier producing a fine water mist over the shop floor. Why must this feature the risk assessment?
o: It is an aerosol-generating source that could disperse droplets to inhale
It is relevant only to the building's annual energy audit
It only affects the humidity readings shown on a wall chart
Humidifiers of this kind are always completely banned in every factory
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: A humidifier or any equipment creating a water mist is an aerosol source; if the water is contaminated, droplets can be inhaled, so the assessment must identify it and set controls for the water feeding it.

n.1: It is a health-risk source, not just an energy consideration.
n.2: The concern is inhalable aerosol, not merely a humidity reading.
n.3: Humidifiers are not banned; they must be assessed and controlled.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: The written scheme should describe the correct operation of the water system. Why is this description important?
o: So that the water system can be advertised more easily to potential buyers and investors
So that this written description can fully replace all staff training
So operators know the conditions controls should hold and can spot deviations
So that the document can be entered into an industry design competition
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Describing how the system should run — temperatures, flows and conditions — gives operators a clear reference so they can recognise when it drifts out of control and trigger the scheme's remedial actions.

n.0: Advertising the system is unrelated to safe operation.
n.1: A written description supports, but does not replace, training.
n.3: A design competition is not a purpose of the scheme.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Two years after it was written, a site's risk assessment has never been looked at again despite a major re-plumbing of the building. What is the main failing?
o: The assessment was simply written on the wrong grade of paper
The assessment used far too few proper technical words
The assessment should have been thrown away after twelve months
The assessment was not reviewed after a significant alteration that could change the risk
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Significant alterations to the pipework are a clear trigger to review the assessment; leaving it untouched means new dead legs, routes or plant may be uncontrolled and unassessed.

n.1: The vocabulary used is not the compliance failing here.
n.2: Assessments are reviewed and updated, not discarded after a year.
n.0: The medium it is written on is irrelevant to its validity.

Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.q: Overall, what is the fundamental purpose of producing and maintaining the risk assessment and written scheme together?
o: To create paperwork that only the building's insurers will ever actually read as a rule
To transfer all of the legal duties away from the employer entirely
To satisfy a simple filing requirement that has no practical effect at all
To identify the risk and then set out and sustain the measures that keep people safe
Risk Assessment & Written Scheme.w: Taken together they identify where and to whom the risk arises and then define, allocate, monitor and sustain the controls that prevent exposure — the whole point being to protect people's health, not merely to hold records.

n.0: Their audience is those who manage and are exposed to the system, not insurers.
n.1: They support the duty holder in meeting duties; they do not transfer them away.
n.2: They exist to control real risk, not merely to fill a filing requirement.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: Legionella bacteria multiply most readily in water that sits within which temperature range?
o: 0 to 15°C
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: The recognised danger zone where Legionella grows most readily is roughly 20 to 45°C.

n.0: Below about 20°C the bacteria stay dormant and do not multiply significantly.
n.1: Between 46 and 59°C growth slows and the bacteria begin to die off.
n.3: At 60°C and above the bacteria are killed quickly, so this range is a control not a risk.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: Why is temperature control regarded as the traditional and primary method of controlling Legionella in a hot and cold water system?
o: It means the outlets can be used far less often than before
It removes the need to keep any written monitoring records at all
It keeps the water either too cold or too hot for the bacteria to thrive
It is far cheaper than fitting any thermostats or valves to the system
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Keeping cold water cold and hot water hot holds the system outside the 20 to 45°C growth range.

n.0: Regular use of outlets is still needed to prevent stagnation.
n.1: Records must still be kept to prove the controls are working.
n.3: Cost is not the reason; effective bacterial control is.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: At what temperature should water be stored in a calorifier (hot water cylinder) to control Legionella?
o: Stored at 50°C or above at all times
Stored at around 55°C or slightly above
Stored at 70°C or above at all times
Stored at 60°C or above at all times
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Hot water should be stored at 60°C or above to keep the bacteria from multiplying.

n.0: 50°C is the minimum at the outlet, not the storage temperature.
n.1: 55°C is below the required storage minimum of 60°C.
n.2: 70°C is higher than needed and risks scalding and energy waste.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: Hot water should reach the tap at a minimum of 50°C within how long of the tap being run?
o: One minute
Five minutes
Two minutes
30 seconds
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Hot water must reach at least 50°C within one minute of running the tap.

n.3: Thirty seconds is shorter than the recognised one-minute allowance.
n.2: Two minutes is the run time used for cold water, not hot.
n.1: Five minutes is far too long and would indicate a fault.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: In a healthcare premises, what minimum hot water temperature should be reached at the outlet within one minute?
o: At least 50°C at the outlet
At least 52°C at the outlet
At least 60°C at the outlet
At least 55°C at the outlet
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: In healthcare settings the hot water target at the outlet is at least 55°C within one minute.

n.0: 50°C is the general minimum but healthcare requires higher.
n.1: 52°C is not the recognised healthcare figure.
n.2: 60°C is the storage temperature, not the outlet target.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: Cold water should be kept below which temperature to control Legionella?
o: Kept below around 18°C at the outlet
Kept below around 25°C at the tap
Kept below around 15°C at the outlet at all times
Kept below 20°C to stay out of the growth range
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Cold water should be kept below 20°C to stay out of the bacterial growth range.

n.2: Below 15°C is ideal but the control limit is 20°C.
n.0: 18°C is not the recognised limit.
n.1: 25°C is inside the danger zone and unsafe.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: What does the term 'sentinel outlets' mean on a hot and cold water system?
o: The nearest and the furthest outlets on a loop or system
The outlets that happen to be located only in the plant rooms
Any outlet that has been fitted with a thermostatic mixing valve
The two outlets that are used most often by staff each day
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Sentinel outlets are the outlets nearest to and furthest from where water enters the system or loop.

n.1: Sentinels are chosen by position on the system, not by being in plant rooms.
n.2: Having a mixing valve does not make an outlet a sentinel.
n.3: Frequency of use does not define a sentinel outlet.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: How often should the temperatures at sentinel outlets normally be checked?
o: Monthly
Annually
Quarterly
Weekly
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Sentinel outlet temperatures are normally checked monthly.

n.3: Weekly checks are more frequent than the routine requirement.
n.2: Quarterly is too infrequent for sentinel monitoring.
n.1: Annual checks apply to a wider set of outlets, not sentinels.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: What is the minimum flow temperature that should be recorded leaving a calorifier?
o: 50°C, which is actually the minimum required at the tap outlet
55°C, roughly the figure used only at healthcare outlets
65°C, which sits a little above the required minimum flow
60°C, the minimum flow that should leave the calorifier
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: The calorifier flow temperature should be at least 60°C.

n.0: 50°C is the outlet minimum, not the calorifier flow.
n.1: 55°C is below the required flow figure.
n.2: 65°C is higher than the minimum required, though not itself unsafe.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: What is the minimum return temperature that should be recorded coming back to a calorifier on a circulating hot water system?
o: At least 50°C returning back to the calorifier
Around 60°C, which is the flow and storage figure
Around 45°C, which sits inside the danger zone
Around 55°C, above the minimum the return needs
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: The return temperature to the calorifier should be at least 50°C.

n.1: 60°C is the flow and storage figure, not the return minimum.
n.2: 45°C is inside the danger zone and below the required return figure.
n.3: 55°C is higher than the minimum needed for the return leg.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: You run a hot tap and after one minute the thermometer reads 48°C. What is the correct response?
o: Run the tap for another five minutes then leave it
Turn the calorifier down to stop scalding
Accept it as it is above 45°C
Record the reading and report it as out of range
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: 48°C is below the 50°C minimum, so the reading is recorded and reported to the responsible person.

n.2: Being above 45°C is not the standard; the outlet must reach 50°C.
n.1: Turning storage down would make the problem worse, not better.
n.0: Leaving it after a long run does not fix an out-of-range outlet.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: A colleague suggests turning the hot water storage down to 55°C so users are less likely to be scalded. Why is this wrong?
o: It would make the outlet checks a little quicker
At 55°C legionella can still survive in storage
Scalding simply cannot happen from stored water
It would end up using more energy overall each day
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Storing below 60°C allows Legionella to survive and multiply, so storage must stay at 60°C or above.

n.3: Energy use is not the safety reason for keeping 60°C.
n.2: Scalding can occur, which is exactly why the safe control is a mixing valve, not lower storage.
n.0: Speed of checks is irrelevant to the decision.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: What is the correct way to reduce the risk of scalding at an outlet without lowering the storage temperature?
o: Store the hot water at only 50°C in the cylinder instead
Fit a much longer pipe run between the cylinder and tap
Fit a thermostatic mixing valve at the outlet
Only ever use that particular tap for cold water
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: A thermostatic mixing valve blends the hot supply down at the point of use while storage stays at 60°C.

n.0: Storing at 50°C would allow bacterial growth.
n.1: A longer pipe run does not safely control the delivered temperature.
n.3: Removing hot use does not address the scald control needed.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: When taking a hot water outlet temperature with a surface probe, how long should you normally allow the tap to run before recording?
o: Until the temperature stabilises, up to one minute
Until the basin below the tap is completely full
For exactly ten seconds, then record the reading
For a fixed five minutes, whatever it reads
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: You run the tap until the temperature stabilises, which for hot water is within one minute.

n.1: Filling the basin is not how the run time is judged.
n.2: Ten seconds is too short for the reading to settle.
n.3: Running a fixed five minutes wastes water and is not the method.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: You take a cold tap reading and after two minutes it reads 22°C. What should you do?
o: Accept it because 22°C is close enough to the 20°C limit
Turn the tap off and simply mark it down as passed
Record the reading and report it as out of range
Wait ten minutes and only record it if it rises further
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: 22°C after two minutes is above the 20°C limit, so it is recorded and reported.

n.0: Being close is not the same as meeting the below-20°C limit.
n.1: Marking it as passed would be a false record.
n.3: Waiting longer does not correct an out-of-range cold outlet.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: Who should an out-of-range temperature reading be reported to?
o: The manufacturer who originally supplied the equipment
Whichever member of the public happens to be nearest
The responsible person appointed for water safety on the site
Nobody at all, provided only a single outlet is affected
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Out-of-range readings are reported to the responsible person so corrective action can be taken.

n.0: The manufacturer is not the person managing the site risk.
n.1: Members of the public are not responsible for the water system.
n.3: Even a single failing outlet must be reported.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: Why must temperature readings be written down at the time they are taken?
o: So that the readings can conveniently be changed at a later date if needed
Only because a member of the public has asked to see them
Because the thermometer will simply stop working otherwise
To provide a documented record proving the controls are being monitored
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Recording readings provides evidence that the control scheme is being monitored and maintained.

n.0: Records must never be altered after the event.
n.1: The record is for the duty holder and inspectors, not only public request.
n.2: The thermometer works regardless of whether you record.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: A cold water tap reads 24°C straight away and drops only to 23°C after two minutes. What is the most likely explanation?
o: The cold supply is being warmed somewhere, such as near a hot pipe
This is a perfectly normal and acceptable temperature for cold water
The tap is simply being used far too often by people
The thermometer is faulty and reads much too high
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: A cold outlet staying above 20°C suggests warming, often from nearby heat sources, and must be investigated.

n.1: 23°C is above the 20°C limit and is not acceptable.
n.2: Frequent use would tend to keep cold water cooler, not warmer.
n.3: A single high reading is more likely a real fault than a probe error.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: Which set of outlets, in addition to sentinels, is typically checked on a longer interval such as annually?
o: A representative selection of other outlets across the system
Only the specific outlets that happened to fail at the last inspection
Outlets that have had their mixing valves removed beforehand
Outlets located out in the staff car park and grounds
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: A representative range of other outlets is checked on a longer cycle, often annually, to confirm system-wide control.

n.1: Checks are not limited to previously failed outlets.
n.2: Removing mixing valves is not how outlets are selected.
n.3: Outlets are chosen across the served system, not by irrelevant locations.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: What temperature confirms that a calorifier is storing hot water safely?
o: Any temperature above 45°C
60°C or above
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Stored hot water at 60°C or above controls Legionella.

n.3: 58°C is below the storage minimum.
n.2: 59°C is still just below the required 60°C.
n.0: Above 45°C alone is not enough; growth continues up to about 45°C and survives to 60°C.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: You are asked to check the two sentinel outlets on a hot water loop. Which outlets are these?
o: The two most decorative and modern-looking taps found in the building
Two taps simply chosen at random from anywhere on the loop
The two taps sitting closest to the building's front door
The first outlet after the calorifier and the last one on the loop
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Sentinels on a loop are the nearest outlet to the calorifier and the furthest one on the return.

n.0: Appearance is irrelevant to sentinel selection.
n.1: Sentinels are chosen by position, not randomly.
n.2: Distance from the door does not define a sentinel.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: Why is it important that a hot outlet reaches temperature within one minute rather than eventually?
o: Because thermometers are only able to read for one single minute in practice
To save water at the outlet and for no other reason than that
Because a slow rise suggests poor circulation where bacteria can grow
So the record card entry fits neatly onto one printed line
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: A hot outlet that is slow to heat points to dead legs or poor circulation where bacteria can establish.

n.0: Thermometers can read for longer than a minute.
n.1: Water saving is a benefit but not the safety reason.
n.3: The one minute is a control standard, not a paperwork limit.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: During a monthly sentinel check the furthest hot outlet reads 46°C after one minute. What action is correct?
o: Accept it, treating it as acceptable within the danger zone
Re-label the outlet as a cold tap so it need not comply
Turn the calorifier down so the readings all match up
Record and report it as failing the 50°C outlet minimum
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: 46°C is below the 50°C outlet minimum, so it is recorded and reported for investigation.

n.0: Being within the danger zone is the problem, not an acceptance.
n.1: Relabelling does not correct the failure.
n.2: Lowering the calorifier would worsen the risk.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: What is the main risk of water sitting in a rarely used outlet, sometimes called a dead leg?
o: The water in the pipe becomes far too cold to use safely
The pipe is very likely to freeze solid quite quickly
The water warms into the danger zone and then stagnates
The tap on that outlet will start to run much faster
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Little-used pipework lets water stagnate and drift into the 20 to 45°C growth range.

n.0: Stagnant water tends to warm, not become too cold.
n.1: Dead legs are a stagnation risk, not primarily a freezing risk.
n.3: Flow rate is not affected in the way described.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: Which thermometer or probe is suitable for recording an outlet water temperature quickly and accurately?
o: A domestic oven thermometer taken from the kitchen
A bare hand simply held against the pipe
A calibrated digital thermometer with a suitable probe
An old, unmarked mercury thermometer left lying in a drawer
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: A calibrated digital thermometer with the correct probe gives a quick, reliable reading.

n.0: An oven thermometer is not designed for water outlet checks.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: During an annual check, a mixed selection of outlets is tested. What is the value of checking outlets beyond the sentinels?

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: A hot storage calorifier reads 62°C, the sentinel hot outlets both reach 52°C within a minute, and cold outlets are below 20°C within two minutes. What is the correct conclusion?

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: After running a hot outlet for a minute you get 50°C exactly. How should this be treated?
o: As a fail, because the reading is not above 50°C
As meeting the minimum standard and recorded as a pass
As requiring the calorifier to be turned off straight away
As a cold outlet reading rather than a hot one

n.3: 50°C at a hot tap is a hot, not cold, reading.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: You find the cold water in a tank reaches 20°C only after standing overnight in a warm plant room. What lasting action helps keep it below 20°C?

20°C or above, matching the cold-water storage limit
60°C or above, hot enough to control legionella

At least 40°C, still in the danger zone
At least 50°C at the outlet
At least 20°C, barely above cold

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: Occupants report scalding-hot water at a washbasin fed directly from a 60°C system. What is the correct control measure?

Remove the tap from the monthly monitoring schedule to avoid disputes
Lower the hot water storage temperature to about 45°C at the calorifier
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Storage must stay at 60°C to control Legionella; the scald risk at the point of use is managed by fitting a thermostatic mixing valve (TMV) that blends water to a safe delivery temperature.

n.1: Reducing the calorifier to 50°C undermines storage control; scald risk is handled by a TMV.
n.2: Removing the outlet from monitoring hides the problem rather than controlling risk.
n.3: Dropping storage to 45°C puts water into the danger zone; storage must remain at 60°C.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: Why must the hot water storage temperature never be reduced below 60°C as a way of preventing scalding?
o: Because the boiler thermostat simply cannot hold any setting under 60°C whatsoever
Because a lower storage temperature causes far too much scale to form inside the vessel
Because water below 60°C fails to remove the limescale from the outlets
It would let stored water fall into the 20–45°C growth range and feed legionella
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Reducing storage below 60°C risks bringing stored water into the 20–45°C danger zone where Legionella multiplies; scald risk must instead be managed with a TMV.

n.0: Thermostats can be set below 60°C; the prohibition is about safety.
n.1: Scale formation is not the reason storage is kept high; bacterial control is.
n.2: Limescale removal is not the purpose of the 60°C requirement.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: After taking a temperature reading that is outside the acceptable range, what is the operative's immediate correct action?
o: Wait until the next monthly visit before mentioning the result
Adjust the calorifier thermostat upward on your own initiative
Record the reading and report it to the responsible person
Discard the reading and retake it until it comes in range
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Out-of-range readings must be recorded accurately and reported to the responsible person so that corrective action can be arranged and tracked.

n.0: Delaying the report to the next visit leaves a potential risk uncontrolled.
n.1: Unilateral thermostat changes are not the operative's decision.
n.3: Discarding readings until a favourable one appears falsifies the record.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: How frequently should the temperature of the water in a cold-water storage tank normally be checked as part of wider (non-sentinel) monitoring?
o: Only when the building's occupants report a specific water quality complaint
Every week, at the same time as little-used outlet flushing
At least annually, comparing incoming and stored-tank temperatures
Every month, alongside the sentinel outlet temperature checks
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: HSG274 Part 2 places cold-water tank temperature checks in the wider annual regime, comparing incoming mains and stored temperatures to confirm the tank is not warming water into the danger zone.

n.0: Monitoring is proactive and scheduled, not triggered only by complaints.
n.1: Weekly activity relates to flushing outlets, not tank temperature.
n.3: Monthly checks apply to sentinel outlets, not the tank temperature.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: A tank thermometer reads 24°C in a cold-water storage cistern during summer. What does this indicate?
o: Stored cold water is inside the danger zone and the warming should be investigated
The tank is performing correctly, since it is still below the 45°C upper limit
The reading is normal, because tank water is always a bit warmer than the mains supply
The cistern is far too cold and its temperature should now be raised
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: At 24°C the stored cold water sits within the 20–45°C danger zone; causes such as solar gain, proximity to heat sources or poor insulation should be investigated and the finding reported.

n.2: Cold storage should stay below 20°C; being warmer than the mains is a fault, not a normal condition.
n.1: Being under 45°C is irrelevant; cold water must be below 20°C, and 24°C exceeds that.
n.3: Cold water is never deliberately heated; the concern is that it is too warm, not too cold.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: When measuring the temperature at a mixed (blended) outlet fitted with a TMV, what should the operative bear in mind?
o: The blended temperature is deliberately reduced, so hot control is checked upstream
The blended outlet reading is the true test of hot water storage control
The blended reading replaces the need to check the incoming hot supply
A blended outlet should still reach 60°C to prove Legionella control
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: A TMV lowers the delivery temperature for scald safety, so a blended outlet will not read the hot control temperature; the hot supply must be checked upstream of the valve.

n.1: A blended reading reflects the mixed output, not the hot storage control temperature.
n.2: The blended reading does not replace an upstream hot-supply check.
n.3: Requiring 60°C at a blended tap would defeat the TMV's scald-prevention purpose.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: A calorifier flow gauge shows 62°C but the return reads 44°C on a circulating system. What is the correct interpretation?
o: Only the flow temperature really matters here, so the return figure can be disregarded
The return is below 50°C and within the danger zone, so it fails and is reported
The system passes because the average of the two readings is above 50°C
Both readings are acceptable because the flow comfortably exceeds 60°C
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: The return must be at least 50°C; at 44°C it sits inside the 20–45°C danger zone, indicating poor circulation, so the result fails and must be recorded and reported.

n.0: The return temperature is a required check that reveals circulation problems and cannot be disregarded.
n.2: Averaging the two readings is not a recognised criterion; each has its own minimum.
n.3: A compliant flow does not excuse a failing return; both must meet their minimums.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: What is the main purpose of measuring temperature at the outlets furthest from the hot water source?
o: To check the calorifier thermostat is calibrated
To confirm hot water stays above the range even at the far end
To verify the incoming cold mains temperature there
To confirm the outlet is used often enough
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: The furthest outlet is where hot water is most likely to have cooled; checking it confirms the 50°C-plus condition is maintained throughout the system, not just near the source.

n.0: Thermostat calibration is verified at the calorifier, not inferred from a distant outlet.
n.2: A hot outlet check assesses hot delivery, not the incoming cold mains temperature.
n.3: Usage frequency is a separate stagnation concern, not the purpose of the far-outlet temperature check.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: Which instrument setup gives the most reliable reading when checking outlet water temperatures?
o: A calibrated thermometer, run until the temperature stabilises
An uncalibrated probe read after only a few seconds of running flow
A hand held over the flow to judge if it feels hot or cold
A single instantaneous reading taken the moment the tap opens
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: A calibrated thermometer, with the outlet run until the reading stabilises, gives an accurate and repeatable result that can be trusted against the pass criteria.

n.2: Judging by hand is subjective, unsafe and cannot be recorded as a measured value.
n.3: An instantaneous reading at opening does not reflect the settled temperature the criteria are based on.
n.1: An uncalibrated probe read too soon produces an unreliable figure that may pass or fail incorrectly.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: During a monthly check a hot sentinel outlet reaches 50°C only after running for three minutes. How should this be treated?
o: A failure of the one-minute criterion, recorded and reported
A cold-water fault to be investigated on the cold side only
A pass, because the outlet eventually reached 50°C
Irrelevant, because only the final steady temperature matters
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Hot water must reach 50°C within one minute; taking three minutes fails the time criterion and suggests problems such as a long dead-leg or poor circulation, so it must be recorded and reported.

n.1: This is a hot-supply timing issue, not a cold-water fault.
n.2: Reaching temperature eventually is not a pass.
n.3: The time taken to reach temperature is part of the criterion.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: Why are temperature readings recorded and retained rather than simply noted verbally?
o: So the operative can be paid according to how many outlets were tested
Because thermometers legally must upload readings to a central database
To give an auditable record showing the system stays under control
Because the water supplier requires a copy before it will bill the site
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Written records give an auditable trail showing temperatures have been maintained and out-of-range results acted upon, which is central to demonstrating ongoing legionella control.

n.0: Records exist for control and audit, not to calculate pay.
n.1: There is no legal requirement for thermometers to auto-upload.
n.3: The record supports the duty holder's control, not billing.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: A little-used shower is flushed weekly, but its monthly hot check reads 46°C at one minute. What does this reading most likely indicate?
o: Hot water is not reaching the required temperature, so the result must be reported
The shower should now simply be reclassified as a cold outlet
The reading now proves the weekly flushing regime can simply be stopped
The outlet is fully compliant, because it comfortably exceeds 45°C
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: A hot outlet must reach 50°C within one minute; 46°C falls short and sits within the danger zone, so the shortfall must be recorded and reported for investigation.

n.1: A hot outlet that underperforms is not reclassified as cold; the hot fault is investigated.
n.2: A failing temperature is a reason to maintain controls, not to stop flushing.
n.3: Exceeding 45°C is not the standard; hot delivery must reach 50°C, so 46°C fails.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: At what interval are TMV performance and outlet checks such as thermostatic controls typically verified within the wider monitoring regime?
o: Every day, before the building is first occupied by anyone at all
At set intervals such as annually, within scheduled servicing
Only once, at the time the valve is first commissioned
Every week, in step with the little-used outlet flushing
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: TMV servicing and similar thermostatic checks fall within the wider regime carried out at set intervals, commonly annually, distinct from the monthly sentinel temperature checks.

n.0: Daily checks are not required for TMV performance verification.
n.2: A one-off commissioning check is insufficient; TMVs need periodic verification.
n.3: Weekly activity relates to flushing, not to TMV servicing.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: A calorifier is stratified so the top reads 61°C but a drain point near the base reads 42°C. Why is the base reading a concern?
o: Cooler water at the base sits in the danger zone and can harbour legionella
It shows the vessel is oversized and can therefore safely be run a good deal cooler
It only really matters for the return leg, not for the stored volume
It is acceptable, because the top of the vessel is above 60°C anyway
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Stratification can leave the vessel base in the 20–45°C danger zone; the whole stored volume should reach 60°C, so a 42°C base reading is a genuine proliferation risk to be reported.

n.1: A cool base indicates poor mixing or a fault, not a licence to run cooler.
n.2: Base stratification concerns the stored water, not only the return leg.
n.3: A hot top does not compensate for a cool base.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: Which situation best explains why a cold outlet might read 22°C despite the incoming mains being 12°C?
o: The cold pipe is warming, running near a hot pipe or warm space
The thermometer is faulty and adds ten degrees to every reading
The mains reading is wrong, as cold water cannot warm in pipework
Cold water is naturally warmer at outlets than the mains by design
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Cold water warming above 20°C in distribution usually reflects heat gain, such as cold pipes routed near hot services or through warm risers; the cause should be investigated and reported.

n.1: A consistent physical cause is more likely than a fixed instrument offset.
n.2: Cold water certainly can warm in pipework; that is the risk being detected.
n.3: A rise into the danger zone is a fault, not by design.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: On a hot circulating loop, which pair of temperatures represents a correctly performing system?
o: Flow 61°C and return 52°C
Flow 50°C and return 40°C
Flow 58°C and return 47°C
Flow 55°C and return 44°C
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: The flow should be at least 60°C and the return at least 50°C; only 61°C flow with 52°C return meets both minimums.

n.1: A 50°C flow fails the 60°C minimum and 40°C return is in the danger zone.
n.2: A 58°C flow is below the 60°C minimum and 47°C return below 50°C.
n.3: The 55°C flow is below 60°C and the 44°C return sits in the danger zone.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: Who holds ultimate accountability for ensuring temperature monitoring results are acted upon at a site?
o: The individual occupants who happen to use the affected outlets
Whichever operative happened to take that particular month's readings
The manufacturer of the calorifier that was originally installed at the premises
The responsible person or duty holder appointed to manage the water system
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: The appointed responsible person / duty holder is accountable for ensuring monitoring is carried out and that out-of-range findings are investigated and corrected.

n.1: The operative records and reports results but is not the accountable duty holder.
n.2: The equipment manufacturer has no accountability for ongoing site monitoring.
n.0: Occupants are not responsible for managing the water system's control regime.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: Why should an operative allow a hot tap to run and stabilise before recording the temperature at the outlet?
o: To reduce the volume of water counted on the site's metered water bill
To confirm the settled delivery temperature reflects the true circulating supply
To use up the cooler standing water so occupants get a fresher supply
To flush limescale out of the tap's aerator before the reading is taken
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Running the tap clears cooled water sitting in the local pipework so the stabilised reading reflects the actual circulating hot supply against which the one-minute criterion is judged.

n.0: Metered water cost is irrelevant to the technical reason for letting it settle.
n.2: Comfort of supply is incidental; the purpose is a representative measured value.
n.3: Descaling the aerator is not the reason; the aim is an accurate supply temperature.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: A newly commissioned wing has long pipe runs, and the furthest hot outlet reads 49°C at one minute while nearer outlets pass easily. What is the most likely underlying issue?
o: Heat loss along the long run is dropping delivery below 50°C at the far end
The calorifier is set far too high and really ought to be turned right down
The nearer outlets are being over-tested and are biasing the whole survey
The thermometer gradually loses accuracy the further it is from the plant room
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: A far outlet just failing while near ones pass points to heat loss down a long run or weak circulation; the shortfall below 50°C must be recorded and reported for remedial work such as improved circulation or insulation.

n.1: Turning the calorifier down would worsen delivery temperatures, not fix the distant shortfall.
n.2: Testing nearer outlets does not bias a distant reading; each outlet is measured independently.
n.3: A calibrated thermometer does not lose accuracy with distance; the cause is heat loss.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between the 50°C outlet figure and the 60°C storage figure?
o: They are interchangeable and either can be used anywhere
The 50°C figure actually applies to storage and 60°C to the outlet
Storage is at 60°C so delivery still meets 50°C at the tap
The tap must always be hotter than storage to prove flow
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Storing at 60°C gives headroom so that, after unavoidable heat loss in distribution, water still arrives at 50°C or above at the outlet within one minute.

n.0: The two figures serve different points in the system and are not interchangeable.
n.1: The figures are reversed here: 60°C is for storage and 50°C for the outlet.
n.3: The tap cannot be hotter than the source; delivery is expected to be at or below storage temperature.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: During a routine visit the responsible person's log shows last month's failing hot outlet was never re-checked after repair. What is the correct response?
o: Assume the repair has worked and mark the outlet compliant without any testing
Re-test the outlet, confirm it meets the standard, and record the result
Delete the previous failing entry so the log looks consistent
Wait a further month before doing any follow-up measurement
