Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: A remedial action is only closed out once a follow-up reading confirms the outlet meets the criteria; the operative should re-test and record the verified result.

n.0: Marking it compliant without measurement leaves the correction unverified and the record false.
n.2: Deleting a failing entry falsifies the audit trail and hides that action was needed.
n.3: Delaying verification leaves a potentially uncontrolled outlet unconfirmed for longer than necessary.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: A dead-leg of redundant pipework tees off a hot supply. Why does it pose a temperature-control concern?
o: It raises the calorifier flow temperature above the 60°C target
Water in the stagnant leg cools into the danger zone
It forces the return temperature above the 50°C limit
It causes the cold mains to exceed 20°C at every outlet
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: A dead-leg holds stagnant water that cools into the 20–45°C danger zone and is not reached by normal flow or heating, so it should be identified and preferably removed.

n.0: A dead-leg does not raise the calorifier flow temperature.
n.2: A dead-leg does not drive the return above its limit.
n.3: A hot-side dead-leg does not govern the cold mains temperature.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: Two adjacent basins share a hot supply: one reads 54°C and a TMV-blended one reads 41°C, both at one minute. How should the results be judged?
o: Both pass, because together the two readings average above 45°C
Both fail, because neither of them reached the 60°C storage figure
The unmixed outlet passes 50°C; the blended one is a TMV delivery
Both fail, because a hot outlet must always exceed 55°C in any building
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: The unmixed hot outlet at 54°C passes the 50°C-in-one-minute standard, while the blended outlet is deliberately reduced by the TMV, so its 41°C reflects safe delivery and hot control is verified upstream of that valve.

n.0: Averaging outlet readings is not a recognised criterion.
n.1: 60°C is a storage requirement, not the outlet delivery standard.
n.3: The 55°C figure applies to healthcare; here the hot standard is 50°C.

Temperature Monitoring & Control.q: What is the primary reason temperature control is used as a routine method of managing Legionella in a water system?
o: It removes the need for any cleaning or disinfection of the storage tanks
Higher storage temperatures reduce the site's overall energy costs
Heated water tastes noticeably better to the building's occupants
Keeping water outside the 20-45°C range suppresses bacterial growth
Temperature Monitoring & Control.w: Temperature control works by keeping hot water hot (>=60°C stored, >=50°C delivered) and cold water cold (<20°C), holding water outside the 20-45°C range in which Legionella multiplies.

n.0: Temperature control complements, but does not replace, cleaning and disinfection.
n.1: Maintaining hot storage uses energy rather than saving it; the purpose is safety.
n.2: Taste is irrelevant to the control rationale, which is bacterial suppression.

Monitoring & Records.q: Why is routine monitoring of water systems carried out?
o: To check the control measures work and show compliance
To reduce the size of the water bill for the whole site
To keep the plant room looking tidy and well organised
To make the water taste noticeably better for users
Monitoring & Records.w: Monitoring checks that controls such as temperature are effective and provides recorded evidence of compliance with the written scheme.

n.1: Monitoring does not lower water charges.
n.2: Tidiness is unrelated to the purpose of monitoring.
n.3: Monitoring is about controlling legionella risk, not taste.

Monitoring & Records.q: How often should hot and cold sentinel outlet temperatures normally be checked?
o: Every three years
Monthly
Once when the building opens
Only if someone complains
Monitoring & Records.w: Sentinel hot and cold outlet temperatures are typically monitored monthly under HSG274 Part 2.

n.0: Three-yearly is far too infrequent for temperature monitoring.
n.2: A single check at opening does not confirm ongoing control.
n.3: Waiting for complaints means the risk is not being managed proactively.

Monitoring & Records.q: Little-used outlets that are not part of normal use should be flushed how often to keep water moving?
o: Yearly
Only in summer
Never, they can be left standing
Weekly
Monitoring & Records.w: Infrequently used outlets should be flushed weekly to prevent water stagnating and legionella multiplying.

n.0: Yearly leaves water standing far too long between uses.
n.1: Stagnation is a risk all year, not only in summer.
n.2: Leaving outlets standing allows stagnation and bacterial growth.

Monitoring & Records.q: How often should showerheads and spray taps typically be cleaned, descaled and disinfected?
o: Daily
Every five years
Only when replaced
Quarterly
Monitoring & Records.w: Showerheads and spray taps are normally cleaned, descaled and disinfected on a quarterly basis, or more often if scaling is heavy.

n.1: Five-yearly allows scale and biofilm to build up unchecked.
n.0: Daily cleaning is unnecessary and not the standard frequency.
n.2: Waiting until replacement leaves fouled heads in service for too long.

Monitoring & Records.q: A written record of a temperature check should include, as a minimum:
o: Only the final temperature reading and nothing else recorded
The date, item checked, reading, who did it and any action
The colour chosen for the pipe insulation nearby
Just the initials of whoever did the check that day
Monitoring & Records.w: A good record captures the date, the outlet or item checked, the result, who carried it out and any action, so it can be reviewed later.

n.0: A lone reading gives no context of where, when or by whom.
n.3: Initials alone do not record what was checked or the result.
n.2: Insulation colour is not relevant monitoring information.

Monitoring & Records.q: What is an 'action level' in a monitoring regime?
o: The height above the floor at which a water tank is fitted
A target for how fast to complete the whole round
The maximum number of outlets allowed on a floor
A result out of range that triggers remedial action
Monitoring & Records.w: An action level is a result outside the acceptable range that must prompt investigation and corrective action.

n.0: It has nothing to do with the mounting height of a tank.
n.1: It is about water safety limits, not the speed of the task.
n.2: It is not a count of outlets.

Monitoring & Records.q: You take a monthly reading and the hot sentinel outlet reaches only 48°C after running for one minute. What should you do?
o: Write down 55°C instead so the record sheet looks correct
Leave the box blank and simply move straight on
Turn the tap off and ignore the low reading entirely
Record the reading and report it for remedial action
Monitoring & Records.w: The reading is below the expected value, so it must be recorded accurately and escalated so remedial action can be taken.

n.0: Writing a false figure falsifies records and hides a real risk.
n.1: A blank hides the problem and breaks the record trail.
n.2: Ignoring an out-of-range result leaves the fault uncorrected.

Monitoring & Records.q: Cold water storage tanks should normally be inspected at what interval?
o: Every ten years
Never once installed
Every week
Around once a year
Monitoring & Records.w: Cold water storage tanks are typically inspected at least annually for cleanliness, condition and debris.

n.0: Ten-yearly is far too long between inspections.
n.2: Weekly inspection of a tank is not the standard requirement.
n.1: Tanks must be inspected periodically, not left unchecked for life.

Monitoring & Records.q: Why are trends in monitoring readings over time useful?
o: They can reveal a control slowly drifting before it fails a limit
They set the market price of any new monitoring equipment that is bought
They remove the need to take any monitoring readings at all
They decide who ultimately pays for the site's water supply
Monitoring & Records.w: Comparing results over time can show a gradual decline in performance so it can be corrected before a control is lost.

n.1: Trends do not determine equipment pricing.
n.2: Trends come from readings; they cannot replace taking them.
n.3: Trends are about water safety, not billing responsibility.

Monitoring & Records.q: When is legionella sampling normally used?
o: As a complete, standalone replacement for routine temperature control
An extra check where control is in doubt or the scheme requires it
Purely to prove that the water tastes clean and fresh
To measure how hard the water is before any descaling work
Monitoring & Records.w: Sampling supports monitoring where control is uncertain or specifically required, but it does not replace routine temperature control.

n.0: Sampling supplements control; it never replaces temperature management.
n.2: Sampling for legionella is not a taste test.
n.3: Sampling for legionella does not measure water hardness.

Monitoring & Records.q: You open last month's monitoring sheet and find it completely blank with no readings. What is the correct action?
o: Throw the blank sheet away and simply start a fresh one
Report the gap so the responsible person can address the missed monitoring
Copy this month's readings straight into last month's empty boxes to fill it
Fill it in now with some made-up figures for last month's checks
Monitoring & Records.w: A missed set of records is a real gap in evidence and must be reported so it can be investigated and put right, never fabricated.

n.0: Destroying the sheet removes evidence that monitoring was missed.
n.2: Copying current readings into a past month falsifies the history.
n.3: Inventing past figures is falsification and misleads everyone.

Monitoring & Records.q: What temperature should hot water be stored at in the calorifier to control legionella?
o: No more than 20°C
At least 60°C
Exactly 45°C
Around 37°C
Monitoring & Records.w: Hot water should be stored at 60°C or above, which prevents legionella from multiplying.

n.0: 20°C is within the range where legionella thrives, not a safe storage temperature.
n.3: 37°C is close to ideal growth temperature for legionella.
n.2: 45°C is still within the growth range and too low for safe storage.

Monitoring & Records.q: Hot water should reach what temperature at the sentinel taps within one minute of running?
o: It should reach 50°C or above at the tap
It should reach below 20°C at the tap
It should reach roughly 45°C at the tap
It should reach only around 30°C at the tap
Monitoring & Records.w: Hot water should reach 50°C or above at the outlet within one minute to confirm the distribution temperature is being maintained.

n.1: Below 20°C would indicate no hot water control at all.
n.2: 45°C is short of the 50°C the outlet should reach.
n.3: 30°C sits within the legionella growth range.

Monitoring & Records.q: Cold water should stay below what temperature at the sentinel outlets after running for two minutes?
o: Below 20°C at the outlet
Below 45°C at the outlet
Below 55°C at the outlet
Below 37°C at the outlet
Monitoring & Records.w: Cold water should be below 20°C at the outlet after two minutes to keep it out of the range that favours legionella.

n.1: 45°C is well within the growth range and unacceptable for cold water.
n.2: 55°C would be hot water, not cold.
n.3: 37°C is close to ideal legionella growth temperature.

Monitoring & Records.q: A thermostatic mixing valve (TMV) is fitted to a shower. Which routine check helps confirm it is safe?
o: Carefully repainting the outside of the valve body once every month
Recording only the temperature of the surrounding room
Removing the valve entirely to speed up the water flow
A periodic check and service, including the fail-safe shut-off
Monitoring & Records.w: TMVs need periodic checking and servicing, including the fail-safe that shuts off flow if the cold supply fails, to prevent scalding while managing legionella risk.

n.0: Painting the valve does nothing to confirm it functions safely.
n.2: Removing the valve creates a scalding hazard and defeats its purpose.
n.1: Room temperature is not what a TMV check assesses.

Monitoring & Records.q: You finish flushing a set of little-used outlets. What should you write on the record?
o: Nothing at all, because flushing does not need to be recorded
Only a short note simply stating that 'work was done'
Just a reminder to come back and check them next year
The date, which outlets were flushed and your name
Monitoring & Records.w: Every monitoring task, including flushing, should be recorded with the date, what was done and who did it so control can be evidenced.

n.0: Flushing is a control task and must be recorded like any other.
n.1: 'Work was done' is too vague to be useful evidence.
n.2: Little-used outlets need weekly flushing, so a yearly note is wrong.

Monitoring & Records.q: Who should out-of-specification monitoring results be reported to?
o: No one, as long as you plan to recheck it again next month
The building's visitors, so that they are kept fully informed
The responsible person or duty holder named in the scheme
A colleague in a different department, purely for their interest
Monitoring & Records.w: Out-of-range results must be escalated to the responsible person so remedial action can be arranged promptly.

n.0: Delaying a month leaves a known risk uncontrolled.
n.1: Visitors have no role in managing the water safety scheme.
n.3: An unrelated colleague cannot authorise remedial action.

Monitoring & Records.q: Which of these best describes falsifying a monitoring record?
o: Recording an unexpected low temperature honestly
Writing a reading you did not actually take
Noting the exact time a check was done
Adding the action you took after a fault
Monitoring & Records.w: Entering figures that were never measured is falsification and is a serious safety failing that hides real risk.

n.0: Recording a genuine low reading is exactly what monitoring is for.
n.2: Noting the time is normal, accurate record keeping.
n.3: Recording remedial action is good practice, not falsification.

Monitoring & Records.q: Why should a written scheme's monitoring regime be followed exactly rather than sampled at random?
o: It makes the required paperwork noticeably shorter
It ensures every control point is checked on time
It allows readings to be estimated rather than measured
It lets you skip the outlets that are hard to reach
Monitoring & Records.w: Following the scheme ensures all identified control points are monitored at the intervals needed to keep the system safe.

n.0: The aim is complete coverage, not less paperwork.
n.2: Readings must be measured, never estimated.
n.3: Hard-to-reach outlets still need checking on schedule.

Monitoring & Records.q: During the monthly round you notice a stored cold water tank reading of 24°C. What does this suggest?
o: The thermometer must be faulty, so the reading can safely be ignored
The cold water is warmer than it should be and needs reporting
The tank is perfectly within its normal working limits
Cold water sitting at 24°C is actually the safest of all
Monitoring & Records.w: Cold water above 20°C is out of specification and must be recorded and reported so the cause can be found and fixed.

n.2: 24°C exceeds the 20°C cold-water limit, so it is not within limits.
n.0: Assuming the instrument is faulty and ignoring the result hides a possible real problem.
n.3: Warmer cold water favours legionella growth; it is not safest.

Monitoring & Records.q: How long should water hygiene monitoring records generally be kept?
o: Only until the very end of that working day
They do not really need to be kept for any time at all
For no longer than a single week after being taken
For a suitable period, usually at least five years
Monitoring & Records.w: Records should be retained for a suitable period, commonly at least five years, so trends and compliance can be reviewed.

n.0: A single day gives no history to review.
n.1: Records must be kept; they are the evidence of control.
n.2: A week is far too short to show trends or prove compliance.

Monitoring & Records.q: A calorifier drain check is part of the scheme. What is being looked for?
o: The colour of the vessel's outer metal casing
The humidity level of the surrounding plant room air
Sediment or debris settling at the base of the vessel
Whether the manufacturer's label is still readable
Monitoring & Records.w: Draining a small amount from the base checks for accumulated sediment, which can shield bacteria and reduce heating efficiency.

n.0: Casing colour tells you nothing about internal cleanliness.
n.1: Room humidity is unrelated to what a calorifier drain reveals.
n.3: A label check is not the purpose of a calorifier drain.

Monitoring & Records.q: You realise you forgot to record the outlet reference next to a temperature you took. What is the best action?
o: Guess a likely outlet reference to fill in the missing gap
Go back, confirm which outlet it was and complete the record
Cross out and discard the whole temperature reading you took
Leave the incomplete record as it is and hope it is never queried
Monitoring & Records.w: An accurate record needs the correct outlet identified, so the detail should be confirmed and completed properly.

n.0: Guessing risks recording the reading against the wrong outlet.
n.2: Deleting a genuine reading loses valid monitoring data.
n.3: An incomplete record cannot be relied on and may hide a problem.

Monitoring & Records.q: What is the main reason for keeping monitoring records legible and clear?
o: So the record book looks neat and tidy for any passing visitors
So the record book gets used up a good deal faster than usual
So anyone reviewing them can understand and act on the results
So the entries can be written in a private personal code
Monitoring & Records.w: Records must be clear so the responsible person or an inspector can read the results, spot problems and confirm control.

n.0: Appearance for visitors is not the purpose of a record.
n.1: There is no benefit to filling books quickly.
n.3: Coded records defeat the point of a clear, reviewable record.

Monitoring & Records.q: On a shower service you descale a heavily scaled head. Why does this matter for legionella control?
o: Scale and biofilm can harbour legionella and shield it from heat and disinfection
Scale gradually changes the colour of the water coming out
Scale only affects the water pressure at the head and nothing else at all
Descaling simply makes the shower run noticeably more quietly
Monitoring & Records.w: Scale and biofilm provide surfaces and nutrients where legionella can grow and be protected from heat and disinfectant.

n.1: Colour change is not the health concern with scale.
n.2: Scale is a legionella harbour, not only a pressure issue.
n.3: Noise is not the reason for descaling in this context.

Monitoring & Records.q: The written scheme says weekly flushing but a set of outlets has only been flushed once this month. What should you do?
o: Quietly cross the outlets off the flushing list
Flush them now, record it and report the missed weeks
Assume that once a month is probably close enough
Backdate three weekly entries to make it look complete
Monitoring & Records.w: The gap is a real lapse in control, so the outlets should be flushed, recorded honestly, and the missed weeks reported for review.

n.0: Removing outlets from the list ignores a required control task.
n.2: Monthly flushing does not meet a weekly requirement.
n.3: Backdating entries falsifies records that never happened.

Monitoring & Records.q: What does a good record of remedial action allow the site to demonstrate?
o: That no monitoring will ever be needed again in future
That the building's overall water use has steadily increased
That out-of-range results were noticed and then put right
That the responsible person can now safely be replaced
Monitoring & Records.w: Recording the action taken shows problems were identified and corrected, closing the loop on control.

n.0: Corrective actions do not remove the need for ongoing monitoring.
n.1: Remedial records are about safety, not water consumption.
n.3: Records do not determine staffing of the responsible person.

Monitoring & Records.q: Why is temperature the main control usually monitored in hot and cold systems?
o: Legionella cannot multiply when water is kept hot or cold enough
It is the only figure that a simple thermometer is ever able to show
Temperature has no real effect on the bacteria at all
Temperature is simply the cheapest thing to write down
Monitoring & Records.w: Keeping hot water hot and cold water cold holds legionella outside its growth range, which is why temperature is the primary control monitored.

n.3: It is chosen for effectiveness, not for being cheap to record.
n.1: Thermometers can show many things; that is not the reason.
n.2: Temperature strongly affects legionella growth.

Monitoring & Records.q: You take a reading and the digital thermometer gives an obviously impossible value of 210°C. What is the correct step?
o: Write 210°C in the record because that is what it displayed every time
Recheck with a working instrument and record the true reading
Round it down to 60°C so the record looks normal
Skip that outlet entirely and move on to the next one
Monitoring & Records.w: A clearly faulty reading should be rechecked with a reliable instrument so the record reflects the true temperature.

n.0: Recording a value you know is false makes the record meaningless.
n.2: Inventing 60°C is falsification and hides the real result.
n.3: Skipping the outlet leaves a gap in required monitoring.

Monitoring & Records.q: What is the purpose of recording who carried out each monitoring task?
o: It is only really needed for brand-new members of staff joining
It is what decides who gets paid overtime at the month end
It removes the need to write down the date of the task at all
It gives accountability and lets any questions be followed up
Monitoring & Records.w: Naming the person gives accountability and allows anyone reviewing the record to follow up on what was done.

n.0: It applies to everyone doing the task, not just new starters.
n.1: Recording names is for traceability, not payroll.
n.2: The name is in addition to the date, not a substitute for it.

Monitoring & Records.q: A monthly sentinel temperature is defined as being taken at which outlets?
o: The outlets nearest and furthest on each supply
The single outlet with the newest tap fitted to it
Only the outlet located in the site manager's office
Every single outlet in the building, checked monthly
Monitoring & Records.w: Sentinel outlets are the nearest and furthest points on each supply, which represent the extremes of the system's performance.

n.1: The age of the tap does not define a sentinel point.
n.2: A single chosen office does not represent the system extremes.
n.3: Checking every outlet monthly is not what sentinel monitoring means.

Monitoring & Records.q: You are asked by a busy colleague to 'just sign off' a check you did not actually do. What should you do?
o: Decline and explain the check must genuinely be done and recorded
Just sign it now to save time, since these checks nearly always pass
Sign a slightly lower temperature just to be on the safe side
Sign it but write a small question mark beside the entry
Monitoring & Records.w: Signing for a check that was not carried out is falsifying a safety record and must be refused; the check should be done properly.

n.1: Signing off undone work is falsification regardless of how it usually turns out.
n.3: A question mark does not make a false sign-off acceptable.
n.2: Any invented figure for an undone check is still a false record.

Monitoring & Records.q: Why might sampling be requested even when temperatures look correct?
o: Where control is in doubt or the scheme requires it
To avoid ever having to check the temperatures again
Only to check the mineral content of the water supply
Because sampling is always cheaper than taking temperatures
Monitoring & Records.w: Sampling can be used as an extra confirmation where confidence in control is low or where the scheme requires it, alongside temperature monitoring.

n.1: Sampling supplements, and does not remove, temperature checks.
n.2: Legionella sampling is not a mineral-content test.
n.3: Sampling is generally more involved, not a cheap shortcut.

Monitoring & Records.q: A cold tank inspection finds debris and an insect screen missing. What is the right recorded response?
o: Remove the tank lid and leave it off to let it dry out
Record and report the findings for cleaning and a new screen
Note only that the tank generally 'looked fine' on the day
Say nothing at all and wait until next year's inspection
Monitoring & Records.w: Contamination and a missing screen are defects that must be recorded accurately and reported so remedial cleaning and repair happen.

n.0: Removing the lid exposes the tank to more contamination.
n.2: Writing 'looked fine' is a false record that hides real defects.
n.3: Waiting a year leaves a contaminated, unprotected tank in use.

Monitoring & Records.q: What information turns a raw temperature figure into a useful monitoring record?
o: The date, the outlet, the result and who took the reading
Just the general fact that it was a fairly warm day outside
The make and model of the thermometer that was used
How many other people were standing nearby at the time
Monitoring & Records.w: Context, the date, the specific outlet, the reading and the person, is what makes a figure meaningful and reviewable.

n.1: The weather does not identify the outlet or the result.
n.2: The instrument brand is not essential monitoring context.
n.3: The number of bystanders is irrelevant to the record.

Monitoring & Records.q: During flushing you find an outlet has been capped off and disused. What should the record show?
o: A rough guess at when the outlet was probably last used
That the outlet is now a dead leg to report for removal
That it was flushed normally along with all the others
Nothing at all, because it no longer counts as an outlet
Monitoring & Records.w: A capped, disused outlet is a potential dead leg and should be recorded and reported so it can be assessed for removal.

n.0: Guessing past use adds nothing and is not a factual record.
n.2: You cannot flush a capped outlet, so recording a normal flush is false.
n.3: Dead legs are a risk and must be recorded, not ignored.

Monitoring & Records.q: Why is it important that the person recording a result does not adjust it to look acceptable?
o: Rounded figures are simply a good deal easier to add up together later
Adjusted figures use noticeably less ink on the sheet
Adjusted figures hide real risks and can lead to people being harmed
The exact number recorded never really matters in practice
Monitoring & Records.w: Altering a reading conceals a genuine control failure, so the risk goes unaddressed and people can be exposed.

n.0: Ease of adding up never justifies falsifying a safety figure.
n.1: Ink use is irrelevant to record integrity.
n.3: The exact reading matters because it shows whether control is met.

Monitoring & Records.q: A TMV serving a care-home bath fails its temperature check. What is the priority?
o: Increase the hot water supply to the bath to try to compensate
Note it down but leave the bath in normal daily service
Loosen the mixing valve by hand to adjust it yourself
Record the failure and escalate it promptly for servicing
Monitoring & Records.w: A failed TMV is a scalding and control risk, so it must be recorded and escalated for servicing or removal from use.

n.0: Raising the hot supply increases the scalding hazard.
n.1: Leaving a failed TMV in service risks scalding vulnerable users.
n.2: Adjusting the valve by hand is not a proper repair and is unsafe.

Monitoring & Records.q: What is the main benefit of writing the action taken next to an out-of-range reading?
o: It proves that the original reading must have been taken wrongly
It cancels any need to report the result to anyone
It makes the poor reading disappear from the record
It shows the problem was followed up and properly closed out
Monitoring & Records.w: Recording the action demonstrates the issue was investigated and resolved, completing the audit trail.

n.0: An action note does not mean the original reading was wrong.
n.1: Recording action does not remove the duty to report where required.
n.2: The original reading stays in the record; the action is added, not a replacement.

Monitoring & Records.q: You arrive to do the monthly checks but the site's thermometer is missing. What is the correct approach?
o: Estimate the temperatures roughly by feeling the warmth of the pipes by hand
Report it and get a suitable calibrated instrument before recording
Skip this month's checks entirely and record nothing at all
Copy last month's figures straight across into this month's record
Monitoring & Records.w: Accurate monitoring needs a proper, working instrument, so it should be sourced before any readings are taken and recorded.

n.0: Feeling pipes cannot give a reliable, recordable temperature.
n.2: Skipping and recording nothing leaves a gap in required monitoring.
n.3: Copying old figures fabricates readings that were never taken.

Monitoring & Records.q: Why should monitoring frequencies in the scheme not be reduced just because results have been good?
o: Operatives can cut the frequencies whenever it happens to be convenient
Only the responsible person may change the regime after review; operatives follow it
Good results mean the checks can now be stopped altogether for good
The monitoring frequencies really only matter during the winter months
Monitoring & Records.w: The written scheme sets the frequencies, and any change is a decision for the responsible person after proper review, not an operative on the day.

n.0: Operatives must follow the scheme, not vary it for convenience.
n.2: Good results confirm control is working; they do not justify stopping.
n.3: Legionella risk is present year round, not only in winter.

Monitoring & Records.q: What does the term 'out of specification' mean on a monitoring sheet?
o: A reading that just happened to be taken on a weekend day
A result that falls outside the acceptable limits set in the scheme
Any reading whatsoever that sits above the freezing point of water
A result that was written down in the wrong colour of ink
Monitoring & Records.w: Out of specification means the measured value falls outside the safe limits defined by the written scheme and needs action.

n.0: The day of the week does not make a reading out of specification.
n.2: Being above freezing is far too broad and unrelated to the limits.
n.3: Pen colour has nothing to do with specification limits.

Monitoring & Records.q: A visiting inspector asks to see evidence that showerheads are being descaled. What best demonstrates this?
o: A verbal assurance that it is done regularly enough
Dated records naming who cleaned and descaled each head
A single photo of one clean showerhead
The purchase receipt for the descaler bought
Monitoring & Records.w: Complete, dated records of each descale, showing what was done and by whom, are the evidence of ongoing compliance.

n.0: A verbal claim is not documented evidence of control.
n.2: A single photo does not show the routine across all heads over time.
n.3: Buying descaler does not prove it was actually used on schedule.

Monitoring & Records.q: Why is it good practice to record even a normal, in-range reading?
o: It builds the evidence trail and lets trends be tracked
It just fills the page up so the work looks busy
In-range readings are meant to be kept secret
Only failing readings are really worth writing down
Monitoring & Records.w: Recording every reading, pass or fail, provides continuous evidence of control and the data needed to spot trends.

n.3: Recording only failures loses the baseline that proves control is normally maintained.
n.2: There is nothing secret about routine readings.
n.1: The value is the evidence trail, not appearing busy.

Monitoring & Records.q: You spot that two months of readings are all identical to the last digit for every outlet. What might this suggest?
o: The system is working perfectly and needs no attention
The readings may have been copied rather than genuinely taken
Nothing here is really worth mentioning to anyone
Thermometers reliably give identical results anyway
Monitoring & Records.w: Real readings naturally vary, so suspiciously identical figures can indicate copying and should be raised for checking.

n.0: Identical results across outlets and months are a warning sign, not proof.
n.2: A possible falsified record is exactly worth mentioning.
n.3: Genuine thermometer readings vary and are rarely identical.

Monitoring & Records.q: What should happen to the monitoring record when a fault has been fixed?
o: The original fault entry is quietly erased from the sheet
The corrective action and a satisfactory recheck are recorded
The whole record sheet is replaced with a fresh clean one
Nothing more is written down once the fault has been fixed
Monitoring & Records.w: Recording the corrective action and a satisfactory follow-up reading closes the loop and shows the fault was resolved.

n.0: Erasing the fault removes the evidence it existed and was handled.
n.2: Replacing the sheet destroys the genuine history.
n.3: Leaving no closing note fails to show the fault was fixed.

Monitoring & Records.q: Why does keeping hot water hot and cold water cold reduce the need for chemical treatment?
o: Temperature control alone keeps legionella out of its growth range
Cold water gradually dissolves and destroys all the bacteria present
Hot water automatically adds chlorine into the whole system
Chemical treatment is completely illegal in any water system
Monitoring & Records.w: Effective temperature control holds water outside the 20-45°C range where legionella multiplies, so it is the primary control.

n.1: Cold water slows growth but does not dissolve bacteria.
n.2: Hot water does not generate chlorine on its own.
n.3: Chemical treatment is permitted and used where needed; it is not illegal.

Monitoring & Records.q: An operative records a shower as 'descaled' but only wiped the outside because they ran out of time. Why is this record a problem?
o: It should have been typed up neatly rather than written by hand
It records a control task as done when it was not carried out
Descaling of shower outlets never actually needs recording
It was entered using the wrong day-and-month date format
Monitoring & Records.w: Recording an incomplete task as done gives false assurance that a control is in place when it is not.

n.0: Handwritten records are acceptable; the problem is the false claim.
n.2: Descaling is a control task that does need recording.
n.3: The date format is not the safety issue here.

Monitoring & Records.q: Overall, what do complete and honest monitoring records give the responsible person?
o: Permission to ignore any action levels that are reached
A perfectly legitimate reason to stop inspecting the system altogether
A convenient way to avoid having to train up competent staff
Confidence that the controls are working and evidence to prove compliance
Monitoring & Records.w: Accurate records show the controls are effective and provide the documented proof of compliance the responsible person needs.

n.0: Action levels must always be acted on, whatever the records show.
n.1: Good records support continued inspection, not stopping it.
n.2: Records do not remove the need to train competent staff.

Monitoring & Records.q: A legionella sample comes back positive but your temperature records for that outlet look correct. What is the right response?
o: Destroy the temperature records to avoid any confusion later
Report it so the result and the controls can be reviewed
Ignore the sample entirely because the temperatures were fine
Retake the sample yourself and keep the new result private
Monitoring & Records.w: A positive sample must be escalated so the responsible person can review both the result and the controls and decide on remedial action.

n.0: Destroying records removes evidence and is never acceptable.
n.2: A positive result cannot be dismissed just because temperatures were logged correct.
n.3: Keeping a result private hides a potential risk from those who must act on it.

Monitoring & Records.q: Why must routine monitoring tasks such as temperatures and flushing be written down and kept?
o: So the paper can be recycled at the end of each and every month
Because regular handwriting practice is a requirement laid down in law
The records demonstrate the controls are working and prove compliance
To decorate the plant room walls with a few colourful charts
Monitoring & Records.w: Records show the control measures are being carried out and are working, which is needed to demonstrate compliance.

n.0: Recording is about evidence of control, not producing paper to recycle.
n.1: There is no legal requirement about handwriting practice.
n.3: Records are kept as evidence, not for decoration.

Monitoring & Records.q: When a monitoring result is out of specification, what must happen in addition to recording it?
o: It should be averaged with good readings to hide it
It should be left for next year's check to sort out
It must trigger remedial action and be escalated
It should be quietly deleted so the log stays clean
Monitoring & Records.w: Out-of-specification results must lead to remedial action and be escalated to the responsible person.

n.0: Averaging a bad reading away conceals the problem instead of fixing it.
n.1: Leaving a fault for a year leaves the risk uncontrolled.
n.3: Deleting a failing result hides a genuine risk and falsifies records.

Monitoring & Records.q: Which of these routine tasks would normally be recorded in the monitoring log?
o: The full names of every visitor signing in at the main reception desk
Temperature checks, flushing little-used outlets and TMV servicing
The daily newspaper headlines seen that morning
The lunch orders placed by the site staff that day
Monitoring & Records.w: Temperature checks, flushing and TMV servicing are control tasks that must be recorded to show the scheme is being followed.

n.0: A visitor book is a separate record, not part of the water monitoring log.
n.3: Lunch orders have nothing to do with water safety monitoring.
n.2: Newspaper headlines are irrelevant to the monitoring record.

Monitoring & Records.q: SCENARIO: While recording your monthly checks you realise last month's page was never signed or completed. What should you do?
o: Tear out the incomplete page and throw it in the bin
Do nothing, since only this month's page really matters
Report the gap to the responsible person
Fill in last month with completely invented readings
Monitoring & Records.w: A gap in the records should be reported so it can be investigated and the monitoring regime corrected.

n.0: Destroying records removes evidence and is never acceptable.
n.1: Ignoring a gap means a lapse in control could go unnoticed.
n.3: Inventing readings falsifies safety-critical records.

Monitoring & Records.q: SCENARIO: A little-used shower has not been flushed for several weeks and there is no record of any flushing. What is the safe, responsible action?
o: Remove it from the flushing schedule to stop it showing overdue
Run it once briefly and mark several past weeks as completed
Leave it, because a rarely used shower is genuinely low risk
Flush it as required, record it, and report the missed flushing
Monitoring & Records.w: Little-used outlets should be flushed regularly; you should flush it, record the task, and report the missed flushing for action.

n.0: Deleting it from the schedule hides the risk rather than controlling it.
n.1: Back-dating weeks that were never done falsifies the record.
n.2: Rarely used outlets are actually higher risk due to stagnation.

Monitoring & Records.q: A site manager asks why the team records monthly sentinel outlet temperatures when 'the system has never had a problem'. What is the primary purpose of this monitoring?
o: To calculate how much hot water the whole building uses each month
To confirm the water is safe to drink without any further chemical treatment
To provide documented evidence the control regime works and demonstrate compliance
To satisfy the water company's billing rules for a metered supply
Monitoring & Records.w: HSG274 Part 2 explains that routine monitoring, including monthly sentinel temperatures, exists to prove the control measures remain effective and to demonstrate compliance with the risk assessment and ACOP L8.

n.0: Sentinel monitoring records temperature and time-to-temperature, not volume used.
n.1: Temperature monitoring controls legionella risk; it does not certify potability.
n.3: Monitoring for legionella control is unrelated to water-company billing.

Monitoring & Records.q: Which combination best describes what a properly completed monitoring record entry should contain?
o: Only the temperature reading itself and a tick to show it was acceptable
The date, the task or outlet, the reading, the result, who did it and any action taken
The outlet reference plus the initials of whoever happened to be on shift during that week
A photograph of the thermometer with the time automatically stamped onto the picture
Monitoring & Records.w: A good record is traceable and complete: date, what was checked, the reading obtained, whether it passed or failed, who carried it out and what action followed if it was out of range.

n.0: A bare reading with a tick omits date, location, operative and action.
n.2: An outlet and vague initials with no reading or result cannot evidence control.
n.3: A photo alone is not a structured record and misses result and action.

Monitoring & Records.q: Outlets that are used only occasionally are flagged on the monitoring schedule. How frequently should such little-used outlets normally be flushed and the action recorded?
o: Only when the outlet is next needed by an occupant
Annually, at the same time as the cold water tank inspection
Weekly, or as often as indicated by the risk assessment
Once a quarter, aligned with the shower cleaning programme
Monitoring & Records.w: HSG274 Part 2 advises flushing infrequently used outlets at least weekly (or more often if the assessment requires) to prevent stagnation, and the flushing must be logged.

n.3: Quarterly is far too infrequent to control stagnation in seldom-used outlets.
n.0: Waiting until an outlet is needed allows water to stagnate and undermines the control regime.
n.1: Annual flushing would leave water standing for long periods, allowing biofilm and legionella growth.

Monitoring & Records.q: How often are showers and other spray-forming outlets typically cleaned, descaled and disinfected, with the work recorded?
o: Every five years, in line with the record retention period
Quarterly, or more often if scale build-up demands it
Only after a positive legionella sample is confirmed
Monthly, at the same time as the sentinel temperature checks
Monitoring & Records.w: HSG274 Part 2 recommends that showerheads and hoses are dismantled, cleaned, descaled and disinfected quarterly as a typical baseline, adjusted by risk and the rate of scaling.

n.0: Five years is the record-keeping period, not a cleaning frequency.
n.2: Waiting for a positive sample means the control has already failed.
n.3: Monthly is more onerous than the typical quarterly guidance.

Monitoring & Records.q: A cold water storage tank feeds a domestic system. As part of the monitoring regime, how often should its condition typically be inspected and the findings recorded?
o: At least annually, checking cleanliness, condition, lid and screens
Every five years or so, to match the usual record-retention period exactly
Every month, alongside the sentinel temperature checks
Every week, alongside the little-used outlet flushing
Monitoring & Records.w: HSG274 Part 2 recommends inspecting cold water storage tanks at least annually and cleaning/disinfecting them where the inspection shows it is needed, with results recorded.

n.1: Five years relates to keeping records, not to inspecting the tank.
n.2: Monthly is the sentinel temperature interval, not tank inspection.
n.3: Weekly inspection of the tank interior is impractical and not required.

Monitoring & Records.q: During monthly checks an operative records a hot sentinel outlet at 44°C after running for one minute, below the expected level. What is the correct first response?
o: Leave the entry blank and simply re-test at the next monthly visit
Round the figure up to 50°C so that the record clearly shows a pass
Record it as an action level, investigate, and carry out remedial action
Note it as acceptable, because the water still felt fairly warm at the tap
Monitoring & Records.w: An out-of-range reading is an action level: it must be recorded honestly, the cause investigated, remedial action taken and the responsible person informed, as required by ACOP L8 and HSG274.

n.1: Altering the figure to show a pass is falsification and leaves a real legionella risk uncontrolled.
n.0: Leaving it blank hides the failure and delays action for a month while risk persists.
n.3: Whether water 'feels warm' is not a valid criterion; 44°C is below the control level and needs action.

Monitoring & Records.q: A responsible person suggests replacing routine temperature monitoring with occasional legionella sampling to save time. Why is this not acceptable?
o: Sampling gives an instant result right at the outlet, unlike the temperature checks on site
Sampling supplements temperature control but does not replace it as the main measure
Sampling is only ever used in cooling towers and never in hot and cold systems
Sampling is cheaper to carry out, so it should always be the primary method
Monitoring & Records.w: HSG274 Part 2 is clear that microbiological sampling can supplement monitoring but is not a substitute for maintaining and checking temperature control, which remains the principal routine control.

n.0: Sampling results take days of laboratory culture, so they give no instant assurance.
n.2: Sampling can be used in hot and cold systems too, but as a supplement.
n.3: Cost does not make sampling the primary method; it is a supplementary check.

Monitoring & Records.q: Why is it valuable to review monitoring readings as a trend over several months rather than judging each reading in isolation?
o: A gradual drift can reveal a developing fault before it breaches an action level
Trends remove any need at all to keep the individual monthly records on file anymore
Trends let individual poor readings be averaged out and then simply ignored
Trends are required only so that the water supplier can set its tariff
Monitoring & Records.w: Reviewing trends can expose a slow deterioration, such as a storage temperature creeping down, allowing intervention before an outright failure occurs.

n.1: Individual records must still be kept; trends are derived from them, not a substitute.
n.2: Trends are used to spot problems early, not to average away and dismiss poor readings.
n.3: Trend analysis supports risk control, not supplier tariffs, which are unrelated.

Monitoring & Records.q: For how long should legionella monitoring, inspection and maintenance records generally be retained?
o: At least five years
Until the next monthly check is completed
Only while the current operative remains employed on site
Six months, then destroyed to save storage
Monitoring & Records.w: ACOP L8 and HSG274 advise keeping records of the risk assessment, control scheme and monitoring for a suitable period, commonly at least five years.

n.1: Overwriting or discarding records each month destroys the audit trail entirely.
n.3: Six months is well short of the recommended retention period and would not support an investigation.
n.2: Retention is tied to a defined period, not to the tenure of any individual staff member.

Monitoring & Records.q: Thermostatic mixing valves (TMVs) appear on the maintenance schedule. Which of the following should be checked and recorded as part of their routine servicing?
o: That the valve reduces the incoming mains pressure to a set value
That the blended outlet temperature is safe and fail-safe works
That the valve carries the installer's business card nearby
That the valve body is painted the correct colour for the room
Monitoring & Records.w: TMV servicing checks the blended temperature is correct for the application and that the thermal shut-off operates, because a failed TMV can deliver water at a temperature favouring legionella or cause scalding.

n.0: A TMV blends hot and cold to a safe temperature; pressure reduction is a separate device's function.
n.2: A nearby business card is not a functional or recordable safety check.
n.3: The colour of the valve body has no bearing on temperature control or safety.

Monitoring & Records.q: Which check on a calorifier (hot water cylinder) should form part of the routine monitoring records?
o: The flow and return temperatures, confirming correct storage
The colour of the insulation jacket fitted around it
The postcode of the manufacturer stamped on the plate
The number of pipe brackets holding up the outlet
Monitoring & Records.w: Monitoring a calorifier includes recording flow and return temperatures to confirm water is stored at 60°C or above and returned at 50°C or more, plus periodic checks for debris at the drain.

n.1: The colour of insulation is irrelevant to whether the stored water reaches control temperature.
n.2: The manufacturer's postcode is administrative trivia, not a monitoring parameter.
n.3: The count of pipe brackets has no relevance to legionella temperature control.

Monitoring & Records.q: An operative is behind on flushing and considers signing the log to show outlets were flushed when they were not. Why must records never be falsified?
o: False records hide risk and can lead to illness and prosecution
Because falsified records slow down the next operative's paperwork
Because the ink used for making corrections is expensive to buy
Because the water supplier audits every single log entry weekly
Monitoring & Records.w: Falsifying records conceals uncontrolled risk, prevents proper action, breaches the duty of honesty in ACOP L8 record-keeping, and can contribute to outbreaks and enforcement action.

n.1: The issue is uncontrolled legionella risk, not paperwork speed.
n.2: The cost of ink is irrelevant to the safety consequences.
n.3: Water suppliers do not audit internal legionella logs.

Monitoring & Records.q: On a monitoring schedule, which outlets are chosen as the hot water 'sentinel' points?
o: Only the outlets that are fitted with a thermostatic mixing valve
The outlets closest to and furthest from each calorifier or loop
Any two outlets that are picked at random each and every month
The two outlets that are used most heavily by the building's occupants
Monitoring & Records.w: Sentinel outlets are the first (nearest) and last (furthest) on a hot water circuit, chosen because they represent the extremes of the temperature the system can deliver.

n.0: Blended TMV outlets mask the true hot temperature, so are unsuitable.
n.2: Random monthly selection prevents consistent trend comparison.
n.3: Heaviest-use outlets are not necessarily the temperature extremes.

Monitoring & Records.q: Once completed, monitoring records should be reviewed. Who is ultimately accountable for ensuring the records are checked and acted upon?
o: The responsible person or duty holder named in the written scheme
The building occupant who happened to last use the outlet in question
The external laboratory that calibrates the thermometer
The most junior member of the site maintenance team
Monitoring & Records.w: The duty holder appoints a responsible person who is accountable for the control scheme, including reviewing monitoring records and ensuring remedial actions are completed.

n.1: Building occupants have no accountability for reviewing the monitoring regime.
n.2: A calibration lab certifies instruments; it plays no part in reviewing site records.
n.3: Accountability rests with the named responsible person, not the most junior operative.

Monitoring & Records.q: A cold sentinel outlet is recorded at 23°C after running for two minutes on a warm day. What does the record require next?
o: Nothing, because cold water temperature is not part of legionella control
Waiting a full six months to see whether winter lowers the reading
Deleting the entry, since ambient warmth always explains a high reading
Log it as out of range, investigate the cause and take the remedial action needed
Monitoring & Records.w: Cold water should stay below 20°C within two minutes; a reading of 23°C is an action level requiring the cause to be found (for example warming from nearby hot pipes) and corrected, all recorded.

n.0: Cold water temperature is a key control; keeping it below 20°C limits growth.
n.1: Delaying six months leaves a raised temperature uncontrolled through the risk period.
n.2: Assuming ambient warmth without investigation could miss a genuine fault.

Monitoring & Records.q: A contractor descales the showers but leaves the site without completing the log. From a monitoring and records standpoint, what is the correct position?
o: No record is needed at all, because the contractor is not directly employed here
A quick verbal report to the caretaker counts as a sufficient permanent record
The task is only fully valid once it is recorded with date, outlet, result and who did it
The next site operative can simply invent some plausible details to close off the log
Monitoring & Records.w: Work is only demonstrably done when documented; the record must capture what was cleaned, when, the outcome and who performed it, regardless of employment status.

n.0: Contractor status does not remove the need to record maintenance.
n.1: A verbal report is not a durable, auditable record.
n.3: Inventing details is falsification and destroys record integrity.

Monitoring & Records.q: A monitoring reading remains out of range after the operative's first remedial attempt. What should the records-and-reporting process require next?
o: Mark the outlet as decorative so that it no longer needs any checking
Close the log entry and move on to the next scheduled outlet
Escalate to the responsible person so further action follows
Reduce the monitoring frequency to avoid repeat failures
Monitoring & Records.w: When first-line remedial action does not restore control, the failure must be escalated to the responsible person, who decides on further measures; the escalation itself is recorded.

n.0: Falsely reclassifying an outlet to dodge checks is dishonest and dangerous.
n.1: Closing an unresolved failure leaves the risk uncontrolled.
n.3: Cutting monitoring frequency hides recurring failures rather than resolving them.

Monitoring & Records.q: In broad terms, what does an effective monitoring and records regime allow a duty holder to demonstrate?
o: That the control measures in the risk assessment are in place and working
That every occupant has read the site's water safety policy
That the whole building uses noticeably less energy than neighbouring premises
That the plumbing was installed by an approved manufacturer
Monitoring & Records.w: The central value of monitoring records is evidencing that the risk assessment's control measures are being implemented and remain effective over time.

n.1: Occupant awareness is not what temperature and flushing records show.
n.2: Energy comparison is unrelated to legionella control evidence.
n.3: Installer approval is a design matter, not proof of ongoing control.

Monitoring & Records.q: When recording a hot sentinel temperature, what target should the water reach at the outlet, and within what time?
o: At least 50°C within one minute of running
Exactly 38°C at the moment the tap is opened
No higher than 20°C within two minutes of running
At least 43°C within five minutes of running
Monitoring & Records.w: HSG274 Part 2 states hot water should reach at least 50°C at the sentinel outlet within one minute of running (55°C in healthcare); the reading and time are recorded.

n.3: 43°C is a scald-risk/blended figure, not the hot sentinel control temperature.
n.2: 20°C in two minutes is the cold water target, not the hot sentinel target.
n.1: 38°C is a typical blended TMV delivery temperature, not the hot sentinel requirement.

Monitoring & Records.q: What is the recorded target for a cold water sentinel outlet?
o: Above 60°C to prevent stagnation
At least 50°C within one minute of running
Between 38°C and 46°C at all times
Below 20°C within two minutes of running
Monitoring & Records.w: Cold water should remain below 20°C, measured after running the outlet for up to two minutes, to keep temperatures outside the range that favours legionella growth.

n.1: 50°C in one minute is the hot sentinel target, not the cold requirement.
n.2: 38-46°C describes blended outlet temperatures, which would be dangerously warm for cold water.
n.0: Above 60°C applies to hot water storage, not cold supply.

Monitoring & Records.q: When monitoring a calorifier's return leg, what minimum temperature should the returning water record to keep the whole circuit protected?
o: At least 50°C so the whole loop stays out of the growth range
Somewhere below about 20°C on the return
Around 38°C or so on the returning leg
Exactly 100°C, at boiling point, at all times
Monitoring & Records.w: Hot water should be stored at 60°C or above and circulate so that it returns to the calorifier at no less than 50°C, ensuring the loop stays above growth temperatures throughout.

n.1: Below 20°C is a cold water target; a hot return that cool would indicate serious failure.
n.2: Around 38°C sits within the legionella growth range and is far too low for the return leg.
n.3: 100°C is boiling and neither required nor safe for a distribution return.

Monitoring & Records.q: Reviewing the flushing log, the responsible person finds a three-week gap where a wing was closed for refurbishment. What is the correct records action before reopening those outlets?
o: Ignore the gap entirely because the closed wing had no occupants at the time
Flush and, where the assessment requires, disinfect the outlets, recording the work first
Remove the wing's outlets from the monitoring schedule on a permanent basis
Backdate the flushing entries to fill the gap so the log looks continuous
Monitoring & Records.w: Standing water during closure raises risk; the outlets should be flushed (and disinfected if the assessment requires) and that remedial work recorded before the wing is brought back into use.

n.0: Lack of occupants during closure is exactly why the water stagnated.
n.2: Deleting the outlets from monitoring abandons control rather than restoring it.
n.3: Backdating entries is falsification and hides a genuine period of stagnation.

Monitoring & Records.q: An enforcing inspector visits and asks to see how the water system is being managed. Which document set best demonstrates ongoing compliance?
o: The manufacturer's glossy brochure for the taps and the fittings
A verbal assurance given by the site caretaker on the day of the inspection
The risk assessment, the written scheme and up-to-date monitoring records
The original boiler purchase invoice, sitting entirely on its own
Monitoring & Records.w: Compliance is evidenced by the current risk assessment, the written control scheme and complete, up-to-date monitoring and maintenance records showing the scheme is being followed.

n.0: A product brochure describes equipment, not how risk is being controlled over time.
n.1: Verbal assurance is not auditable evidence of a managed regime.
n.3: A purchase invoice shows procurement, not ongoing control of the system.

Monitoring & Records.q: When checking a TMV-served basin used by vulnerable people, which blended-outlet temperature would you expect to record as within the safe delivery range?
o: Around 41°C, within the typical safe blended range
At least 60°C to match the storage temperature
Below 20°C, as for a cold-only outlet
Exactly 50°C, the hot sentinel figure
Monitoring & Records.w: TMVs deliver a blended temperature typically around 38-46°C to prevent scalding of vulnerable users; a recorded value near 41°C sits within that safe range.

n.1: 60°C at the outlet would scald; that figure is the storage temperature, not the blended delivery.
n.2: Below 20°C is a cold sentinel target and would be far too cold for a blended washing outlet.
n.3: 50°C is the hot sentinel control temperature, above the safe blended delivery range for a TMV outlet.

Monitoring & Records.q: An entry shows a temperature reading but no operative's name or initials against it. Why does this weaken the record?
o: There is no traceability for who took the reading or whether to trust it
It stops the water supplier from issuing a compliance certificate for the site
It makes the ink much harder to read on the page later
It prevents the reading from being converted into Fahrenheit
Monitoring & Records.w: Without identifying who took a reading, the record loses traceability and accountability, so its reliability cannot be assured during review or investigation.

n.2: Legibility of ink is unrelated to the missing accountability information.
n.3: Unit conversion is unaffected by whether a name is present.
n.1: Water suppliers do not issue certificates from these internal logs; the issue is traceability.

Monitoring & Records.q: Over four months a calorifier's stored temperature records read 62, 61, 60 and 58°C. What does this trend indicate and require?
o: A perfect result needing no attention because none has failed yet
That the thermometer should be thrown away as clearly faulty
A downward drift to investigate before it breaches control
That monitoring should now stop since the figures are close
Monitoring & Records.w: Even though the latest figure is still near target, a steady decline signals a developing fault (such as a failing thermostat or scaling) that trend review lets you catch early.

n.0: A downward drift is a warning sign, not a perfect result.
n.1: A consistent fall points to a system issue, not a faulty instrument.
n.3: A concerning trend is a reason to maintain, not stop, monitoring.

Monitoring & Records.q: After a failed reading is put right, what should the monitoring record show about the remedial action?
o: Only that a failure occurred, with the outcome column left blank
The failure fully erased once the fix is completed on the site
Just a brief note reading 'see me' with no further detail at all
What action was taken, by whom, when, and that control was restored
Monitoring & Records.w: A complete record closes the loop: it states the corrective action, who did it, the date, and the follow-up reading confirming the outlet is back within its control limits.

n.0: Recording the failure but not the outcome leaves control unclear.
n.1: Erasing the failure destroys the evidence trail.
n.2: A vague 'see me' note is not an auditable account of what was done.

Monitoring & Records.q: During a quarterly clean an operative finds a showerhead heavily scaled and discoloured. Beyond cleaning it, what should the records reflect?
o: That the cleaning frequency need never change regardless of how much scaling occurs
The condition found, the descale and disinfection done, and any frequency review
Only the date it was done, with the poor condition left completely unmentioned
That the head was deliberately hidden from view to avoid alarming occupants
Monitoring & Records.w: The record should capture the condition observed, the remedial cleaning and disinfection performed, and prompt consideration of whether the cleaning interval needs shortening given the scaling rate.

n.0: Heavy scaling is exactly the trigger to review and possibly increase cleaning frequency.
n.2: Omitting the poor condition loses the information needed to justify any frequency change.
n.3: Concealing a component is dishonest and does nothing to control the risk.

Monitoring & Records.q: Two similar buildings have different monitoring frequencies for the same task. What most likely explains this legitimately?
o: One building simply happens to have more spare staff time available
Each building's own risk assessment sets its monitoring frequency
The colder of the two buildings can safely skip monitoring altogether
Frequencies are picked at random, so any difference is meaningless
Monitoring & Records.w: Monitoring frequencies are risk-based: the site-specific assessment determines how often each task is done according to the system, its users and its history.

n.0: Available staff time does not set safety-critical intervals; risk does.
n.2: No building can lawfully skip monitoring entirely; temperature can rise anywhere.
n.3: Frequencies are deliberately assessed, not chosen at random.

Monitoring & Records.q: As part of cold water monitoring, why is the incoming supply temperature also recorded where practicable?
o: To confirm the mains water meets the minimum drinking-water fluoride levels required
To set a baseline and reveal if the cold system is warming above the incoming value
To decide the correct colour coding for the cold pipework in the plant room
To help calculate the building's total metered water bill for the quarter
Monitoring & Records.w: Recording the incoming cold temperature provides a baseline; a rise between the supply and outlets shows the system is picking up unwanted heat, which needs investigation.

n.0: Fluoride and drinking-water chemistry are separate from temperature monitoring.
n.2: Pipe colour coding follows standards, not the incoming temperature.
n.3: Billing is unrelated to temperature monitoring for legionella control.

Monitoring & Records.q: A duty holder cannot produce any monitoring records when an outbreak is investigated. Why is this a serious position?
o: Because printing new records later is technically difficult
Because the thermometer's warranty will immediately be voided
Because without records there is no evidence controls were applied
Because the water supplier will increase the standing charge
Monitoring & Records.w: Absent records, the duty holder cannot demonstrate that the required controls were carried out; this undermines any legal defence and deprives investigators of the data needed to trace the fault.

n.0: The difficulty of reprinting is trivial next to the loss of evidence.
n.1: A thermometer warranty has no bearing on the compliance failure.
n.3: Standing charges are unrelated to legionella record-keeping.

Monitoring & Records.q: Good practice is for someone to review and sign off the monitoring records periodically. What does this review primarily achieve?
o: It transfers all of the duty holder's legal responsibility onto whoever signs
It confirms readings are within limits, spots trends and confirms failures were fixed
It entirely removes the need to actually carry out the monitoring checks in the first place
It noticeably increases the resale value of the whole building
Monitoring & Records.w: Periodic review verifies that readings sit within control limits, identifies adverse trends, and checks that any out-of-range results were investigated and resolved.

n.0: Signing a review does not shift the duty holder's responsibility.
n.2: Reviewing records does not replace performing the checks.
n.3: Resale value has nothing to do with a records review.

Monitoring & Records.q: At a non-TMV kitchen tap the operative records the hot water reaching 43°C after a minute and holding there. What does the record indicate?
o: A pass, because just about any warm water is acceptable at a kitchen tap
A perfectly acceptable cold outlet sitting within its correct range
A sign that the tap should simply be relabelled as a blended outlet
A failure to reach the 50°C hot control temperature, needing action
Monitoring & Records.w: A direct hot outlet should reach at least 50°C within a minute; 43°C sits within the legionella growth range and is an action level requiring the cause to be found and corrected.

n.0: 'Any warm water' is not the standard; the outlet is below its 50°C control temperature.
n.1: 43°C is far above the sub-20°C cold target, so it cannot be treated as an acceptable cold reading.
n.2: Relabelling a plain hot tap does not fix an undersupplied temperature and would mask the failure.

Monitoring & Records.q: What is the minimum stored-water temperature you would expect to confirm and record for a hot water calorifier serving a domestic system?
Monitoring & Records.w: Hot water should be stored at 60°C or above so that legionella cannot multiply and is killed on contact; the monitoring record confirms this storage temperature.

n.0: 38°C is a blended delivery temperature, well inside the growth range for storage.
n.1: 45°C is below the storage requirement and still within the range where legionella can grow.
n.2: 20°C is the cold water ceiling, not a hot storage target.

Monitoring & Records.q: A meeting room that was mothballed for two months is about to be brought back into use. What should the monitoring and records regime require for its outlets?
o: Permanent removal of all these outlets from the flushing schedule
Only a written note that the meeting room has reopened, with no physical action taken
Immediate normal use, since such a short closure carries no risk
Flushing, and disinfection if required, with the remedial work recorded before use
Monitoring & Records.w: Water standing for two months can allow growth; the outlets should be flushed, and disinfected where the assessment requires, with the action recorded before the room returns to use.

n.0: Removing the outlets from the schedule abandons control rather than restoring it.
n.1: A note without physical flushing leaves potentially stagnant water in service.
n.2: A two-month closure is ample time for stagnation and raised risk.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: What is the main reason a cold water storage tank must have a close-fitting lid?
o: To keep out light, dust, insects, debris and vermin
To raise the water pressure delivered around the building
To make the heavy tank easier to lift and move about
To stop the water inside from freezing during winter
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A close-fitting lid keeps out light, dust, insects, debris and birds or vermin that would contaminate the stored water and encourage bacterial growth.

n.1: A lid has no effect on pressure, which comes from the tank's height.
n.2: A lid is a hygiene barrier, not a lifting aid; tanks are fixed.
n.3: Insulation, not the lid, protects against freezing.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: You lift a tank lid and find it does not seal down properly, leaving a gap around one edge. Why is this a problem?
o: The gap will lower the temperature of the stored water
It will make the ball valve close far too quickly
The water will slowly drain out through the gap
Light, insects, dust and debris can get in and contaminate the stored water
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A gap lets in light, insects, dust and vermin, all of which contaminate the water and promote microbial growth, so the lid must be refitted to seal fully.

n.2: Water sits in the base of the tank and cannot escape through a gap at the top rim.
n.0: A gap lets warm air and light in and tends to raise temperature, not lower it.
n.1: The ball valve operation is unaffected by the lid seal.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Keeping light out of a cold water storage tank is important mainly because light encourages the growth of:
o: Limescale deposits building up across the tank walls
Rust forming on the metal fittings inside the tank
Air bubbles collecting throughout the body of the water
Algae and other micro-organisms in the stored water
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Daylight promotes the growth of algae and other micro-organisms in stored water, so a light-tight lid helps keep the water safe.

n.0: Limescale is caused by hard water and heat, not by light.
n.1: Rust is caused by moisture and oxygen, not by light.
n.2: Air bubbles are not caused by light entering the tank.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: A tank lid is made of a translucent plastic that lets daylight pass through into the tank. What should be done?
o: Fit a light-proof cover so daylight cannot reach the water
Add more water so that light cannot reach right to the bottom
Paint the inside of the tank black to block the light coming through
Leave it as it is, since a little daylight keeps the water fresh
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Daylight reaching the water encourages algae and microbial growth, so the tank needs a light-proof lid or cover.

n.1: Extra water does not block light entering through a translucent lid and still allows growth near the surface.
n.2: Painting the inside adds a coating not approved for drinking water and does not stop light entering.
n.3: Light never keeps water fresh; it encourages micro-organisms to grow.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Which of these does a properly fitting tank lid help to prevent?
o: Birds, insects and vermin entering the stored water
Water hammer knocking loudly through the pipework system
The supply pump from running completely dry
A loss of water pressure at the building's taps
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A close-fitting lid is a physical barrier that stops birds, insects and vermin entering and fouling the stored water.

n.1: Water hammer is caused by fast-closing valves, not by the tank lid.
n.2: Low-water protection for a pump is a separate control, not the lid's job.
n.3: Pressure depends on the tank height, not on whether the lid fits.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: You open a tank and see droppings and feathers floating on the surface. What is the most likely cause?
o: The tank is simply too large for the building it serves
The water has been chlorinated far too heavily
Birds have got in through a missing or ill-fitting lid
The insulation has come loose inside the tank body
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Droppings and feathers show birds have entered through a missing or poorly fitting lid, which is a serious contamination that needs cleaning and disinfection.

n.1: Chlorination does not produce droppings or feathers.
n.0: Tank size does not put droppings into the water.
n.3: Insulation is fitted on the outside of the tank and would not create droppings.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Why should the lid of a cold water storage tank be checked as part of a routine inspection?
o: To measure exactly how much water is currently in the tank
To confirm it fits closely and keeps contaminants out
To check the water pressure available at the outlets
To see whether the tank will soon need repainting
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Checking the lid confirms it still fits closely and continues to exclude light, insects, dust and vermin from the stored water.

n.0: Water level is judged by the float valve, not the lid.
n.2: Pressure checks are done at outlets, not by inspecting the lid.
n.3: Repainting is not part of a standard tank inspection.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Where should insect and vermin screens be fitted on a cold water storage tank?
o: Inside the tank, directly on the float valve arm
On the outlet pipe that feeds water to the whole building
On the overflow, warning pipe and any vent openings
Only across the tank inlet coming from the mains
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Screens are fitted on the overflow, warning pipe and vent openings because these are the routes through which insects and vermin could otherwise enter the tank.

n.0: The float valve does not open to the outside, so needs no screen.
n.1: The outlet carries water away and needs no insect screen.
n.3: The mains inlet is pressurised and not an entry route for pests.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: You inspect a tank overflow pipe and find the mesh screen is torn. What is the risk?
o: The stored water will gradually lose its normal supply pressure
The overflow will no longer carry any excess water away safely
Insects and small animals can get into the tank through the open overflow
The tank will begin to fill much more slowly than it did before
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A torn screen lets insects and small animals travel up the overflow into the tank, so it must be repaired or replaced to keep them out.

n.0: Screen condition has no effect on water pressure.
n.1: A torn screen does not block the overflow; water can still flow out.
n.3: Fill rate is controlled by the float valve and inlet, not the overflow screen.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: What is the purpose of a screen fitted to a tank's air vent?
o: To stop the stored water gradually evaporating from the tank
To let air in and out while keeping insects and dust out
To reduce the noise made as the water fills the tank
To filter limescale out of the incoming mains supply
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A vent screen allows the tank to breathe as the level changes while preventing insects, dust and debris from entering through the vent.

n.0: A closed lid limits evaporation; the vent screen excludes contaminants.
n.2: A screen is a hygiene barrier, not a noise reducer.
n.3: Vent screens do not treat mains water or remove limescale.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: An overflow (warning) pipe should be arranged so that:
o: It is left open and unscreened to allow the maximum airflow
It discharges straight down directly into the nearest available foul drain
It is screened and turns down to discharge visibly, warning of a fault
It runs uphill from the tank up towards the roof to discharge
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A warning pipe is screened against insects and turns down to a visible discharge point so an overflow is noticed and does not become an entry route.

n.0: Leaving it open and unscreened invites insects and vermin into the tank.
n.1: Connecting into a drain risks back-siphonage and hides the warning.
n.3: An overflow must fall away from the tank; it cannot run uphill.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: You find a wasps' nest built inside a tank vent where no screen is fitted. What does this tell you?
o: The tank's overflow pipe must therefore be working correctly
The tank is clearly the correct size for the demand
The stored tank water is too cold for any bacteria
The vent needs a screen fitted to keep insects out
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Insects nesting in the vent show the opening is unprotected, so a screen must be fitted to keep insects out of the stored water.

n.0: An unscreened, nested vent is a fault, not evidence the overflow works.
n.1: Insect ingress is unrelated to whether the tank is correctly sized.
n.2: An insect nest tells you nothing about water temperature.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Which statement about insect screens on a storage tank is correct?
o: They are only needed on storage tanks that are kept outdoors
They can be safely removed once the tank has been cleaned out
They should be replaced with a fine muslin cloth draped over the openings
They should be intact, correctly fitted and checked at inspections
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Screens must be intact, correctly fitted and checked at each inspection so they keep excluding insects and vermin throughout the tank's service.

n.0: Indoor tanks have overflows and vents insects use, so screens are needed too.
n.1: Screens are a permanent barrier and must never be left off after cleaning.
n.2: Loose cloth is not a durable approved screen and can rot, clog or fall in.
