Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Screens on the overflow and vent of a tank mainly protect the water from:
o: Physical entry of insects, spiders and small vermin
Sudden surges of excessive water pressure inside the storage tank
Dissolved limescale carried in from very hard water
Unusually high chlorine levels coming from the mains
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Screens are a physical barrier against insects, spiders and small vermin entering the tank through its openings.

n.2: Screens cannot remove dissolved limescale, which is a chemical property of the water.
n.3: Screens do not affect chlorine concentration.
n.1: Screens have nothing to do with controlling water pressure.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Why must cold water storage tanks and their pipework be insulated?
o: To reduce the weight the tank support must carry
To hold the water above 60°C for safety
To help keep the stored cold water below 20°C
To make the water flow faster to the taps
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Insulation helps keep stored cold water below 20°C, the temperature above which Legionella and other bacteria multiply more readily.

n.3: Insulation does not speed up flow, which depends on head and pipe size.
n.1: Cold water should stay cold and low; only hot water is held hot, and never in a cold tank.
n.0: Insulation adds a little weight and is not about reducing structural load.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Cold water should be stored and distributed below which temperature to limit bacterial growth?
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Keeping cold water below 20°C limits the growth of Legionella and other bacteria, which multiply fastest between roughly 20°C and 45°C.

n.0: 30°C is well inside the range where bacteria multiply readily.
n.1: 45°C is near the top of the growth range and far too warm for stored cold water.
n.2: 5°C is colder than required; the recognised control limit for cold water is below 20°C, not 5°C.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: You measure the stored water in a tank at 24°C. What does this indicate?
o: The tank's ball float valve has failed and jammed fully shut
The tank is clearly oversized and simply needs draining down
The water is too warm, so controls such as insulation need review
The stored water is comfortably within the cold water limit
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: At 24°C the cold water is above the 20°C limit and in the bacterial growth range, so insulation, location and turnover should be reviewed to bring it down.

n.0: A failed-shut float valve stops the tank filling; it does not raise the water temperature.
n.1: A high temperature does not prove the tank is oversized, and draining is not the fix.
n.3: 24°C is above the 20°C cold water limit, so it is not safely within it.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: A cold water tank is sited in a warm plant room next to hot pipes. Why is this a concern?
o: Heat gain can raise the stored water above 20°C
The tank will fill more quickly than normal
The overflow screen will corrode faster
The mains pressure will drop across the building
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Warm surroundings and nearby hot pipes transfer heat into the tank, raising the water above 20°C into the bacterial growth range, so insulation or relocation is needed.

n.1: Ambient heat does not change how fast the tank fills.
n.3: Room temperature does not affect mains supply pressure.
n.2: Heat gain warms the water; it is not primarily a corrosion issue for the screen.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Which practice best helps keep stored cold water cool?
o: Wrapping the tank in a dark, heat-absorbing cover
Insulating the tank and keeping it away from heat sources
Leaving the tank lid off so warm air escapes
Placing the tank directly above the building boiler
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Insulating the tank and siting it away from heat sources keeps the stored water below 20°C and limits bacterial growth.

n.0: A dark, heat-absorbing cover would gain heat rather than keep the water cool.
n.2: Removing the lid lets in light, insects and warm air and does not keep the water cool.
n.3: Placing a tank above a boiler adds heat and warms the water.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Insulation on a cold water storage tank should be:
o: Taken off during the summer months so the tank cools naturally
Made from any absorbent material to soak up damp
Fitted only to the base of the tank underneath
Complete and sound, including the lid where appropriate
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Insulation should be complete and sound so the whole tank is protected from heat gain and stays below 20°C, including insulating the lid where appropriate.

n.0: Removing insulation in summer exposes the tank to warmer ambient air and heat gain.
n.2: Insulating only the base leaves the sides and top exposed to heat.
n.1: Absorbent material that stays damp encourages mould and is not suitable tank insulation.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Why is the temperature range of about 20°C to 45°C important in water hygiene?
o: It is the range at which limescale dissolves the fastest
It is the range at which the water first begins to freeze
It is the range in which Legionella bacteria multiply most readily
It is the range at which chlorine disinfectant works best
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Legionella and similar bacteria multiply most readily between about 20°C and 45°C, which is why cold water is kept below 20°C and hot water above 60°C.

n.0: Limescale forms with heat, but this range is defined by bacterial growth.
n.1: Water freezes at 0°C, nowhere near this range.
n.3: Chlorine effectiveness is not why this range is highlighted.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: You find the insulation on a rooftop tank is missing on the sunny side. What is the likely effect?
o: The tank will start to overflow far more often than before
Solar heat gain warms the stored water above 20°C
The float valve will gradually stick fully open
The stored water pressure will noticeably increase
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: With insulation missing, sunshine heats that side of the tank and can push the stored water above 20°C into the bacterial growth range.

n.0: Missing insulation warms the water; it does not cause overflowing.
n.2: A warm tank side does not make the float valve stick open.
n.3: Insulation does not affect the water pressure.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Which of the following is essential when keeping a cold water storage tank in good hygienic condition?
o: Keeping it free of scale, sludge, sediment, rust and debris
Leaving deposits in the base to help seal any small leaks
Adding a scoop of clean sand to help the particles settle out
Keeping it filled with as much water as possible at all times
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A hygienic tank must be free of scale, sludge, sediment, rust, biofilm and debris, as these harbour and feed bacteria.

n.1: Deposits are not a sealant; they foul the water and support bacterial growth.
n.2: Adding sand introduces contamination and material for bacteria to grow on.
n.3: Overfilling has nothing to do with cleanliness and does not keep the tank hygienic.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: You open a tank lid and see a layer of brown sludge and sediment across the bottom. What should happen?
o: The water level should simply be raised above the sludge layer
Nothing, since sediment always settles harmlessly at the base
The tank should be drained, cleaned and disinfected to remove it
A splash of neat bleach poured in and the lid closed again
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Sludge and sediment harbour bacteria and biofilm, so the tank must be cleaned and disinfected to restore a hygienic condition.

n.0: Raising the level leaves the contamination in the tank feeding the water.
n.1: Settled sludge is not harmless; it is a reservoir for bacterial growth.
n.3: An unmeasured splash of bleach is not a controlled disinfection.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Biofilm inside a storage tank is a concern because it:
o: Acts as a useful protective coating for the tank
Improves the taste of the stored water
Shelters and feeds bacteria such as Legionella
Keeps the water below 20°C
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Biofilm is a slimy layer that shelters and provides nutrients for bacteria including Legionella, so it must be removed by cleaning and disinfection.

n.1: Biofilm degrades water quality; it does not improve taste.
n.0: Biofilm is harmful growth, not a protective coating.
n.3: Biofilm has no cooling effect and often signals warm, stagnant conditions.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: A dead pigeon is found floating in a storage tank. What is the correct response?
o: Top the tank right up so that the body sinks out of sight
Remove it, then clean and disinfect the tank before returning it to use
Ignore it, because the water will dilute any contamination present
Scoop it out and then simply carry on using the water straight away as normal
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A dead animal is a gross contamination, so the carcass is removed and the tank cleaned and disinfected before the water is used again.

n.0: Hiding the body does nothing to remove the contamination.
n.2: Dilution does not make contaminated water safe.
n.3: Removing the body alone leaves bacterial contamination behind.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Why should debris and dead insects never be left inside a storage tank?
o: They noticeably increase the pressure of the incoming mains supply
They cool the stored water down far below safe levels
They decompose and provide nutrients for bacterial growth
They give the stored water a strong taste of chlorine
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Decomposing debris and insects release nutrients that feed bacteria and support biofilm, so they must be removed by cleaning.

n.0: Material in the tank has no effect on mains pressure.
n.1: Debris does not cool the water.
n.3: Debris does not create a chlorine taste.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: When a tank is cleaned, rust and corrosion on the internal surfaces should be:
o: Left well alone, since the rust protects the metal underneath it
Painted over using ordinary gloss paint from the store
Removed and the surface made good with approved materials
Covered with a loose plastic sheet placed inside the tank
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Rust provides a rough surface for bacteria and biofilm, so it is removed and the surface made good with materials approved for contact with drinking water.

n.0: Rust is active corrosion, not protection, and harbours growth.
n.1: Ordinary gloss paint is not approved for wholesome water and can taint it.
n.3: A loose plastic sheet is not an approved lining and traps debris and bacteria.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Which finding inside a tank most clearly means it needs cleaning and disinfection?
o: Stored water sitting steadily at around 12°C all day
Sediment, slime and debris covering the base
Intact insect screens fitted neatly across the overflow pipe
A securely fitting, fully light-proof tank lid
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Sediment, slime and debris are contamination that harbours bacteria, so the tank needs cleaning and disinfection.

n.0: Water at 12°C is safely below the 20°C limit and is a good sign, not a fault.
n.3: A secure, light-proof lid is correct and desirable.
n.2: Intact overflow screens are exactly what an inspection wants to find.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Why should a cold water storage tank not be much larger than the building actually needs?
o: Oversized tanks let water sit and warm, causing stagnation
A large tank noticeably lowers the incoming mains water pressure
Bigger tanks cannot be fitted with a close-fitting lid at all
Larger tanks will always leak far more than smaller ones do
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: An oversized tank stores more water than is used, so it turns over slowly, sits longer, warms up and stagnates, which encourages bacterial growth.

n.1: Tank size does not reduce mains pressure.
n.2: Large tanks can and should still have close-fitting lids.
n.3: Size does not determine whether a tank leaks.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: What does 'turnover' of stored water mean in a storage tank?
o: The number of times the tank lid is opened across a year
The stored water gradually changing colour as the weeks pass
The tank being physically turned upside down to empty it out
Stored water being used and replaced regularly with fresh water
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Turnover is the regular use and replacement of the stored water with fresh mains water, which keeps it from stagnating and warming.

n.0: Lid openings are unrelated to water turnover.
n.1: A colour change is a sign of a problem, not the meaning of turnover.
n.2: Turnover refers to water exchange, not physically inverting the tank.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: A tank was sized for a large workforce that has since shrunk, so most of the water is rarely used. What is the risk?
o: The incoming mains pressure will become dangerously high
The tank will completely run dry every single day
The water stagnates and warms, encouraging growth
The insulation will absorb the extra stored water
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: With low demand the water sits for long periods, warms toward ambient and stagnates, giving bacteria time and conditions to multiply.

n.0: Reduced demand does not raise mains pressure.
n.1: Low demand means the tank is used less, so running dry is unlikely.
n.3: Insulation does not absorb water; it limits heat transfer.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Stagnant water in a storage system is a hazard mainly because:
o: It steadily raises the water pressure throughout the pipework
It makes the stored water freeze far more easily
It lets bacteria multiply and any disinfectant residual fade
It becomes far too cold to be used safely at all
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: When water stagnates it warms, the disinfectant residual decays and bacteria have time to multiply, increasing the risk of Legionella.

n.3: Stagnant water tends to warm toward ambient, not become dangerously cold.
n.0: Stagnation does not raise system pressure.
n.1: Stagnation is linked to warming and growth, not to freezing.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Which action helps maintain good turnover and reduce stagnation in a storage tank?
o: Sizing the tank to match real daily demand
Keeping the tank permanently brim full and unused
Fitting the largest tank that will physically fit
Blocking off the outlet to save water
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Matching tank size to genuine daily demand keeps the stored water moving and refreshed, reducing the time it sits and warms.

n.2: An over-large tank stores water that is not used and encourages stagnation.
n.1: A full, unused tank is the definition of stagnant storage.
n.3: Blocking the outlet stops turnover entirely and would let the water stagnate.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: You notice a large storage tank that is divided so both halves stay in use. Why can this design help?
o: It doubles the mains water pressure to the building
It removes the need for any lid on the storage tank
It stops the water ever needing to be tested again
It keeps water moving through both sections and avoids a still volume
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Keeping both sections in flow avoids a large stagnant volume and helps maintain turnover so the water does not sit and warm.

n.0: A divided tank does not change mains pressure.
n.1: Every storage tank still needs a close-fitting lid.
n.2: Good design reduces risk but monitoring is still needed.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: An unused, capped section of an old oversized tank still holds standing water connected to the system. This is best described as a:
o: A handy method of keeping the stored water cool
A normal and perfectly acceptable water storage arrangement
A useful reserve supply to draw on in busy periods
A dead leg or stagnant volume that should be removed
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Standing water in an unused section acts as a dead leg where water stagnates and bacteria grow, so it should be removed from the system.

n.0: Still, unused water tends to warm and stagnate, not stay cool.
n.1: An unused volume that never turns over is not acceptable.
n.2: Stagnant standing water is a hazard, not a safe reserve.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: How often should a cold water storage tank typically be inspected as a minimum?
o: Once every five years
Once every ten years
Only when a fault is reported
At least once a year
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Storage tanks should be inspected at least annually to check condition, cleanliness, temperature and that the lid and screens are intact.

n.0: A five-year gap is far too long to spot contamination or damage in time.
n.2: Waiting for a reported fault means problems go unnoticed until they are serious.
n.1: A ten-year interval leaves the tank unchecked for a dangerously long period.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: During a routine tank inspection, which of these should be checked?
o: Nothing inside the tank at all, so as not to disturb the stored water
Lid fit, insect screens, water clarity, temperature and material condition
Only the colour of the outside surface of the storage tank
Just the name of the plumber who originally fitted the tank
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A proper inspection covers the lid fit, insect screens, clarity of the water, temperature and the condition of the tank and its fittings.

n.0: The inside condition, clarity and temperature must be checked, not avoided.
n.2: External colour alone tells you nothing about the hygiene of the stored water.
n.3: Who fitted the tank is not a condition check.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: You open a tank for inspection and cannot see the bottom because the water is cloudy. What does this suggest?
o: That the stored water is perfectly clean and fit for use
Possible contamination or sediment needing investigation
That the tank is correctly insulated against any warming
That the tank lid is a good fit and sealing properly
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Cloudy water suggests suspended sediment or contamination, so the cause must be investigated and the tank cleaned and disinfected as needed.

n.0: Clean stored water should be clear, not cloudy.
n.2: Cloudiness is unrelated to whether the tank is insulated.
n.3: Water clarity is a separate check from lid fit.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Why is it good practice to record the findings of each tank inspection?
o: To do away entirely with the need for a close-fitting lid
So that the tank will no longer need to be cleaned out again in future
To track the tank's condition over time and to show that checks are being done
Because completing the written record itself increases the water pressure
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Written records show the tank is being monitored, track changes in condition over time and demonstrate that the required checks are carried out.

n.0: A record cannot substitute for the physical barrier of a lid.
n.1: Recording an inspection does not remove the need to clean a dirty tank.
n.3: Records have no effect on water pressure.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: On inspection you find the tank temperature is fine but a screen is missing and there are dead flies inside. What should you do?
o: Report it, clean and disinfect as needed, and refit the screen
Record only the temperature and take no action
Leave the screen off, since the water temperature is fine
Add more cold water to the tank to dilute the dead flies
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A missing screen and insect debris are faults that let contamination in, so they must be reported, the tank cleaned and disinfected as needed, and the screen refitted.

n.1: A good temperature does not cancel out the contamination and open entry route.
n.2: Leaving the screen off keeps the tank open to insects and vermin.
n.3: Dilution does not remove the flies or the contamination they cause.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Checking the stored water temperature during inspection is important because it confirms whether:
o: The paint finish on the tank walls is still sound
The incoming mains water supply pressure is set correctly
The cold water is being kept below 20°C as required
The tank is currently sitting at exactly half full
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Measuring the temperature confirms whether the cold water is being kept below 20°C, the key control against bacterial growth.

n.0: Paint condition is a separate visual check, not shown by temperature.
n.1: Temperature readings do not measure mains pressure.
n.3: Temperature does not indicate the water level.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Who should carry out cleaning and disinfection of a storage tank found to be contaminated?
o: Nobody, since tanks simply clean themselves over time
Any passer-by who happens to be available at the time
The first person to notice it, without any training at all
A competent, trained person following a safe procedure
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Cleaning and disinfection must be done by a competent, trained person following a safe, controlled procedure so the work is effective and safe.

n.1: An untrained passer-by could do the job wrongly or unsafely.
n.0: Tanks do not self-clean; contamination remains until removed.
n.2: Noticing a problem does not make someone competent to carry out disinfection.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Materials used inside a cold water storage tank, such as the lining or float valve, should be:
o: Made from untreated, absorbent material that soaks up the water
Any spare parts that physically fit the tank and its valve
WRAS-approved and suitable for contact with wholesome water
Chosen only for the lowest price available from the supplier
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Components in contact with drinking water must be approved as suitable so they do not taint the water or support bacterial growth.

n.0: Absorbent, untreated materials can leach substances and harbour bacteria.
n.1: Parts that merely fit may not be approved and could contaminate the water.
n.3: Price alone does not ensure a material is safe for drinking water.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: What is the job of the ball (float) valve in a storage tank?
o: To filter debris out of the water as it leaves the tank
To hold the tank lid down firmly and securely in place
To control the inflow and keep the water at the correct level
To heat the stored water up to a legionella-safe temperature
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: The float valve opens and closes the inlet to maintain the correct water level, preventing both overflow and running dry.

n.0: It controls level, not filtration of the outgoing supply.
n.1: It has nothing to do with securing the lid.
n.3: The float valve does not heat water and cold water should not be heated.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: You find water trickling from the overflow pipe continuously. What is the most likely cause?
o: The float valve is not shutting off the inflow properly
The insect screen fitted to the tank inlet is far too fine
The tank has been far too heavily insulated
The tank lid is fitting a little too tightly on top
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A continuous overflow usually means the float valve is failing to shut off the inflow at the correct level, so it needs adjusting or replacing.

n.1: A fine screen restricts insects, not the water level control.
n.2: Insulation controls temperature and cannot cause a continuous overflow.
n.3: A tight-fitting lid is desirable and does not cause overflowing.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: After a storage tank has been cleaned and disinfected, before returning it to normal use you should:
o: Leave the lid off for a whole week to air the tank
Remove the insect screens to help it refill faster
Confirm disinfection is complete and the water is safe to use
Immediately paint the outside of the tank body
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: The disinfection process must be properly completed and the water confirmed safe before the tank is brought back into normal service.

n.3: Painting the outside is unrelated to safely returning the tank to use.
n.1: Removing screens exposes the freshly cleaned tank to insects and vermin.
n.0: Leaving the lid off lets in light, dust and insects and undoes the cleaning.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: A galvanised tank shows heavy rust and flaking on its inner walls. What does this indicate about the material?
o: The tank must be virtually brand new on the inside
It is corroding and gives surfaces where bacteria grow
It is in ideal condition for storing clean water
The rust actually makes the stored water safer to drink
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Rust and flaking show the material is corroding, creating rough surfaces and particles that harbour bacteria and biofilm, so the tank needs attention or replacement.

n.0: Advanced rusting indicates an old or failing tank, not a new one.
n.2: Heavy corrosion is the opposite of ideal condition.
n.3: Rust contaminates the water rather than making it safer.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Which combination best describes a well-managed cold water storage tank?
o: Close-fitting lid, intact screens, insulated, inspected
Open top, no screens, in a warm location, cleaned once a decade
Translucent lid, torn screens, sited right beside the hot boiler
Oversized, always full, uninsulated and never once inspected
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A well-managed tank has a close-fitting light-proof lid, intact insect screens, adequate insulation, clean water and regular inspection, all of which control bacterial growth.

n.1: An open, unscreened tank in a warm spot invites contamination.
n.2: A translucent lid, torn screens and heat are all faults.
n.3: An oversized, uninsulated, uninspected tank stagnates and warms.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Why should a cold water storage tank be kept solely for wholesome water and not connected to other uses?
o: To stop contaminated water flowing back and fouling the supply
To reduce the number of insect screens the tank needs
To help keep the stored water a little bit warmer
To make the storage tank fill up much faster during peak demand periods
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Keeping the tank dedicated to wholesome water and protected against backflow stops contaminated water from other systems entering and fouling the supply.

n.1: Screens are still required on the overflow and vent regardless of what the tank feeds.
n.2: Cold water should be kept cool, not warmed, so warming is never a goal.
n.3: Sharing the tank with other uses does not speed up filling and adds contamination risk.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Why must a cold water storage tank have a close-fitting lid or cover?
o: To keep out light, insects, dust and debris
To make the tank easier to lift and move
To raise the water temperature above 20°C
To increase the water pressure in the system
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A close-fitting lid keeps out light, insects, dust and debris that would encourage legionella growth and contamination.

n.2: Cold water should be kept below 20°C, not warmed above it.
n.3: A lid does not affect the pressure in the system.
n.1: Tanks are not designed to be lifted; the lid is about hygiene.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Cold water in a storage tank should be kept below which temperature to control legionella?
o: Below 60°C, which is the usual hot-water storage figure
Below 30°C, which is roughly hand-warm to the touch
Below 45°C, the very top of the legionella danger zone
Below 20°C, the recognised cold-water storage limit
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Legionella multiplies between 20°C and 45°C, so stored cold water should be kept below 20°C.

n.0: 60°C is the storage temperature for hot water, not cold.
n.1: 30°C is well inside the range where legionella multiplies.
n.2: 45°C is at the top of the danger zone, not a safe cold limit.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: What is fitted to a cold water tank's overflow and vent pipes to stop pests getting in?
o: A pressure relief valve
A thermostatic mixing valve
A one-way check valve on the inlet
An insect or vermin screen
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A fine insect or vermin screen on the overflow and vent stops insects, birds and rodents entering and contaminating the water.

n.0: A pressure relief valve protects hot water systems, not against pests.
n.1: A mixing valve blends hot and cold water and does not screen pests.
n.2: A check valve prevents backflow, not the entry of insects or vermin.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Why should a cold water storage tank be insulated?
o: To speed up how quickly the stored water heats up
To stop the storage tank from overflowing at the top
To help keep the stored water below 20°C
To increase the amount of water that the tank can hold
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Insulation keeps the stored cold water cool and below 20°C, out of the temperature range where legionella multiplies.

n.0: Cold water should be kept cool, not heated up.
n.1: Overflow is controlled by the ball valve and overflow pipe, not insulation.
n.3: Insulation does not change the tank's capacity.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: How often should the condition of a cold water storage tank normally be inspected as a minimum?
o: Once every five years
Once every ten years
At least once a year
Only when a fault is reported
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Tanks should be inspected at least annually to check for debris, corrosion, a secure lid, light ingress and water clarity and temperature.

n.0: Five yearly is far too infrequent for a stored water tank.
n.3: Waiting for a fault means problems go unnoticed until it is too late.
n.1: Ten yearly leaves the tank unchecked for a dangerously long time.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: You open a cold water tank lid and find dead insects, silt and a film of algae on the water. What should you do?
o: Put the lid back and leave it until the next yearly check comes round
Add some extra insulation to the tank and simply move on
Report it and arrange for the tank to be cleaned and disinfected
Skim off the bits you can see and then take no further action at all
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Insects, silt and algae mean the tank is contaminated, so it must be reported and properly cleaned and disinfected.

n.0: Leaving known contamination lets legionella grow unchecked.
n.1: Insulation does not remove the contamination already in the tank.
n.3: Skimming the surface leaves the underlying contamination behind.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: During a tank inspection you notice daylight shining in through a gap in the lid. Why does this matter?
o: Light has no real effect on the water, so the gap can safely be ignored
Light encourages algae and organisms that help legionella grow
Light noticeably increases the water pressure in the tank
Light makes the stored water freeze over much more quickly
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Light entering the tank encourages algae and other organisms that support legionella, so the lid must exclude light completely.

n.0: Light ingress is a real hygiene problem and must be fixed.
n.2: A gap in the lid does not raise water pressure.
n.3: Light does not freeze water; if anything it warms it.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: A cold water storage cistern is found with a loose-fitting timber board resting on top instead of a proper cover. Under HSG274 Part 2, why is this a significant Legionella risk?
o: It stops the float valve working and starves the outlets
Bare timber improves insulation and lowers water below 20°C
It makes the cistern easier to inspect so no action is needed
It lets light, dust, insects and debris in, promoting growth
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A close-fitting, dust- and insect-proof lid is required to keep out light, dust, insects, debris and vermin. A loose board lets contaminants and light in, encouraging microbial and Legionella growth.

n.0: A board on top does not affect float valve operation; the risk is contamination, not supply failure.
n.1: Bare timber is not effective insulation and does not seal the cistern; it can also shed contaminants into the water.
n.2: Ease of inspection does not offset the contamination the open gap allows; the cover must still be close-fitting.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: What is the primary purpose of fitting an insect/vermin screen to the overflow and warning pipe of a cold water storage cistern?
o: To act as a backflow prevention device for the incoming main
To stop insects and vermin entering through the open pipe
To slow the flow so the overflow discharges more gently
To filter scale and sediment out of the stored water supply
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Overflow, warning and vent pipes are potential entry points; fitting screens keeps insects and vermin from getting into the cistern.

n.2: Screens are not intended to regulate flow rate of an overflow discharge.
n.0: A screen is not a backflow prevention device; a suitable air gap and valve arrangement handle backflow.
n.3: Screens keep pests out; they do not remove scale or sediment already in the water.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: During an inspection an operative measures the stored water in a loft cistern at 23°C. According to HSG274 Part 2, what does this indicate?
o: At the ideal storage temperature, so no action is needed
Too high, favouring growth, so the cause should be found
The float valve has failed and must be replaced at once
The cistern is oversized and should be drained permanently
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Stored cold water should be kept below 20°C. At 23°C it is within the range that favours Legionella proliferation, so the cause (e.g. poor insulation, warm surroundings) should be investigated and corrected.

n.0: Above 20°C is a warning sign, not an acceptable condition.
n.2: A high temperature does not indicate a failed float valve.
n.3: The finding is a temperature exceedance to investigate, not to abandon the cistern.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Why should a cold water storage cistern be correctly sized for the building's actual demand rather than deliberately oversized?
o: Oversized cisterns hold water longer, causing stagnation and warming
Oversized cisterns need much larger float valves that fail far more often
Oversized cisterns noticeably raise the mains water pressure at the outlets
Oversized cisterns cost more to insulate and are harder to lift into a loft
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A cistern sized far above demand turns water over too slowly. The long residence time allows stagnation and warming, both of which encourage Legionella growth.

n.1: Float valve reliability is not the hygiene rationale here.
n.2: Cistern size does not raise mains pressure; it feeds outlets by gravity.
n.3: Cost and handling are practical issues, not the hygiene reason.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: A cistern lid has a vent left uncovered so the cistern can 'breathe'. What is the correct arrangement under HSG274 Part 2?
o: Enlarge the vent so much more air can circulate over the water surface
Connect the vent to the overflow so that both discharge together
Seal the vent completely so that no air can enter the cistern
Fit the vent with an insect and vermin screen while allowing airflow
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Vents are required for the cistern to equalise pressure as the level changes, but they must be screened so insects, vermin and debris cannot enter.

n.0: Enlarging the opening increases the contamination risk rather than reducing it.
n.1: A vent and an overflow serve different functions and should not be combined.
n.2: Fully sealing the vent can cause pressure problems; screening is the correct control.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Which combination of materials and finish is appropriate for a cold water storage cistern used for wholesome (potable) water?
o: Galvanised steel fitted with an internal copper heating coil
WRAS-approved, non-corroding materials suitable for potable water
Reclaimed timber lined internally with heavy-duty plastic sheeting
Untreated mild steel finished with a bituminous internal coating
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Cisterns should be made from WRAS-approved, non-corroding materials suitable for contact with potable water, so they do not taint the water or shed corrosion products.

n.0: A heating coil warms the stored water, the opposite of keeping cold water below 20°C.
n.2: Improvised timber and sheeting are not approved potable-water materials.
n.3: Untreated mild steel corrodes and sheds rust; ad-hoc bituminous coatings are unsuitable.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: An operative opens a cistern and finds a layer of brown sludge and scale on the base. What is the most appropriate action sequence?
o: Add more insulation around the outside of the cistern to cool the water down
Clean and, where required, disinfect the cistern, then find why the sediment built up
Top the cistern up and simply record the water level as satisfactory
Raise the float valve setting so that the cistern then holds a much greater volume of water
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Sludge, scale and sediment provide nutrients and shelter for Legionella. The cistern should be cleaned and disinfected as required, and the underlying cause investigated to prevent recurrence.

n.0: External insulation does not remove existing sediment inside.
n.2: Recording it satisfactory ignores a clear contamination finding.
n.3: Raising the level does not clean the cistern and can worsen turnover.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: How does keeping stored cold water below 20°C help control Legionella?
o: It sterilises the incoming mains water before the cistern
It kills any legionella already present in the tank within minutes
It keeps the water outside the range in which legionella multiplies
It removes the need to keep the cistern clean and covered at all
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Legionella proliferates roughly between 20°C and 45°C. Holding cold water below 20°C keeps it outside the range where the bacteria multiply readily.

n.0: Temperature control does not sterilise the incoming supply.
n.1: Cold storage suppresses multiplication but does not rapidly kill legionella.
n.3: Temperature control works alongside cleanliness and covering, not instead.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: A cistern is installed directly against a hot water cylinder in a warm airing cupboard. Why is this location a concern?
o: The close proximity noticeably reduces the mains pressure feeding the cistern
The hot cylinder will draw cold water backwards into the cistern
Heat gain from the surroundings can raise the stored water above 20°C
The warm air will dry out the float valve washer and cause leaks
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Storing cold water next to warm plant lets heat transfer into the cistern, pushing the temperature toward or above 20°C and favouring Legionella growth. Cisterns should be sited away from heat sources and insulated.

n.0: Proximity to a cylinder does not reduce incoming mains pressure.
n.1: A hot cylinder does not siphon water back into a feed cistern.
n.3: Warm air is not why float valves fail; the concern is water temperature.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: What is the main hygiene reason for insulating a cold water storage cistern and its associated pipework?
o: To cut down the noise made by water entering the cistern
To increase the total volume of water that the cistern is able to hold
To make the float valve inside operate a little more quietly
To limit heat gain and keep the stored cold water below 20°C
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Insulation limits heat gain from warm surroundings, helping keep the stored cold water below 20°C and out of the Legionella growth range.

n.0: Noise reduction is not the water-hygiene purpose of insulation.
n.1: Insulation does not change the cistern's capacity.
n.2: Float valve noise is unrelated to the hygiene reason for insulation.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: How often should cold water storage cisterns typically be inspected as part of a Legionella control scheme?
o: Only when a fault is eventually reported by one of the building's occupants
Once every ten years, at the time of a major building refurbishment
At least annually, or more frequently where conditions require
Only once, during commissioning, and then never inspected again after
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Cisterns should be inspected on a regular, scheduled basis, commonly at least annually, with more frequent checks where the risk assessment or conditions indicate.

n.0: Waiting for occupant complaints is reactive and misses developing contamination.
n.1: Ten-yearly intervals are far too long for a Legionella control scheme.
n.3: Commissioning checks alone do not maintain ongoing control.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: During a routine visit an operative notices the cistern lid is present but has a gap around a pipe penetration where daylight is visible. What is the correct interpretation?
o: Daylight helps the operative see the water level, so the gap is acceptable
The gap lets light and contaminants in and should be sealed to restore the cover
The gap provides necessary ventilation and so it must simply be left open as it is
The gap shows the cistern is correctly sized and needs no further action
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: The cover must be close-fitting and light-excluding. A gap at a pipe penetration lets in light, dust and insects and must be sealed while still allowing screened venting.

n.0: Admitting daylight encourages microbial growth; the gap is a defect, not a convenience.
n.2: Ventilation is provided by a screened vent, not by an unsealed gap around a pipe.
n.3: A gap in the cover has nothing to do with correct sizing.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Why are dead insects, leaves and other debris found floating in a cistern considered a Legionella control problem?
o: They lower the stored water temperature below the safe range
They noticeably improve the taste of the stored water
They increase the mains pressure entering the cistern
They provide nutrients that support microbial growth
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Organic debris supplies nutrients for biofilm and micro-organisms, supporting Legionella growth. Their presence also shows the cover or screens are failing to keep contaminants out.

n.0: Debris does not cool the water; if anything it signals failed protection.
n.1: Contaminants degrade water quality; they do not improve it.
n.2: Floating debris has no effect on incoming mains pressure.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: A building has two cisterns supplying the same system, but valves are set so nearly all draw-off comes from one cistern. What is the water-hygiene concern?
o: The little-used cistern stagnates and warms into a legionella reservoir
The heavily used cistern will end up running permanently dry
The arrangement guarantees the water always stays below 20°C
Having two cisterns will always double the mains pressure that is available
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Where flow is not balanced, the little-used cistern experiences low turnover, stagnation and warming, allowing it to become a reservoir for Legionella. Turnover across storage should be maintained.

n.1: The heavily used cistern is fed by its float valve and refills; it does not run permanently dry.
n.3: Multiple cisterns do not increase mains pressure.
n.2: Poor turnover tends to raise, not guarantee low, stored water temperature.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: What is the correct function of the warning pipe (as distinct from the overflow) on a cold water storage cistern?
o: To vent the air displaced as the cistern fills up
To drain the whole cistern completely for cleaning
To supply water to the lowest outlet in the building
To visibly warn the level has risen too high
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: The warning pipe discharges in a visible position to warn that the level has risen above normal, indicating a passing or failed float valve, before the higher overflow is reached. It must be screened against pests.

n.0: Venting is provided by a screened vent, not the warning pipe.
n.1: Draining for cleaning is done via a drain-down point.
n.2: The warning pipe is not a supply pipe to outlets.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: A float (ball) valve is found dripping continuously so the cistern overflows intermittently. Beyond wasting water, why does this matter for Legionella control?
o: A faulty valve and open overflow can admit pests and signal lost control
A continually passing valve actually proves the cistern is sized correctly
Continuous overflowing keeps the stored water permanently below 20°C always
Overflowing raises the mains water pressure across the whole building supply
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A passing float valve causes discharge through the overflow, and a running overflow with a compromised screen is an entry route for insects and vermin. The valve should be repaired to restore proper level control.

n.1: A leaking valve indicates a defect, not correct sizing.
n.2: Overflowing does not reliably control temperature; it is a fault.
n.3: An overflowing cistern does not raise mains pressure.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Which statement best describes how sediment at the bottom of a cistern and biofilm on its walls relate to Legionella?
o: They keep the stored water cool and therefore actually reduce the overall risk
They shelter and feed micro-organisms, protecting legionella from controls
They only ever matter in hot water systems, not in cold cisterns
They are quite harmless as long as a tight lid is fitted
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Sediment and biofilm provide nutrients and physical shelter, protecting Legionella and other organisms and making temperature or biocide control less effective. Cisterns must be kept clean.

n.0: They do not cool the water; they increase risk.
n.2: Sediment and biofilm are a recognised cold-water storage problem, not just a hot-water issue.
n.3: A fitted lid helps keep contaminants out but does not neutralise sediment and biofilm already present.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: An operative is asked to disinfect a cistern found heavily contaminated. What is the correct principle before returning it to service?
o: Clean out the debris and sludge first, then disinfect the now-clean surfaces
Leave the sediment in place so the disinfectant has something to work on
Disinfect it first and then clean out all the debris afterwards
Simply refill it with fresh mains water without cleaning or disinfecting
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Physical cleaning to remove sludge and debris should precede disinfection, because organic matter consumes and shields against biocide. Cleaning then disinfection lets the biocide act effectively on clean surfaces.

n.1: Sediment protects micro-organisms from disinfectant rather than helping it work.
n.2: Disinfecting over debris wastes biocide and leaves shielded organisms.
n.3: Refilling without cleaning or disinfecting leaves a contaminated cistern in service.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Why should the cold water storage cistern feed the system so that water is drawn off and replaced regularly (good turnover)?
o: So the cistern can then quite safely be left completely uncovered without any risk at all
So fresh, cooler mains water regularly replaces the stored water, limiting stagnation
So protective scale forms faster and coats the base of the cistern
So that a much smaller and far cheaper float valve can be fitted to the cistern inlet
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Regular turnover means stored water is frequently replaced with fresh, cooler mains water, reducing residence time, stagnation and the temperature rise that favour Legionella.

n.0: Good turnover does not remove the need for a close-fitting cover.
n.2: Scale is a contaminant to be removed, not encouraged.
n.3: Turnover is about water quality, not float valve cost.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: On a hot summer visit an operative records the incoming mains at 15°C but the top of the stored water at 24°C. What is the most likely cause to investigate?
o: The overflow screen mesh is far too fine and is heating up the stored water
The incoming mains supply is contaminated and should be shut off
Heat gain and stratification from warm surroundings and poor insulation
The tank's float valve is oversized for the cistern it serves
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A large gap between incoming mains and stored temperature, with the surface warmest, points to heat gain from warm surroundings and inadequate insulation. Insulation, siting and turnover should be reviewed.

n.0: A screen mesh does not heat water; the rise comes from heat gain.
n.1: Cool incoming mains at 15°C is normal, not proof of contamination.
n.3: Float valve size does not warm the stored water.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Which of the following is the correct reason a cold water storage cistern must be provided with a properly fitting, light-tight cover?
o: A close cover raises the stored water temperature enough to aid disinfection
Light and airborne contaminants promote algal and microbial growth
A cover removes any need to insulate the cistern at all
A cover increases the flow rate delivered to the taps
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Excluding light discourages algae, and a close-fitting light-tight cover keeps out dust, insects, debris and vermin that would otherwise support microbial and Legionella growth.

n.0: Cold storage should stay below 20°C; a cover is not to warm it.
n.2: A cover and insulation address different risks; one does not replace the other.
n.3: A cover has no effect on the flow rate delivered to outlets.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: A newly installed plastic cistern has a screened vent, screened overflow and close-fitting lid, but the lid is a light translucent colour that lets daylight through. What should be done?
o: Replace or over-cover the lid so it excludes daylight fully
Remove the pest screens so the translucent lid can ventilate it
Nothing, because the lid is close-fitting and that is all that matters
Paint the inside of the cistern black to absorb the daylight
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A cover must exclude light as well as fit closely. A translucent lid admits daylight that encourages algae and microbial growth, so it should be replaced or over-covered with a light-excluding cover.

n.2: Close fit alone is not enough; light exclusion is also required.
n.1: Removing pest screens introduces a contamination route and does not solve the light problem.
n.3: Painting the interior introduces non-approved materials in contact with potable water and does not address the translucent lid correctly.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: What is the correct arrangement of the cold feed (outlet) and the inlet on a storage cistern to encourage good mixing and turnover?
o: Inlet and outlet set so water flows across the cistern to the draw-off, avoiding dead zones
Inlet and outlet both fitted at the base so no fresh water reaches the surface
Inlet and outlet placed immediately next to each other on the same side
Outlet fitted at the very top so only the warmest surface water is drawn off
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Positioning the inlet and outlet so water flows across the cistern promotes turnover and mixing, avoiding short-circuiting and stagnant dead zones where Legionella can develop.

n.1: Drawing only from the base leaves surface water stagnant and is poor practice.
n.2: Adjacent inlet and outlet short-circuit the flow, leaving most water stagnant.
n.3: Drawing only warm surface water leaves cooler water below stagnant.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: An operative finds rust staining and flaking on the interior of an old galvanised cistern. Why is corrosion a water-hygiene concern?
o: Rust actually lowers the water temperature and genuinely improves its overall quality
Corrosion noticeably increases the mains pressure reaching the outlets
Rust particles and rough surfaces harbour sediment and biofilm that support growth
Rust proves the cistern is still made from fully WRAS-approved material
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Corrosion products create sediment and rough surfaces that trap debris and biofilm, providing nutrients and shelter for micro-organisms including Legionella. Non-corroding, approved materials are required.

n.0: Rust does not cool the water and degrades, not improves, its quality.
n.1: Corrosion has no effect on mains pressure.
n.3: Visible corrosion indicates unsuitable or degraded material, not approved material.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: A cistern in a seldom-used wing shows very low turnover on the risk assessment. Which control is most appropriate to reduce Legionella risk?
o: Raise the stored water temperature to try to pasteurise it
Leave it exactly as found, since low use means low risk
Restore turnover and keep it clean, cool and covered
Remove the cistern lid to let the water cool naturally
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Low turnover leads to stagnation and warming. The control is to restore regular use or flushing, right-size storage where possible, and maintain cleanliness, temperature and covering.

n.0: Warming stored cold water is the opposite of the required control and increases risk.
n.1: Low use actually raises stagnation risk; it must be actively managed, not ignored.
n.3: Removing the lid exposes the water to light and contaminants, worsening risk.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: What is the correct purpose of maintaining a suitable air gap where the mains inlet discharges into a storage cistern?
o: To filter out sediment from the incoming supply
To warm the incoming water up before it is stored
Backflow protection so stored water cannot return to the mains
To raise the noise so a passing valve can be heard
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: A suitable air gap between the inlet and the water level provides backflow prevention, stopping potentially contaminated stored water from siphoning back into the wholesome mains.

n.1: An air gap does not warm the water; the aim is cold storage.
n.0: The gap is a backflow safeguard, not a sediment filter.
n.3: Its purpose is contamination prevention, not making noise.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: During cleaning, an operative removes the lid and rests tools and a jacket on the open cistern rim. Why is this poor practice?
o: It increases the mains water pressure while the lid is removed
It causes the cistern's float valve to close permanently
It risks dropping dirt and microbes into the open water
It could lower the stored water temperature much too far
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: With the cover off, the water is exposed. Placing dirty items over or near the opening risks dropping dirt, debris and micro-organisms into the water. Good hygiene discipline is essential during any cistern work.

n.0: Removing the lid does not change mains pressure.
n.1: Items on the rim do not lock the float valve closed.
n.3: Tools on the rim do not meaningfully cool the water.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Which record is most important to keep after inspecting or cleaning a cold water storage cistern under a Legionella control scheme?
o: Only the brand of disinfectant used, with no dates or findings noted
A note of who was on site, but nothing about the cistern's condition
A dated record of the condition found, temperatures and actions taken
No record at all is needed, provided the cistern simply looked acceptable
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Control schemes require documented evidence: dated records of condition, temperatures, cleaning or disinfection carried out and remedial actions support monitoring and demonstrate control.

n.0: The disinfectant brand alone, without dates or findings, is not evidence.
n.1: Attendance without condition data fails to record the cistern's state.
n.3: Records are required even when conditions look acceptable.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: A cistern's insect screen on the overflow is found torn. Why should it be repaired or replaced promptly?
o: It leaves an open route for insects and vermin to enter the cistern
A torn screen gradually lowers the temperature of the stored water below normal
A torn screen dangerously slows the overflow's discharge of water
A torn screen increases the mains water pressure to the building
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: The screen's job is to block pests at an opening in the cistern. Once torn, insects and vermin can enter, contaminating the water, so it must be repaired or replaced without delay.

n.1: A screen has no role in controlling water temperature.
n.2: Overflow discharge speed is not the safety concern; contamination entry is.
n.3: A damaged screen does not affect mains pressure.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Why is a very large single cistern often replaced or subdivided into smaller cisterns in modern Legionella-conscious design?
o: Divided storage improves turnover and keeps supply on during cleaning
Larger single cisterns always keep the water cooler and are preferred
Smaller cisterns remove any need to fit covers and insect screens
Smaller cisterns hold the water long enough for it to warm up naturally
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Matching storage to demand improves turnover and reduces stagnation; dividing storage lets one part be isolated and cleaned while supply continues, aiding both hygiene and maintenance.

n.1: Oversized storage tends to stagnate and warm rather than stay cool.
n.2: Smaller cisterns still require covers and screens.
n.3: Allowing water to warm through long residence is undesirable, not a design aim.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: An operative is asked why cold water storage temperature is checked at the ball valve inlet and at the cistern outlet. What does comparing these readings help reveal?
o: Whether the overflow warning pipe is discharging into the correct foul drain outside
Whether the incoming mains water is being over-chlorinated somewhere back at the source
Whether the stored water is warming above the incoming supply toward the growth range
Whether the cistern's float valve is fitted in the correct colour coding
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Comparing incoming and stored/outgoing temperatures shows any heat gain within the cistern. A significant rise toward 20°C flags stagnation or heat gain needing attention.

n.0: Overflow routing is a separate check from stored temperature.
n.1: These checks do not measure chlorine levels at source.
n.3: Float valve colour is irrelevant to temperature monitoring.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: A cistern serving a healthcare ward is found with a poorly fitting lid and warm, discoloured water. Given the vulnerable occupants, what is the appropriate response?
o: Ignore the finding because the ward taps happen to be used fairly often
Treat it as priority: report, clean, disinfect and correct defects
Delay any action until the next annual service falls due
Simply top it up with fresh water and loosely refit the lid
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Warm, discoloured water with a failed cover in a setting with vulnerable people is high priority. It should be reported and remediated promptly: cleaning/disinfection as required plus correcting the cover, temperature and turnover.

n.0: Frequent use does not excuse contaminated, warm stored water for at-risk patients.
n.2: Vulnerable occupants make delay to the next annual service unacceptable.
n.3: Topping up and refitting a loose lid does not clean the water or restore a cover.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: Which statement about the relationship between cleanliness and temperature control in cold water storage is correct?
o: A clean cistern can safely store its water at absolutely any temperature
Temperature control only ever applies to hot water, not to cold storage
Cleanliness and keeping water below 20°C are complementary controls
Keeping the water below 20°C means cleanliness no longer matters at all
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Legionella control relies on multiple barriers. Keeping the cistern clean and keeping stored water below 20°C work together; neither on its own removes the need for the other.

n.0: Even a clean cistern must keep cold water below 20°C.
n.1: Keeping cold water below 20°C is a specific cold-storage requirement.
n.3: Low temperature suppresses growth, but sediment and biofilm still risk.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: An operative finds a cistern where the overflow and warning pipe have been joined into a single pipe with no screen at the open end. What is the correct assessment?
o: The pipe should simply be sealed shut to stop any discharge
The open end must be fitted with an insect and vermin screen to keep pests out of the cistern
Acceptable, because an unscreened open end lets the cistern breathe
Acceptable, because combining the pipes usefully saves material
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: Any pipe open to the cistern interior is a pest entry route and must be screened. The open discharge end requires an insect/vermin screen while still allowing the pipe to discharge.

n.3: Saving material does not justify an unscreened open route for pests into the cistern.
n.2: Venting is provided by a screened vent; an unscreened open pipe is a contamination risk, not acceptable breathing.
n.0: Sealing an overflow/warning pipe would stop it protecting against high water level; it must discharge but be screened.

Cold Water Storage Tanks.q: After cleaning and disinfecting a contaminated cistern, what is the correct final step before returning it to normal use?
o: Flush out the disinfectant to acceptable levels, then refill with wholesome water
Return it to use immediately while it is still at the full disinfectant concentration
Leave the disinfectant in the stored water permanently for ongoing protection
Drain it right down and simply leave it empty to prevent any future growth
Cold Water Storage Tanks.w: After disinfection the cistern and system must be flushed/rinsed so residual disinfectant is reduced to acceptable levels, then refilled with wholesome water before being returned to service.

n.1: Supplying water at full disinfection concentration is unsafe for use.
n.2: High-concentration disinfectant is not left in potable stored water.
n.3: Leaving the cistern empty removes the supply and does not return it to service.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: What is a calorifier?
o: A vessel that stores and heats the hot water supply
A pump that circulates cold water around the building
A filter fitted to strip sediment from the mains supply
A tank holding cold water before it reaches the taps
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: A calorifier is a storage vessel that heats and holds hot water ready for use in the building.

n.1: A calorifier stores and heats water; it is not a circulating pump.
n.2: A calorifier is a heated storage vessel, not a sediment filter.
n.3: Cold water storage is a separate cistern, not a calorifier.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: At what temperature should the water stored in a hot water calorifier be kept?
o: Between 45°C and 50°C
At or above 40°C
At or above 60°C
Between 20°C and 45°C
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Storing hot water at 60°C or above controls legionella because the bacteria do not survive well at that temperature.

n.3: 20°C to 45°C is the range where legionella multiply, so it is unsafe for storage.
n.1: 40°C is too low and sits within the range that lets legionella grow.
n.0: 45°C to 50°C is still within or near the growth range and is too low for safe storage.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Why is hot water stored at 60°C or above rather than at a lower, more energy-saving temperature?
o: Because legionella bacteria are killed off at that temperature
Because water that hot simply tastes noticeably better
Because storing it that hot lowers the water pressure at all the taps
Because it stops the pipes across the building from rusting
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: At 60°C and above legionella bacteria are killed, so keeping storage hot is the main control measure.

n.1: Taste is not the reason; the temperature controls bacteria.
n.2: Storage temperature is about killing bacteria, not pressure.
n.3: Temperature is chosen to kill legionella, not to prevent corrosion.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: The temperature range in which legionella bacteria multiply most readily is generally given as:
o: Between 60°C and 80°C
Between 0°C and 10°C
Between 20°C and 45°C
Between 50°C and 60°C
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Legionella multiply readily between about 20°C and 45°C, which is why hot storage is kept above this band.

n.0: Above 60°C the bacteria are killed, not multiplying.
n.1: Below 20°C the bacteria stay dormant rather than multiplying readily.
n.3: 50°C to 60°C is above the main growth band and is used to hold water safe.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A calorifier is best described as which part of the hot water system?
o: The thermostatic mixing valve fitted at the tap outlet
The heated storage vessel that supplies hot water to outlets
The expansion vessel mounted on the heating circuit
The cold feed cistern located in the roof space
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: The calorifier is the heated store that feeds hot water out to the taps and other outlets.

n.0: A mixing valve blends water at the outlet; it does not store it.
n.2: An expansion vessel absorbs pressure changes and stores nothing.
n.3: The cold feed cistern supplies cold water in, not the heated store.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Keeping a calorifier at the correct hot temperature is described in water hygiene guidance as:
o: Something only required in swimming pools
A key control measure against legionella
A measure that increases the risk of legionella
An optional step only needed in summer
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Maintaining correct storage temperature is one of the main control measures for legionella in hot water systems.

n.3: Temperature control is needed year round, not only in summer.
n.0: It applies to hot water systems in all types of building, not only pools.
n.2: Correct hot temperature reduces the risk; it does not increase it.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Which statement about a hot water calorifier is correct?
o: It should be run cold to remove any risk of scalding
It should heat the stored water so it is delivered hot right through the system
It should keep the water lukewarm to save on fuel
It is only ever used to store cold drinking water
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: A calorifier's job is to heat and store water so it reaches the outlets hot enough to control bacteria.

n.2: Lukewarm water sits in the growth range and is unsafe.
n.3: A calorifier stores hot water, not cold drinking water.
n.0: Running it cold would encourage bacteria; scalding is controlled by mixing valves, not by cooling storage.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Where in a calorifier does sludge and sediment tend to collect?
o: At the base of the vessel
Only in the flow pipe leaving the vessel
Evenly spread through the whole vessel
At the very top of the vessel
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Sludge and sediment settle and collect at the base of the calorifier under gravity.

n.3: Sediment settles downward, so it does not gather at the top.
n.1: Debris settles inside the vessel rather than collecting only in the outgoing flow pipe.
n.2: It does not stay evenly spread; it settles to the bottom.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Why is sludge at the base of a calorifier a particular concern for legionella control?
o: It improves the flow of hot water reaching the taps upstairs
It makes the stored water hotter than it was ever intended to be
It has no effect on legionella in the calorifier at all
It can shelter legionella and provide nutrients for them
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Sludge and sediment shelter legionella and provide nutrients, protecting the bacteria from heat.

n.0: Sludge restricts and fouls the system rather than improving flow.
n.1: Sludge does not raise the water temperature; it insulates cooler pockets.
n.2: Sludge harbours bacteria, so it does have an effect.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: What should be done about the sludge that collects in the base of a calorifier?
o: It should be left in place, as it protects the metal base
It should be drained off and the base de-sludged periodically
It should be topped up with extra sediment to seal the base
It should be heated to a higher temperature and simply ignored
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: The base is drained and de-sludged periodically so bacteria have nowhere to shelter.

n.0: Leaving sludge in place lets it shelter legionella, so it must be removed.
n.2: Adding sediment increases the risk; the aim is to remove it.
n.3: Heating alone does not clear the sludge, which still shelters bacteria.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: During calorifier inspection, why is a drain valve at the lowest point of the vessel important?
o: It measures the flow temperature of the hot water
It lets settled sediment and sludge drain from the base
It vents trapped air out from the top of the vessel
It mixes cold water in to help prevent scalding
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: A low-level drain valve allows the settled sludge at the base to be flushed out during maintenance.

n.0: Temperature is read with a thermometer or sensor, not a drain valve.
n.2: Air is vented at the top; the base drain is for removing sludge.
n.3: Scald protection is provided by mixing valves, not by the drain point.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A calorifier is opened for inspection and a layer of soft brown sludge is found in the base. What does this indicate?
o: That the stored water is being kept far too hot
That the vessel is working perfectly and needs no action at all
That the drain valve is fitted at the wrong height
A build-up that can harbour legionella and must be removed
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Sludge in the base is a build-up that can shelter legionella and must be drained and cleaned out.

n.1: Sludge build-up is a fault to correct, not a sign of perfect operation.
n.0: Sludge relates to settled debris, not to the water being too hot.
n.2: The presence of sludge does not tell you the drain height is wrong; it tells you the base needs de-sludging.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Which of these best explains how sediment protects legionella from heat inside a calorifier?
o: It circulates the bacteria harmlessly out to the drain
It removes all the nutrients the bacteria need to grow
It raises the whole vessel to well above 60°C throughout
It insulates and shelters the bacteria in cooler pockets at the base
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Sediment insulates and shelters bacteria in cooler pockets, protecting them from the hot stored water.

n.0: Sediment settles and stays put; it does not flush bacteria away.
n.1: Sediment supplies nutrients and debris rather than removing them.
n.2: Sediment does not heat the vessel; it shields cooler areas.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: De-sludging a calorifier as part of routine control is mainly carried out to:
o: Raise the stored water temperature to above 80°C at all times
Reduce the flow rate delivered to the building's outlets
Remove settled deposits that can support bacterial growth
Add fresh nutrients into the stored hot water supply
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: De-sludging removes the settled deposits that would otherwise support and shelter bacterial growth.

n.0: De-sludging clears deposits; it does not set the storage temperature.
n.1: It keeps the vessel clean; it is not done to reduce flow.
n.3: The aim is to remove nutrient-rich debris, not to add nutrients.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Which practice helps keep the base of a calorifier free from harmful sediment?
o: Never opening the vessel once it is installed
Regular draining and inspection of the base
Keeping the drain valve permanently sealed
Lowering the storage temperature below 50°C
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Regular draining and inspection of the base removes sediment before it can shelter bacteria.

n.0: Never opening the vessel lets sludge build up unchecked.
n.2: A permanently sealed drain prevents the base being cleared of sludge.
n.3: Lowering the temperature encourages bacterial growth rather than controlling it.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: What is meant by 'stratification' inside a hot water calorifier?
o: Hot water sitting on cooler layers, so temperature varies with height
Sludge slowly dissolving evenly throughout all of the stored water
The water sitting at exactly the same temperature throughout the vessel
Air becoming trapped somewhere along the hot flow pipe
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Stratification is layering, where hotter water rises to the top and cooler water sits below, so temperature varies with depth.

n.1: Stratification refers to temperature layers, not to sludge dissolving.
n.2: Even temperature throughout is the opposite of stratification.
n.3: Trapped air in a pipe is a separate issue from temperature layering in the store.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Because of stratification, which part of a calorifier is most likely to be cooler than the rest?
o: The top of the vessel
The base of the vessel
The outgoing flow connection
The insulation on the outside
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Cooler water settles low, so the base of the calorifier is most likely to be below the target temperature.

n.0: Hot water rises, so the top is usually the hottest part.
n.2: The flow leaves from the hotter upper region, not the cool zone.
n.3: External insulation is not part of the stored water's temperature layering.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Why does the whole volume of water in a calorifier need to reach the control temperature, not just the top?
o: Because the outgoing flow pipe draws only from the coldest bottom layer
Cooler layers, especially at the base, can let legionella survive
Because only the base water ever actually reaches the taps
Because the top layer is the part that cools down fastest
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: If cooler layers remain, particularly at the base, legionella can survive there, so the whole volume must reach temperature.

n.0: The flow normally draws from the hotter top, which is why the neglected base is the risk.
n.2: Water is drawn from the hotter upper region, but surviving base bacteria can still spread.
n.3: The concern is the cool base surviving, not the top cooling fastest.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A thermometer at the top of a calorifier reads 62°C, but a check at the base reads 41°C. What is the most likely explanation?
o: The whole vessel is actually safely above 60°C throughout its volume
The base thermometer must simply be reading far too high a value
Hot water has settled and collected right down at the very base
The vessel is stratified and the base is not reaching temperature
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: A hot top and cool base is classic stratification, showing the base is not reaching the control temperature.

n.0: A base of 41°C means the vessel is not safely above 60°C throughout.
n.1: 41°C is a low reading, not a falsely high one.
n.2: Hot water rises to the top; cooler water collects at the base.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Stratification in a calorifier is a hygiene concern mainly because:
o: It can leave a cool zone at the base within the growth range
It makes the water at the taps far too hot to use safely at all
It usefully removes sludge from the base of the vessel
It increases the overall storage capacity of the vessel
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Stratification can leave the base in the 20°C to 45°C growth range, allowing legionella to multiply.

n.1: Stratification leaves a cool base; it does not overheat the tap water.
n.2: Stratification does not clear sludge; cool bases and sludge often occur together.
n.3: It does not change the vessel's capacity; it changes the temperature distribution.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: To overcome stratification and make sure the base heats up, a calorifier may be fitted with or checked for:
o: A cold water bypass fitted to cool the vessel base
Extra sludge left in the base to help hold the heat in
Adequate heat input and, where fitted, a shunt pump to mix the contents
A reduced storage temperature setting on the thermostat
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Enough heat input, sometimes with a shunt pump to circulate the contents, helps bring the whole volume including the base up to temperature.

n.0: Cooling the base with a bypass would make the problem worse.
n.1: Sludge insulates cool pockets and shelters bacteria; remove it.
n.3: Lowering the setting would leave more of the vessel too cool.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Which reading pattern in a calorifier would suggest the whole volume is safely up to temperature?
o: Top and base both reading at or above 60°C
Top at 60°C but the base sitting right down at only 35°C
Top at only 45°C with the base up at 60°C
Top at 55°C and the base lagging at 40°C
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: When both the top and the base sit at or above 60°C, the whole volume has reached the control temperature.

n.1: A base at 35°C shows a cool zone in the growth range, so it is not safe throughout.
n.2: A top at 45°C is below the safe storage value.
n.3: A base at 40°C is within the growth range and not up to temperature.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Which of these is the correct way to think about a calorifier's stored temperature?
o: The average of the top and the base is really all that counts
Only the hottest layer of water at the very top actually matters
The coolest part of the volume, not just the hottest, must be controlled
Only the temperature of the incoming cold feed needs checking
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Control depends on the coolest part of the stored water reaching temperature, because that is where bacteria could survive.

n.0: An average can hide a cool base still in the growth range.
n.1: The hot top can mask a dangerously cool base.
n.3: The cold feed temperature does not show the store is heated through.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: On a hot water calorifier, which two temperatures are routinely monitored to check the system is working?
o: The flow temperature and the return temperature
The drain-off water and the outside air temperature
The insulation surface and the plant room floor slab
The cold feed inlet and the general room temperature
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: The flow leaving the calorifier and the return coming back are the two temperatures routinely monitored to confirm hot water is maintained.

n.1: Drain water and outside air are not the routine monitoring points for the hot circuit.
n.2: Surface and floor temperatures are not the hot water flow and return.
n.3: Room and cold feed temperatures do not confirm the hot circuit is holding heat.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: The flow temperature from a hot water calorifier should normally be at least:
o: Around 40°C, which sits within the growth range
Around 30°C, well inside the growth range
Around 45°C, near the top of the growth range
At least 60°C leaving the calorifier
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Hot water should leave the calorifier at 60°C or above so it stays hot as it travels round the system.

n.0: 40°C is within the growth range and unsafe as a flow temperature.
n.1: 30°C is well within the growth range and far too low.
n.2: 45°C is too low; it sits near the top of the growth range.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: The return temperature of a hot water circuit coming back to the calorifier should commonly be kept at least:
o: At least 50°C on return
Around 30°C on the return leg
About 10°C on the return leg
Roughly 20°C on the return leg
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: The return should stay at 50°C or above so that no part of the circulating loop drops into the growth range.

n.1: 30°C is within the growth range and shows the loop has cooled too far.
n.3: 20°C is far too low and well inside the growth range.
n.2: 10°C would mean the hot loop has effectively gone cold.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A calorifier flow reads 60°C but the return reads 43°C. What does the low return most likely mean?
o: The system is performing exactly as it was intended to
The return thermometer must be reading much too high
The stored water is far too hot and must be reduced
Hot water is losing too much heat around the loop
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: A return well below the recommended value shows the water is losing too much heat around the loop, allowing cool zones to form.

n.0: A return in the growth range is a fault, not intended performance.
n.1: 43°C is a low reading, not a falsely high one.
