n.2: A low return points to heat loss, not the store being too hot.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Why is monitoring the return temperature as well as the flow temperature important?
o: Only the return-side water ever actually reaches the building's taps
The flow temperature simply cannot be measured directly
The return is always a good deal hotter than the flow
It confirms the whole loop stays hot, not just the outlet
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Checking the return confirms that water is still hot after travelling round the building, so no cool zones have developed.

n.0: Taps are fed from the flow side; the return brings unused water back.
n.1: The flow temperature can be measured directly at the calorifier.
n.2: The return is normally slightly cooler than the flow, not hotter.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: If routine monitoring shows the calorifier return temperature has been steadily falling over several weeks, the appropriate response is to:
o: Investigate the cause, as heat loss may be creating cool zones
Ignore it, because the return temperature does not really matter
Seal the return pipe so that no water can come back at all
Lower the flow temperature right down to match the falling return
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: A falling return should be investigated because heat loss in the circulation loop can create cool zones where legionella grow.

n.1: The return temperature is a key monitoring value and must not be ignored.
n.2: Sealing the return would stop circulation and make the risk worse.
n.3: Lowering the flow to match a poor return spreads the problem instead of fixing it.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Recording flow and return temperatures on a regular schedule is an example of:
o: A task that removes any need to keep the water hot at all going forward
A one-off check that is only needed at installation time
Routine monitoring that shows the control scheme is working
An optional extra that carries no real hygiene value at all
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Regular flow and return records are routine monitoring that demonstrates the temperature control scheme is being maintained.

n.0: Monitoring confirms the water is hot; it does not remove the need to keep it hot.
n.1: Monitoring is ongoing, not a single check at installation.
n.3: It has clear hygiene value as evidence that control is being kept.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: What is the purpose of a secondary circulation (secondary return) on a hot water system?
o: To keep the hot water moving so that it stays hot throughout the building
To filter sediment out of the hot water as it circulates
To supply cold water to all of the drinking taps around the building
To store extra hot water ready for periods of peak demand
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: A secondary return continuously circulates hot water so it stays hot in the pipework and does not cool in long runs.

n.1: Sediment removal is done by draining and cleaning, not the loop.
n.2: The secondary return handles hot water, not the cold supply.
n.3: Storage is the calorifier's job; the loop keeps water moving.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Without a working secondary return, what tends to happen to hot water in long pipe runs?
o: It gets hotter and hotter the further it has to travel
It is somehow filtered completely clean of all bacteria
It turns into perfectly safe cold drinking water
It cools down and can drop into the legionella growth range
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: In long dead legs or runs without circulation, stationary hot water cools into the range where legionella multiply.

n.0: Water loses heat as it sits in pipes; it does not get hotter.
n.1: Cooling in the pipe does not remove bacteria; it encourages their growth.
n.2: It becomes tepid rather than a safe cold supply.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A secondary circulating pump on the hot water system helps control legionella by:
o: Adding a fresh supply of nutrients into the returning water
Storing sludge in the pump until the next service
Keeping the loop water moving and above the control temperature
Cooling the circulating water right down to save energy
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: The circulating pump keeps water moving so the whole loop stays above the control temperature and does not stagnate.

n.0: It moves water; it does not add nutrients.
n.1: Sludge is drained from the calorifier base, not stored by the pump.
n.3: The pump keeps water hot; it is not there to cool it.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Outlets sited a long way from the calorifier are best kept safe by:
o: Fitting a separate cold water cistern somewhere nearby
Reducing the calorifier's stored water temperature
Simply leaving the taps unused for long periods between draw-offs
A secondary return loop that circulates hot water close to them
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: A secondary return brings circulating hot water close to distant outlets so the water reaching them stays hot.

n.2: Leaving taps unused causes stagnation, increasing the risk.
n.1: Reducing storage temperature lets more of the system fall into the growth range.
n.0: A cold cistern does not address keeping the hot supply hot at distant outlets.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: At a large site, taps at the far end of a wing run only warm even after running for a while, while taps near the plant room run hot quickly. This most likely points to:
o: The calorifier is being stored at a far too high temperature
A problem with the secondary circulation reaching that wing
The cold water supply to the building has been switched off
Too much sludge has built up inside the individual tap spouts
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Distant outlets that never get properly hot suggest the secondary circulation is not maintaining temperature to that part of the building.

n.0: If storage were too hot, distant taps would run hotter, not cooler.
n.2: A cold supply being off would affect cold water, not the hot outlets.
n.3: Warm water across a whole wing points to circulation, not spouts.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Which statement about the secondary return temperature is correct?
o: It is expected to arrive cold by the time it reaches the calorifier
It should be allowed to drop to room temperature overnight
It should stay hot, commonly 50°C or above, right round the loop
It only really matters on cold water systems, not hot ones
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: The secondary return should stay hot, commonly at least 50°C, so the whole loop remains above the growth range.

n.0: A cold return would mean the loop has stagnated and cooled dangerously.
n.1: Letting it fall to room temperature overnight would allow bacteria to multiply.
n.3: The secondary return is a feature of the hot water system, not the cold.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: How does a point-of-use (instantaneous) water heater differ from a calorifier in terms of legionella risk?
o: It heats water on demand and stores little, so lower risk
It stores a much larger volume of warm water than a calorifier
It always runs cooler than a calorifier and is more dangerous
It removes the need to keep any water hot anywhere on site
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Instantaneous heaters heat water only as it is drawn, so with little or no stored warm water the storage risk is lower.

n.1: A point-of-use heater stores little or no water, unlike a large calorifier.
n.2: Its lower stored volume gives lower, not higher, storage risk.
n.3: Other parts of a system, and scald control, still need managing; the heater does not remove all requirements.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Why is a point-of-use heater serving a single tap generally considered lower risk for legionella storage?
o: There is little or no stored water in the growth range
It heats water on demand rather than storing it for days
It runs at a much lower temperature than a calorifier
It has a large sludge trap fitted at its base
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: With little or no standing warm water, there is far less opportunity for legionella to multiply in storage.

n.2: Lower risk comes from little stored water, not from running cooler.
n.3: Point-of-use heaters are small and generally have no large sludge trap.
n.1: They heat on demand rather than holding water for days.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A small unvented hot water cylinder differs from an open-vented calorifier mainly in that it:
o: Cannot ever store its water above 45°C at all
Never needs its stored temperature checked at any point
Has no need for any water hygiene controls whatsoever
Is a sealed, pressurised store fed from the mains
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: An unvented cylinder is a sealed, pressurised vessel supplied directly from the mains rather than from an open cistern.

n.0: It is designed to store water hot, typically at 60°C or above.
n.1: It still stores hot water and its temperature must be checked.
n.2: Being sealed does not remove the need for hygiene controls.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Even where instantaneous heaters reduce storage risk, what consideration still applies at the outlet?
o: The water must always be kept below 20°C right at the tap itself
There is no risk of any kind at all at the outlet
The heater must first store the water for a whole week
Scald risk, since water delivered hot can burn at the tap
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Hot water delivered to an outlet can scald, so scald control at the tap remains a consideration even with low storage risk.

n.0: Scald is managed by mixing at the tap, not by cooling the supply.
n.1: Hot outlets do carry a scald risk, so they are not risk-free.
n.2: Instantaneous heaters heat on demand and store no water.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Which of these hot water arrangements stores the largest volume of warm water and so needs the most storage-related control?
o: A single point-of-use water heater serving just one basin
A small instantaneous electric shower heater on the wall
A central calorifier serving the whole building
A sealed kettle kept in the staff kitchen area
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: A central calorifier holds a large stored volume, so it carries the greatest storage-related legionella control requirement.

n.0: A single point-of-use heater stores little or no water.
n.1: An instantaneous shower heater heats on demand with minimal storage.
n.3: A kettle is boiled and emptied in use and is not part of the stored hot water system.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A washroom is fed by a small local instantaneous heater rather than the main calorifier. What is the correct view of its legionella risk?
o: It needs no attention or management of any kind whatsoever
Lower storage risk, but its outlet and pipe still need managing
It carries exactly the same storage risk as the main calorifier
It is more dangerous than the calorifier just because it is smaller
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Little stored water lowers the storage risk, but the outlet and any pipework to it still need managing.

n.0: Even low-risk fittings need basic management such as regular use and scald control.
n.2: With little stored water its storage risk is lower than the large calorifier's.
n.3: Smaller stored volume makes it lower risk for storage, not more dangerous.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A calorifier is taken out of service for internal inspection and cleaning. Before opening it, the operative should first:
o: Add fresh sludge inside to protect the internal metal surfaces
Turn the storage temperature right up to 90°C before opening the vessel
Open the vessel up while it is still completely full and hot
Isolate and safely drain the vessel following the correct procedure
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: The calorifier must be isolated and safely drained down following the correct procedure before it can be opened for inspection.

n.0: Sludge is removed during cleaning, never added.
n.1: Raising the temperature does not prepare it and adds a burn hazard.
n.2: Opening a full, hot vessel is unsafe and risks scalding.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Internal inspection and cleaning of a calorifier is carried out mainly to:
o: To deliberately add a fresh new nutrient supply into the stored water
To raise the pressure in the hot water mains supply
To remove scale, sludge and debris that can harbour bacteria
To lower the storage temperature of the water permanently
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Cleaning removes the scale, sludge and debris that provide shelter and nutrients for bacteria.

n.0: The purpose is to remove nutrient sources, not to add them.
n.1: Cleaning is about hygiene, not raising mains pressure.
n.3: Cleaning does not aim to lower the storage temperature; the water is still kept hot.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: To save energy, a site manager suggests turning the calorifier down so the stored water sits at 50°C. Why is this the wrong decision for water hygiene?
o: 50°C is easily hot enough to sterilise the whole system
Lowering the temperature always removes sludge from the base
It would make the circulating return temperature too high
Storage below 60°C lets legionella survive and multiply in the vessel
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Dropping storage below 60°C moves the vessel toward the growth range, letting legionella survive and multiply.

n.0: 50°C does not reliably kill legionella; keep storage at 60°C or above.
n.1: Lowering the temperature does not remove sludge; it encourages growth.
n.2: Lower storage would tend to lower the return, not raise it.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Staff are worried about scalding from hot taps. What is the correct way to control scald risk without lowering the calorifier storage temperature?
o: Remove the hot water supply from the entire building, leaving only cold
Turn the calorifier off completely between each use
Store the water at only 40°C in the calorifier
Fit thermostatic mixing valves at the outlets to blend the water down
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Thermostatic mixing valves blend hot and cold at the point of use, controlling scald risk while storage stays safely hot.

n.2: Storing at 40°C would create ideal conditions for legionella.
n.1: Switching the calorifier off between uses lets the water cool into the growth range.
n.0: Removing the hot supply is not a practical or safe control for a working building.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Which statement about scald control and storage temperature is correct?
o: Lower storage to prevent scalding and simply accept the legionella risk too
Scald risk means hot water should never be stored above 45°C
A TMV fully replaces the need to store the water hot at all
Keep storage at 60°C or above and control scalding at the tap with a TMV
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: The safe approach is to store water hot at 60°C or above for legionella control and use a thermostatic mixing valve to limit the temperature at the tap.

n.0: Lowering storage trades one hazard for a worse one.
n.1: Storing at 45°C or below invites legionella growth.
n.2: A TMV controls delivery but does not remove the need to store hot.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: After a calorifier has been cleaned and refilled, a sensible check before returning it to normal use is to:
o: Confirm it heats through and that flow and return reach control temperatures
Leave it standing cold overnight so the fresh water can settle
Skip all the temperature checks entirely, since the vessel has only just been cleaned
Add some fresh sediment back into the base to help protect the metal
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Confirming the vessel heats through and that flow and return reach the correct temperatures shows control has been restored after cleaning.

n.1: Leaving it cold overnight lets the fresh fill cool into the growth range.
n.2: Cleaning does not guarantee correct temperatures, so checks are still needed.
n.3: Sediment is what was removed; adding it back would defeat the cleaning.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: An operative finds a calorifier has been left running at 52°C 'to prevent scalding'. The correct action is to:
o: Turn the storage down further to around 45°C
Restore storage to 60°C or above and fit TMVs for scald control
Leave it as it is because 52°C feels safe
Drain the vessel completely and leave it empty
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Storage should be restored to 60°C or above, with scald risk managed by thermostatic mixing valves at the outlets.

n.0: Lowering it to 45°C makes conditions even better for legionella.
n.2: 52°C is within reach of the growth range and is not a safe storage temperature.
n.3: Draining and leaving it empty does not provide the building with safe hot water and is not the required fix.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: During a monthly check an operative finds the calorifier base drain has never been opened and heavy sediment is suspected. What is the appropriate response?
o: Arrange for the base to be drained and de-sludged in maintenance
Record the finding and then take no further action
Raise the storage temperature right up to 90°C instead
Weld the drain valve shut so it cannot ever leak
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: A base that has never been drained should be de-sludged as part of maintenance so bacteria have nowhere to shelter.

n.3: Sealing the drain shut prevents the base ever being cleared of sludge.
n.2: Overheating the store does not remove the settled sludge, which still shelters bacteria.
n.1: Recording without acting leaves the sludge in place and the risk uncontrolled.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: At what temperature should a calorifier store hot water to control legionella?
o: Below 20°C
60°C or above
About 45°C
Between 20°C and 30°C
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Hot water should be stored at 60°C or above, a temperature at which legionella cannot survive.

n.3: 20–30°C is within the range where legionella actively multiplies.
n.2: 45°C is at the top of the danger zone and does not kill legionella.
n.0: Below 20°C is the target for cold water, not hot storage.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Why is sludge and sediment at the base of a calorifier a concern?
o: It makes the stored water heat up far too quickly
It shelters legionella from the hot water above it
It improves the flow and return balance of the loop
It raises the storage temperature above 60°C on its own
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Sludge and sediment settling at the base protect legionella and other bacteria from the heat of the stored water, so the base must be drained and de-sludged.

n.0: Sludge insulates and slows heat reaching the base; it does not speed heating.
n.2: Sludge worsens performance and hygiene; it does not improve balance.
n.3: Sludge does not raise storage temperature; it creates cool, sheltered layers.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: What does stratification inside a calorifier mean, and why is it a problem?
o: The storage tank overflows badly because it has been overfilled
Cooler layers form, so not all the water reaches safe temperature
The flow and the return pipes both read exactly the same temperature
The water is heated far above 60°C and simply wastes energy
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Stratification is where cooler layers form in the cylinder so part of the water sits in the danger zone below 60°C rather than reaching safe temperature.

n.3: The problem is cool layers, not overheating or wasted energy.
n.0: Stratification is about temperature layers, not overfilling or overflow.
n.2: Equal flow and return temperatures would indicate good, not poor, heating.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Which temperatures are checked on a calorifier to confirm it is working correctly?
o: The room and outdoor air temperatures
The flow and return temperatures
The overflow and vent temperatures
The cold feed and float valve temperatures
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: The flow (outgoing) and return temperatures are checked to confirm the whole cylinder is reaching and holding a safe temperature.

n.2: Overflow and vent pipes are features of cold tanks, not calorifier performance checks.
n.3: Cold feed and float valve temperatures relate to the cold supply, not hot storage output.
n.0: Room and outdoor air temperatures do not tell you about the stored hot water.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: You take a calorifier's flow temperature at 62°C but the return is only 48°C. What does this most likely indicate?
o: The cylinder is running far too hot and should now be turned down
Everything is completely fine here and no further action is needed
Cool layering or sludge, so it needs draining and further checks
The cold water tank lid is missing somewhere up in the roof space
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: A return well below the flow suggests cool layers or sludge at the base, so the calorifier should be drained, de-sludged and re-checked.

n.0: The problem is a low return in the danger zone, not overheating.
n.1: A 48°C return sits in the danger zone and must not be ignored.
n.3: These readings are about the calorifier, not the cold tank lid.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: You open a calorifier's drain point during service and a large amount of brown sludge runs out. What should you do?
o: Close the drain quickly again to avoid losing any hot water
Ignore it completely, as sludge is perfectly normal and harmless
Lower the storage temperature below 60°C to let it settle out
Drain and de-sludge the base fully, then record and report it
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Brown sludge shelters bacteria, so the base should be drained and de-sludged fully, with the finding recorded and reported.

n.0: Stopping early leaves the sludge and its bacteria in place.
n.1: Sludge is not harmless; it protects legionella from the heat.
n.2: Dropping below 60°C would make the problem worse, not settle it.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Why is hot water stored at 60°C or above rather than at a warm 40°C?
o: Legionella is killed at 60°C but thrives near 40°C
40°C water is too hot and would scald users at the tap
40°C water slowly damages the calorifier over time
Storing at 60°C uses less energy than storing at 40°C
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: At 60°C legionella is killed, whereas around 40°C sits in the range where the bacteria multiply readily.

n.1: 40°C is a warm, comfortable temperature, not a scalding one.
n.2: It is legionella growth, not tank damage, that rules out 40°C storage.
n.3: Storing hotter uses more energy, not less; safety is the reason.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: To confirm a calorifier is not stratified, what should be true of the stored water?
o: The water should be cooler at the outlet than the base
Only the base needs to be hot where sludge sits
The whole cylinder, from top to bottom, reaches a safe temperature
Only the very top of the cylinder needs to be hot
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Avoiding stratification means the entire cylinder from top to bottom reaches a safe temperature, leaving no cool layers.

n.3: A hot top with a cool base is exactly the stratification to be avoided.
n.1: A cool top over a hot base is still stratified and unsafe.
n.0: The outlet should not be cooler; cool layers are the hazard.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A calorifier stores hot water for distribution around a building. To control legionella, at what minimum temperature should the stored water be held?
o: 50°C, which is the minimum figure for water reaching the outlets
65°C, which sits a little above the storage requirement
60°C, which is hot enough to kill legionella over time
55°C, which sits just below the recognised storage figure
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: ACOP L8 / HSG274 Part 2 require hot water in a calorifier to be stored at 60°C or above, which is hot enough to kill legionella bacteria over time.

n.0: 50°C is the minimum for water reaching outlets, not for stored water.
n.1: 65°C exceeds the requirement; the standard minimum for storage is 60°C.
n.3: 55°C is below the storage standard and allows legionella to persist.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: During a monthly check you record the calorifier flow at 61°C but the return leg at only 44°C. What does the low return reading most likely indicate?
o: Normal operation that needs no further action at all
The whole system is over-heated and should be turned down
A faulty thermometer reading that can simply be ignored
Cooling in the circulation loop, so parts reach the growth range
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: The return should be at least 50°C. A return of 44°C shows the water has cooled below the control temperature as it circulates, allowing legionella to multiply in the cooler parts of the loop; the cause must be investigated and corrected.

n.0: A return below 50°C is outside the required standard and is not acceptable normal operation.
n.1: A 44°C return is too cold, not too hot; turning the system down would worsen the problem.
n.2: A reading this far below standard must be acted on, not dismissed as instrument error without checking.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Why does sludge and sediment collecting at the base of a calorifier present a particular legionella risk?
o: It raises the stored water temperature above the safe limits
It shelters bacteria in the cooler base debris where they multiply
It actually improves the circulation of water throughout the whole vessel
It only makes the water discolour but is otherwise harmless
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Sludge and scale settle at the base, where the water is often coolest. The debris provides nutrients and shelters legionella from the heat, so the base must be checked and periodically drained/de-sludged.

n.3: Sediment is not merely cosmetic; it harbours bacteria and biofilm and is a genuine health risk.
n.0: Debris tends to keep the base cooler, not hotter; it does not raise temperature above safe limits.
n.2: Sediment obstructs and stagnates flow at the base rather than improving circulation.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: 'Stratification' inside a hot water calorifier refers to which of the following?
o: The vessel operating above its rated working pressure
A protective scale layer forming on the vessel walls inside
Hot water flowing far too quickly through the outlets
Layers of water at different temperatures forming inside
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Stratification is the layering of water by temperature. Cooler water settles to the bottom while hotter water rises, so the base can sit in the legionella growth range even when the top of the vessel is hot.

n.0: It is a thermal layering effect, unrelated to pressure.
n.1: Stratification is temperature layering, not scale on the walls.
n.2: It concerns temperature distribution, not flow rate.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: What is the correct purpose of a secondary circulation (hot water return) system on a large building?
o: To store a further quantity of hot water away from the calorifier
To lower the flow temperature deliberately and so save some energy
To keep hot water circulating so it stays above 50°C along long runs
To reduce the cold water that enters the calorifier vessel
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: A secondary return keeps hot water constantly moving around long distribution runs so temperature does not drop; the return to the calorifier should be at least 50°C, preventing cool stagnant legs where legionella grows.

n.0: It is a circulation loop, not additional storage capacity.
n.1: Its purpose is to maintain temperature, not lower it to save energy.
n.3: It circulates hot water; it does not regulate incoming cold water.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A site manager proposes lowering the calorifier storage temperature from 60°C to 52°C to cut energy bills and reduce scald risk. Under ACOP L8, is this acceptable?
o: Yes, provided that all the outlets still manage to reach 45°C
Yes, if a chemical dosing system is added to the system at the same time
No; storage must stay at 60°C, and scalding is controlled with TMVs
Yes, because 52°C is warm enough to prevent any bacterial growth
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Storage must be kept at 60°C or above for legionella control; it must never be reduced to save energy or manage scalding. Scald risk is controlled at the point of use with thermostatic mixing valves (TMVs), not by lowering stored temperature.

n.0: Reducing storage to 52°C breaches the control standard regardless of outlet temperature.
n.1: Chemical dosing does not permit abandoning the 60°C storage standard.
n.3: 52°C is within the range where legionella can survive in storage and is not safe.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Hot water reaching outlets should achieve at least what temperature within one minute of running?
o: 50°C, the outlet delivery figure
60°C, the calorifier storage standard
45°C, a mixed-water target after a TMV
55°C, the healthcare premises figure
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: HSG274 Part 2 requires hot water to reach the outlet at 50°C or above within one minute of running, confirming hot water is being delivered throughout the system.

n.1: 60°C is the storage standard for the calorifier, not the outlet minimum.
n.2: 45°C is a mixed-water target after a TMV, not the hot supply temperature.
n.3: 55°C applies to healthcare premises; the general outlet standard is 50°C.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: When checking a calorifier for temperature control, why is the reading taken at the base of the vessel especially important?
o: The base is where the safety relief valve is fitted onto the vessel
The base of the vessel is always the very hottest point inside it
The base is the coolest point, so it confirms the whole volume has reached temperature
The base reading is only really needed in order to check the water pressure in the vessel
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Because cooler water and sediment settle at the bottom, the base is typically the coldest point. Confirming it is at temperature verifies the entire stored volume, not just the hot upper layer, is being controlled.

n.0: The base check is about the coolest water, not the safety valve.
n.1: The base is normally the coolest point due to stratification.
n.3: The base check is about temperature, not pressure.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Point-of-use (instantaneous) water heaters are sometimes preferred for infrequently used outlets. What is their main legionella advantage?
o: They heat water only when needed, so little water can stagnate
They store large volumes of warm water permanently right beside each tap
They remove the need to monitor any temperatures at all
They allow the stored water to be run safely below 60°C
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Instantaneous heaters warm water on demand and hold little or no stored volume, so there is minimal opportunity for water to sit warm and stagnate, reducing the legionella risk associated with storage.

n.1: Their advantage is the opposite: they hold little or no stored volume.
n.2: Monitoring is still required as part of the scheme.
n.3: They do not license running below control temperatures; scald control is via TMVs.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Before a calorifier can be internally inspected and cleaned, which step is essential?
o: Drain the vessel down and isolate it safely to reach the interior
Raise the stored water temperature to 70°C for a full hour beforehand
Add extra cold water to dilute any sediment sitting in the base
Increase circulation to flush the debris out through the outlets
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Internal inspection and cleaning require the calorifier to be drained down and safely isolated so the interior, particularly the base, can be examined and any sludge removed.

n.1: Raising temperature does not remove sludge or allow internal inspection.
n.2: Adding cold water only cools the store; it does not enable inspection.
n.3: Circulation cannot flush settled sludge out; the vessel must be drained.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: On a healthcare premises, at what minimum temperature should hot water reach the outlets, reflecting the higher-risk population?
o: Around 43°C, the safe blended bath temperature
About 45°C, a fairly typical blended-water figure
At least 50°C, which is only the general premises standard
At least 55°C, the higher healthcare outlet standard
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: In healthcare settings serving vulnerable people, HSG274 Part 2 sets the higher outlet standard of 55°C within one minute, above the general 50°C, to give an added margin of protection.

n.2: 50°C is the general premises standard; healthcare adopts the stricter 55°C figure.
n.1: 45°C is a blended-water figure after a TMV, not the hot delivery temperature.
n.0: 43°C is around the maximum safe mixed temperature at a bath/shower, not a hot supply standard.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A duty-holder wants to protect users from scalding at wash-hand basins in a care home without lowering the stored hot water temperature. What is the correct approach?
o: Reduce the temperature at the calorifier down to 48°C during the night only in daily use
Fit thermostatic mixing valves (TMVs) at the outlets to blend the hot water down
Remove the hot water supply from the wash-hand basins in the home entirely
Insulate the pipework so that the hot water cools before it reaches the tap
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Scald protection is delivered at the point of use with TMVs, which blend stored 60°C water down to a safe temperature at the tap while storage and distribution stay hot for legionella control.

n.0: Dropping the calorifier to 48°C breaches the storage standard and risks growth.
n.2: Removing the hot supply is impractical and does not address safe warm-water delivery.
n.3: Insulation keeps water hot; it does not cool it.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: The temperature range within which legionella bacteria multiply most readily is approximately:
o: 50°C to 60°C, where the bacteria are steadily being killed off
0°C to 15°C, where any growth is slow at best
20°C to 45°C, the main range for multiplication
60°C to 70°C, where the bacteria are rapidly destroyed
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Legionella multiplies in the approximate range of 20°C to 45°C. Storing hot water at 60°C and keeping cold water below 20°C both keep water out of this growth band.

n.0: At 50°C to 60°C legionella is being killed off, not multiplying.
n.1: Below about 20°C legionella survives but does not readily multiply.
n.3: Above 60°C legionella is rapidly destroyed, so this is not a growth range.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A calorifier's flow temperature reads a healthy 62°C, yet a distant outlet on the same system only reaches 47°C after two minutes. What is the most likely underlying issue?
o: The calorifier thermostat is set far too high
The cold water supply is contaminating the outlet
The outlet thermometer is reading too low and needs replacing
Poor circulation or a stagnant leg cools the water en route
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Hot water leaving at 62°C but arriving at 47°C shows heat loss on the way, typically from inadequate secondary circulation or a long dead-leg where water sits and cools, dropping into the growth range.

n.0: A high flow temperature is not the fault; the problem is heat lost between the calorifier and the outlet.
n.1: Cold-water contamination would suggest a faulty valve, but the pattern here points to distribution heat loss and poor circulation.
n.2: Assuming instrument error without investigating the circulation would leave a genuine legionella risk unaddressed.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Why should the whole stored volume of a calorifier reach the control temperature rather than just the water near the outlet?
o: To prevent the pressure safety valve from operating far too frequently
To reduce the whole building's energy consumption
To speed up delivery of hot water to the taps
Cooler zones at the base can let legionella grow and seed the system
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: If only the upper part of the vessel is hot, cooler water at the base sits in the growth range and can contaminate the whole system. The entire volume must reach 60°C so no reservoir of bacteria remains.

n.1: Heating the full volume is a control measure, not an energy-saving one.
n.2: It concerns eliminating cool zones for safety, not the speed of hot water delivery.
n.0: It is about bacterial control across the stored volume, not safety-valve operation.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Small unvented hot water cylinders are increasingly common in smaller premises. Compared with a large stored calorifier system, what is generally true?
o: Lower storage risk, but scald protection still matters
They must always be run below 60°C to avoid over-pressure
They eliminate the need for any temperature checks at all
They are exempt from legionella control because they are sealed
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: A small unvented cylinder holds far less water than a large calorifier, so the storage risk is lower, but it still stores hot water and must be kept at 60°C, with scalding controlled at outlets by TMVs where needed.

n.1: Unvented cylinders are designed to run at 60°C safely.
n.2: Temperature monitoring is still needed to confirm the standards.
n.3: Being sealed does not exempt a cylinder from control.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: As part of the routine scheme, how often are calorifier flow and return temperatures typically checked?
o: Annually
Only when a fault is reported
Once every three years
Monthly
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: HSG274 Part 2 recommends checking calorifier flow and return temperatures monthly to confirm the system is holding 60°C flow and 50°C return.

n.2: A three-yearly interval is far too infrequent to detect a temperature fault before risk develops.
n.1: Checks are planned and routine, not left until a problem is reported.
n.0: Annual is too infrequent for flow/return; the annual task is typically the more detailed base inspection.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A calorifier has a drain valve at its base. As part of legionella control this valve is used to:
o: Regulate the pressure of the incoming cold water supply main
Bleed trapped air from the very top of the vessel
Increase the delivered flow temperature during periods of high demand
Draw off and check base water, and remove settled sludge
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: The base drain lets the operator draw off water from the coolest point to check its temperature and clarity, and to de-sludge the vessel by flushing out settled sediment.

n.0: Incoming cold pressure is managed by supply valves, not this drain.
n.1: Air is vented from the top of a vessel, not the base valve.
n.2: A drain valve does not raise flow temperature.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A large calorifier serves a hotel. To confirm the full volume is being heated, an operative draws water from the base drain and measures 51°C, while the flow reads 61°C. What does this suggest?
o: The whole system is fully compliant and clearly needs no further action at all
The building therefore has no legionella risk of any kind at all
The flow thermometer at the very top must simply be faulty
Stratification is occurring, with a cooler base layer needing investigation
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: A base reading of 51°C against a 61°C flow shows the bottom of the vessel is significantly cooler, a sign of stratification. The cooler base layer sits nearer the growth range and must be investigated and corrected.

n.0: A 10°C difference with a base near the growth range is not full compliance.
n.1: A cooler base layer is exactly the kind of condition that can allow legionella.
n.2: Both readings are plausible; the issue is a genuine cool layer at the base.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Why is it important that hot water pipework, including the secondary return, is adequately insulated?
o: To cut heat loss so water stays above 50°C, out of the growth range
To increase the water pressure available at all of the outlets
To reduce the noise made by the water as it flows through the pipes
To allow the storage temperature to be safely reduced further instead
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Insulation reduces heat loss along the pipes, helping keep circulating hot water above 50°C so it does not cool into the 20-45°C growth range between the calorifier and the outlets.

n.1: Insulation conserves heat; it does not raise water pressure.
n.2: Noise reduction is not the reason; the aim is thermal control.
n.3: Good insulation supports maintaining 60°C storage, not reducing it.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: During an annual inspection the base of a calorifier is found to hold a thick layer of brown sludge. What is the correct response?
o: Leave it alone, as the sludge protects the vessel from internal corrosion
Add more cold water into the vessel to try to dilute and settle the sludge down
Raise the storage temperature permanently in order to burn the sludge off
Drain, clean and de-sludge the vessel, then confirm the temperatures on refilling
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Settled sludge harbours legionella and biofilm, so the vessel must be drained, physically cleaned and de-sludged. On refilling, temperatures are confirmed to ensure the whole volume reaches 60°C.

n.0: Sludge shelters bacteria and provides nutrients; it is a hazard.
n.1: Adding cold water increases sediment and cools the store.
n.2: Heat alone does not remove accumulated sludge; physical cleaning is needed.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: What is the correct minimum temperature for hot water returning to the calorifier through the secondary circulation loop?
o: It should be at least 55°C
It should be at least 50°C
It should be at least 45°C
It should be at least 48°C
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: The secondary return should be at least 50°C when it reaches the calorifier, confirming the circulating hot water has stayed hot throughout the loop and not fallen into the growth range.

n.0: 55°C is higher than required; the minimum return standard is 50°C.
n.2: 45°C is below the return standard and sits within the growth range.
n.3: 48°C is still below the 50°C minimum required for the return.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Two calorifiers are installed in parallel with a shared pipework arrangement, but one is kept on standby and rarely used. What is the legionella concern?
o: The rarely used standby vessel simply consumes far too much energy while idle
Water in the idle standby vessel stagnates and cools, becoming a reservoir
Parallel calorifiers cannot be temperature controlled at all
The duty calorifier will overheat to try to compensate for it
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: A rarely used standby vessel can hold stagnant water that cools into the growth range, acting as a reservoir that seeds the system when it is brought into use; standby units should be kept hot or regularly cycled and monitored.

n.0: The concern is stagnation and growth, not the energy an idle vessel uses.
n.2: Parallel calorifiers can be temperature controlled; stagnation is the issue.
n.3: The duty calorifier does not overheat; the risk is the stagnant standby.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A thermometer pocket (test point) is fitted to the flow and return of a calorifier primarily to:
o: To provide a convenient point for adding biocide chemicals into the loop
To let trapped air escape from the circulation loop
To allow accurate temperature readings without opening up the system
To reduce the water pressure in the return pipe
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Thermometer pockets let an operative insert a probe and take accurate flow and return readings quickly and safely, without breaking into the pipework, supporting routine monthly monitoring.

n.0: Test pockets are for temperature measurement, not for dosing chemicals into the system.
n.1: Air is vented through dedicated vents, not through a thermometer pocket.
n.3: A thermometer pocket does not regulate or reduce pressure in the return.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Following a period when a building was closed and the hot water system stood idle, what should be done to the calorifier and distribution before reoccupation?
o: Nothing needs doing at all, provided the calorifier had been left switched on as a rule
Drain the whole system down permanently and rely on point-of-use heaters
Bring the system up to temperature and flush all outlets to clear stagnant water
Simply lower the temperature to save energy until the occupants return
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: After a shutdown, stagnant water may have cooled into the growth range, so the calorifier is brought back up to 60°C and every outlet is flushed through to clear stagnant water before people use the system.

n.0: Even if left on, distant legs and outlets may have stagnated and must be flushed.
n.1: Permanent draining is not the standard response; the system is recommissioned.
n.3: Lowering the temperature after a shutdown increases risk.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Which statement best explains why running a calorifier below 60°C 'to save energy' is not permitted for legionella control?
o: It increases the building's overall water pressure to an unsafe level
It moves the stored water towards the 20-45°C range where legionella multiplies
It makes all the outlets deliver their water far too quickly
It causes the storage vessel to corrode noticeably more quickly
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Lowering storage below 60°C brings the stored water closer to the 20-45°C growth range, allowing legionella to multiply. Temperature control is the primary safeguard and must not be relaxed to save energy.

n.0: Storage temperature has no meaningful effect on the building's water pressure.
n.2: Storage temperature does not control how quickly outlets deliver water.
n.3: Corrosion is a maintenance concern but is not the legionella reason storage must stay at 60°C.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A calorifier's incoming cold feed is measured at 24°C on a warm day. Why is this relevant to the hot water system's legionella risk?
o: Warmer incoming water reduces the heat needed, so it is beneficial
Warm feed is already in the growth range and adds thermal load
The feed temperature has no bearing on hot water safety
A warm feed means the calorifier can be run cooler safely
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Cold water above 20°C is already in the growth range and gives the calorifier a warmer, higher-risk starting point. The vessel must still bring the entire volume to 60°C, and the cold-side warming should also be investigated.

n.0: Warmer feed water is a risk factor, not a benefit; it is closer to the growth range.
n.2: The temperature of the feed water directly affects risk and the heating duty of the calorifier.
n.3: A warm feed is a reason for vigilance, not for running the calorifier cooler.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Sentinel outlets on a hot water system are best described as:
o: Just any three outlets that are picked completely at random on the day each month
The nearest and furthest outlets from the calorifier, representing the system
Only the outlets that are fitted with mixing valves
The outlets that are never used from one year to the next
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Sentinel outlets are the first and last (nearest and furthest) on each loop. Monitoring them monthly gives a representative picture of temperatures across the whole hot water distribution.

n.2: Sentinel status is about position on the system, not whether a TMV is fitted.
n.3: Unused outlets are a separate stagnation concern; sentinels are chosen for their representative position.
n.0: Sentinels are fixed representative points, not random each month, so trends can be tracked.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: On a hospital ward, a TMV-served shower reads a mixed 41°C while the hot supply feeding the TMV reads 58°C. How should this be interpreted?
o: The TMV is safely blending 58°C down to 41°C
The hot supply is too cold and must be raised at once
The whole system must be shut down immediately for safety
The mixed temperature is dangerously high and the TMV failed
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: The 58°C hot supply meets the healthcare standard, and the TMV is correctly blending it to a safe 41°C at the shower to prevent scalding, while storage and distribution stay hot for legionella control.

n.1: 58°C meets the healthcare hot supply standard.
n.2: The readings show correct operation, so no shutdown is needed.
n.3: 41°C is a safe blended temperature; the TMV is working.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Why should thermostatic mixing valves (TMVs) be positioned as close as possible to the outlet they serve?
o: To allow the incoming hot water supply to be run below 50°C safely
To keep the run of cooled, blended-temperature pipework short
To make the valve a good deal easier to reach for routine cleaning
To increase the rate of water flow delivered at the tap or outlet
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Blended water leaving a TMV is in the legionella growth range, so the pipe between the valve and outlet should be as short as possible to limit the volume of warm water that could support bacterial growth.

n.0: The hot supply must still meet its standard; close mounting doesn't allow cooler.
n.2: Ease of access is a minor benefit, not the control reason.
n.3: Position relative to the outlet does not increase flow rate.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A calorifier is described as having 'inadequate turnover'. What does this mean for legionella risk?
o: The whole vessel is being heated to well above 60°C almost constantly
The circulation pump is left running continuously, day and night
The stored water is replaced too slowly, so it can sit warm and stagnate
Hot water is being used up faster than it can be reheated
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Poor turnover means water sits in the vessel for long periods. If any part is below 60°C, stagnant warm water can allow legionella to grow, so vessel sizing and demand should suit actual usage.

n.0: Overheating above 60°C is not what inadequate turnover means; the concern is stagnant warm water.
n.1: Continuous pump operation actually improves circulation rather than causing poor turnover.
n.3: That describes excessive demand outstripping heating, a different issue from low turnover.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: An operative is asked to record calorifier readings in the site log. Which set of values would indicate the system is meeting the standard?
o: Flow 61°C, return 52°C
Flow 55°C, return 45°C — both low
Flow 58°C, return 47°C — both under
Flow 60°C, return 43°C — return low
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Flow must be at least 60°C and return at least 50°C. Flow 61°C with return 52°C satisfies both, showing the water is stored hot and stays hot around the loop.

n.1: Flow 55°C and return 45°C are both below their minimums and near the growth range.
n.2: A 58°C flow is below the 60°C standard and a 47°C return is below 50°C.
n.3: The 60°C flow just meets the standard but the 43°C return is well below 50°C.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: A single-feed 'combination' style calorifier serving both storage and demand is found running with the base at 40°C. What is the priority action?
o: Increase the outlet flow rate right up in an attempt to mix the cold and hot layers together
Treat it as a control failure: investigate, restore full heating and check for sludge
Reduce the demand placed on the vessel and then simply monitor it once again next month
Record it as satisfactory, because the top of the vessel is nice and hot
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: A base at 40°C sits squarely in the growth range and is a temperature-control failure. The cause (stratification, poor heating, sludge) must be investigated and the whole volume restored to 60°C, with the base checked and cleaned.

n.0: Raising flow does not reliably heat the base.
n.2: A base in the growth range needs prompt action, not a month's monitoring.
n.3: A hot top with a 40°C base is not satisfactory.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: Where a calorifier cannot practically achieve 60°C throughout because of its design, what is the correct course of action?
o: Seek expert advice and apply additional control measures
Simply switch the vessel off entirely between periods of use
Ignore the base temperature and monitor only the flow
Accept a lower storage temperature as perfectly normal
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: If temperature control cannot be fully achieved, the risk assessment must be reviewed and competent/expert advice sought so that supplementary control measures are put in place; the shortfall is never simply accepted.

n.1: Switching the vessel off between uses creates stagnation and cooling.
n.2: Ignoring the base leaves the coolest, highest-risk zone unmonitored.
n.3: A lower storage temperature must not be accepted as normal.

Hot Water & Calorifiers.q: What is the main reason records of calorifier temperatures and cleaning should be kept as part of the water safety scheme?
o: Only to satisfy the water supplier's monthly metering and billing requirements
To decide when the outlet taps should be replaced
To demonstrate the control scheme is followed and reveal trends early
To calculate the whole building's overall energy bills
Hot Water & Calorifiers.w: Records provide evidence that monitoring and cleaning are being carried out as required, and reviewing them reveals adverse trends, such as a slowly falling return temperature, so action can be taken before a control failure occurs.

n.0: Records exist for the safety scheme and duty of care, not the supplier's billing.
n.1: Tap replacement is maintenance, not the purpose of these records.
n.3: Records support control and compliance, not energy-bill calculation.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: What is a 'dead leg' on a water system?
o: A pipe that carries water at high pressure to a tap
A pipe fitted with a working outlet that is used every day
The main incoming supply pipe from the street mains
A length of pipe closed at one end with little flow
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A dead leg is a section of pipe, often closed off at one end, where water is not drawn through and so sits and stagnates.

n.0: A pressurised pipe in daily use keeps water moving.
n.1: A pipe with an outlet used every day has good turnover.
n.2: The incoming main is a live, flowing supply.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why does water sitting in a blind end or dead leg become a legionella risk?
o: It sits under too much pressure for any bacteria to survive
It stays still and warms up, letting bacteria and biofilm grow
It is constantly refreshed with fresh cold mains water
It is chlorinated far more heavily than the rest of the system
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Still, warming water in a dead leg gives legionella the stagnation, warmth and biofilm it needs to grow.

n.0: Dead legs are low or no pressure, and pressure does not kill legionella.
n.2: A dead leg is not refreshed; that lack of turnover is the problem.
n.3: Trapped water loses any disinfectant residual over time, not gains it.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: In a dead leg with no through-flow, how does any fresh water reach the closed end?
o: Quickly, because mains pressure pushes it right through the closed end
Automatically, pumped through on a regular timed cycle each day
Not at all, so it stays cool because no water ever reaches it
Only very slowly by diffusion, so the water effectively stagnates
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: With no outlet drawing water through, the closed end is refreshed only by slow diffusion, so it stagnates.

n.0: A closed end has no exit, so pressure cannot push a flow through it.
n.1: There is no automatic timed cycle on an ordinary dead leg.
n.2: Water does reach it and sits there warming to the surrounding temperature.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Which best describes why a blind-ended pipe helps legionella grow?
o: The fast flow through it scours away any bacteria present
Ultraviolet light inside the pipe kills off the bacteria
The very cold temperature freezes any bacteria in the water
Stagnant, warm water and biofilm collect there undisturbed
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A blind end holds undisturbed warm water and biofilm, the ideal conditions for legionella to multiply.

n.0: There is no fast flow in a blind end; the water is static.
n.1: There is no UV light inside ordinary pipework.
n.2: Water in a blind end tends to reach room temperature, not freeze.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: What tends to happen to the temperature of water trapped in a long dead leg?
o: It always stays reliably below 20 degrees C, whatever the surroundings are
It stays at exactly the same temperature as the live main from which it branches off
It drifts towards the surrounding room temperature, often into the growth range
It always stays reliably above 60 degrees C, whatever the surroundings are
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Trapped water loses or gains heat towards the ambient temperature, frequently landing in the 20-45 degrees C growth range.

n.0: It only stays cold if the surroundings are cold, often not the case.
n.1: Because it is not flowing, it drifts towards ambient, away from the main.
n.3: It only stays hot if kept hot; a dead leg normally cools down.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A dead leg is a concern mainly because it combines which conditions?
o: Stagnation, warmth and nutrients from biofilm together
Freezing temperatures combined with constant movement
High pressure together with thorough daily flushing
High flow, cold water and a fresh disinfectant residual
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Stagnation, warmth and biofilm nutrients together are the recipe for legionella growth in a dead leg.

n.1: Freezing and constant movement would suppress growth, not encourage it.
n.2: High pressure and daily flushing would keep the section safe.
n.3: High flow, cold and fresh disinfectant are protective, not a risk.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: How does a live, regularly used pipe differ from a dead leg in legionella terms?
o: The live pipe holds no water at all in the periods between uses
The live pipe holds warmer water, which makes it more dangerous
The live pipe has water moving through it, so it rarely stagnates
There is no real difference between a live pipe and a dead leg
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Regular flow through a live pipe keeps water moving and turned over, unlike the static water in a dead leg.

n.0: A live pipe stays full and pressurised between uses; it does not empty.
n.1: A live cold pipe is kept cool, and flow reduces risk rather than raising it.
n.3: Flow versus stagnation is central to legionella control.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: When a run of pipework is no longer used, what is the correct way to remove the risk?
o: Cut it out right back to the live main so no stub is left to stagnate
Paint the pipe a bright colour so it is easy to identify
Fit an extra isolation valve on it and simply close it
Cap the end and leave the redundant pipe in place
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Removing redundant pipe right back to the live main leaves no stub of standing water to stagnate.

n.3: A capped pipe still holds a length of stagnant water and remains a dead leg.
n.2: A closed valve still leaves standing water beyond it that stagnates.
n.1: Painting the pipe identifies it but does nothing about the stagnant water inside.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why is simply capping off a disused pipe not good enough?
o: Caps are illegal fittings and are not permitted on water systems
A fitted cap will always begin to leak within just a few days
Capping the branch raises the system water pressure dangerously
The capped length still holds standing water that stagnates and grows legionella
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A cap seals the end but the water trapped behind it becomes a stagnant dead leg.

n.0: Caps are commonly used fittings and are not illegal.
n.1: A properly fitted cap does not necessarily leak.
n.2: Capping a short branch does not create a dangerous pressure rise.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A sink has been removed but the pipe that fed it has been capped just below the old tap position. What should be done?
o: Cut the redundant pipe back to the live main and cap it there
Insulate over the capped pipe and then simply take no further action at all
Leave the capped pipe exactly as it is for now and just move on
Open the cap about once a month to let a little air in
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: The disused branch should be removed back to the live main so no stagnant dead leg is left.

n.1: Insulation alone does not remove the stagnant water inside the redundant pipe.
n.2: Leaving the long capped stub leaves stagnant water that can grow legionella.
n.3: Letting air in does not refresh the water and does not fix the dead leg.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: When cutting back a redundant pipe, how close to the live main should the cut be made?
o: About one metre away from the main is close enough
As close as practicable so almost no dead length remains
Roughly halfway along the old branch
Right at the old outlet position only
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Cutting back close to the live main leaves the shortest possible stub, minimising standing water.

n.0: A metre of pipe left on the main is still a dead leg holding stagnant water.
n.2: Cutting halfway leaves a long stagnant stub still connected.
n.3: Cutting at the old outlet removes nothing useful and leaves the whole branch as a dead leg.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A shower in a rarely used changing room has been taken out, and the supply pipe left capped at full length behind the wall. What is the best action?
o: Remove the redundant pipework back to the live supply
Fit a longer cap so it seals more tightly
Record it on the plan and leave it capped off
Flush the capped pipe from the mains end just once a year
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: The capped full-length branch is a dead leg and should be removed back to the live supply.

n.3: A capped pipe has no outlet, so it cannot be flushed through from the mains.
n.1: A better cap still traps the same stagnant water.
n.2: Recording it does not remove the stagnation risk it poses.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: An old water heater has been removed and its feed pipe capped where the heater used to stand. Why is this a problem?
o: The capped feed is now a dead leg of standing water
The cap will make the remaining hot water far too hot
There is no real problem at all once the heater is gone
The capped pipe will freeze the rest of the system
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: The capped feed pipe holds standing water with no turnover, forming a dead leg where legionella can grow.

n.1: A cap on a redundant feed does not raise the temperature of live water.
n.2: The redundant capped pipe stagnates and should be removed.
n.3: A capped branch does not freeze the working system.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why is closing an isolation valve, rather than removing the pipe, an unsatisfactory way to deal with a disused branch?
o: The standing water beyond the closed valve still stagnates
Isolation valves are simply not allowed on cold water systems
The closed valve is certain to seize itself fully open
A closed valve steadily raises the water temperature beyond it
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Water trapped beyond a closed valve has no turnover and stagnates just like any other dead leg.

n.1: Isolation valves are normal, permitted components of water systems.
n.2: The concern is the stagnant water, not the valve seizing open.
n.3: Closing a valve does not heat the water beyond it.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: What is the recommended action for an outlet, such as a tap, that is only used occasionally?
o: Turn the water pressure right up to that particular outlet
Flush it regularly, at least once a week, to keep the water turning over
Cap it off permanently in between the occasional uses
Leave it exactly as it is, because occasional use is quite enough
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Little-used outlets should be flushed regularly, at least weekly, to move fresh water through and prevent stagnation.

n.0: Raising pressure does not move water through an outlet that is not being opened.
n.2: Capping it turns a usable outlet into a dead leg; if not needed it should be removed.
n.3: Occasional use is often not frequent enough to prevent stagnation.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why does an oversized pipe or storage vessel increase legionella risk?
o: Bigger vessels are automatically self-cleaning on the inside
Water turns over slowly, so it sits longer and can stagnate
Large pipes always run at a very high water velocity throughout
The extra volume keeps all the water below 20 degrees C
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Oversized pipes and tanks hold more water than is used, so turnover is poor and water stagnates.

n.0: Large vessels are not self-cleaning; sediment and biofilm build up.
n.2: Oversizing lowers velocity, it does not raise it.
n.3: A large volume does not keep water cold; slow turnover often lets it warm.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: What does 'low turnover' of water in part of a system mean for legionella control?
o: The water is kept permanently above 60 degrees C in that part
Water is replaced so quickly that bacteria can never settle
Water sits still for long periods, giving the bacteria plenty of time to multiply
The disinfectant residual in the standing water is automatically boosted
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Low turnover means water lingers, giving legionella the standing time it needs to grow.

n.0: Low turnover usually drifts into the warm growth range, not stays hot.
n.1: That describes high turnover, which is protective.
n.3: Standing water tends to lose disinfectant residual, not gain it.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A cold water storage tank is far larger than the building actually needs. Why is this a concern?
o: It uses far less energy overall, so there is really no downside at all
The stored water turns over slowly and can warm and stagnate
The stored water will end up far too cold for anyone to use
The tank will constantly overflow from being too large
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: An oversized tank holds more water than is drawn each day, so turnover is poor and the water can warm and stagnate.

n.0: There is a clear downside: poor turnover and stagnation risk.
n.2: Slow turnover tends to let cold water warm, not make it colder.
n.3: A float valve controls the level, so it does not overflow constantly.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A hotel bedroom is only used a few times a year, so its basin and shower are rarely run. What is the sensible control measure?
o: Increase the hot water temperature for that room only
Do nothing, as the room is rarely occupied
Include the outlets in a regular flushing routine
Disconnect the water and cap the pipes at the outlets
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Rarely used outlets should be flushed regularly so fresh water moves through and does not stagnate.

n.3: Capping at the outlets turns them into dead legs; unused pipework should be removed, not capped.
n.0: Raising temperature for one room does not move water through unused outlets.
n.1: Doing nothing lets the standing water stagnate between the infrequent uses.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: How often, as a minimum, should seldom-used outlets generally be flushed to control stagnation?
o: At least weekly
Once a year at the annual service
Once every six months
Only when the water looks discoloured
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Guidance is to flush little-used outlets at least weekly to keep water moving and prevent stagnation.

n.2: Six-monthly is far too infrequent to prevent stagnation.
n.3: Waiting for visible discolouration means the problem has already developed.
n.1: An annual flush leaves long periods for stagnation to occur.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Which situation is most likely to cause stagnation in a water system?
o: A branch of pipework that is hardly ever used
A short pipe run in constant use
A well-sized pipe carrying water at normal flow
A tap that is opened many times every day
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A branch that is hardly ever used has poor turnover, so water sits and stagnates.

n.3: A tap used many times a day keeps water moving and turned over.
n.1: A short pipe in constant use has good turnover and low stagnation risk.
n.2: A correctly sized pipe at normal flow keeps water moving well.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Legionella multiplies most readily within which temperature range?
o: Between about 0 and 5 degrees C
Below the freezing point of water
Between about 20 and 45 degrees C
Between about 60 and 70 degrees C
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: The 20 to 45 degrees C range is where legionella grows fastest, so systems aim to keep water outside it.

n.0: At 0 to 5 degrees C bacteria are dormant, not multiplying.
n.1: Below freezing the bacteria do not multiply.
n.3: At 60 to 70 degrees C legionella is killed, not growing.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A long cold water pipe runs through a warm building before reaching the tap. What is the risk?
o: The cold water actually gets colder as it travels along
The cold water warms up towards the growth range on the way
The standing water somehow becomes badly over-chlorinated inside the pipe
The pipe simply cannot carry any cold water at all
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A long run through warm surroundings lets cold water pick up heat and drift into the 20-45 degrees C range.

n.0: Passing through warm areas warms the water rather than cooling it.
n.3: The pipe carries cold water fine; the issue is it warming up along the way.
n.2: Standing in a warm pipe does not add chlorine to the water.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Cold water should be kept below what temperature to hold down legionella growth?
o: 45 degrees C
55 degrees C
60 degrees C
20 degrees C
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Cold water is kept below 20 degrees C so it stays out of the temperature range where legionella multiplies.

n.0: 45 degrees C is well inside the growth range, not a safe cold target.
n.1: 55 degrees C is a hot water distribution target, not a cold one.
n.2: 60 degrees C is a hot storage target, far too warm for cold water.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Hot water is normally stored and distributed at which temperatures to control legionella?
o: Stored at 45°C and distributed to the outlets at about 40°C
Stored at 20°C and distributed to the outlets at about 15°C
Stored at 30°C and distributed to the outlets at about 25°C
Stored at 60°C and distributed to reach outlets at 50°C or above
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Storing hot water at 60 degrees C and delivering it at 50 degrees C or above keeps it out of the growth range and controls legionella.

n.0: 45°C and 40°C are within the growth range, not a safe hot regime.
n.1: 20°C and 15°C are cold-water figures, far too low for hot water control.
n.2: 30°C and 25°C sit right inside the growth range and would encourage legionella.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why does a long hot water pipe run to a distant outlet raise legionella risk?
o: The hot water gets even hotter and scalds the pipe
Long runs always keep the water above 60°C throughout
Long runs are said to remove all bacteria before water arrives
The water cools as it travels and enters the growth range
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Over a long run, hot water loses heat and can drop into the 20-45 degrees C range where legionella grows.

n.0: Hot water loses heat over distance; it does not gain it.
n.1: Long runs tend to let hot water cool below target, not stay above 60°C.
n.2: Cooling in a long run does not sterilise the water; it can make matters worse.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A tap in an outbuilding is fed by a very long pipe from the main building. What temperature problem is likely?
o: Both hot and cold arrive far colder than intended
Cold arrives warmer and hot arrives cooler than intended
The delivered temperatures are unaffected by the pipe length
Both hot and cold arrive far hotter than intended
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Over a long run the cold gains heat and the hot loses it, so both can drift towards the growth range.

n.0: The cold does not get colder over a long run; it warms up.
n.3: The hot does not get hotter; it cools down over distance.
n.2: Long runs clearly do affect the delivered temperatures.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: When a hot tap is opened, roughly how quickly should the water reach its proper hot temperature?
o: Only after half an hour of running
Within about one minute of running the tap
Within about ten minutes of running the tap
It does not matter how long it takes
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Hot water should reach at least 50 degrees C at the outlet within about one minute; longer means the run is too long or poorly insulated.

n.2: Ten minutes indicates a badly designed or uninsulated run holding cooling water.
n.0: Half an hour would mean a very large volume of cooled water sitting in the pipe.
n.3: It does matter: slow-to-heat outlets signal cooled, higher-risk water in the pipe.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why should cold water pipes be insulated (lagged)?
o: Only to stop the pipe from looking untidy on the wall
To help keep the water below 20°C by shielding it
To make the water flow through the pipe much faster
To raise the water temperature above 20°C deliberately
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Insulating cold pipes shields them from surrounding heat so the water stays below 20 degrees C.

n.0: Appearance is not the reason; temperature control is.
n.2: Insulation does not change the flow rate.
n.3: The aim is to keep cold water cool, not to warm it up.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why are hot water pipes insulated?
o: To cool the water down into the bacterial growth temperature range
Purely to save on the material cost of the pipework itself
To let the hot pipe be run right next to cold pipes safely
To help keep the water hot and cut heat loss along the run
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Lagging hot pipes reduces heat loss so the water stays above the growth range all the way to the outlet.

n.0: Insulation keeps hot water hot; it does not cool it to the growth range.
n.1: The purpose is temperature control and energy saving, not pipe cost.
n.2: A hot pipe still needs separating from cold pipes; insulation is not enough.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: What can happen if a cold water pipe is run right next to a hot water pipe?
o: The cold pipe simply cools the hot water down to a safe level
Nothing at all happens, because adjacent pipes never affect each other
The cold water automatically stays below 20 degrees C regardless
Heat transfers across from the hot pipe and warms the cold water into the growth range
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A hot pipe alongside a cold pipe warms it by conduction and radiation, pushing the cold water into the growth range.

n.0: The much larger heat in the hot pipe warms the cold, not the other way round.
n.1: Adjacent pipes clearly do affect each other's temperature.
n.2: Sitting next to a heat source is exactly what stops it staying below 20°C.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Besides insulating pipes, what else helps keep cold water below 20 degrees C?
o: Leaving cold pipes uninsulated so they can lose their heat
Bundling the cold and hot pipes tightly together in the runs
Routing cold pipes well away from hot pipes and other heat sources
Running cold pipes through the warm boiler house for convenience
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Keeping cold pipes clear of hot pipes, heaters and other heat sources stops the cold water from warming up.

n.0: Cold water gains heat from a warm room; it needs insulation, not exposure.
n.1: Bundling hot and cold together transfers heat into the cold pipe.
n.3: A boiler house is a warm place that would heat the cold water.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: In a service duct, the cold water pipe runs tight against an uninsulated hot flow pipe. What should be done?
o: Separate them and insulate both of the pipes so the cold stays below 20°C
Just leave them together as they are, since it saves valuable duct space
Move only the cold pipe even closer to the hot flow pipe
Wrap both of the pipes together inside a single shared sleeve
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: The pipes should be separated and insulated so heat from the hot pipe cannot warm the cold water into the growth range.

n.1: Saving space by warming the cold water is not acceptable.
n.2: Moving the cold pipe closer makes the heating worse.
n.3: One sleeve around both still lets heat pass from hot to cold.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: What is the main purpose of insulating water pipes in legionella control?
o: Drain it down and leave it empty and open to the air
Raise the pressure inside it and leave it fully closed
Cap it off and forget about it until it is needed again
Flush it regularly so the water does not stagnate in it
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Insulation maintains temperatures, keeping hot water above and cold water below the legionella growth range.

n.0: Leaving it drained and open invites contamination and does not control the risk.
n.1: Raising pressure without flow does not move fresh water through it.
n.2: Capping and forgetting it lets the water stagnate as a dead leg.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A cold water pipe passes through a warm plant room with no lagging. Why is this a risk?
o: The pipe will eventually burst from all the warmth
The plant room actually keeps the cold water below 20 degrees C
There is no real risk provided the water inside is moving occasionally
The warm room heats the unlagged cold water into the growth range
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: An unlagged cold pipe in a warm plant room absorbs heat and can rise into the 20-45 degrees C range.

n.0: Warmth does not burst a pipe; the concern is the water temperature.
n.1: A warm room heats the water; it does not keep it cold.
n.2: Occasional movement does not overcome constant heating; lag and separate it.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why should pipes, fittings and materials in a water system be WRAS-approved (approved for use with drinking water)?
o: They are tested not to encourage bacteria or contaminate water
They deliberately change the colour of the water for easy identification
They noticeably make the water flow faster through the system
They are always the very cheapest option that is available
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: WRAS-approved materials are tested to be suitable for potable water and not to support microbial growth or leach contaminants.

n.3: Approval is about safety and suitability, not being the cheapest.
n.2: Approved materials do not speed up flow.
n.1: Approved materials do not colour the water.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why do flexible hoses and rubber components carry extra legionella risk?
o: They are made of stainless steel that will never corrode or foul each time
They are unable to hold any water at all inside the hose body
Materials such as EPDM can release nutrients and support biofilm growth
They always run at well over 60 degrees C during normal use
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Flexible hoses and rubber parts like EPDM can release nutrients and harbour biofilm, feeding legionella growth.

n.0: They are typically rubber-based, not stainless steel.
n.1: They hold water like any other pipe, which is part of the problem.
n.3: Flexible hoses are not kept permanently above 60 degrees C.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: What is the concern with certain rubber washers, seals and hoses in a water system?
o: They make the water permanently sterile and totally bacteria-free
They have no effect on water quality whatsoever, one way or the other
They can release nutrients that feed bacteria and support biofilm
They reliably keep the water above the legionella growth range
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Some rubber and elastomer components leach nutrients and hold biofilm, which supports legionella growth.

n.0: They do not sterilise water; they can do the opposite.
n.1: They can clearly affect water quality by supporting growth.
n.3: They do not keep water hot.
