Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why should materials that support biofilm be avoided in water systems?
o: Biofilm shelters and feeds legionella from disinfectant
Biofilm is said to make the water flow more smoothly through pipes
Biofilm keeps the water permanently cold in the pipe
Biofilm has no real link to legionella survival at all
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Biofilm harbours legionella and other bacteria and shields them from temperature and chemical control.

n.1: Biofilm roughens surfaces and can restrict flow, not smooth it.
n.2: Biofilm does not control temperature.
n.3: Biofilm is strongly linked to legionella survival and growth.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why are corrosion-resistant materials preferred in water pipework?
o: Rusty internal surfaces kill legionella on contact instantly
Rough, corroded surfaces let biofilm and bacteria build up
Corroded pipes carry the water at a safer temperature
Corrosion has no bearing at all on legionella risk
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Corrosion creates rough, scaled surfaces and sediment that shelter biofilm and bacteria, so corrosion-resistant materials are preferred.

n.2: Corrosion does not control water temperature.
n.0: Rust does not kill legionella; it can shelter it.
n.3: Corrosion is relevant because it fosters biofilm and sediment.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A flexible braided hose has been fitted to connect a tap, and the outlet is used only now and then. Why is this a raised risk?
o: The hose cannot hold any standing water inside it
Braided hoses are always WRAS-approved and completely risk-free
The hose can support biofilm and low use lets water stagnate
The hose keeps the water above 60°C at all times
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A flexible hose can harbour biofilm, and infrequent use leaves standing water in it, combining two risks.

n.0: The hose holds standing water, which is part of the problem.
n.1: Not all braided hoses are approved, and even approved ones need turnover.
n.3: The hose does not keep water hot.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why should non-approved or unsuitable fittings not be used on a water system?
o: They guarantee the water always stays below 20°C at every tap
They may leach substances or support growth, contaminating water
They always cost noticeably more than the approved fittings do
They make the water flow far too quickly through the pipework
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Unsuitable fittings can leach materials into the water or support bacterial growth, so only approved fittings should be used.

n.0: A fitting does not control the water temperature.
n.2: Cost is not the reason; suitability for potable water is.
n.3: Fittings do not generally speed up flow to a dangerous level.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Which design principle helps reduce legionella risk in pipework?
o: Add plenty of extra spare branches ready for future use
Store as much water as the storage tank will possibly hold
Keep pipe runs and stored water to the minimum needed
Make all of the pipes as long and as wide as possible
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Minimising pipe length and stored water improves turnover and reduces where stagnant water can sit.

n.0: Spare branches left in place become dead legs.
n.1: Storing excess water reduces turnover and encourages stagnation.
n.3: Long, wide pipes hold more standing water and lower velocity, raising risk.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: What is a key aim when designing or running a water system to control legionella?
o: Keep as many unused branches on the system as you possibly can
Store the water for as long as possible before it is used
Let the water sit still so any sediment can settle out
Keep water moving and turned over throughout the whole system
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Keeping water moving and turned over stops it stagnating and drifting into the growth range.

n.0: Unused branches become dead legs and should be removed.
n.1: Long storage lowers turnover and raises risk.
n.2: Letting water sit still is exactly what encourages legionella.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why should low-flow or no-flow branches be avoided in system design?
o: Water sits in them and stagnates, which encourages legionella
They keep the whole of the system much too cold to be useful
They carry the water far too fast through the pipework to be at all safe
They use up too much of the system's disinfectant residual
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Branches with little or no flow hold standing water that stagnates, so good design avoids them.

n.1: Low-flow branches tend to warm up, not keep the system cold.
n.2: The problem is too little flow, not too much.
n.3: Stagnant branches tend to lose disinfectant, not consume it.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: If a section of pipework must be kept for possible future use, what should be done in the meantime?
o: Drain it down and leave it empty and open to the air
Raise the pressure inside it and leave it fully closed
Flush it regularly so the water does not stagnate in it
Cap it off and forget about it until it is needed again
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A section that must be retained should be flushed regularly to keep water moving until it is brought back into use.

n.0: Leaving it drained and open invites contamination and does not control the risk.
n.1: Raising pressure without flow does not move fresh water through it.
n.3: Capping and forgetting it lets the water stagnate as a dead leg.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A branch is being left in place because a new sink may be fitted there next year. What is the correct interim control?
o: Insulate the branch and simply leave it capped off
Include the branch in the weekly flushing regime
Cap the branch off and take no further action at all
Close a valve on the branch and then leave it be
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: While retained for future use, the branch should be flushed regularly so the water in it does not stagnate.

n.0: Insulation does not stop stagnation of the standing water inside.
n.2: A capped branch with no flushing is a dead leg that stagnates.
n.3: A closed valve still leaves standing water beyond it that stagnates.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why should a water system be designed to avoid dead legs wherever possible?
o: Dead legs keep the trapped water permanently sterile
Dead legs somehow make the water flow far too fast through them
Dead legs hold stagnant water that lets legionella multiply
Dead legs push the system pressure far too high
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Dead legs trap standing water where legionella can grow, so designs aim to eliminate them.

n.3: Dead legs do not raise system pressure.
n.1: Dead legs have little or no flow, not fast flow.
n.0: Dead legs harbour bacteria rather than keeping water sterile.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A cafe kitchen has a rarely used pot-filling tap on a long branch. Which design improvement best reduces the risk?
o: Add a second dead-ended branch alongside the existing one
Widen the branch pipe so that it is able to hold more water
Leave it in place and simply rely on the annual service visit as well
Remove the tap and its branch back to the live main if not needed
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: If the outlet is genuinely not needed, removing it and its branch back to the live main eliminates the dead leg.

n.0: Adding another dead-ended branch creates a second stagnation point.
n.1: Widening the pipe increases the standing volume and worsens turnover.
n.2: Relying on an annual service leaves long periods for stagnation.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Overall, which set of actions best keeps pipework free of legionella growth?
o: Remove dead legs, keep the water moving, and hold correct temperatures
Fit extra flexible hoses and use plenty of non-approved fittings
Cap all the unused pipes, store plenty of water, and let it sit still
Run the cold pipes right beside the hot pipes and skip insulation
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Removing dead legs, maintaining flow and holding hot and cold temperatures out of the growth range are the core controls.

n.1: Extra flexible hoses and non-approved fittings add nutrients and biofilm sites.
n.2: Capping and storing water that then sits encourages stagnation and growth.
n.3: Running cold beside hot and skipping insulation warms the cold water into the growth range.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: What is a 'deadleg' in a water system?
o: A busy pipe that carries only hot water to the taps
A pipe with little or no flow where water stagnates
The main incoming supply pipe to the whole building
A pipe fitted with an insect screen fixed on the end
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A deadleg is a section of pipe with little or no throughflow, so water sits and stagnates, letting legionella grow.

n.0: A busy hot water pipe with regular flow is not a deadleg.
n.2: The live incoming main has constant flow and is not a deadleg.
n.3: An insect screen is a tank fitting and does not define a deadleg.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why does stagnant water in pipework increase the legionella risk?
o: Moving water encourages far more bacteria than still water
Still, warm water lets legionella multiply undisturbed
Still water is always noticeably colder than moving water
Stagnant water pushes the mains pressure up far too high
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Where water is stagnant it can warm into the danger zone and sit undisturbed, giving legionella the conditions to multiply.

n.0: Regular flow and turnover reduce growth; they do not encourage it.
n.2: Stagnant water drifts toward room temperature, not colder.
n.3: Stagnation does not increase the mains pressure.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: When a length of pipework is taken out of use, what is the correct way to deal with it?
o: Remove it right back to the live main, not just cap the end
Cap off the end and leave the rest of the pipe fully in place
Insulate the whole pipe well and leave it still connected
Fit a valve and turn it off, but leave the pipe full of water
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Disused pipework should be removed right back to the live main so no stagnant deadleg is left behind.

n.1: Capping the end still leaves a stagnant deadleg full of standing water.
n.2: Insulating a still-connected disused pipe does not stop the water stagnating.
n.3: A closed valve leaves the branch full of water that will stagnate.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why should hot and cold water pipes be kept apart and properly insulated where they run together?
o: To make the pipes easier to paint in different identifying colours later
To stop cold pipes warming and hot pipes cooling into the danger zone
To let the two pipes share a single common support bracket
To increase the flow rate through both of the pipes
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Keeping them apart and insulated stops the cold pipe warming above 20°C and the hot pipe cooling below 60°C into the danger zone.

n.0: Colour coding is a labelling matter, not the reason for separation.
n.2: Sharing a bracket is not a water hygiene reason to separate the pipes.
n.3: Separation and lagging control temperature; they do not raise flow rate.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why do long runs of pipework increase the legionella risk?
o: Hot water cools and cold water warms toward the danger zone along the run
Long pipes will always leak a great deal more than short pipes do
Long pipes raise the storage temperature of the calorifier feeding them
Long pipes simply cannot be insulated properly along their whole length at all
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Over a long run, hot water loses heat and cold water gains heat, drifting into the 20–45°C danger zone where legionella grows.

n.1: Length does not by itself make a pipe leak more.
n.2: Pipe length does not change the calorifier's storage temperature.
n.3: Long pipes can and should be insulated to hold temperature.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: You find a capped, disused pipe branch that stays warm to the touch and is full of standing water. What should you do?
o: Open the cap to let the standing water drain onto the floor
Leave it as it is, because it already has a cap on the end
Add more lagging to the branch and take no other action
Report it and arrange for the deadleg to be removed
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A warm, water-filled capped branch is a stagnant deadleg, so it should be reported and removed back to the live main.

n.0: Draining onto the floor is unsafe and does not remove the deadleg.
n.1: A cap does not fix the problem; the stagnant water remains inside.
n.2: Lagging alone leaves the stagnant water and deadleg in place.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: During a survey you find a little-used outlet at the end of a long branch that is rarely turned on. What is the best control?
o: Cap the outlet off and leave the branch full of standing water
Ignore it, since one unused outlet cannot cause a real problem
Flush it regularly, or remove the branch if it is genuinely not needed
Turn up the calorifier temperature to try to compensate for it
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Little-used outlets are managed by regular flushing to keep water turning over, or by removing the branch entirely if it is not needed.

n.0: Capping it leaves a stagnant deadleg of standing water behind.
n.1: A single stagnant outlet can seed legionella into the wider system.
n.3: Raising the calorifier temperature does not move the stagnant water.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A dead leg is a length of pipework in which water is retained and rarely, if ever, drawn off. Why is a dead leg a specific legionella concern under HSG274 Part 2?
o: The pipe wall cools the water below 20°C, which sterilises the section
The stagnant retained water warms into the growth range and supports legionella
The retained water somehow moves fast enough to strip protective scale from the wall
Dead legs raise the system pressure, which forces bacteria out of the outlet
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: HSG274 Part 2 identifies dead legs as areas where water stagnates, warms towards 20-45 degrees C and allows biofilm and legionella to proliferate because there is little or no turnover.

n.2: Stagnant water in a dead leg is not moving at all; scale stripping is not the mechanism of concern.
n.0: Stagnant retained water tends to drift towards ambient/warm temperatures, not sterile cold conditions.
n.3: A dead leg does not raise system pressure, and pressure does not expel bacteria.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: During a survey you find an old branch pipe that once fed a demolished sink; it is capped about 600 mm from the live main and never used. What is the correct remedial action under HSG274 Part 2?
o: Leave the capped stub in place because the cap already isolates the stagnant water
Remove the redundant pipework right back to the live main so no stub remains
Fit a second cap on the end to double-seal the retained water
Insulate the capped stub so the retained water cannot warm up
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Capping does not solve the problem; the capped section still holds stagnant water. HSG274 Part 2 requires redundant pipework to be removed back to the point of connection with the live/circulating main.

n.0: A cap still leaves a stagnant, warming volume of water connected to the system; it is not a solution.
n.2: A second cap adds nothing; the retained water still stagnates and can grow legionella.
n.3: Insulation slows temperature change but the stagnant retained water remains a colonisation risk; the stub must be removed.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Which of the following best describes why oversized pipework increases legionella risk?
o: Larger bore reduces the surface area available for biofilm per litre of water
Larger bore increases the velocity so much that biofilm cannot form anywhere
Larger bore always keeps the water colder than the surrounding room air
Larger bore holds more water at lower velocity, so turnover falls and water stagnates
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Oversized pipes carry a greater volume at reduced velocity, so turnover falls and water dwells longer, allowing it to reach growth temperatures and support biofilm.

n.0: Larger bore increases wetted surface and dwell time, worsening biofilm potential.
n.1: Oversizing lowers velocity, it does not raise it, and biofilm forms readily.
n.2: Slow turnover lets water drift towards ambient temperature, not stay cold.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A cold water pipe runs for several metres alongside an uninsulated hot water flow pipe in a warm plant room. What is the main risk to the cold supply?
o: The cold water will freeze because of its close proximity to the hot pipe
Heat gain warms the cold water above 20 degrees C, into the legionella growth range
The cold water will become over-chlorinated by heat coming off the hot pipe
The cold pipe will lose pressure to the hot pipe through their shared bracket
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Cold pipes routed near hot pipes or heat sources pick up heat; if the cold water rises above 20 degrees C it enters the 20-45 degrees C range where legionella multiplies. Cold pipes should be kept away from heat and lagged.

n.0: Proximity to a hot pipe warms the cold water, it does not freeze it.
n.2: Heat does not add chlorine; warming and stagnation help disinfectant decay.
n.3: Pressure is not transferred between separate pipes through a bracket.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: An infrequently used outlet at the end of a long branch is identified as a stagnation risk but cannot yet be removed. What interim control does HSG274 Part 2 recommend?
o: Fit a longer run of pipe to increase the stored volume at the outlet
Raise the cold water temperature at the outlet above 25°C
Flush the outlet regularly, usually weekly, to bring fresh water
Close the branch isolation valve and leave water standing
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Where little-used sections cannot be removed, the recommended interim control is regular flushing (commonly weekly) to move fresh water through and stop stagnation, until the redundant length can be removed.

n.0: Adding pipe increases stored volume and dwell time, worsening stagnation.
n.1: Warming cold water into the low-20s pushes it towards the growth range, the opposite of what is wanted.
n.3: Isolating and leaving water standing makes stagnation worse, not better.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Which pipework material choice is most consistent with HSG274 Part 2 guidance for minimising microbial risk in a water system?
o: WRAS-approved materials that resist corrosion and microbial growth
Any material to hand, so long as it is cheap and quick
Natural rubber hoses, because they flex and fit fast
Materials that leach nutrients so as to feed a biofilm
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: HSG274 Part 2 and the Water Fittings Regulations require materials in contact with wholesome water to be WRAS-approved (or equivalent), resisting corrosion and not providing nutrients that support microbial growth.

n.1: Suitability for potable water and approval status matter far more than cost or ease of fitting.
n.2: Natural rubber components can leach nutrients and harbour biofilm and legionella and are discouraged.
n.3: Encouraging biofilm is exactly what should be avoided; nutrient-leaching materials are unsuitable.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why are flexible flexible-hose connectors (such as those under taps or to appliances) flagged as a specific risk in HSG274 Part 2?
o: They contain chlorine reservoirs that over-dose the outlet
They cannot be connected to WRAS-approved fittings at all
The rubber lining can degrade and harbour biofilm
They are always undersized and raise water velocity too high
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Flexible hoses often use EPDM or similar elastomers that can degrade, shed nutrients and support biofilm and legionella growth; their use should be minimised and approved low-risk types selected.

n.0: They do not store or over-dose chlorine.
n.1: They can be connected to approved fittings; the issue is the lining.
n.3: The concern is the lining and biofilm, not excessive velocity.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A designer wants to reduce stagnation risk in a new washroom. Which design principle aligns with HSG274 Part 2?
o: Minimise pipe run lengths and stored volume so water is turned over quickly
Route long individual branches to each outlet for future flexibility
Provide generous spare capacity by oversizing pipes for possible future demand
Add several capped spur connections for future appliances
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Good design minimises pipe length, dead legs and stored volume so that water is used and replaced frequently, keeping it moving and reducing the chance of it reaching growth temperatures.

n.2: Oversizing lowers turnover and promotes stagnation and warming.
n.1: Long individual branches create low-turnover legs that stagnate.
n.3: Capped spurs are dead legs in waiting and should be avoided, not designed in.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: What is the essential difference between a 'dead leg' and a 'blind end' in system terminology used in HSG274 Part 2?
o: A dead leg still feeds an outlet but is rarely used; a blind end feeds nothing
A dead leg is always hot pipework, and a blind end is always cold pipework
A blind end circulates constantly while a dead leg never holds water
There is no real difference; both terms mean continuously flushed pipework
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A dead leg is a pipe leading to an outlet that is used infrequently; a blind end (or dead end) is pipework that is capped and no longer serves any outlet. Both retain stagnant water and are colonisation risks.

n.1: The distinction is about use and termination, not hot versus cold.
n.2: Neither circulates continuously; both are low- or no-turnover.
n.3: There is a difference; neither is continuously flushed pipework.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A ward is temporarily closed and its outlets will not be used for six weeks. To manage the pipework stagnation risk, the safest approach is to:
o: Do nothing at all, as closed rooms present no water risk whatsoever
Drain the whole system fully and then leave it empty and open to the air
Flush outlets regularly during closure, or drain down and disinfect before reuse
Isolate the branch entirely and rely on residual disinfectant holding for six weeks
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: For temporarily unused outlets, HSG274 Part 2 advises maintaining regular flushing to keep water fresh, or draining down; before bringing outlets back into use after prolonged inactivity, disinfection/flushing is needed.

n.0: Stagnant water in unused outlets is a well-recognised risk and cannot be ignored.
n.1: Leaving pipework empty and open invites contamination and does not make reuse safe.
n.3: Residual disinfectant decays; six weeks of standing water will stagnate and colonise.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Which statement about biofilm in pipework is correct according to HSG274 Part 2 principles?
o: Biofilm is only ever a concern in outdoor cooling towers, not in pipework
It forms on wet pipe surfaces and shelters legionella from disinfectant
Biofilm dissolves away harmlessly whenever water simply flows past it
Biofilm forms only in hot water that is kept above 60 degrees C
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Biofilm forms on the wetted internal surfaces of pipework and equipment; it provides nutrients and shelter for legionella and other organisms and can protect them from disinfectant, and it is worst where water stagnates.

n.0: Biofilm is a concern throughout hot and cold systems, not only cooling towers.
n.2: Flow does not dissolve established biofilm; it can shed organisms into the water.
n.3: Biofilm forms across a wide temperature range, not only in hot water.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A maintenance operative removes a redundant length of pipe but leaves a short tee stub about 400 mm long projecting from the live pipe. Why is this still a problem?
o: The stub increases the flow velocity through it and slowly erodes the tee joint over time
The stub raises the mains pressure and can eventually burst the fitting
The stub is a residual dead leg holding stagnant water that can warm and colonise
The stub reduces the volume of stored water and so starves the outlets
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Any length of pipe left projecting from the live main forms a residual dead leg that retains stagnant water, warms towards growth temperatures and can seed the live water with legionella. Removal should be flush to the live pipe.

n.0: A short dead stub carries little flow; erosion is not the issue.
n.1: The stub does not raise mains pressure.
n.3: The concern is stagnation, not any reduction in stored volume.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: In a cold water system, which condition most directly pushes stored or standing water into the legionella growth range?
o: Cold water warming above 20°C in stagnant, poorly insulated pipe
Cold water held below 20°C in well-insulated, frequently used pipe
Continuous high-velocity flow through short, direct pipe runs
Rapid turnover of water in a correctly sized storage cistern
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Legionella multiplies between roughly 20 and 45 degrees C. Cold water that warms above 20 degrees C, especially where it stagnates in uninsulated pipe near heat, is at greatest risk.

n.1: Cold water kept below 20°C and moving is the safe condition, not the risk.
n.2: High turnover through short runs keeps water fresh and cool.
n.3: Rapid turnover in correctly sized storage limits warming and stagnation.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why does HSG274 Part 2 recommend lagging (insulating) cold water pipework as well as hot?
o: Only to reduce the noise of the water flowing through the pipes
Only to prevent condensation from dripping down onto the floors and ceilings below
To slow the flow of water so that the outlets are quieter in use
To limit heat gain warming cold water into the range and keep hot water hot
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Insulation on cold pipes limits heat gain so the water stays below 20 degrees C, and insulation on hot pipes limits heat loss so the water stays hot; both help keep water outside the 20-45 degrees C growth range.

n.0: Noise reduction is not the guidance's purpose for lagging.
n.1: Condensation control is a secondary benefit, not the main reason.
n.2: Lagging does not slow flow, and slowing flow increases stagnation risk.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A hotel installs a bank of eight guest showers but typically only two are ever used. From a stagnation perspective, the best control is to:
o: Cap the pipes to the six unused showers, close up near the shower head
Turn up the cold water pressure feeding the whole bank of showers
Leave the six unused showers fully plumbed in and simply never use them
Rationalise the installation to what is actually needed, or use or flush every head on a regular rota
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Provision far in excess of demand creates low-turnover branches. HSG274 Part 2 favours matching provision to need, or, where outlets are retained, rotating use/flushing so every branch turns over regularly.

n.2: Unused but plumbed showers become dead legs that stagnate.
n.0: Capping at the head still leaves a stagnant branch feeding the cap; it does not remove the risk.
n.1: Raising pressure does not address the stagnant water in unused branches.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Which of the following would a competent surveyor most likely record as a dead leg on a schematic?
o: A capped pipe left in place after a urinal was removed
A circulating hot water return pipe kept above 50 degrees C
A rising main feeding the whole building continuously
A frequently used kitchen tap on a short direct branch
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A capped pipe left after equipment removal serves no outlet and retains stagnant water; it is a classic dead leg / blind end that should be removed back to the live main.

n.3: A frequently used tap on a short branch turns over regularly and is not a dead leg.
n.1: A hot circulating return is continuously moving water, not a dead leg.
n.2: A continuously used rising main is live, high-turnover pipework.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A little-used tap is flushed weekly for control. What is the correct way to carry out the flush to gain the benefit?
o: Run it until the water fully turns over and reaches the incoming supply temperature
Open the tap for just one second so a small amount of water passes through
Only flush the hot side and leave the cold side of the tap fully untouched
Flush at maximum spray to create as much aerosol as you possibly can
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A flush must draw fresh water through the whole retained length, so it should run until the standing water is displaced and the temperature reaches that of the incoming supply; aerosol should be minimised during flushing.

n.1: A one-second flush does not displace the standing water in the branch.
n.2: Both hot and cold sides retain standing water and both need flushing.
n.3: Maximising aerosol increases inhalation risk; aerosol should be minimised.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why is proximity of stored or standing water to heat sources such as boilers, plant, or south-facing walls specifically noted in stagnation risk assessment?
o: Heat sources genuinely have no measurable effect on the water temperature within the pipes
Local heating raises the water above 20 degrees C, into the legionella growth range
Heat sources chlorinate all the nearby water completely automatically
Heat sources actually cool the nearby pipework down and can freeze the water
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Local heat from plant, boilers or solar gain warms adjacent cold pipework and stored water; combined with stagnation this pushes the temperature into the 20-45 degrees C growth range.

n.0: Adjacent heat sources measurably warm pipework and are a recognised risk factor.
n.2: Heat does not add disinfectant to the water.
n.3: Heat sources warm rather than cool and freeze the water.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A site has a large storage cistern sized for a demand that no longer exists, so the water sits for days. Which control best addresses the stagnation this causes?
o: Raise the storage water temperature to about 30°C to help
Increase the cistern size further to add buffer capacity
Seal the cistern lid permanently and stop inspecting it
Right-size the storage so turnover matches actual demand
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Storage should be matched to demand so water is turned over roughly daily; oversized storage lets water dwell and warm. Reducing stored volume to suit real demand restores turnover.

n.0: Warming stored water to 30 degrees C puts it squarely in the growth range.
n.1: Adding capacity worsens dwell time and stagnation.
n.2: Sealing the lid and stopping inspection removes control and does not address turnover.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Which of these is the strongest reason to remove rather than merely isolate a redundant pipe branch with a valve?
o: Isolation valves cost considerably more than simply removing the pipe
Valves always leak and cause flooding within a few days
An isolated branch raises the flow rate to all other outlets
The isolated branch still holds standing water that stagnates
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Closing a valve leaves a stagnant, water-filled length beyond it. If the valve is later opened, or leaks by, that colonised water can enter the live system. Removal back to the live main eliminates the retained volume.

n.0: Cost is not the guidance reason; the retained stagnant water is.
n.1: Valves do not always leak within days; this is not the rationale.
n.2: Isolating a branch does not meaningfully raise flow to other outlets.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: On a schematic review you notice a shower fed by a long, small-bore hot branch that is used once a fortnight. Which two factors combine to make this a high stagnation risk?
o: High water turnover combined with a cold-only supply
Frequent use and an oversized bore that keeps the water cold
Long, low-turnover run and infrequent use letting water sit
A short run length combined with continuous daily use
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A long branch used only occasionally means water sits for extended periods; in that time hot water cools and cold water warms towards the 20-45 degrees C range, and stagnation supports biofilm and legionella.

n.0: High turnover is protective; this branch has low turnover.
n.1: The branch is used infrequently, not frequently.
n.3: Short runs with continuous use are low risk, the opposite of this.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: What is the recommended approach to a strainer, filter or expansion vessel that creates a low-flow or dead volume in the pipework?
o: Deliberately warm them to keep the trapped water above 25°C at all times
Assess them as stagnation points and manage them within maintenance
Permanently remove all strainers and filters from every single water system
Ignore them entirely, since small components hold far too little water to matter
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Components such as strainers, filters and expansion vessels can create localised low-flow or dead volumes where water stagnates; they should be identified in the risk assessment and managed by suitable maintenance, flow-through or flushing.

n.0: Warming them into the growth range is the opposite of good control.
n.2: These have legitimate functions; manage them rather than remove all.
n.3: Even small dead volumes can harbour biofilm and seed the system.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A new extension is plumbed and left filled with water but not commissioned or used for three months before occupation. What is the key stagnation control before hand-over?
o: Nothing, because brand-new pipework is sterile and cannot support any growth
Leave the water standing so that any disinfectant residual builds up
Simply run all the taps once on the actual day of occupation
Keep the system flushed throughout the delay, or disinfect and flush before use
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Filled but unused new pipework stagnates just like existing pipework. It should be kept flushed through the delay or, where that has not happened, disinfected and thoroughly flushed before occupation.

n.0: New pipework is not sterile; it wets, forms biofilm and can support growth once water stands.
n.1: Standing water depletes rather than builds disinfectant residual and stagnates.
n.2: A single run on the day does not overcome three months of stagnation throughout the system.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Which practice most reduces the length of dead legs at the design stage of a hot and cold water installation?
o: Adding extra spare tee connections ready for possible future outlets
Place infrequently used outlets as close as possible to the circulating pipework
Connecting infrequently used outlets as far as possible from circulation
Running each outlet on its own long individual supply from the plant room
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Keeping infrequently used outlets close to the circulating loop or a busy branch keeps the low-turnover length short, minimising the dead-leg volume that can stagnate.

n.0: Spare tees are dead legs in waiting and should be avoided.
n.2: Placing them far from circulation lengthens the low-turnover run.
n.3: Long individual supplies to each outlet maximise dead-leg length.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Standing water in a poorly used section of pipe has been found at 32 degrees C. What does this reading indicate for legionella control?
o: It is safely below the growth range, so no further action at all is needed here
It sits in the 20–45°C range that favours legionella multiplication and needs control
It is above the growth range, and so the legionella present is being killed off quickly
The temperature does not matter at all, provided the water still looks nice and clear
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: 32 degrees C is well within the 20-45 degrees C band in which legionella multiplies most readily; the stagnation and temperature together indicate a real risk requiring flushing, temperature control or removal of the section.

n.0: 32°C is inside, not below, the growth range.
n.2: Legionella is not killed until well above 50°C; 32°C encourages growth.
n.3: Clear-looking water can still be heavily colonised.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why should the number of joints, tees and fittings in a water system be kept to the minimum necessary?
o: Because copper fittings sterilise the water and should be avoided
Because every fitting adds cost that must be recovered from users
Because fittings always reduce the pressure below usable levels
Because fittings create low-flow zones and surfaces where biofilm forms
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Each additional tee or fitting introduces potential dead volumes, turbulence-free pockets and extra wetted surface where biofilm forms; minimising them supports smoother flow and reduces stagnation opportunities.

n.0: Copper does not sterilise water; this is not a reason to avoid fittings.
n.1: Cost is not the microbial-control reason for minimising fittings.
n.2: Fittings do not automatically drop pressure below usable levels.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A facilities team proposes leaving a decommissioned wing's pipework full of water 'in case the wing reopens'. What should the risk assessment conclude?
o: A large dead leg that will stagnate; drain and isolate it or remove it
Acceptable, provided the doors leading into the wing are kept securely locked
Acceptable, because the unused water slowly self-disinfects over time
Acceptable, since full pipes are always safer than empty ones
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: An entire wing of unused, water-filled pipework is effectively a very large dead leg. It will stagnate; the safe options are to drain down and physically disconnect, or maintain flushing, with disinfection and flushing before any reuse.

n.1: Locking doors does nothing about the stagnating water in the pipes.
n.2: Water does not self-disinfect; residual decays and organisms multiply.
n.3: Full pipes that never turn over stagnate; full is not always safer.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: During refurbishment, a plumber tees off the live cold main to feed a temporary standpipe that will be used for a few weeks. What ongoing control does the stagnation risk demand while it is in place?
o: Cap it off at the standpipe end when the works finish, and leave the tee in place
Use it daily or flush it regularly, and remove it back to the main once done
Insulate only the tee connection and take no other action at all
Leave it connected indefinitely afterwards in case it proves useful
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A temporary connection is a dead leg unless it turns over; it should be used or flushed regularly while needed and then removed back to the live main promptly, not capped and abandoned.

n.3: Leaving it indefinitely creates a permanent, unused dead leg.
n.0: Capping the end leaves a stagnant branch on the tee; the whole connection should be removed.
n.2: Insulating the tee does not address the stagnant water; regular use/flushing and removal are needed.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Which combination of factors does HSG274 Part 2 associate with the greatest risk of legionella proliferation in pipework?
o: Frequent use, short pipe runs and water reliably held below 20 degrees C
Continuous circulation and hot water reliably held above 55 degrees C
Stagnation, water at 20-45 degrees C, biofilm and suitable nutrients present together
A high disinfectant residual combined with very rapid water turnover
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Proliferation is favoured when several conditions coincide: stagnant or low-flow water, temperatures of 20-45 degrees C, established biofilm and a source of nutrients. Control aims to remove one or more of these.

n.0: That is the low-risk, well-controlled scenario, not the high-risk one.
n.1: Circulation and hot water above 55 degrees C suppresses legionella.
n.3: High residual and rapid turnover are protective, not high-risk.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: An operative is asked to record 'sentinel' outlets for temperature monitoring. In relation to stagnation, which outlets are typically most useful to include?
o: Only the single outlet that is nearest the incoming main, whatever its level of use
Only those outlets that happen to be used continuously all day long
The furthest and nearest outlets to the source, plus low-use or long-branch ones
Any three of the outlets chosen completely at random each and every month
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Sentinel outlets are usually the nearest and furthest points on a system, chosen to represent temperature control across it; including known low-use or long-branch outlets targets the places where stagnation and temperature drift are most likely.

n.0: A single near outlet does not represent the far, higher-risk parts of the system.
n.1: Continuously used outlets are least likely to stagnate and are not the priority.
n.3: Random monthly selection undermines trend monitoring and may miss high-risk points.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Why is simply capping a redundant pipe considered an inadequate control, even though it stops water escaping?
o: The capped length still holds stagnant water linked to the system
Capping raises the pressure in the retained length of pipe until it bursts
Capping cools the retained water below the growth range for good
Capping is only inadequate when the cap is made of plastic
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A cap seals the end but the pipe behind it still holds water that no longer turns over; connected to the live system, this stagnant volume warms and supports growth, and can seed the live water. That is why removal to the live main is required.

n.1: A capped dead length does not build pressure to bursting.
n.2: Capping does not cool the water; stagnant water tends to drift towards ambient/warm.
n.3: The material of the cap is not the point; the retained stagnant water is.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A cold water branch reads 22 degrees C at the sentinel outlet, above the target. Which investigation best addresses a likely pipework cause?
o: Check for heat gain, poor insulation, and dead legs or low turnover
Increase the outlet flow restrictor so the water slows right down in the branch
Immediately raise the storage temperature to try to compensate
Assume the thermometer is faulty and record the target value
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A cold outlet above about 20 degrees C points to heat gain and/or low turnover. The pipework investigation looks for adjacent heat sources, inadequate lagging and stagnant or dead-leg sections, then corrects them.

n.3: Falsifying records hides a genuine control failure and is unacceptable.
n.2: Raising storage temperature does not fix a warm cold-water branch and may worsen scald risk.
n.1: Slowing the flow increases dwell time and warming, making the problem worse.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: In relation to pipework layout, what does 'keeping water moving' primarily achieve for legionella control?
o: It erodes the pipe walls so biofilm cannot attach anywhere
It removes the need to control the temperature at all
Water is used and replaced before it can stagnate
It heats the water through friction to a safe level
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: Regular turnover means water does not dwell long enough to warm into the growth range or lose its disinfectant residual, and it disrupts the conditions biofilm needs to build up; it is a core stagnation control.

n.0: Normal flow does not erode pipe walls, and biofilm still forms.
n.1: Movement supports but does not replace temperature control.
n.3: Friction does not usefully heat the water; the benefit is turnover.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: A drinking water dispenser is fed by a 4-metre small-bore pipe that only delivers a few litres a day. Which description and control are correct?
o: It should be fed by an even longer pipe run to increase the stored volume
It is a high-turnover run that needs no specific stagnation control at all
It is perfectly safe, as long as the dispenser is a well-known branded unit
A low-turnover branch at risk; keep it short, insulate it and flush it
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: A long, low-draw branch turns over slowly and can warm and stagnate. Controls are to minimise the branch length, keep it cool with insulation and away from heat, and ensure regular turnover or flushing.

n.0: Lengthening the pipe increases dwell time and stagnation.
n.1: A few litres a day through 4 metres is low turnover, not high.
n.2: The dispenser's brand does not remove the pipework stagnation risk.

Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.q: Which record-keeping action best supports ongoing management of dead legs and stagnation identified in a risk assessment?
o: Recording only the outlets that passed their temperature checks
Keep an up-to-date schematic marking dead legs and low-use outlets, and log flushing
Discarding the old schematics as soon as a single survey is complete
Relying on operatives' memory instead of written flushing records
Pipework, Deadlegs & Stagnation.w: An up-to-date schematic/asset register that marks dead legs and low-use outlets, together with logs of flushing and of redundant pipework removed, lets the responsible person track and demonstrate that stagnation risks are being controlled over time.

n.0: Recording only passes hides the at-risk outlets that most need action.
n.2: Discarding schematics loses the baseline needed to manage change and dead legs.
n.3: Memory is not auditable or reliable; written records are required to demonstrate control.

TMVs & Scalding.q: What does a thermostatic mixing valve (TMV) do?
o: Blends hot and cold at the tap to give safe warm water
Cools the whole hot water system to a safe temperature
Stores a reserve of tepid water ready for later use
Heats stored water hotter to kill off any legionella
TMVs & Scalding.w: A TMV mixes stored hot water with cold water so the water leaving the outlet is warm but not scalding.

n.1: It does not cool the system; storage stays hot and only the outlet water is tempered.
n.2: It has no storage; it blends on demand as water is drawn.
n.3: A TMV does not heat water; it only blends hot and cold.

TMVs & Scalding.q: A TMV allows a building to protect people from scalding WITHOUT doing what?
o: Fitting the valve close to each outlet served
Servicing the mixing valve on a regular basis
Lowering the hot storage temperature below 60°C
Drawing cold water into the blended supply
TMVs & Scalding.w: The point of a TMV is to control scald risk while the stored water stays at 60°C or above for legionella control.

n.0: TMVs should be fitted close to the outlet, so this is not something avoided.
n.1: Regular servicing is required, not avoided.
n.3: A TMV must draw cold water to blend, so this is essential, not avoided.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Why must hot water storage NOT be turned down below 60°C to stop scalding?
o: Lower storage lets legionella grow in the stored water
It would end up using rather more energy over time
It would gradually damage the storage cylinder over time
It would make the stored water taste unpleasant
TMVs & Scalding.w: Storing hot water below 60°C brings it into the range where legionella can multiply, so scalding is controlled with a TMV instead.

n.1: Lower temperatures generally use less energy, and energy is not the issue.
n.2: Lower temperatures do not damage the cylinder; the risk is bacterial growth.
n.3: Taste is not the safety concern; legionella growth is.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Where should a TMV be sited in relation to the outlet it serves?
o: At the incoming cold water main
Halfway along the distribution pipe
As close to the storage cylinder as possible
As close to the outlet as practicable
TMVs & Scalding.w: Siting the TMV close to the outlet keeps the length of blended tepid water short, limiting where legionella could grow.

n.2: Near the cylinder would leave a long run of tepid blended water in the growth range.
n.0: The cold main is not where blending needs to happen.
n.1: Halfway along still leaves a long section of warm blended water.

TMVs & Scalding.q: A care home manager asks an operative to turn the hot water cylinder down to 45°C so frail residents cannot be scalded. What is the correct response?
o: Switch the hot water supply off completely during the daytime
Turn the cylinder down to 50°C as a sensible compromise
Keep storage at 60°C or above and fit TMVs at the outlets
Turn the cylinder down to 45°C exactly as requested
TMVs & Scalding.w: Storage must stay at 60°C or above for legionella control, and scalding is prevented with TMVs at the outlets.

n.0: Switching off does not control legionella and disrupts the supply.
n.1: 50°C storage is still below the 60°C needed to control legionella.
n.3: Storing at 45°C sits in the legionella growth range and is unsafe.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Why is the blended water leaving a TMV itself a legionella risk?
o: It is drawn only from the incoming cold water supply
It is warm and sits in the range where legionella can grow
The valve has stripped all of the chlorine out of it
It is stored for long periods in the valve before being used
TMVs & Scalding.w: The tepid blended water and the valve internals sit in the bacterial growth range, so TMVs need regular cleaning and servicing.

n.0: Blended water is a mix of hot and cold, not cold only.
n.2: A TMV does not strip chlorine from the water.
n.3: The blended water is made on demand, not stored.

TMVs & Scalding.q: What is a typical safe delivery temperature for a TMV-served bath or shower used by vulnerable people?
o: Around 55°C, close to distribution temperature
Around 41°C, a warm, non-scalding blend
Around 20°C, in the cold water range
Around 60°C, the hot storage temperature
TMVs & Scalding.w: Blended delivery of roughly 41°C gives a warm, usable temperature that is well below the scalding threshold.

n.0: 55°C is close to the distribution temperature and would present a scald risk.
n.2: 20°C is cold water territory, not a usable bath or shower temperature.
n.3: 60°C is the storage temperature and would scald.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Which of these is a reason a TMV needs regular servicing?
o: It eventually runs out of the cold water that it keeps in store
The valve gradually loses its coloured hot and cold identification coding over time
Scale and debris can affect the valve and let the delivery temperature drift
The valve wears out and slowly starts to heat the water itself
TMVs & Scalding.w: Scale, debris and wear can stop the TMV holding its set temperature, so servicing, descaling and temperature checks are needed.

n.0: A TMV does not store cold water, so it cannot run out.
n.1: Colour fading is cosmetic and not the reason for servicing.
n.3: A TMV blends; it does not heat water.

TMVs & Scalding.q: A TMV should only be fitted where what applies?
o: Wherever the building simply has a boiler installed
Wherever the pipework happens to be easy to reach
Where there is a genuine scald risk that justifies it
Wherever there is any hot water outlet of any kind at all
TMVs & Scalding.w: TMVs add a legionella risk and maintenance burden, so they are fitted only where a real scald risk to users justifies them.

n.0: Having a boiler does not by itself create a scald risk needing a TMV.
n.1: Ease of access does not decide whether a TMV is needed.
n.3: Not every hot outlet needs a TMV; only those with a scald risk.

TMVs & Scalding.q: In which type of premises are TMVs most commonly required?
o: Open outdoor storage yards, compounds and loading areas
Unoccupied data centres with no washing facilities
Healthcare premises, care homes, schools and nurseries
Warehouses that have no hand-washing facilities at all
TMVs & Scalding.w: TMVs are commonly required where at-risk users such as patients, elderly people and children use baths, showers and washbasins.

n.0: Outdoor storage yards do not have the vulnerable users TMVs protect.
n.1: Unoccupied data centres have no users at risk of scalding.
n.3: Warehouses with no washing facilities have no scald-risk outlets.

TMVs & Scalding.q: What tension does a TMV help to resolve on a water system?
o: Removing limescale from the water while quietly adding minerals
Increasing the flow rate while reducing the pipe size
Saving energy while keeping the storage cylinder cold
Keeping water hot for legionella control while still preventing scalding of the users
TMVs & Scalding.w: Legionella control needs hot stored water, but vulnerable users need protection from scalding, and the TMV delivers safe warm water while storage stays hot.

n.2: A TMV does not keep the cylinder cold; storage stays hot.
n.1: A TMV does not change flow rate or pipe sizing to resolve any conflict.
n.0: A TMV does not remove limescale or add minerals.

TMVs & Scalding.q: A nursery asks why it cannot simply run all its taps cool from the tank to avoid scalding toddlers. What should you explain?
o: Running the taps cool saves water and completely removes all of the risk
Cool stored water lets legionella grow; keep storage hot and fit TMVs at the taps
Cool water straight from the tank is perfectly safe and needs no controls
Toddlers are not really at risk from hot water, so no controls are needed
TMVs & Scalding.w: Storing or standing water in the tepid range encourages legionella, so the system stays hot and TMVs temper the water at the point of use.

n.0: Running taps cool does not remove the legionella risk.
n.2: Cool stored water is a legionella risk, not automatically safe.
n.3: Toddlers are highly vulnerable to scalding, so protection is needed.

TMVs & Scalding.q: What is the approximate maximum blended temperature a TMV should deliver to a bath used by at-risk people?
o: About 50°C, which is the minimum required at a hot tap outlet
About 55°C, which is a typical hot water distribution temperature
About 60°C, which is the usual hot water storage temperature
About 43°C, the recognised upper blended limit for a bath
TMVs & Scalding.w: Delivery to baths for vulnerable users is limited to around 43°C as an upper figure to avoid scalding.

n.0: 50°C is above the safe blended limit and risks scalding.
n.1: 55°C is a distribution temperature, not a safe blended delivery figure.
n.2: 60°C is the storage temperature and would cause scalds quickly.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Why should a TMV be removed if the outlet it serves is no longer used?
o: Removing it saves the purchase cost of the valve
It makes the run of pipework look tidier
It frees up space in the busy plant room
A disused TMV holds warm, stagnant water where legionella grows
TMVs & Scalding.w: An unused TMV and its short blended run become a stagnant, warm dead leg that supports legionella growth, so both should be removed.

n.0: Cost saving is not the health reason for removal.
n.1: Tidiness is not why a redundant TMV must be removed.
n.2: Space is not the safety concern behind removal.

TMVs & Scalding.q: A strainer or filter is often fitted on the inlets to a TMV. What is its purpose?
o: To add a dose of disinfectant into the blended water supply
To slow the flow right down so the water cools
To catch debris and grit that could stop the valve working
To gently warm the incoming cold water first
TMVs & Scalding.w: Inlet strainers trap debris so it cannot jam the valve or affect the blended temperature, and they must be cleaned during servicing.

n.3: A strainer does not heat the cold water.
n.0: A strainer does not dose disinfectant.
n.1: A strainer removes debris; it is not there to cool the water.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Non-return (check) valves at a TMV are there to do what?
o: Store extra water ready for later periods of low demand
Stop hot and cold water crossing over between the two supplies
Increase the delivered water temperature at the outlet
Filter limescale out of the blended water at the tap
TMVs & Scalding.w: Check valves prevent crossflow between the hot and cold supplies, which could otherwise upset temperatures or contaminate a supply.

n.0: Check valves do not store water.
n.2: Check valves do not raise the delivery temperature.
n.3: Check valves prevent backflow; they do not filter scale.

TMVs & Scalding.q: A hospital ward keeps its stored hot water at 62°C but wants patients protected from scalding at the basins. What is the right approach?
o: Reduce the stored water to just 42°C so that the basins are safe
Blend in cold water only at the cylinder itself
Remove the hot water supply from the ward entirely
Fit TMVs at the basins while storage stays at 62°C
TMVs & Scalding.w: Keeping storage hot controls legionella, and TMVs at the basins deliver safe warm water to patients.

n.0: Reducing storage to 42°C puts it in the legionella growth range.
n.1: Blending at the cylinder leaves a long tepid run in the growth range.
n.2: Removing the hot supply is not a legionella control and harms care.

TMVs & Scalding.q: After a TMV is first commissioned, what should be checked periodically thereafter?
o: That it still delivers water at the correct set temperature
That its casing colour still matches the surrounding pipework
That the cold water supply to it has been fully isolated
That the outlet it feeds has now been sealed off
TMVs & Scalding.w: Regular checks confirm the TMV still delivers the safe set temperature, since scale and wear can cause it to drift.

n.1: Colour matching is cosmetic, not a safety check.
n.2: Isolating the cold supply would stop the TMV blending correctly.
n.3: Sealing the outlet would take it out of use, not maintain it.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Which statement about a TMV and legionella control is correct?
o: The TMV disinfects the whole system as the water passes through it
The TMV controls legionella, so system temperatures no longer matter
The TMV removes the need to run any hot water in the system
The TMV controls scalding; temperatures still control legionella
TMVs & Scalding.w: A TMV only manages scald risk at the outlet; keeping storage and distribution hot still does the legionella control.

n.0: A TMV does not disinfect the system.
n.1: A TMV does not control legionella; hot temperatures do.
n.2: Hot water is still needed and must reach outlets hot behind the TMV.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Why is only a short length of pipe wanted between a TMV and its outlet?
o: A long run of pipe would end up costing a great deal too much in pipe materials
A long run of pipe would make the blended water arrive far too hot
A long run of pipe would reduce the water pressure at the outlet too far
A long run of blended tepid water would sit in the legionella growth range
TMVs & Scalding.w: The blended water is warm, so keeping the run short limits the volume of water sitting in the bacterial growth range.

n.0: Pipe cost is not the health reason for a short run.
n.1: A long run would let the blended water cool, not heat up.
n.2: Pressure loss is minor compared with the growth risk.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Servicing a TMV typically includes which of the following?
o: Repainting the outside of the valve body casing
Increasing the calorifier storage temperature to 70°C
Cleaning, descaling and disinfecting the internal parts
Fitting a larger cold water storage tank to the system
TMVs & Scalding.w: TMV servicing involves cleaning, descaling and disinfecting the internals and checking the delivery temperature.

n.0: Painting is not part of a hygiene service.
n.1: Raising storage to 70°C is not part of servicing a TMV and increases scald risk.
n.3: A TMV service does not involve fitting a larger tank.

TMVs & Scalding.q: A school has a row of washbasins used by young children. Where should scald protection be applied?
o: By fitting TMVs at the basins while keeping the stored water hot
By removing the hot taps from all of the basins
By lowering the whole hot water supply down to 40°C
By running the basins from a rainwater collection butt
TMVs & Scalding.w: TMVs at the children's basins give safe warm water while the stored hot water stays at a temperature that controls legionella.

n.1: Removing hot taps leaves no warm water and does not control legionella.
n.2: Lowering the whole supply to 40°C sits in the legionella growth range.
n.3: Rainwater is not a suitable or safe supply for washbasins.

TMVs & Scalding.q: What happens inside a well-designed TMV if the cold water supply suddenly fails?
o: It simply lets full-temperature hot water flow straight to the outlet
It shuts down or greatly reduces the flow to prevent scalding
It switches the outlet over to the separate mains cold main
It stores the hot water safely until the cold supply returns
TMVs & Scalding.w: A TMV has a fail-safe so that loss of the cold supply causes it to shut off or reduce flow, protecting the user from scalding.

n.0: Passing full hot water through would defeat the safety purpose of the valve.
n.2: A TMV does not reroute to a separate cold main.
n.3: A TMV does not store water for later.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Who benefits most from TMVs being fitted?
o: Only the maintenance staff who are working directly on the water system every time
People who cannot react quickly to hot water, such as the very young or infirm
Only occasional visitors passing briefly through the building each day
People who never use any hot water anywhere in the building at all
TMVs & Scalding.w: TMVs protect vulnerable users who may not sense or move away from scalding water quickly enough.

n.0: Maintenance staff are not the primary group scald protection is for.
n.2: General visitors are not the specific at-risk group TMVs target.
n.3: People who never use hot water are not exposed to the scald risk.

TMVs & Scalding.q: A landlord suggests fitting TMVs to every outlet in an office block 'to be safe'. Why is this not the right approach?
o: Fitting TMVs to every single outlet would push the delivered water temperature far too high
Each TMV adds legionella risk and upkeep, so fit only where a scald risk justifies it
Offices are simply not permitted to have any hot water supply at all
TMVs are actually completely illegal to install in any office premises
TMVs & Scalding.w: Because a TMV is itself a legionella risk, valves are fitted only where vulnerable users create a genuine scald risk, not everywhere.

n.0: TMVs lower, not raise, the delivered temperature.
n.2: Offices are permitted hot water; the point is not to over-fit valves.
n.3: TMVs are not illegal in offices; they are simply not always needed.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Legionella multiplies most readily in water at which range?
o: Above 70°C, where the water is extremely hot
At exactly 60°C and no other temperature
Below 5°C, where the water is very cold
Roughly 20°C to 45°C, in the warm range
TMVs & Scalding.w: Legionella grows in the roughly 20-45°C range, which is why storage is kept above 60°C and blended water is kept close to the outlet.

n.0: Above 70°C the bacteria are killed rapidly, not growing.
n.1: At 60°C the bacteria do not thrive; growth is in the lower warm range.
n.2: Below 5°C is too cold for the bacteria to multiply.

TMVs & Scalding.q: A residential care unit finds a resident's shower TMV is delivering water at 50°C. What does this indicate?
o: The hot water storage temperature should now be lowered
The cold water supply to it should be turned off
The TMV is working perfectly and needs no attention
The TMV has drifted off its setting and needs servicing
TMVs & Scalding.w: A blended delivery of 50°C is too hot and shows the valve has drifted, so it needs checking, servicing or resetting.

n.2: 50°C is above the safe blended range, so it is not working correctly.
n.1: Turning off the cold supply would make the water hotter, worsening the problem.
n.0: Lowering storage below 60°C is never the fix; the TMV should be corrected instead.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Why does keeping hot water stored at 60°C or above help control legionella?
o: High temperatures remove all of the dissolved minerals
High temperatures continually add chlorine to the water
High temperatures make the water flow much faster
Legionella does not survive well at high temperatures
TMVs & Scalding.w: At 60°C and above legionella is killed off quickly, which is why hot storage is kept high while a TMV handles scald risk.

n.0: Heat does not remove minerals as a control measure.
n.1: Heat does not add chlorine to water.
n.2: Flow speed is not how temperature controls the bacteria.

TMVs & Scalding.q: A TMV is described as being fitted 'at the point of use'. What does this mean?
o: Right at the tap, shower or bath that it serves
Up on the building's cold roof storage tank itself
Only inside the plant or boiler room, well upstream
Out at the incoming mains water meter position
TMVs & Scalding.w: Point of use means the valve is fitted close to the actual outlet, keeping the blended tepid run as short as possible.

n.1: The roof tank is a storage point, not the point of use.
n.2: The boiler room is far from the outlet, leaving a long tepid run.
n.3: The water meter is at the incoming supply, not the outlet.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Which of these is the safest way to reduce scalding at a bath used by an elderly resident?
o: Fit a TMV set to a safe blended temperature at the bath
Tell the elderly resident to add the cold water themselves
Turn the boiler thermostat down to around 44°C
Remove the hot tap from the bathroom altogether
TMVs & Scalding.w: A TMV delivers a reliably safe temperature at the bath without lowering storage below the level needed for legionella control.

n.1: Relying on the resident to add cold is unreliable for a vulnerable person.
n.2: Turning the boiler to 44°C leaves stored water in the legionella growth range.
n.3: Removing the hot tap leaves no usable warm water for bathing.

TMVs & Scalding.q: During a TMV service, why is the inlet strainer cleaned?
o: A blocked strainer actually heats the water passing through it
A clean strainer changes the colour of the water at the tap
The strainer holds a store of disinfectant for the valve
A blocked strainer restricts the flow and upsets the blended temperature
TMVs & Scalding.w: Debris in the strainer disturbs the flow balance and can stop the valve holding a safe blended temperature, so it is cleaned.

n.0: A blocked strainer does not heat water; it restricts flow.
n.1: A strainer does not affect water colour.
n.2: A strainer does not store disinfectant.

TMVs & Scalding.q: A facilities officer wants to prove a TMV is still safe. Which check is most relevant?
o: Weighing the valve to confirm that it is the correct model
Checking the colour of the valve body against a reference chart
Measuring the temperature of the blended water at the outlet
Counting how many outlets there are across the whole building
TMVs & Scalding.w: Measuring the delivered temperature confirms the TMV is still blending to a safe, non-scalding figure.

n.0: The valve's weight is irrelevant to its function.
n.1: The valve's colour tells you nothing about its performance.
n.3: Counting outlets does not confirm a specific valve is working.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Why can a TMV not be treated as 'fit and forget'?
o: It automatically self-cleans thoroughly every single day
It never needs any attention at all once it is installed
It is fully sealed and cannot collect any deposits inside
Its warm internals scale up and can harbour legionella
TMVs & Scalding.w: The TMV sits in the warm growth range and accumulates scale and biofilm, so it needs regular servicing, cleaning and disinfection.

n.0: A TMV does not self-clean daily.
n.1: It does need attention; ignoring it creates a legionella risk.
n.2: A TMV can and does collect scale and debris internally.

TMVs & Scalding.q: A busy commercial kitchen has a hand wash basin used only by staff. Does it necessarily need a TMV?
o: No hand-wash basin anywhere ever needs a TMV fitted
Only if the commercial kitchen also has a dishwasher
Yes, every single basin must always have a TMV fitted
Not necessarily; a TMV is fitted where there is a real scald risk
TMVs & Scalding.w: Healthy adult staff are not the vulnerable group TMVs are aimed at, so a TMV is fitted based on assessed scald risk, not automatically.

n.0: Some basins genuinely need TMVs, so 'never' is wrong.
n.1: A dishwasher does not decide whether a basin needs a TMV.
n.2: A TMV is not mandatory on every basin regardless of user.

TMVs & Scalding.q: What is the correct relationship between storage temperature and the TMV setting?
o: Storage stays hot at 60°C+ and the TMV blends it down at the outlet
Storage is set to exactly match the TMV's blended outlet temperature
The TMV actually raises the storage temperature up to its own setting
The TMV setting alone decides what the storage temperature will be
TMVs & Scalding.w: Hot storage is kept above 60°C for legionella control and the TMV independently blends it down at the outlet to a safe figure.

n.3: The TMV setting does not control the cylinder thermostat.
n.1: Storage must stay hot; it is not lowered to match the outlet.
n.2: A TMV blends down, it cannot raise the storage temperature.

TMVs & Scalding.q: A shower TMV in a care home has not been serviced for over two years. What is the main concern?
o: The valve will have completely run out of its stored supply of water
The coloured indicator on the valve body will simply have faded
Scale and biofilm may have built up, causing legionella risk and temperature drift
The outlet served by the valve will have physically moved position
TMVs & Scalding.w: Without servicing, the warm valve accumulates scale and biofilm that can harbour legionella and cause the delivered temperature to drift.

n.0: A TMV does not store water, so it cannot run out.
n.1: Faded colour is cosmetic and not a health concern.
n.3: An outlet does not move because a valve is unserviced.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Which describes the safe delivery temperature idea for TMV-served outlets?
o: As hot as the stored water, at around 60°C straight from the tap
Warm enough to use but low enough not to scald, around 41°C
Whatever temperature the individual user happens to prefer, with no limit
As cold as the incoming mains cold-water supply, at around 12°C
TMVs & Scalding.w: The blended water is set to a comfortable, usable temperature of about 41°C that is safely below the scalding threshold.

n.0: 60°C storage temperature at the outlet would scald.
n.2: There is a safe upper limit; it is not left unlimited.
n.3: Mains-cold water is not usable for washing or bathing.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Why should the pipe run of hot water reaching the TMV still be hot?
o: So that the blended water comes out hotter at the tap
So legionella is controlled right up to the valve
So the TMV will never need any servicing in future
So the separate cold supply is no longer needed
TMVs & Scalding.w: Keeping the supply hot up to the TMV means the water is under legionella control until the moment it is blended down at the outlet.

n.0: The blended water is deliberately cooler, not hotter, than the supply.
n.2: The TMV still needs servicing regardless of the hot supply.
n.3: The cold supply is still needed for the TMV to blend.

TMVs & Scalding.q: A nursing home has an unused disabled bathroom with a bath TMV. What is the legionella concern and action?
o: Warm water stands in the TMV and pipe, so flush it or remove the outlet
There is no legionella concern at all here because the outlet is never used
It should simply be left exactly as it is for the time being
The hot water storage temperature ought to be reduced
TMVs & Scalding.w: An unused TMV outlet becomes warm, stagnant water in the growth range, so it must be flushed regularly or removed if no longer needed.

n.1: Being unused makes it more of a risk, not less, because water stagnates.
n.2: Leaving it untouched allows stagnation and growth.
n.3: Reducing storage temperature is never the answer to a stagnation problem.

TMVs & Scalding.q: What does 'TMV' stand for?
o: Treated mains valve
Temperature monitoring vent
Thermostatic mixing valve
Thermal maintenance vessel
TMVs & Scalding.w: TMV stands for thermostatic mixing valve, which blends hot and cold to a safe delivered temperature.

n.3: It is not a maintenance vessel; it is a valve that blends water.
n.1: It is not a monitoring vent.
n.0: It is not a mains valve for treated water.

TMVs & Scalding.q: A caretaker proposes removing TMVs from a school's showers to cut maintenance. Why is this unsafe?
o: The showers would deliver full-temperature stored hot water and scald pupils
The stored water would badly overheat without the valves fitted
The pipework across the whole school would soon freeze up
The showers would then draw far too much cold water through
TMVs & Scalding.w: Without the TMV, the outlet would deliver stored hot water at scalding temperature to vulnerable pupils.

n.1: Storage temperature is not controlled by the outlet TMV.
n.2: Removing a TMV does not cause pipes to freeze.
n.3: Removing a TMV does not increase cold water use.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Which combination correctly controls both legionella and scalding?
o: Cool storage below 45°C with no TMVs
Hot storage above 60°C with no scald protection anywhere
Cold-only supply to all outlets
Hot storage above 60°C plus TMVs at at-risk outlets
TMVs & Scalding.w: Hot storage controls legionella and TMVs at the vulnerable outlets control scalding, giving both protections together.

n.0: Cool storage below 45°C fails legionella control.
n.1: Hot storage with no scald protection leaves vulnerable users at risk of scalding.
n.2: A cold-only supply gives no usable hot water and does not address the balance.

TMVs & Scalding.q: After first installing and setting a TMV, when is an early performance check commonly made?
o: Never again at all once the valve has first been set up
Soon after commissioning, then at regular intervals
A full ten years after it was first installed on site
Only once the valve has completely failed in service
TMVs & Scalding.w: An early check soon after commissioning, followed by regular checks, confirms the valve is holding its safe set temperature.

n.0: A set-and-never-check approach ignores temperature drift over time.
n.2: A ten-year gap is far too long for a safety-critical valve.
n.3: Waiting for total failure risks scalding before it is caught.

TMVs & Scalding.q: A day centre for people with learning disabilities is planning new washrooms. What advice fits?
o: Skip the TMVs altogether, since it is only adults using the washrooms
Fit the TMVs only on the cold water taps in the washrooms
Lower the hot water storage temperature instead of fitting any TMVs
Fit TMVs on baths, showers and washbasins, as users face higher scald risk
TMVs & Scalding.w: Users who may not react to hot water quickly are at higher scald risk, so TMVs are fitted at the relevant outlets while storage stays hot.

n.0: These adults are a vulnerable group, so TMVs are appropriate.
n.1: TMVs are fitted on the hot/blended outlets, not on cold taps.
n.2: Lowering storage would fail legionella control.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Why is a TMV preferred over simply mixing hot and cold with two separate taps for vulnerable users?
o: Two separate taps are cheaper, so they are always the required choice
Two separate taps control the legionella risk far better than a valve
A TMV needs no cold water supply connected in order to work
It reliably holds a safe temperature and reacts if a supply changes
TMVs & Scalding.w: A TMV automatically maintains the set blended temperature and fails safe if the cold supply drops, protection two manual taps cannot give.

n.0: Cost does not make two manual taps the safe choice for vulnerable users.
n.1: Neither taps nor a TMV control legionella; temperatures do that.
n.2: A TMV does need a cold supply to blend.

TMVs & Scalding.q: A washroom TMV serves a bidet and a basin from one valve some distance away. What is the drawback?
o: The valve will end up delivering the water much too hot at both outlets
The valve will then never need any routine cleaning or servicing
The long shared run of blended tepid water sits in the growth range
The cold water supply to the valve becomes completely unnecessary
TMVs & Scalding.w: A single distant TMV feeding several outlets creates a long run of warm blended water that can support legionella growth.

n.0: A correctly set valve does not deliver water too hot; the tepid run is the issue.
n.1: The valve still needs regular cleaning and servicing.
n.3: The cold supply is still needed for blending.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Which best describes why storage is kept hot rather than warm?
o: Warm water gradually damages the internal parts of every fitted TMV
Hot water is a good deal easier to pump around a system
Warm water is noticeably more expensive to produce
Warm water encourages legionella, whereas hot storage suppresses it
TMVs & Scalding.w: Warm storage in the growth range promotes legionella, so water is stored hot to suppress the bacteria while a TMV handles scald risk.

n.0: TMVs are designed to take hot supply, so warm water is not about protecting them.
n.1: Pumping ease is not why storage is kept hot.
n.2: Cost is not the reason; the reason is bacterial control.

TMVs & Scalding.q: An operative measures a care home basin TMV at 41°C blended and 60°C on the incoming hot supply. What does this show?
o: The TMV has failed and now needs to be removed
The hot storage is too hot and must be reduced
The system is controlling legionella and the TMV is preventing scalding
The cold supply is cross-contaminating the hot supply
TMVs & Scalding.w: Hot supply at 60°C shows legionella control is maintained and a 41°C blend shows the TMV is delivering safe, non-scalding water.

n.0: A 41°C blend shows the TMV is working, not failed.
n.1: 60°C is the correct storage temperature and should not be reduced.
n.3: There is no cross-contamination; the readings are exactly as intended.

TMVs & Scalding.q: A hotel wants to fit TMVs on the guest bath taps in a wing used mainly by elderly holiday groups. What temperature should the baths be set to deliver?
o: Around 55°C to match the distribution temperature
Around 30°C so it is never warm enough to scald
Around 41°C, safely below the scalding threshold
Around 60°C to match storage
TMVs & Scalding.w: A blended bath delivery of about 41°C is warm and comfortable while staying safely below the scalding threshold for older guests.

n.0: 55°C is a distribution temperature and would scald.
n.3: 60°C is the storage temperature and would cause rapid scalds.
n.1: 30°C is too cool for a comfortable bath and is not what TMVs are set to.

TMVs & Scalding.q: Why is checking the fail-safe shut-off part of TMV maintenance?
o: To confirm the valve still stops the flow if the cold supply fails
To confirm the valve is still able to heat the water on demand quickly
To confirm the valve stores enough cold water in reserve
To confirm the valve changes colour whenever it runs hot
TMVs & Scalding.w: The fail-safe check proves the TMV will shut down if the cold supply is lost, so a user cannot be scalded by full-temperature water.

n.1: A TMV does not heat water, so this is not what is tested.
n.2: A TMV does not store cold water.
n.3: Colour change is not a TMV function or a maintenance check.
