Whenever someone simply happens to want to use the shower anyway
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Infrequently used outlets, including showers, should be flushed at least weekly, running each until the hot reaches hot and the cold reaches cold, to prevent stagnation in the branch and fitting.

n.0: Monthly is too long; water stagnating for a month in a warm branch grows Legionella.
n.2: Flushing is an ongoing weekly control, not a task done only around an audit.
n.3: Relying on chance use gives no reliable control; a weekly flush is required.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: When flushing a little-used spray tap or shower to limit the release of aerosol, what is the recommended technique?
o: Remove the head entirely and let water jet out under full pressure
Open the outlet gently and slowly to reduce splashing and aerosol
Open it fully and quickly so the flush is over sooner
Flush only the cold side to avoid producing any warm mist
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Opening the outlet gently and slowly keeps flow smooth and minimises splashing and aerosol release during flushing, protecting the operative from any contaminated droplets.

n.2: Opening fully and fast maximises turbulence and aerosol, exactly what should be avoided.
n.0: Jetting water from a headless fitting produces heavy spray and does not clean the head itself.
n.3: Both hot and cold must be flushed so the whole branch is turned over; flushing cold only leaves the hot leg stagnant.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: A shower head on a welfare unit is found permanently caked in scale and slime. What does this build-up mainly represent in terms of risk?
o: Scale and biofilm that harbour and feed Legionella and are then aerosolised in use
Clear evidence that the incoming supply water is too soft and really needs hardening now
A purely cosmetic fault only, with no real bearing on overall water safety
Proof that the disinfectant dose must have been set far too high
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Scale and biofilm in a head or hose provide a surface and nutrients that shelter and support Legionella; when the shower runs, organisms from that fouling are released in the aerosol.

n.1: The build-up indicates fouling to be cleaned, not that the water should be made harder.
n.2: It is not merely cosmetic; the deposit is a reservoir for growth feeding the spray.
n.3: Fouling of this kind reflects a lapse in cleaning, not an excessive disinfectant dose.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: During a routine round you find a shower outlet serving an area that has been decommissioned and will never be used again. What is the correct action?
o: Leave it capped at the head but keep the branch connected
Have the redundant outlet and its branch removed to the main
Turn the temperature up and leave it to self-sterilise
Add it to the weekly flushing list indefinitely
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: A permanently redundant outlet should be removed, including its branch pipe back to the circulating main, so that no dead leg of stagnant water is left to grow Legionella.

n.0: Capping the head still leaves a dead leg of standing water in the branch, which is the very hazard to be eliminated.
n.2: Leaving warm stagnant water in a dead branch promotes growth rather than sterilising anything.
n.3: Flushing a permanently disused outlet forever wastes effort; if it will never be used it should be removed.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: What is the purpose of a flow straightener or aerator fitted into the nose of a tap, and why must it be kept clean?
o: It measures the flow rate for billing and must be left sealed shut
It sterilises the water chemically, so cleaning it would remove that protection
It heats the water at the outlet, so it should never be disturbed
It smooths the flow but traps debris and scale, so clean it with the outlet
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Aerators and flow straighteners shape the stream but present a large fine-mesh surface that collects scale, grit and biofilm; they must be cleaned, descaled and disinfected on the same routine as the rest of the outlet.

n.1: These are mechanical fittings; they do not chemically sterilise the water.
n.2: They do not heat the water and are designed to be removed for cleaning.
n.0: They are not metering devices; leaving them sealed and dirty creates a fouling reservoir at the outlet.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: You are asked to disinfect a shower head that cannot easily be dismantled. Which approach best follows good practice from HSG274 Part 2?
o: Wipe the outside of the head over with a dry cloth only
Soak the removed head and hose in a descaler and disinfectant
Spray air freshener into the head to mask any bad odour
Run the shower hot for a couple of minutes and consider it done
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Good practice is to remove the head and hose where practicable and immerse them in an appropriate descaling and disinfecting solution, physically clearing scale and biofilm from the internal surfaces and jets.

n.0: A dry external wipe does nothing about internal scale and biofilm.
n.2: Masking odour ignores the microbiological hazard.
n.3: A brief hot run does not remove established scale and biofilm.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: A spray tap in a rarely-used first-aid room is included in the weekly flush. What is the aim of running it until the water reaches temperature?
o: To test whether the tap can still reach a scalding hot temperature
To warm the whole first-aid room up nicely before anyone actually uses it
To draw fresh water through and clear stagnant water from the branch
To use up spare water before it is metered at the end of the month
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Flushing until hot runs hot and cold runs cold confirms fresh water from the live system has been drawn right through the branch, clearing the stagnant water where Legionella could otherwise multiply.

n.0: The flush is not a scald test; usable outlets are blended to safe temperatures.
n.1: Heating the room is irrelevant; the purpose is turning over stagnant water.
n.3: Flushing is a microbiological control, not a way to manage metering.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: After cleaning and descaling a set of shower heads on a welfare block, what record should be made?
o: A note in a personal diary that stays only with the operative
A dated written record of the cleaning and disinfection, kept in the log
No written record is needed at all if the heads simply looked clean afterwards
Only a quick verbal note passed on to the very next shift
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Cleaning, descaling and disinfection of outlets must be recorded, with dates, in the site log so the responsible person can demonstrate the control scheme is being carried out.

n.0: A private diary is not part of the site records and cannot be relied on for the log.
n.2: A clean appearance is not evidence; the task must be documented either way.
n.3: A verbal handover leaves no auditable record and is easily lost.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: While flushing outlets you find one shower head heavily fouled and dribbling brown water. Beyond flushing, what should you do?
o: Report the fouled outlet so it can be cleaned and investigated
Ignore it, because brown water is quite normal on a first draw
Say nothing, since simply flushing it is enough on its own here
Break the head open and pour neat bleach straight into the pipe
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: A visibly fouled or scaled outlet is a finding that must be reported to the responsible person so remedial cleaning, disinfection and any further investigation can be arranged; flushing alone does not fix established fouling.

n.1: Persistent brown, fouled water is a defect to report, not a normal first draw.
n.2: Flushing turns over the water but does not remove established fouling.
n.3: Uncontrolled neat dosing is unsafe and not the operative's decision on the spot.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: On a large site, several outlets are described as 'infrequently used'. Which best describes an infrequently used outlet for Legionella control?
o: Any outlet that happens to be sited more than two metres away from a cold storage tank
An outlet that is only ever actually used by visiting contractors on site
An outlet used less often than the water in its branch turns over, needing planned flushing
Any outlet at all that happened to be fitted on after the main building itself was first built
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: An infrequently used outlet is one drawn upon too seldom to keep the water in its branch fresh, so it needs a managed flushing regime, typically at least weekly, to prevent stagnation.

n.0: Distance from a tank alone does not make an outlet infrequently used.
n.1: Who uses it is not the point; how often the water turns over is.
n.3: Age of the fitting does not define frequency of use.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: Why is a long flexible shower hose left lying in the base of the tray a particular concern?
o: It shortens the overall pipe run and raises the water pressure dangerously high
The rubber will always leach harmful chemicals into the water
It is only a trip hazard and has no water-safety effect at all
Water sits stagnant and warm along it, and the bore grows biofilm
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: A shower hose holds a slug of water that sits warm and stagnant between uses; the flexible bore is prone to biofilm, and both are discharged as aerosol when the shower next runs, so hoses need regular cleaning and disinfection.

n.0: A hose does not meaningfully raise system pressure.
n.1: The concern is microbiological growth in retained water, not chemical leaching.
n.2: It may be a trip hazard, but the real issue is stagnation and biofilm inside.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: A temporary welfare cabin has been standing unused on a compound for six weeks with water left in the system. Before the showers are brought back into use, what is the priority?
o: Leave the water exactly as it is, since sealed systems always stay safe
Simply switch the water heater on and let the staff use the showers straight away
Clean and disinfect the heads and hoses, then flush and disinfect the system
Run the showers hard for about ten seconds and then open the site up
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: After a long period of stagnation the outlets and system may have grown Legionella, so heads and hoses should be cleaned and disinfected and the system flushed, and disinfected where the risk assessment requires, before anyone showers.

n.0: Standing water is not sterile; six weeks is classic for growth.
n.1: Warming stagnant water and using it could aerosolise organisms.
n.3: A ten-second run does not turn the system over or clean fittings.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: Which combination of tasks is normally carried out at the quarterly service of a shower under HSG274 Part 2?
o: Repaint the whole shower cubicle and then carefully reseal the shower tray again
Fit a brand-new water heater to serve the whole block
Clean, descale and disinfect the head, hose and any strainer or flow fitting
Replace all of the copper pipework throughout the building
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: The quarterly service centres on the aerosol-generating fittings: cleaning, descaling and disinfecting the head, hose and any strainer, aerator or flow straightener so scale and biofilm cannot accumulate.

n.3: Wholesale pipe replacement is a major works item, not a routine quarterly outlet task.
n.0: Redecorating the cubicle is unrelated to controlling the water-borne hazard.
n.1: Renewing the heater is not part of the routine quarterly cleaning of the outlet.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: A strainer in a spray-tap fitting keeps blocking with grit and scale. What does this recurring blockage tell the operative?
o: The strainer should simply be removed and thrown away so that it cannot block
The mains water pressure is far too high and it must be roughly doubled
Nothing at all, because strainers are actually meant to stay blocked up
The fitting is fouling and should be cleaned and disinfected on schedule, and reported
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Recurrent scale and debris in a strainer show the fitting is fouling; it must be cleaned and disinfected as part of the routine and the persistent problem reported so the cause can be dealt with.

n.0: Discarding the strainer lets debris pass into the outlet and removes a control.
n.1: Blockage from grit and scale is a fouling issue, not a signal to raise pressure.
n.2: A blocking strainer is a maintenance finding, not a normal state to accept.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: Which precaution best protects an operative from inhaling aerosol while cleaning a heavily fouled shower head?
o: Stand directly in the running spray to check the flow of the water thoroughly first
Work as fast as you can with the head running at full pressure to save time
Point the running head straight at your own face to inspect all the jets
Isolate or gently open the outlet to limit spray, and follow the method statement
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: The operative should limit aerosol generation, for example by isolating or gently controlling the outlet, and follow the site method statement and risk assessment, wearing any respiratory protection specified for the task.

n.0: Standing in the spray deliberately exposes the operative to the aerosol being controlled.
n.1: Running at full pressure produces the most aerosol and increases exposure.
n.2: Directing the running head at the face maximises inhalation of contaminated droplets.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: Why does the flushing of little-used outlets need to include the hot supply as well as the cold?
o: Because stagnant warm water in the hot leg favours legionella
Because the cold branch never stagnates at all
So the fitting looks fully tested to an auditor
Because only the hot tap produces any aerosol
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Legionella thrives in warm water, so a stagnant hot branch is a high-risk condition; both hot and cold sides must be flushed until each reaches its proper temperature to clear stagnant water throughout the fitting.

n.1: Cold branches can and do stagnate; they are not exempt from flushing.
n.2: The reason is genuine microbiological control, not appearance for an audit.
n.3: Both hot and cold outlets can aerosolise; that is not the reason for flushing the hot side.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: A responsible person asks why capped-off but still-connected shower branches are unacceptable. What is the best explanation?
o: They just make the wall behind them look rather untidy
They increase the water pressure to everywhere else
They form dead legs where water stagnates and legionella can grow
They are perfectly acceptable as long as the cap fitted is a brass one
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: A capped branch still full of water is a dead leg: the water sits stagnant, can warm up and grow Legionella, and organisms can migrate into the live supply, so redundant branches should be cut back to the main, not just capped.

n.0: Appearance is irrelevant; the objection is the stagnant dead leg it creates.
n.1: A capped dead leg does not usefully raise system pressure; the hazard is stagnation.
n.3: The material of the cap does not remove the dead-leg hazard behind it.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: When a shower has been dismantled, descaled and disinfected, what is important about how the disinfectant is finally dealt with before hand-back?
o: Refit the head while it is still dripping with neat solution
Flush the head and hose so no residue reaches the user
Pour the used disinfectant back into the storage tank
Leave the disinfectant in the head to keep working for good
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: After disinfection the fittings must be rinsed or flushed so that no harmful chemical residue is delivered to the user, then refitted and returned to service; the work and any re-commissioning flush are recorded.

n.0: Refitting a head loaded with neat solution exposes the next user.
n.2: Returning used disinfectant to the tank contaminates the supply.
n.3: Leaving disinfectant sitting risks delivering harmful residue.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: An operative notices a decorative fountain-style spray outlet has been added to a site reception without being on any water-safety schedule. Why is this a concern?
o: Any spray-producing feature can spread Legionella and must be assessed
Decorative features like this one never hold enough water to matter at all
It only really matters if young children are able to reach the spray outlet
It is only a genuine concern if the feature happens to use hot water
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Any feature that produces a spray or aerosol can disperse Legionella if the water is contaminated, so it must be identified, risk-assessed and included in the written control scheme with appropriate cleaning and monitoring.

n.1: Even small aerosolising features can disperse organisms.
n.2: Anyone breathing the aerosol is at risk, not only children.
n.3: Cold-water sprays can still be at growth temperatures and aerosolise.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: A shower on the flushing schedule was missed for three weeks because the operative was off site and no cover was arranged. What is the correct response when this is discovered?
o: Report the missed flushing to the responsible person and follow the site procedure
Backdate the whole log so that the missing weeks all appear complete
Ignore it completely, since one single lapse really makes no difference
Delete the outlet from the flushing schedule altogether so the gap cannot recur
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: A gap in flushing is a control failure that must be reported to the responsible person; the site procedure is then followed, which may call for flushing, cleaning or additional checks before the outlet returns to normal use.

n.1: Falsifying records is dishonest and hides a genuine risk; the gap must be reported truthfully.
n.2: Three weeks of stagnation is significant and cannot be dismissed as making no difference.
n.3: Removing a live outlet from the schedule to hide the lapse leaves it uncontrolled.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between temperature control and the risk from shower aerosols?
o: Correct hot and cold storage limits growth, but showers still need cleaning
Keeping the showers deliberately lukewarm at all times is the safest option
Temperature has no real effect on Legionella at the shower outlets at all
If the water is stored hot enough, the shower heads will never need cleaning
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Correct temperature regimes suppress growth in the system, but the shower delivers blended warm water and its head and hose can still foul, so cleaning, descaling and flushing remain necessary alongside temperature control.

n.1: Deliberately lukewarm water sits in the ideal growth range and is not safe.
n.2: Temperature strongly affects Legionella growth; it is central to control.
n.3: Hot storage does not keep the fittings clean; heads and hoses still foul.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: What is the main reason for keeping a written record of shower head and spray-tap flushing and cleaning?
o: Simply because keeping such records replaces the need to actually clean the outlets at all
To satisfy the water supplier's billing department each and every quarter
To provide evidence the control scheme is carried out and to reveal trends and lapses
So that the operative on site can then claim overtime for the work done
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Records demonstrate that the control measures are being performed as scheduled and let the responsible person spot missed tasks, recurring fouling or other trends that need action.

n.0: A record does not substitute for the physical cleaning.
n.1: The record is a safety document, not a billing input.
n.3: Records exist for safety assurance, not to support pay claims.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: An emergency safety shower and eye-wash in a plant area is very rarely operated. From a Legionella standpoint, how should it be managed?
o: Drained right down and simply left completely dry until an emergency occurs
Filled with disinfectant and left permanently charged in place
Regularly flushed and maintained so the water does not stagnate
Left completely untouched because it is only for emergencies
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: An emergency shower or eye-wash still holds water that can stagnate and aerosolise; it must be flushed and maintained on a regular schedule so it is both microbiologically safe and ready to function in an emergency.

n.0: Draining it dry would leave it unusable in the emergency it exists for.
n.1: Charging it with disinfectant would harm anyone who then needed to use it.
n.3: Leaving it untouched allows stagnation in a unit that produces aerosol.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: Why should the outermost, aerosol-producing fittings such as heads, roses and hoses receive particular attention in the cleaning schedule?
o: Because they are simply the easiest parts of the system to reach
Because the manufacturers require it as a strict condition of the product warranty
They are where scale and biofilm collect and where water turns to aerosol
Because they are the most expensive parts of the shower to replace
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: The head, rose and hose are where scale and biofilm accumulate and where the water is turned into a fine aerosol; contamination there is delivered straight to the user's breathing zone, so they are prioritised for cleaning.

n.0: Accessibility is convenient but is not why these parts matter most.
n.1: Warranty terms are not the health-and-safety rationale.
n.3: Cost is not the reason; the priority is driven by aerosol risk.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: During flushing you must gently open the outlet to limit aerosol. What should you also consider about your own position and PPE?
o: Your position does not matter as long as the tap is opened slowly
Stand clear of the spray path and use the PPE the risk assessment specifies
PPE is quite unnecessary here, because flushing is not really a cleaning task
Face PPE is only ever needed when flushing hot outlets
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Even with gentle opening, some aerosol is produced, so the operative should keep out of the direct spray path and wear the respiratory and other PPE the site risk assessment specifies for the task.

n.0: Where you stand affects exposure; gentle opening reduces but does not remove aerosol.
n.3: Aerosol from cold outlets can also carry organisms, so PPE is not limited to hot outlets.
n.2: Flushing still generates aerosol, so specified PPE remains relevant.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: A site manager suggests simply turning off the water to a bank of little-used showers instead of flushing them, but leaving the pipework charged. Why is this not a safe substitute?
o: It is perfectly acceptable and is actually a better option than flushing them
It would end up making the showers far too hot when they are turned back on
It simply saves far too much water to ever be allowed on a site like this
The isolated but charged branches become dead legs of stagnant water that seed the system
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Isolating showers while leaving the branches full of water simply creates dead legs where Legionella can multiply and later contaminate the live system; either keep them in use and flushed, or remove the redundant pipework.

n.0: Charged, unused branches are exactly the dead legs to be avoided.
n.1: Isolation does not make water hotter; the issue is stagnation in the branch.
n.2: The objection is the stagnation hazard, not the volume of water saved.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: Which of the following would be the clearest sign that a shower fitting needs cleaning and descaling before its next scheduled service?
o: The tiling grout around the whole cubicle has slowly begun to discolour over time
The cubicle door has developed a fairly loud and noticeable squeak
The shower curtain is simply the wrong colour for the whole room
The spray pattern has become uneven and weak, with visible scale round the jets
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: A weakening, uneven spray with visible scale around the jets indicates scale and biofilm are blocking the head, warning that cleaning and descaling are needed and should be reported rather than left to the next quarter.

n.0: Discoloured grout is a cosmetic issue unrelated to the internal state of the head.
n.1: A squeaking door has no bearing on the water hazard in the fitting.
n.2: The curtain colour tells you nothing about scale or biofilm in the outlet.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: When a new shower is installed on a site welfare block, what should happen before it is handed over for use?
o: It is used straight away and only cleaned after a month
The old head from the previous unit is simply refitted
Nothing, because new fittings cannot contain legionella
It is flushed, disinfected, then added to the schedule
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: A new shower should be commissioned properly, flushed and disinfected as required, then entered onto the flushing and cleaning schedule and the site records so it is controlled from the outset.

n.0: Delaying any control for a month leaves the new outlet unmanaged during a vulnerable period.
n.1: Refitting an old, potentially fouled head undermines the new installation.
n.2: New pipework and stored water can still become contaminated; new fittings are not automatically safe.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: How does the presence of biofilm inside a shower hose affect the effectiveness of temperature and disinfectant controls elsewhere in the system?
o: Biofilm only ever matters in large cooling towers, and never in ordinary showers
Biofilm shields legionella from heat and disinfectant, so it stays a source
Biofilm improves disinfectant contact, so it actually helps control
Biofilm has no effect at all once the water leaves the tank
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Biofilm protects Legionella from temperature and biocide, so a fouled hose or head can persist as a local source of organisms even when tank temperatures and system dosing are otherwise satisfactory, which is why physical cleaning is essential.

n.2: Biofilm shields organisms from disinfectant rather than improving contact.
n.3: Biofilm in the outlet fittings very much affects the water delivered to the user.
n.0: Biofilm forms in domestic hot and cold systems and outlets, not only in cooling towers.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: An operative is unsure whether a particular seldom-used spray tap is on the flushing regime. What is the correct course of action?
o: Check with the responsible person and the records
Leave a note for someone else to sort it out one day
Remove the tap so that it no longer needs managing at all
Just assume it is covered by the regime and move on
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Where there is doubt, the operative should confirm with the responsible person and the records; a seldom-used aerosol-producing outlet that has slipped off the regime is a genuine risk that must be positively controlled, not assumed.

n.1: Deferring indefinitely leaves the outlet uncontrolled meanwhile.
n.2: Removing a needed tap is not the operative's decision or the answer.
n.3: Assuming coverage could leave a high-risk outlet unmanaged.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: Which practice would most undermine the control of a shower even if the quarterly cleaning is done on time?
o: Recording the exact cleaning date accurately in the site maintenance log each time
Descaling the shower head thoroughly before it is then properly disinfected
Rinsing the shower head with clean water once it has been fully disinfected
Leaving the shower full of stagnant water between cleans, never flushing it
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Leaving the shower full of stagnant water and never flushing it between cleans lets Legionella multiply in the retained water regardless of the quarterly service, so regular flushing must accompany periodic cleaning.

n.0: Accurate recording supports control rather than undermining it.
n.1: Descaling before disinfecting is correct practice.
n.2: Rinsing after disinfection protects the user from residue.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: A cleaner reports that a shower head 'spits and splutters' at start-up and then runs cloudy. What is the most appropriate interpretation and action?
o: It is just normal air trapped in the line, so no action is needed at all
Turn the water pressure right up until the spitting and spluttering completely stop
It may be scale or fouling; report it and clean, descale and disinfect the head
The head should simply be painted over to hide the discolouration
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: Spitting and cloudy delivery can point to scale, debris or fouling partially blocking the jets; the finding should be reported and the head cleaned, descaled and disinfected as part of controlling the aerosol hazard.

n.0: Dismissing persistent spitting and cloudiness as air ignores a likely fouling problem.
n.1: Raising pressure to force water past a blockage does not clean the fouled head.
n.3: Painting the head does nothing about the internal fouling and is not a control.

Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.q: Overall, which set of measures best summarises safe management of showers and spray taps under HSG274 Part 2?
o: Clean the heads once a year and rely on mains pressure for everything else
Flush all the outlets once, at installation, and then take no further action
Only ever store the water cold and never fit any showers in the building
Clean, descale and disinfect fittings quarterly, flush little-used outlets weekly, remove redundant ones and record it
Showers, Spray Taps & Outlets.w: The core regime is quarterly cleaning, descaling and disinfection of the aerosol-producing fittings, at least weekly flushing of little-used outlets, removal of redundant outlets to avoid dead legs, and full recording and reporting of the work.

n.0: Annual cleaning is too infrequent and mains pressure does not control fouling.
n.1: A single flush at installation provides no ongoing control.
n.2: Showers are a needed facility; manage them rather than ban them.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: When is disinfection of a water system typically required? Choose the best answer.
o: Only once a year, on a fixed date, regardless of the system's condition
Only when the water coming from the outlets looks visibly discoloured
Never at all, provided the system temperatures are properly controlled
After contaminating work, on new or altered systems, or after a positive legionella result
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: Disinfection is required for new or altered systems, after contaminating work, when a system is found dirty, and following a positive result or outbreak.

n.0: Disinfection is triggered by events and findings, not a fixed annual date.
n.1: Discolouration is only one possible sign; many triggers involve no change.
n.2: Temperature control reduces risk but does not remove the need to disinfect.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: A cold water storage tank is opened for inspection and found to contain a layer of sludge and debris on the bottom. What is the correct action?
o: Top the tank right up to dilute the debris and settle it out
Report it and arrange for the tank to be cleaned and disinfected
Add some extra chlorine tablets into the incoming water main
Leave it, since the debris will settle out and cause no harm
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: A tank found to be dirty must be reported and then cleaned and disinfected to remove nutrients and biofilm that support legionella.

n.0: Adding water does not remove the debris or the biofilm on the tank surfaces.
n.2: Dosing the main does not clean an already fouled tank and is not the defined procedure.
n.3: Sediment provides nutrients and shelter for bacteria and must be removed, not left.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: Which of these best describes chemical (chlorination) disinfection of a water system?
o: Adding a measured dose, holding the contact time, then flushing
Raising the water temperature until it is too hot to touch
Pouring bleach into the tank until the water smells strong
Leaving disinfectant in the pipes permanently
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: Chlorination means dosing to a defined concentration, holding it for the required contact time, then flushing the system through.

n.1: That describes thermal disinfection, a different method.
n.2: Disinfection uses a measured, controlled dose to a defined level, not an uncontrolled pour judged by smell.
n.3: Disinfectant is flushed out after the contact time; it is not left in permanently.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: During thermal disinfection of a hot water system, what is the operative aiming to achieve?
o: Coating the inside of all the pipes with a disinfectant
Removing all of the water and leaving the pipes empty
Cooling the whole system down to below 20°C throughout
Getting each outlet up to the required hot temperature for the set time
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: Thermal disinfection raises the temperature through the system so that each outlet reaches and holds the required hot temperature for the defined period.

n.2: Cooling would move water into the range where legionella thrives, not disinfect it.
n.1: Draining alone does not disinfect and leaves biofilm behind.
n.0: Coating pipes with chemical describes a different, chemical method, not thermal disinfection.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: Before handling a concentrated disinfectant chemical, where should an operative look for the correct handling and PPE information?
o: The COSHH assessment and product safety sheet
Nowhere at all, since practical experience alone is enough
A colleague's memory of how the job went last time
The supplier's delivery note that came with the drum
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: The COSHH assessment and safety data sheet set out the hazards, safe handling and the PPE required for the chemical.

n.1: Even experienced operatives must follow documented COSHH controls.
n.2: Relying on memory risks missing hazards and precautions.
n.3: A delivery note records quantity and cost, not safe handling.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: A monitored hot water outlet reads well below the required temperature. What should the operative do?
o: Rub the sensor to warm it and record a passing figure
Record it, report it, and act to correct the cause
Turn the tap off so it cannot be tested again
Ignore it, since a single low reading really does not matter
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: An out-of-range reading must be recorded, escalated to the responsible person, and the underlying cause corrected.

n.0: Faking a reading falsifies records and hides a real risk.
n.2: Disabling the outlet hides the problem instead of fixing it.
n.3: A low temperature can allow legionella to grow and must never be ignored.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: Why is a legionella water sample taken as part of a control scheme?
o: To prove to occupants that the stored water tastes perfectly acceptable
To supplement temperature monitoring and check the regime works
To completely replace the need for any temperature monitoring
To help decide the water rates charged for the whole building
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: Sampling supplements temperature and other control monitoring; it is a check on the regime, not a substitute for it.

n.0: The sample tests for legionella, not for taste or palatability.
n.2: Sampling supports temperature control but does not replace routine monitoring.
n.3: Sampling is a safety check and has nothing to do with billing.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: An operative is asked to carry out a task that is not covered by their training and is not in the written scheme. What should they do?
o: Guess a sensible method and press on with it to save some time
Refuse to ever carry out any water work again in the future
Stop and get competent help or instruction before continuing
Do it in their own way and simply not record it at all
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: Operatives must work within their competence and the written scheme, seeking competent help rather than improvising on unfamiliar tasks.

n.0: Guessing on a safety-critical task risks contamination and harm.
n.1: The issue is this specific task, not all future work; total refusal over-reacts.
n.3: Working unrecorded outside the scheme breaches the control arrangements.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: A colleague suggests writing down a temperature that was never actually measured to save time on the checks. What is the correct response?
o: Record the made-up figure but simply tell nobody about it
Only ever do it for the outlets that are genuinely hard to reach
Refuse; readings must be genuine and records must never be falsified
Agree to it, as long as the invented figure still looks perfectly reasonable
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: Records must be truthful; falsifying a check hides risk and is never acceptable.

n.0: Keeping quiet still leaves a dishonest, unsafe record in place.
n.1: Difficulty of access does not justify inventing a reading.
n.3: A plausible-looking invented figure is still a false record.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: A legionella sample from a shower has come back positive. What is the appropriate response?
o: Remove the shower unit and throw the sample in the bin
Report it and follow the scheme's actions, such as disinfection
Increase the water pressure going to the shower head
Do nothing at all, as one positive result is quite normal
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: A positive result must be escalated to the responsible person and acted on under the scheme, which can include cleaning and disinfection.

n.0: Discarding the evidence prevents proper follow-up and investigation.
n.2: Raising the pressure does nothing to remove or kill the legionella present.
n.3: A positive legionella result is a control failure signal and always needs a response.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: Repairs have just been made to a water main that involved cutting into the pipe and using tools inside it. What should follow the work?
o: A permanent increase in the stored water temperature
Disinfection of the affected section before it goes back into use
Painting the new pipework on the outside to seal it
Nothing further, provided that the joint does not leak
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: Work that could contaminate the system, such as cutting into pipework, should be followed by disinfection before normal use.

n.0: Raising storage temperature permanently is not the defined remedy.
n.2: Painting the outside of a pipe does not disinfect the water inside.
n.3: A watertight joint says nothing about microbial contamination introduced.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: Legionella bacteria multiply most readily in water within which temperature range?
o: Warm water roughly between 20°C and 45°C, around body heat
Water held right at exactly 0°C, at freezing point
Any very hot water kept well above 70°C
Cold water kept steadily below about 5°C
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: Legionella proliferates in water roughly between 20°C and 45°C, which is why systems are kept cold or hot to stay out of that band.

n.3: Cold water below 20°C suppresses growth, which is why cold is kept low.
n.2: Above 60°C legionella dies quickly; 70°C is well above the growth range.
n.1: Freezing point is far below the temperatures at which legionella actively multiplies.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: Which item of PPE is normally required when handling liquid disinfectant that can splash?
o: A high-visibility vest on its own and nothing else is needed
Steel-toe boots on their own are all that is really required
Suitable gloves together with eye protection
No PPE is needed at all provided the work is done quickly
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: Disinfectant chemicals can harm skin and eyes, so suitable gloves and eye protection are required as set out in the COSHH assessment.

n.0: Hi-vis aids visibility but gives no protection against a chemical splash.
n.1: Toe protection does not guard the hands or eyes against splashes.
n.3: Working quickly increases splash risk; PPE is still required.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: After the required contact time in a chlorination disinfection, what is the final key step?
o: Seal the system up and leave the strong chemical sitting inside it
Add a second full dose of precisely the same disinfectant chemical again
Drain the system right down and leave all the pipes empty for a full week
Flush the system through until the disinfectant is cleared to safe levels
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: Once the contact time is complete, the system is flushed through until the disinfectant level returns to that of the normal supply.

n.0: Leaving concentrated disinfectant in the system is unsafe and not part of the procedure.
n.1: A second dose is not the defined next step and wastes chemical without purpose.
n.2: Leaving pipes empty invites stagnation and does not complete the disinfection.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: When carrying out a disinfection, why must an operative follow the written scheme or method statement rather than their own approach?
o: Because it makes the site paperwork look neat and tidy
Because it is only a guideline that can be ignored
Because it decides who on the team gets paid
Because it sets out the correct, safe and consistent procedure
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: The written scheme defines the correct, safe and repeatable procedure, so it must be followed rather than improvised.

n.0: The scheme exists to control risk, not merely to keep records looking neat.
n.1: A written scheme is a control document to be followed, not an optional guideline.
n.2: The scheme governs how work is done safely, not payment.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: A stored hot water calorifier is found to be running at a temperature too low to control legionella. As a remedial action, what should be done?
o: Record and escalate the fault, then reinstate the correct temperature
Empty the calorifier right out and then refill the vessel with cold water
Leave it running low in order to save on energy costs
Cover the calorifier over so as to keep the heat in
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: An out-of-range calorifier temperature is recorded, escalated to the responsible person, and corrected by reinstating the required temperature.

n.2: Running below the control temperature allows legionella to grow; energy saving does not justify it.
n.3: Insulation may help retain heat but does not correct a heat source or setting fault, and alone does not fix the low temperature.
n.1: Filling with cold water moves the system into the growth range, making matters worse.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: A sample point needs disinfecting before a legionella sample is taken. When is the outlet surface-disinfected in this way?
o: Only if the tap visibly looks dirty to the eye
Only after the sample has already been bottled up
Never, because it would change the sample result
Before sampling where the scheme requires it
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: Where the scheme calls for it, the outlet is prepared or disinfected before sampling so the result reflects the water, not surface contamination.

n.0: The requirement follows the scheme, not just visible dirt.
n.1: Disinfecting after bottling cannot protect a sample already taken.
n.2: Correct preparation improves reliability; it is a defined step.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: An operative notices a section of dead, unused pipework (a dead leg) still connected to a live system. What is the correct action?
o: Fill it with disinfectant and cap it off permanently
Cut it out straight away without telling anybody about it first
Report it so it can be removed or properly managed
Ignore it entirely because nobody uses that tap
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: Dead legs allow stagnation and should be reported so they can be removed or brought under proper management.

n.0: Capping a stagnant leg full of chemical is not the defined remedy.
n.1: Removing pipework without authorisation may breach the scheme; report first.
n.3: Unused, stagnant pipework is exactly where legionella can proliferate.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: During a chemical disinfection, spillage of concentrated disinfectant onto the floor occurs. What is the first priority?
o: Deal with it safely under the COSHH and spill procedure, in correct PPE
Cover the spill over with a cloth and quietly say nothing to anyone at all
Keep on working and simply mop it up again later on
Pour plenty of clean water over it and then walk away
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: A chemical spill is dealt with promptly and safely under the COSHH and spill procedures, wearing the correct PPE.

n.1: Hiding a spill leaves an unmanaged hazard and breaches safe-working duties.
n.2: Leaving a chemical spill creates a slip and exposure hazard for everyone nearby.
n.3: Adding water can spread the chemical or create fumes and does not make the area safe.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: Following a confirmed legionnaires' disease outbreak linked to a building's water system, what response is expected?
o: A single extra temperature check taken at the one affected outlet
Business as usual until the season eventually changes over
Painting a set of warning signs onto all of the affected taps
Immediate action under the scheme: disinfection and expert help
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: A confirmed outbreak triggers urgent remedial action under the scheme, usually including disinfection and involvement of competent specialists.

n.0: One temperature check does not address contamination that has already caused illness.
n.1: An outbreak is a serious control failure demanding immediate action, not a wait.
n.2: Signage does not remove the source of the outbreak.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: Why should disinfectant chemicals be used in a well-ventilated area where possible?
o: To reduce the build-up of harmful fumes and protect those working nearby
Because good ventilation is a requirement set by the water meter itself
To make the water that comes out taste noticeably better
To speed up the rate at which the water then flows through all the pipework
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: Good ventilation limits the build-up of harmful vapours from disinfectants, protecting the operative and others as required under COSHH.

n.1: Water meters have nothing to do with ventilation requirements.
n.2: Ventilation is a safety measure, not a way to alter taste.
n.3: Airflow in the room has no bearing on water flow in the pipes.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: An operative completes a check but the reading is a clear failure. What must the record show?
o: No entry at all recorded for that particular outlet
An averaged figure from several nearby outlets instead
The true failed result, so action can then be taken
A passing result, so as not to alarm anyone at all
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: The genuine result, including a failure, must be recorded and reported so the correct remedial action follows.

n.0: Leaving the entry blank conceals the failure and breaks the record.
n.1: Averaging masks the failing outlet and does not reflect what was measured.
n.3: Recording a false pass hides a real risk and is falsification.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: What is the correct sequence for cleaning and disinfecting a dirty storage tank?
o: Refill it immediately, then add chemical to the running supply
Drain it, physically clean out debris, disinfect, then flush and refill
Wipe over the outside of the tank only and leave it
Disinfect it first, then leave the dirt and debris in place
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: The tank is drained and physically cleaned to remove debris, then disinfected, then flushed and returned to service.

n.0: Dosing a running supply does not remove the debris fouling the tank.
n.2: Cleaning only the outside leaves the contaminated internal surfaces.
n.3: Disinfectant works poorly over sludge, so cleaning must come first.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: An operative finds the lid of a cold water storage tank is missing, leaving the water open to dirt and insects. What should they do?
o: Leave a note for the next operative to deal with it in six months' time
Report it, fit a close-fitting lid, and disinfect the tank if needed
Do nothing at all, because the water still looks perfectly clear
Drop in a handful of chlorine tablets and simply move on
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: An uncovered tank is a contamination risk; it should be reported, covered properly, and cleaned and disinfected if contaminated.

n.2: Clear-looking water can still be contaminated by dust, insects and droppings entering an open tank.
n.3: Tablets do not clean out contamination already present or replace the missing lid.
n.0: Delaying six months leaves the tank open to ongoing contamination.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: After a thermal disinfection, why is each outlet run for the required time at temperature?
o: So the heat and hot water reach and disinfect every part of the system
To deliberately waste a large volume of hot water down the drain day to day
To gently warm up the room that the outlet happens to be in
To carry out a pressure test on the system while it is hot
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: Running each outlet at temperature for the set time ensures the heat reaches the full system so no part is missed.

n.1: The controlled run is a necessary part of the method, not deliberate waste.
n.2: Any room warming is incidental and not the reason for the procedure.
n.3: The purpose is disinfection by heat, not a pressure test.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: Which statement about legionella sampling is correct?
o: A positive result can be safely ignored so long as the water still looks clear
Sampling supports the control regime and does not replace routine monitoring
Samples are only ever taken once during a system's entire lifetime
A single negative result means the temperature checks can now stop
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: Sampling supplements the control regime; routine monitoring such as temperature checks continues regardless of a sample result.

n.0: A positive result signals a control problem and must be acted on, whatever the water looks like.
n.2: Sampling is repeated as the scheme requires, not just once.
n.3: A single negative result does not prove ongoing control, so monitoring must continue.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: A shower head is found to be heavily scaled and covered in slime. As a remedial action, what should be done?
o: Wrap tape around the head to hide the scale
Remove, clean, descale and disinfect or replace the head
Leave it in place, as the scale is harmless
Turn the shower to cold only and leave the head on
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: Scale and slime harbour legionella, so the head should be cleaned, descaled and disinfected or replaced.

n.0: Concealing the scale leaves the contamination in place and creates aerosols in use.
n.2: Scale and biofilm shelter bacteria and provide nutrients, so they are not harmless.
n.3: Running cold does not remove the contamination and cold showers still create spray.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: What must an operative do before using a disinfectant they have not used before?
o: Read and understand the COSHH assessment and safety data sheet
Taste a small amount of the product to confirm it is still active
Mix it with another chemical to make it act stronger
Assume it behaves the same as every other chemical
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: Each chemical has its own hazards; the COSHH assessment and safety data sheet must be read and understood before use.

n.3: Different disinfectants have different hazards, dilutions and precautions.
n.1: Tasting a disinfectant is dangerous and never a valid test.
n.2: Mixing chemicals can create toxic gases and is strictly avoided unless specified.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: After remedial work to correct a fault, why is the completed action written up in the records?
o: So that all of the paperwork can be shredded afterwards
To simply fill in time at the end of the working day
So the responsible person and future operatives know what was done
Because records are only ever kept for brand-new systems
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: Recording what was found and corrected keeps the responsible person informed and provides a traceable history for the future.

n.0: Records must be kept, not destroyed after completion.
n.1: Records serve a control purpose; they are not busywork.
n.3: Records are maintained for existing systems too.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: A recently refurbished bathroom block has new pipework that has stood full of water, unused, for several weeks before handover. What is the safe step before use?
o: Flush thoroughly and disinfect the system before use
Raise the incoming water main pressure for a while
Leave the water in place to keep the new pipes wet
Simply open the taps and hand the system over
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: Refurbished pipework left standing must be flushed and disinfected before use, as stagnant water can allow legionella to develop.

n.1: Higher pressure does not disinfect standing water or remove growth.
n.2: Leaving water standing encourages stagnation and growth.
n.3: Handing over stagnant, unflushed pipework passes on contaminated water.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: When mixing a disinfectant to the required strength, what should the operative follow?
o: Simply double the stated amount just to be on the safe side
The dosing instructions in the method statement and on the product
Whatever a passing member of the public happens to suggest at the time
Their own rough judgement of roughly about the right amount
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: The correct concentration comes from the method statement and product instructions, not guesswork, so that disinfection is effective and safe.

n.0: Overdosing wastes chemical, raises hazards and is not the specified strength.
n.2: An unqualified passer-by is not a reliable source for a safety-critical dose.
n.3: An approximate dose may be too weak to work or too strong to handle safely.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: A cold water outlet is reading above the temperature at which cold water should be kept. As remedial action, the operative should first:
o: Run the hot tap right next to it for a good while to compensate for it
Insulate the outlet handle so it feels cooler to the touch
Record it, report it and investigate the cause such as nearby warming
Ignore it, because cold water taps are always a low risk
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: A cold outlet running too warm is out of range, so it is recorded, reported and the cause (such as heat gain) investigated and corrected.

n.0: Running the hot tap adds heat nearby and does not address the warm cold-water problem.
n.1: Insulating the handle does nothing about the temperature of the water.
n.3: Warm cold-water is within the growth range, so it is not low risk.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: Why must disinfectant never be added to a system in a way that could reach people drinking or using the water at full strength?
o: Because it changes the colour of the pipes it passes through
Because using it that way would end up wasting far too much of the chemical
Because it noticeably slows the flow of the water right down through the system
Concentrated disinfectant is harmful; isolate and flush before normal use
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: Concentrated disinfectant is hazardous, so the system is isolated during dosing and flushed to safe levels before it is returned to normal use.

n.0: Pipe colour is irrelevant; the hazard is chemical exposure.
n.1: The concern is protecting people, not the cost of the chemical.
n.2: Disinfectant does not meaningfully change flow speed; toxicity is the issue.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: An outlet has not been used for a long period. To reduce risk before it is put back into regular use, the scheme is most likely to require:
o: Flush it through, cleaning and disinfecting where required
Leave it completely unused and out of service indefinitely
Paint a small hazard warning mark on it and nothing else
Remove the tap from the wall entirely and permanently
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: Little-used outlets are flushed, and cleaned or disinfected where the scheme requires, before regular use resumes to clear stagnant water.

n.1: Leaving it stagnant maintains the risk rather than reducing it.
n.2: A hazard mark does nothing to clear the stagnant water inside.
n.3: The outlet here is being returned to use, which needs flushing.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: While disinfecting, an operative realises the actual system differs from the drawings and they are unsure how to isolate part of it safely. What should they do?
o: Guess which valve to close and simply carry on
Skip the isolation step entirely and proceed
Stop work and seek competent advice before continuing
Carry on regardless and hope the isolation happens to be correct
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: Where the situation exceeds their knowledge, the operative stops and seeks competent advice rather than risk an unsafe disinfection.

n.0: Guessing at valves risks dosing occupied areas or missing sections.
n.1: Skipping isolation can let concentrated disinfectant reach people in use.
n.3: Proceeding on a hope can leave the system unsafely dosed or untreated.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: Which of the following is a valid trigger for disinfecting a domestic-scale hot and cold water system?
o: A tank or system has been found dirty or contaminated
A set of new curtains has just been fitted in the main bathroom
The whole building has recently changed its owner
The building's water bill has noticeably increased
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: Finding a tank or system dirty or contaminated is a recognised trigger for cleaning and disinfection.

n.2: A change of ownership is an administrative event, not a contamination trigger.
n.3: A higher bill relates to usage or price, not water hygiene.
n.1: Fitting curtains has no bearing on the water system's cleanliness.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: After a disinfection is complete and the system flushed, why might a follow-up legionella sample be taken?
o: To replace all of the future routine temperature checks entirely in the end
To help confirm the disinfection worked, alongside the control regime
To work out the hardness of the water supplying the building
To bill the client for a further piece of additional work
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: A post-disinfection sample can help confirm the treatment worked, supplementing rather than replacing ongoing control monitoring.

n.0: Temperature control continues; the sample does not replace it.
n.2: The sample tests for legionella, not for water hardness.
n.3: Sampling is a technical check, not a billing device.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: An operative is dosing a system and starts to feel dizzy from the chemical fumes. What is the correct immediate action?
o: Stop, get to fresh air, and follow the COSHH and emergency procedure
Add more of the chemical so the whole job can be finished sooner
Push on through it and finish the dosing as quickly as possible
Take the mask off so it is easier to breathe while still working
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: Feeling unwell from fumes means stopping, getting fresh air and following the emergency and COSHH procedures.

n.1: Adding more chemical increases fumes and the hazard.
n.2: Continuing while affected by fumes risks serious harm.
n.3: Removing respiratory protection increases exposure and makes matters worse.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: During routine checks an operative finds a fault they cannot fix themselves. What is the correct step?
o: Attempt an unfamiliar repair anyway to appear more capable
Ignore it entirely and simply complete the round
Record and report it so competent help can be arranged
Erase the check so that no fault is left on record
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: A fault beyond the operative's competence is recorded and reported so that competent help can correct it.

n.0: Attempting an unfamiliar repair risks making the fault worse or unsafe.
n.1: Ignoring a fault leaves a control failure unaddressed.
n.3: Deleting the check hides the fault and falsifies the record.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: Which best describes the purpose of a contact time during chemical disinfection?
o: The length of time it takes to fill the storage tank right to the top
The time the operative spends away on their break
The time before the next annual service falls due
The time the disinfectant is left to act before it is flushed away
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: The contact time is the period the disinfectant is held in the system so it can act effectively before flushing.

n.0: Filling the tank is a separate step, not the contact time.
n.1: A break has nothing to do with the chemical acting on the system.
n.2: The annual service interval is unrelated to a single disinfection's contact time.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: A tank found to be contaminated has been cleaned and disinfected. Before it is returned to normal supply, the operative should:
o: Seal the tank tightly shut for a whole month
Flush it through until the water is back to normal
Immediately take a hot shower from the outlet to test it
Leave the disinfectant sitting in the tank for users
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: After disinfection the tank is flushed until the water returns to normal supply quality before it serves users.

n.0: Sealing a tank shut for a month risks stagnation.
n.2: Testing by showering exposes a person to unflushed water and aerosols.
n.3: Leaving disinfectant in the supply exposes users to a harmful chemical.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: Why is it important that an operative only carries out water hygiene tasks they are trained and competent to do?
o: Because untrained work is always noticeably faster to finish
So the operative can then go on to charge a much higher rate
Simply to keep the toolbox and the work van tidy and organised
Because wrong work on a safety-critical system creates real risk
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: Water systems are safety-critical, so working within competence prevents mistakes that could create a legionella risk.

n.0: Untrained work is not reliably faster and risks dangerous errors.
n.1: Competence is about safety, not setting a rate.
n.2: Tool tidiness has nothing to do with competence requirements.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: A monitoring reading is on the edge of the acceptable range and the operative is unsure whether it passes. The best action is to:
o: Round the figure right down to a clear fail and then simply leave it
Round it up to a clear pass so that the record looks fine
Do not record it at all until they are completely certain of it
Record the actual reading and check the scheme, then escalate if still unsure
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: The true reading is recorded and, where its meaning is unclear, the operative checks the scheme and escalates rather than guessing.

n.0: Rounding to a fail misrepresents the measured value.
n.1: Rounding to a pass falsifies the reading and may hide a problem.
n.2: Delaying the record risks the reading being forgotten or the entry missed.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: After building work that generated dust and debris near an open water tank, what is the sensible hygiene step?
o: Leave the tank open so any airborne dust can settle out of it slowly
Assume the lid kept everything out and simply do nothing more
Increase the water temperature inside the cold water tank
Check the tank for contamination and clean and disinfect it if debris entered
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: Work that could contaminate a system means checking the tank and cleaning and disinfecting it if debris has got in.

n.0: Leaving the tank open invites more contamination rather than resolving it.
n.1: Assuming no ingress without checking risks leaving contamination in place.
n.2: Warming cold stored water moves it into the growth range, worsening risk.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: An operative is offered a shortcut that skips part of the written disinfection procedure to finish before lunch. What should they do?
o: Follow the full written procedure; skipping steps can leave the system unsafe
Skip only the final flushing step and complete everything else
Halve every one of the contact times in order to save a bit of time
Take the shortcut, since the end result is very probably going to be perfectly fine
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: The full written procedure must be followed, because omitting steps can leave the system inadequately disinfected and unsafe.

n.1: Skipping flushing can leave harmful chemical in the supply.
n.2: Halving contact times may mean the disinfectant has not acted long enough.
n.3: A shortcut skipping steps risks an ineffective disinfection.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: Which of these is the correct way to store disinfectant chemicals on site between uses?
o: Loose on a shelf beside the food and drink in the site mess room
All mixed together in one big container to save space
In an unlabelled plastic bottle kept under the sink
Securely and labelled, in line with the COSHH assessment
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: Chemicals are stored securely, correctly labelled and as the COSHH assessment requires, kept apart from incompatible substances.

n.0: Storing chemicals with food and drink risks contamination and ingestion.
n.1: Combining different chemicals can react dangerously.
n.2: Unlabelled bottles cause dangerous mix-ups about contents.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: A sample result is delayed and an operative is tempted to sign off the check as clear before the laboratory reports back. What is correct?
o: Wait for the actual result and record what the laboratory reports
Sign it off as clear now to keep the paperwork moving
Record it as a fail now just to be on the safe side
Discard the sample and simply take no result at all
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: The record must reflect the genuine laboratory result, so the operative waits rather than inventing an outcome.

n.1: Signing off before the result is known falsifies the record.
n.2: Recording an invented fail is also a false entry.
n.3: Discarding the sample wastes the test and answers nothing.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: Following a disinfection, why should the operative check that temperatures and other controls are reinstated correctly before leaving?
o: Because a disinfection like this is only ever valid if it is done on a Monday
In order to reset the building's main water meter afterwards
To make sure the ongoing control regime keeps working after the disinfection
So that all the taps end up looking clean and shiny
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: Disinfection is a one-off event; ongoing control such as correct temperatures must be reinstated so day-to-day protection continues.

n.0: Disinfection validity does not depend on the day of the week.
n.1: Checking controls has nothing to do with the water meter.
n.3: Appearance of the taps is irrelevant to reinstating controls.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: An operative arrives to find that the last three weeks of temperature records are all identical, suggesting readings may have been copied rather than measured. What should they do?
o: Take genuine readings now and report the concern to the responsible person
Say nothing about it at all, as the records already look nicely complete
Delete all the old records and quietly start fresh without telling anybody
Copy the very same figures across again so that they all still match
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: Suspected falsified or copied records are a control failure, so the operative takes genuine readings and reports the concern to the responsible person.

n.1: A complete-looking record that may be false still conceals real risk.
n.2: Quietly deleting records destroys evidence and is a form of falsification.
n.3: Copying suspect figures continues the falsification.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: When is a cleaning and disinfection of a water system typically required?
o: Only at the point when the whole building is being demolished
Only once every ten years regardless of any results
Never at all, provided the water simply looks clear
After works, on new systems, or after a positive result
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: Disinfection is carried out after works, on new or refurbished systems, when tanks are dirty, or after a positive result or control failure.

n.0: Demolition is not the trigger; disinfection protects a system that stays in use.
n.1: A fixed ten-year cycle ignores the events that actually require disinfection.
n.2: Clear-looking water can still be contaminated, so appearance is not the test.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: You take a temperature reading at an outlet and it is well outside the required range. What should you do?
o: Record the reading and report it to the responsible person
Wipe the reading off and take no further action at all
Round it up to a passing figure so the paperwork looks fine
Ignore it, since a single reading does not really matter
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: An out-of-range reading is a control failure that must be recorded accurately and reported to the responsible person so action can be taken.

n.2: Falsifying a reading hides a real legionella control failure and is never acceptable.
n.3: A single failing reading can signal a genuine fault and must not be ignored.
n.1: Wiping the reading destroys the evidence needed to put the fault right.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: Why is PPE worn when carrying out a chemical disinfection of a water system?
o: Because PPE noticeably speeds up the disinfection reaction
To protect against chemicals such as chlorine
Only to keep your own work clothes clean and dry
Because the law always bans working without gloves
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: Disinfection chemicals like chlorine are hazardous, so appropriate PPE is worn to protect the operative during the work.

n.0: PPE protects the person; it has no effect on the reaction.
n.2: Keeping clothes clean is not the safety reason for PPE.
n.3: PPE is worn for the specific hazard, not a blanket glove rule.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: When carrying out remedial or disinfection work, which document should you follow?
o: The old newspaper that was left lying in the plant room
Whatever you can just about remember from a similar job last year
A verbal comment you happened to overhear from another trade
The written scheme of control and the agreed method statement
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: Work is done in line with the written scheme of control and the agreed method so the task is carried out correctly and safely.

n.0: Random paperwork in the plant room is not a control document.
n.1: Relying on memory risks missing steps and getting it wrong.
n.2: An overheard comment is not an authorised, reliable method.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: A monthly check shows a cold water tank is dirty, with debris and sediment in the bottom. What is the correct action?
o: Leave it, since storage tanks are always a little bit dirty anyway
Add some extra sediment to weigh it down in the bottom
Stir the sediment up so that it disperses through the water
Report it and arrange for the tank to be cleaned and disinfected
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: A dirty tank is a legionella risk, so it is reported and cleaned and disinfected to remove the debris and sediment.

n.0: A sediment-filled tank is a genuine risk that must be dealt with, not accepted.
n.1: Adding material to the tank makes the contamination and the risk worse.
n.2: Stirring the sediment spreads contamination through the supply instead of removing it.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: A water sample from a shower comes back positive for legionella. What is the appropriate response?
o: Throw the result away and re-sample only if someone later falls ill
Do nothing at all until the next scheduled annual review comes
Report it to the responsible person and follow the plan for disinfection
Increase the shower's flow rate to wash the bacteria away
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: A positive result is reported to the responsible person and the agreed remedial and disinfection actions are carried out to bring the system back under control.

n.0: Discarding a positive result hides a serious risk to health.
n.1: Waiting a year leaves a known contaminated aerosol source in use.
n.3: More flow spreads more contaminated aerosol rather than disinfecting the system.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: After finishing a remedial task and completing a control check, what should the operative do?
o: Record the work and readings and report anything out of range
Only tell a colleague verbally and keep no written record at all
Record only the readings that happened to pass the control check
Leave the site straight away without writing anything down at all
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: Accurate records of the work and readings, with any out-of-range findings reported, keep the responsible person informed and the control scheme reliable.

n.1: A verbal word to a colleague is not a reliable record.
n.2: Recording only passing readings hides the failures needing action.
n.3: Leaving no record means faults and work cannot be tracked.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: A newly installed section of pipework is complete and ready to be brought into use for the first time. Before any water is supplied to users, what must happen?
o: It needs disinfecting only if it is then not going to be used for several weeks
It must be disinfected and then thoroughly flushed before it is returned to normal use
It can be used straight away, because the pipe is brand new and clean
It only needs a quick visual check that no debris was left inside it
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: New, refurbished or altered systems must be disinfected before use, then flushed and returned to normal supply, because installation work can introduce contamination.

n.0: Disinfection of new work is required before use regardless of timing.
n.2: Installation debris and handling can introduce contamination.
n.3: A visual check cannot confirm microbiological safety.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: You are about to disinfect a storage tank that has a visible layer of sediment and slime on the base. What is the correct sequence?
o: Leave the sediment in place so it is not disturbed during disinfection
Clean out the sediment and slime, then disinfect
Disinfect first, then clean out the sediment afterwards
Disinfect only, as the chemical will dissolve the sediment
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: You must clean before you disinfect. Sediment and biofilm shield organisms from the disinfectant, so soiling is physically removed first, then the surfaces are disinfected.

n.2: Disinfecting over sediment lets it protect organisms; cleaning must come first.
n.0: Leaving contamination in place defeats the purpose; it must be cleaned out before disinfection.
n.3: Disinfectant does not reliably dissolve sediment and biofilm; they must be physically removed.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: During chlorination of a system, why must the measured disinfectant dose be held throughout a set contact time?
o: To hold the disinfectant long enough at the right strength to kill organisms
So the treated water looks clearly and visibly different before anyone uses it
To let the added chemical settle down to the very bottom of the pipework
Because the responsible person happens to prefer a much longer job
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: Disinfection depends on both concentration and time; the dose must be maintained at the required level for the full contact time so organisms are reliably inactivated before the system is flushed.

n.1: Effectiveness depends on measured concentration over time, not appearance.
n.2: The disinfectant must stay in contact with all wetted surfaces, not settle out.
n.3: Contact time is a technical requirement of the method, not a preference.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: When thermal disinfection is used on a hot water system, what confirms the process has been carried out correctly?
o: The boiler flow temperature is raised for one hour only
Each outlet in turn reaches the required temperature for the set time
The furthest outlet is checked and the rest are assumed to be the same
The water simply feels hot when the tap is opened
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: In thermal disinfection every outlet must be run until it reaches the required temperature and held there for the specified time, so heat actually reaches each part of the system.

n.0: Raising the boiler temperature does not prove each outlet reached the required temperature for long enough.
n.2: Outlets vary; each must be individually checked, not assumed from one point.
n.3: Feeling hot is not a measurement; a thermometer reading against the required value is needed.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: A routine sample returns a positive legionella result for a water system. In terms of remedial action, this result normally triggers which response?
o: Immediately dismantle and fully replace the entire water system throughout the site
Cleaning and disinfection of the system, alongside investigating the cause
Increase the frequency of sampling and take no other action
Wait for a second confirmatory sample before doing anything
Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.w: A positive legionella result is one of the triggers for disinfection; the system is cleaned and disinfected and the underlying cause investigated and corrected under the written scheme.

n.0: Wholesale replacement is not the first response; clean and disinfect.
n.2: More sampling monitors but does not remove the contamination.
n.3: A positive result requires action, not simply waiting.

Cleaning, Disinfection & Remedial Action.q: After work that may have contaminated the inside of a water main, before it is put back into service you should:
